tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The finance committee has submitted the budget proposal last Monday.
Our compliance officer has worked in the Vienna office since 2018.
While the auditors were checking the ledgers, the CFO interrupted the meeting.
She used to working overtime before the firm hired two junior analysts.
By next June, the board will have approved the merger terms.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A finished time marker such as "last Monday" calls for past simple ("submitted"), not present perfect.

Tip: Spot calendar anchors (yesterday, last week, in 2019) — they usually kill present perfect.

TRUE — Present perfect with "since" correctly signals a situation that began in the past and continues now.

Tip: Pair "since + starting point" with present perfect, not past simple.

TRUE — Past continuous sets the background review; past simple marks the interrupting call.

Tip: Longer background → continuous; shorter interrupt → simple past.

FALSE — Past habit needs "used to" + base verb: "used to work," not "used to working."

Tip: "Used to" + V1 for habits; "be used to" + -ing for familiarity.

TRUE — Future perfect ("will have approved") correctly places completion before a future deadline.

Tip: "By + future time" often flags future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Warm up on the classic tense traps: finished time versus "since," background continuous versus a short interrupt, "used to" form, and future perfect with "by." Read each verb against its time cue before you tick true or false.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The procurement team already left when the supplier's courier arrived.
They had already left when the supplier's courier arrived.
The analyst is knowing every clause in the outsourcing contract.
I am used to preparing quarterly forecasts under tight deadlines.
We completed the due-diligence report in March.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The departure happened first, so past perfect is needed: "had already left."

Tip: When two past events stack, mark the earlier one with past perfect.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly shows that leaving preceded the courier's arrival.

Tip: "Already" often sits comfortably with past perfect in sequenced past narratives.

FALSE — Stative "know" resists continuous form; use "knows" (or "know" after a plural subject).

Tip: Mental-state verbs (know, believe, own) rarely take -ing in exam English.

TRUE — "Be used to" + gerund correctly means "accustomed to" a recurring task.

Tip: "Am/is/are used to + -ing" ≠ "used to + V1."

TRUE — Past simple with "in March" correctly places a finished action in a closed time frame.

Tip: Closed past time → past simple is the safe default.
tasks.solution_overview: This set contrasts past simple with past perfect, tests a stative continuous trap, and separates "used to" habit from "be used to" familiarity. Match the verb form to the timeline before you decide.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The treasury desk has revised the cash-flow model yesterday evening.
By the time investors arrive tomorrow, the pitch deck will have been finalised.
She has been a risk manager here in 2016.
The trainee is belonging to the graduate programme this year.
We used to outsource payroll before we built an in-house HR team.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Yesterday evening" is finished time, so write "revised," not present perfect.

Tip: Present perfect hates explicit finished-time adverbs.

TRUE — Future perfect passive correctly places finalisation before the investors' arrival.

Tip: "By the time + future" often invites "will have + past participle."

FALSE — "In 2016" closes the period; use past simple: "was a risk manager here in 2016."

Tip: "In + year" usually blocks present perfect for a finished role.

FALSE — "Belong" is stative; prefer "belongs," not continuous.

Tip: Possession and membership verbs stay simple in formal exam prose.

TRUE — "Used to outsource" correctly reports a discontinued past habit.

Tip: "Used to + base verb" = past habit that no longer holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Only two sentences survive here. Hunt finished-time clashes with present perfect, check future perfect with "by the time," and reject stative continuous plus the wrong "used to" companion patterns.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The logistics manager has supervised the warehouse since the expansion.
While the negotiators were drafting the clause, counsel objected.
By year-end, the start-up will have raised its Series A round.
Investors used to prefer longer lock-up periods in this sector.
The controller is owning several shares in the subsidiary.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect + "since" correctly links an ongoing role to its start point.

Tip: "Since" points to a start that still matters now — present perfect territory.

TRUE — Continuous background plus simple interrupt is the standard past pairing.

Tip: Ask which action was "in progress" when the other struck.

TRUE — Future perfect places fundraising completion before year-end.

Tip: Corporate deadlines with "by" love future perfect.

TRUE — "Used to prefer" correctly describes a past preference that has changed.

Tip: Preferences and habits both take "used to + V1."

FALSE — Stative "own" should be "owns," not continuous.

Tip: Ownership verbs almost never take continuous in exam English.
tasks.solution_overview: Four sentences are clean; only the stative continuous fails. Confirm "since," background continuous, future perfect with "by," and past habit before you hunt the ownership trap.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The audit partner presented the findings at last week's plenary.
Staff are used to filing expense claims through the new portal.
The research unit has published three working papers this semester.
By Friday noon, legal will have cleared the non-disclosure agreement.
When the CEO entered, the team had already finished the dry run.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past simple correctly anchors a finished presentation to "last week."

Tip: Explicit past time → past simple is rarely wrong.

TRUE — "Are used to filing" correctly means staff are accustomed to the process.

Tip: "Be used to + -ing" = familiarity, not past habit.

TRUE — Present perfect fits an unfinished period ("this semester") with present relevance.

Tip: "This week / this year / this semester" often keep present perfect alive.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places clearance before Friday noon.

Tip: Clock deadlines with "by" are classic future-perfect cues.

TRUE — Past perfect marks the dry run as earlier than the CEO's entrance.

Tip: "Already" before a second past event often signals past perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are grammatical. Use this as a calibration set: past simple with closed time, "be used to," present perfect in an open period, future perfect, and past perfect sequencing.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Marketing has launched the campaign two days ago.
The intern is understanding the margin model after three tutorials.
We had finalised the term sheet before the bank called back.
She is used to commute across town for client visits.
By Q3, operations will have relocated the call centre.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Two days ago" demands past simple: "launched," not present perfect.

Tip: Any "ago" phrase is a finished-time killer for present perfect.

FALSE — Stative "understand" should stay simple: "understands" (or "understand" after we/they).

Tip: Temporary "I'm beginning to understand" is rare; exams prefer the simple form.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly places finalisation before the bank's later call.

Tip: "Before + past event" often licenses past perfect for the earlier action.

FALSE — Familiarity needs gerund: "is used to commuting," not "commute."

Tip: After "be used to," always expect a noun or -ing form.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly schedules relocation completion by Q3.

Tip: Fiscal quarters with "by" are natural future-perfect frames.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch "ago," a stative continuous, and the "be used to" + base-verb trap. Only the past-perfect sequence and the future-perfect relocation hold.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The firm has not yet disclosed the restructuring plan.
While HR was interviewing candidates, the server crashed.
Investors used to relying on annual reports alone.
The economist is believing the inflation forecast is too optimistic.
By the time the bond matures, we will have repaid half the principal.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect with "not yet" correctly signals a still-open disclosure.

Tip: "Yet / already / just" often partner with present perfect in exam English.

TRUE — Continuous interview as background; past simple crash as interrupt.

Tip: IT outages mid-process are classic continuous + simple pairs.

FALSE — Past habit needs base verb: "used to rely," not "relying."

Tip: "Used to + -ing" is almost always wrong; swap to V1 or switch to "be used to."

FALSE — Stative "believe" stays simple: "believes."

Tip: Opinion verbs (believe, agree, prefer) resist continuous form.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places repayment before maturity.

Tip: Bond and loan timelines with "by the time" invite future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Three correct, two traps: "used to relying" and continuous "believe." Keep "yet," background continuous, and future perfect with maturity dates in your checklist.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board has appointed the new CFO in January.
She used to being responsible for investor relations in London.
The consortium is seeming ready to bid on the concession.
We already signed the heads of terms when counsel raised objections.
By dawn, the overnight desk will have hedged the currency exposure.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "In January" is closed past time; use "appointed," not present perfect.

Tip: Month + year style anchors usually force past simple.

FALSE — Past state needs "used to be," not "used to being."

Tip: After "used to," take a base verb or "be," never an -ing form.

FALSE — Stative "seem" should be "seems," not continuous.

Tip: Appearance verbs (seem, appear, look like) stay simple in careful prose.

FALSE — Signing came first, so write "had already signed."

Tip: "Already" + two past events → check whether past perfect is missing.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places the hedge before dawn.

Tip: Overnight trading desks love "by + time" + future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Only one sentence survives. Reject present perfect with "in January," "used to being," stative continuous, and missing past perfect; keep the dawn future perfect.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Revenue has grown steadily for the past five quarters.
The associate was preparing the slide deck when the client cancelled.
Junior traders are used to monitoring screens for twelve-hour shifts.
By the closing bell, the fund will have liquidated its remaining positions.
Management has announced the spin-off at the 2022 AGM.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect continuous-style growth with "for + duration" that reaches now is fine in perfect form.

Tip: "For the past X" usually keeps the window open → present perfect.

TRUE — Past continuous preparation interrupted by past-simple cancellation.

Tip: "Was/were + -ing when…" is the textbook interrupt pattern.

TRUE — "Are used to monitoring" correctly expresses workplace familiarity.

Tip: Long shifts and routines are natural "be used to + -ing" contexts.

TRUE — Future perfect places liquidation before the closing bell.

Tip: Market-session endpoints with "by" cue future perfect.

FALSE — The 2022 AGM is finished time; use "announced," not present perfect.

Tip: Named past events (AGM 2022, last summit) block present perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Four hold; the AGM date breaks present perfect. Confirm open-duration perfect, interrupt continuous, familiarity "be used to," and market future perfect before you fail the dated announcement.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The valuation team finished the model before the roadshow began.
Counsel had reviewed the indemnity clause before the counterparties signed.
I used to travel monthly to the Frankfurt subsidiary.
She is used to negotiating with works councils in Germany.
By next month's board meeting, IT will have migrated the CRM data.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Two past simples can sequence events when order is clear from "before."

Tip: Past perfect is optional when "before/after" already orders the timeline.

TRUE — Past perfect optionally (and correctly) stresses the earlier review.

Tip: Past perfect is never wrong when one past action clearly precedes another.

TRUE — "Used to travel" correctly marks a discontinued travel habit.

Tip: Frequency adverbs (monthly, often) sit well with "used to."

TRUE — "Is used to negotiating" correctly means she finds works-council talks familiar.

Tip: Cross-border labour talks are classic "be used to + -ing" exam content.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places migration before the next board meeting.

Tip: "By next [meeting/date]" is a future-perfect magnet.
tasks.solution_overview: All five work. Notice that past simple + "before" can stand alone, while past perfect is equally acceptable for clarity — then separate habit "used to" from familiarity "be used to," and lock future perfect to the board deadline.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The syndicate desk has priced the bond issue this morning and is still taking orders.
Stakeholders are wanting a clearer capital-allocation narrative.
We used to hedge every FX exposure automatically; now we apply selective hedges.
By the time the regulator publishes its ruling, the bank will have provisioned the fine.
The trainee has joined the graduate scheme in September 2023.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "This morning" can still be an open period if the trading day continues; present perfect fits ongoing relevance.

Tip: Same-day "this morning" often allows present perfect when results still matter.

FALSE — Stative "want" should be "want," not continuous, in formal exam style.

Tip: Desire verbs (want, need, prefer) stay simple unless a special progressive nuance is intended.

TRUE — "Used to hedge" correctly contrasts a past automatic habit with current practice.

Tip: "Used to…; now…" is a clean habit-change pattern.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places provisioning before the ruling's publication.

Tip: Regulatory publication dates with "by the time" invite future perfect.

FALSE — September 2023 is closed; use "joined," not present perfect.

Tip: Exact past months with years almost always take past simple.
tasks.solution_overview: Three pass. Keep open-period perfect and the habit contrast; reject continuous "want" and present perfect with a dated September 2023 join.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: While the analyst was updating the DCF, the peer multiples moved sharply.
The partnership has existed since the 2019 joint venture.
Executives used to holding weekly stand-ups in the open-plan office.
I am used to receiving same-day feedback from the partner.
By December, the plant will have installed the new assembly line.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Continuous update as background; past-simple market move as the shorter event.

Tip: Market moves mid-task are textbook continuous + simple pairs.

TRUE — Present perfect with "since" correctly marks a continuing partnership.

Tip: Corporate existence "since [year]" is classic present-perfect territory.

FALSE — Write "used to hold," not "used to holding," for past habit.

Tip: If you mean habit, drop the -ing after "used to."

TRUE — "Am used to receiving" correctly expresses familiarity with fast feedback.

Tip: "Be used to + -ing" answers "What feels normal to you?"

TRUE — Future perfect correctly schedules installation completion by December.

Tip: Capex milestones with "by + month" cue future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Four correct; only "used to holding" fails. Separate past-habit form from familiarity "be used to," and keep since-perfect plus future perfect intact.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rating agency has already downgraded the issuer twice this year.
When the whistle-blower contacted compliance, the investigation had not yet begun.
The portfolio manager is liking the defensive tilt of the new mandate.
We are used to work under Basel reporting calendars.
By the IPO date, underwriters will have booked the full order book.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect with "already" and "this year" fits an unfinished reporting year.

Tip: "Already + this year" is a present-perfect sweet spot.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly places non-start of the probe before the contact.

Tip: Negative past perfect ("had not yet") is natural for "earlier than" claims.

FALSE — Stative "like" should be "likes," not continuous, in exam register.

Tip: Preference verbs stay simple unless you stress a temporary change of taste.

FALSE — Familiarity needs "are used to working," not bare "work."

Tip: After "be used to," insert -ing (or a noun), never a bare infinitive.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places book-building completion before the IPO.

Tip: Capital-markets deadlines with "by" almost advertise future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder traps: continuous "like" and "be used to" + bare verb. Keep open-year perfect, past-perfect sequencing, and IPO future perfect as your anchors.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The subsidiary posted record EBITDA last quarter.
Researchers have been collecting survey responses for six weeks.
Sales reps used to cold-call every lead; the CRM now prioritises warm contacts.
By the time the customs inspection ends, warehouse staff will have restocked the bay.
The director is having a mansion in the countryside outside Vienna.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past simple correctly ties a finished result to "last quarter."

Tip: Fiscal periods labelled "last…" almost always take past simple.

TRUE — Present perfect continuous correctly stresses ongoing collection over six weeks.

Tip: "Have been + -ing + for" highlights duration still in progress.

TRUE — "Used to cold-call" correctly marks a discontinued sales habit.

Tip: Process-change stories often contrast "used to" with "now."

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places restocking before inspection end.

Tip: Parallel operations with "by the time" invite future perfect.

FALSE — Stative possession needs "has," not "is having," for permanent ownership.

Tip: "Have" for possession ≠ "have" for temporary activities ("having a meeting").
tasks.solution_overview: Four are solid; only stative "is having" for ownership fails. Note the acceptable present perfect continuous for duration and the "have" possession trap.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The mediation team has resolved most disputes since the new charter took effect.
While logistics was rerouting shipments, the port authority imposed a strike notice.
Associates are used to preparing client memos overnight before hearings.
By the refinance date, the borrower will have amortised twenty per cent of the loan.
The CFO used to review every invoice personally before the ERP went live.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect with "since" correctly covers outcomes from charter start until now.

Tip: Policy start dates + continuing results → present perfect.

TRUE — Continuous rerouting as background; past-simple imposition as interrupt.

Tip: External notices mid-process fit the interrupt pattern cleanly.

TRUE — "Are used to preparing" correctly signals overnight-work familiarity.

Tip: Legal and consulting grind often appears with "be used to + -ing."

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places amortisation before refinance.

Tip: Loan milestones with "by" are future-perfect territory.

TRUE — "Used to review" correctly describes a discontinued personal-review habit.

Tip: System go-lives often mark the end of a "used to" habit.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are grammatical at a higher band: since-perfect, interrupt continuous, familiarity "be used to," refinance future perfect, and a clear past habit. Use it to lock pattern recognition under time pressure.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The exchange has suspended trading in the share yesterday for exactly twelve minutes.
When the external auditor arrived, management had already circulated the draft findings.
The committee is consisting of five independent directors and two executives.
We used to depend entirely on one supplier before dual-sourcing.
By dusk, the crisis team will have drafted the holding statement for the press.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Yesterday" is finished time, so write "suspended," not present perfect.

Tip: "Yesterday" never pairs with present perfect in exam English.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly places circulation before the auditor's arrival.

Tip: Drafts "already" in circulation before a visitor → past perfect.

FALSE — Stative "consist" should be "consists," not continuous.

Tip: Composition verbs (consist of, contain, include) stay simple.

TRUE — "Used to depend" correctly marks a past single-supplier habit.

Tip: Supply-chain diversification stories often hinge on "used to."

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places the draft before dusk.

Tip: Crisis timelines with "by dusk/dawn" cue future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Subtler mix: present perfect clashes with "yesterday," and continuous "consist" fails. Keep past-perfect sequencing, past habit, and dusk future perfect.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Ever since the carbon levy rose, exporters have passed more costs to buyers.
The strategist was weighing a divestiture when the antitrust probe surfaced.
Partners used to meeting clients exclusively in person before hybrid work.
I am used to analysing sparse data sets under exam time limits.
By the time the fiscal year closes, treasury will have rolled every maturing swap.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Ever since" + present perfect correctly links a past trigger to continuing cost pass-through.

Tip: "Ever since" almost always wants present perfect in the result clause.

TRUE — Continuous weighing interrupted by past-simple surfacing of the probe.

Tip: Strategy work interrupted by news is a clean continuous + simple pair.

FALSE — Past habit needs "used to meet," not "meeting."

Tip: Hybrid-work contrasts often hide the "used to + -ing" trap.

TRUE — "Am used to analysing" correctly expresses familiarity with sparse-data work.

Tip: Exam and research routines fit "be used to + -ing."

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places swap rolls before year close.

Tip: Year-end treasury checklists with "by the time" invite future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Top band: trust "ever since" + perfect and interrupt continuous, but catch "used to meeting." Keep familiarity "be used to" and year-end future perfect.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The start-up has secured seed funding only after the second pitch last autumn.
Investors had already written down the stake when the turnaround plan leaked.
The board is recognising the need for tighter liquidity covenants this quarter.
She is used to prepare remote due-diligence packs overnight.
By midnight GMT, the arbitrage bot will have closed every open pair trade.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Only after… last autumn" closes the timeline; past simple "secured" is required.

Tip: "After + finished past event" usually blocks present perfect.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly places the write-down before the leak.

Tip: Write-downs "already" before news breaks → past perfect.

FALSE — Here "recognise" is stative awareness; exam English prefers "recognises," not continuous.

Tip: Mental acknowledgement verbs rarely need continuous in formal prose.

FALSE — Familiarity needs "is used to preparing," not a bare infinitive.

Tip: After "be used to," take -ing (or a noun), never V1.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places bot closure before midnight GMT.

Tip: Time-zone cut-offs with "by" are future-perfect cues.
tasks.solution_overview: Only two survive. The hardest traps stack finished-time perfect, stative continuous, and "be used to" + bare verb — keep past-perfect sequencing and midnight future perfect.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Over the past decade, the university has expanded its executive MBA intake steadily.
While counsel was redlining the SPA, valuation multiples shifted overnight.
Deal teams are used to sleeping little during exclusivity periods.
By the lock-up expiry, early investors will have sold a measured first tranche.
The economist has predicted a mild recession in her 2019 white paper.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect with "over the past decade" correctly covers a period reaching now.

Tip: "Over the past…" almost always licences present perfect.

TRUE — Continuous redlining as background; past-simple overnight shift as the shorter change.

Tip: Overnight market moves during drafting fit continuous + simple.

TRUE — "Are used to sleeping" correctly (if bluntly) marks familiarity with deal intensity.

Tip: "Be used to + -ing" can take colloquial verbs in business narratives.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places the measured sale before lock-up expiry.

Tip: Lock-up and vesting dates with "by" cue future perfect.

FALSE — A 2019 white paper is finished time; use "predicted," not present perfect.

Tip: Publication years force past simple for the act of predicting.
tasks.solution_overview: Four pass; the 2019 white-paper prediction fails present perfect. Lock "over the past," interrupt continuous, deal-team "be used to," and lock-up future perfect.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Since the Basel reforms, banks have held thicker capital buffers against credit risk.
The restructuring adviser had outlined three options before the creditors voted.
Procurement used to sole-source critical components from a single Asian plant.
Graduates are used to presenting case solutions under strict time pressure.
By the time the fiscal watchdog reports, the ministry will have published revised deficit figures.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect with "since" correctly links reform start to continuing buffer policy.

Tip: Regulatory "since" markers almost demand present perfect in the result.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly places the outline before the creditors' vote.

Tip: Pre-vote briefings are natural past-perfect territory.

TRUE — "Used to sole-source" correctly reports a discontinued sourcing habit.

Tip: Supply-risk stories often contrast "used to" with today's diversification.

TRUE — "Are used to presenting" correctly expresses exam-style familiarity.

Tip: BBE case drills are textbook "be used to + -ing" contexts.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places publication before the watchdog report.

Tip: Parallel institutional deadlines with "by the time" invite future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: A clean top-band set: since-perfect policy continuity, past-perfect pre-vote briefing, past sourcing habit, graduate familiarity with presenting, and ministry future perfect ahead of the watchdog. All five stand.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If inflation rises, the central bank raises the policy rate.
If the board approves the budget, the firm will hire three analysts next month.
If demand increases, the warehouse will restocks overnight.
If cash flow improves, payroll will processes on Friday.
If the client signs today, logistics would ship the sample kit tomorrow for certain.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — This is a clean zero conditional: present simple in both clauses for a general business rule that always holds when the condition is met.

Tip: For habits and policy rules, keep both sides in present simple — not will.

TRUE — First conditional: a real future possibility takes present simple in the if-clause and will + base verb in the result.

Tip: After if for a real future plan, use present simple, then will in the main clause.

FALSE — The result clause mixes will with a third-person -s form ("will restocks"). After will you need the base form restock.

Tip: Modal will always takes a bare infinitive: will restock, never will restocks.

FALSE — After will the verb must stay bare: will process, not will processes. Agreement -s never follows a modal.

Tip: Scan will + verb: if you see an -s on that verb, the line is broken.

FALSE — A real tomorrow delivery plan needs will ship, not would ship. Would belongs to unreal or polite second-conditional territory.

Tip: Open near-term plans → will; reserve would for unreal or soft hypothetical results.
tasks.solution_overview: Walk each sentence like a checklist: is this a general rule (zero) or a real future plan (first)? Zero keeps present + present; first keeps present + will. Three lines fail on form — will + -s, and would where will is required.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the start-up had more working capital, it would expand into two new regions.
If I were the finance director, I would postpone the share buy-back.
If the supplier would have confirmed earlier, we would have met the launch date.
If margins were higher, the retailer would stock premium SKUs.
If the auditor were available on Monday, we would close the ledger then.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Second conditional: past simple in the if-clause plus would + base verb for an unreal present or future business scenario.

Tip: Unreal now/soon → if + past simple, main clause would + infinitive.

TRUE — Formal were is the preferred subjunctive after if I for unreal advice or role-play, paired with would in the result.

Tip: In exams, prefer If I were … would … over If I was for hypothetical roles.

FALSE — Classic trap: do not put would have in the if-clause. The unreal past condition needs past perfect: If the supplier had confirmed earlier…

Tip: Never write if … would have; use if … had + past participle instead.

TRUE — Standard second conditional for a counterfactual present about margins and assortment.

Tip: Past simple + would is the default unreal-present frame.

TRUE — Were with a third-person singular subject is fine in careful business English for an unreal present condition.

Tip: If X were … would … is exam-safe for unreal present, even with he/she/it.
tasks.solution_overview: These lines test unreal present (second conditional) and the infamous if … would have trap. Keep would only in the result clause; the if-clause wants past simple or were, never would have.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the bank had tightened covenants sooner, the borrower would have refinanced elsewhere.
Had the logistics team booked the slots, the shipment would have cleared customs on time.
Had the CFO hedged the exposure, the firm will avoid the currency loss.
If procurement had dual-sourced the chip, production would not have stalled.
Had marketing tested the creative, the campaign would have launched with fewer revisions.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Third conditional: past perfect in the if-clause and would have + past participle for a closed past outcome.

Tip: Past unreal → if + had + V3, main clause would have + V3.

TRUE — Inverted third conditional: Had + subject + past participle replaces If + subject + had, with the same would have result.

Tip: Had the team … would have … equals If the team had … would have …

FALSE — After inverted Had … the result must stay in the third-conditional world (would have), not will. Will clashes with a finished past condition.

Tip: Inversion still needs would have / could have / might have — never bare will.

TRUE — Classic third conditional on a missed sourcing decision and its past production impact.

Tip: Check both verbs: had dual-sourced + would not have stalled.

TRUE — Another clean Had-inversion third conditional about campaign testing.

Tip: If the sentence starts with Had + past participle phrase, expect would have in the main clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on closed past regrets: past perfect (or Had-inversion) plus would have. The broken line swaps will into a past counterfactual — that tense clash is the giveaway.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the firm had entered the Nordic market last year, it would have a stronger brand there now.
If inventory were lower today, we would have ordered less last quarter.
If the tender is won, the contractor will mobilise within ten days.
If energy prices fall, factories cut night-shift overtime.
If I would be the project lead, I would freeze scope changes.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed conditional: past cause (had entered) with a present result (would have a stronger brand now).

Tip: Past cause → present result: if + past perfect, would + present-state verb.

TRUE — The other common mix: unreal present condition (were lower today) explaining a different past action (would have ordered).

Tip: Present unreal → past result: if + past simple/were, would have + V3.

TRUE — Straightforward first conditional for a still-open tender outcome.

Tip: Open future deal → present + will.

TRUE — Zero conditional describing how plants generally respond when energy prices fall.

Tip: General operations rule → present + present.

FALSE — Avoid would in the if-clause. For an unreal role use If I were the project lead, I would freeze…

Tip: If I would be is almost always wrong; rewrite as If I were / If I was (informal).
tasks.solution_overview: Four lines are healthy mixes of zero, first, and mixed conditionals. Isolate the if-clause that wrongly uses would — that is the only hard fail on this card.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Unless the invoice is paid by Friday, the wholesaler will suspend further deliveries.
If the KPI dashboard updates nightly, managers review exceptions each morning.
If headcount rose next spring, HR will open a graduate scheme.
Provided that compliance clears the script, the webinar will go live at noon.
If liquidity dried up tomorrow, treasurers would draw the revolving facility.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Unless + present simple works like a first-conditional if-not clause, with will in the result.

Tip: Unless ≈ if not; keep present after unless for real future threats.

TRUE — Zero conditional for a recurring overnight data habit and the morning review that follows.

Tip: Habitual systems → present in both clauses.

FALSE — Mixing past simple (rose) with will for a still-possible next-spring plan is inconsistent. Use rises … will open, or rose … would open for unreal.

Tip: Match time frames: real future needs present + will, not past + will.

TRUE — Provided that behaves like if in a first conditional and correctly pairs with will.

Tip: Provided that / as long as take the same tense pattern as if.

TRUE — Second conditional for an unlikely near-term liquidity crunch: past simple + would.

Tip: Unlikely tomorrow-stress → past + would.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch connectors (unless, provided that) — they follow the same tense rules as if. The weak sentence pairs a past-form condition with will for an open future plan.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the joint venture had secured the licence in March, it would be operating at full capacity now.
Had interest rates stayed low, the REIT would refinance the portfolio last autumn.
If customers complained about packaging, the brand redesigns the inserts.
If I were advising the board, I would ring-fence the contingency reserve.
If the merger would have closed in Q2, synergies would have appeared sooner.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed: past perfect condition with a present continuous-style result (would be operating now).

Tip: Past decision → present state: had + V3, then would + be + -ing / would + base.

FALSE — Had … stayed sets a third/mixed past frame, but would refinance (simple) fails to mark the missed autumn action; need would have refinanced.

Tip: A finished past result after Had … needs would have + V3.

TRUE — Zero conditional for a standing customer-service rule.

Tip: Whenever-style complaints → present + present.

TRUE — If I were + would is the polished second-conditional advisory pattern.

Tip: Hypothetical advice voice: If I were …, I would …

FALSE — Another if … would have trap in the condition clause; rewrite as If the merger had closed in Q2…

Tip: Delete would from every if-clause; use had + V3 for past unreal.
tasks.solution_overview: Two failures hide in past counterfactuals: one under-marks the result (would instead of would have), and one illegally places would have after if. The true lines show clean zero, mixed, and If I were patterns.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Should the underwriter demand more disclosure, the issuer will file an amended prospectus.
If unit costs fall below target, the plant will increase daily throughput.
If the franchisee paid royalties on time, the brand renews the territory next year.
Had the warehouse installed scanners earlier, picking errors would have dropped.
If demand softens, dynamic pricing lowers weekend rates automatically.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Formal first-conditional inversion with Should + subject + base verb, then will in the result.

Tip: Should the X … will … = If the X … will … for real future contingencies.

TRUE — Ordinary first conditional on a cost-threshold trigger.

Tip: Present after if + will for operational targets.

FALSE — Past simple paid paired with present renews for a next-year plan is a tense mash-up. Use pays … will renew, or paid … would renew.

Tip: Do not mix a past if-clause with a present-simple future result.

TRUE — Had-inversion third conditional on a past technology investment.

Tip: Had + V3 … would have + V3 is the inversion checklist.

TRUE — Zero conditional for an automated pricing rule.

Tip: System rules that always fire → present + present.
tasks.solution_overview: Should-inversion is just a formal first conditional — keep will in the result. Reject any line that jumps from a past if-clause straight into a present-simple future promise.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the catalogue were printed in colour, retail buyers would place larger orders.
If the courier arrives before noon, the clinic will still process same-day claims.
If R&D had patented the coating, competitors would not copy it so easily now.
If we would receive the escrow release, we will settle the contractors.
Were the exchange rate more stable, exporters would quote longer fixed prices.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Second conditional with were for an unreal present product decision.

Tip: Were / past simple + would marks counterfactual present.

TRUE — First conditional for a real same-day operations window.

Tip: Present + will for open daytime logistics.

TRUE — Mixed: past perfect cause with a present result (would not copy … now).

Tip: Past IP choice → present competitive pain: had + V3, would + base.

FALSE — Double fault: would in the if-clause and will in the result for what should be a simple first conditional (If we receive … we will settle).

Tip: Strip would from if; use present + will for real receipts.

TRUE — Were-inversion second conditional (Were the exchange rate …) equals If the exchange rate were…

Tip: Were + noun phrase … would … is formal unreal present.
tasks.solution_overview: Healthy second, first, mixed, and Were-inversion lines surround one toxic if we would receive … will settle pair. Train your eye to delete would from every if-clause first.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the bond had been rated investment-grade, pension funds would hold larger positions today.
If churn stays under two percent, the SaaS firm will beat its ARR guidance.
Had the pilot failed safety checks, regulators would suspend the route indefinitely.
If staffing were flexible, overtime premiums would fall during peak weeks.
If the auctioneer would have set a higher reserve, the lot would have sold for more.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed conditional: past rating event → present portfolio behaviour (would hold … today).

Tip: Look for now/today after a had-been condition — that signals mixed, not pure third.

TRUE — First conditional on a live KPI threshold and forward guidance.

Tip: Open metric path → present + will.

FALSE — Had the pilot failed frames a closed past check, so the result needs would have suspended, not would suspend (which reads like a present/future habit).

Tip: Past inversion + ongoing would is usually wrong; prefer would have for finished past results.

TRUE — Second conditional about an unreal present HR policy.

Tip: Were + would for counterfactual workforce design.

FALSE — If … would have set is the prohibited pattern; use If the auctioneer had set a higher reserve…

Tip: Past unreal conditions: had + V3 only — never would have after if.
tasks.solution_overview: Distinguish mixed present results from pure third-conditional past results. Two lines fail: one under-marks a past result after Had…, and one still smuggles would have into the if-clause.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: As long as collateral covers the drawdown, the facility will remain available.
If freight rates spiked last winter, importers would switch to rail now.
If the prototype passes EMC tests, manufacturing will tool the moulds.
If I was the risk officer yesterday, I would have blocked the trade.
If volatility increases, option premiums rise across the board.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — As long as + present simple with will is a standard first-conditional credit condition.

Tip: As long as / so long as follow first-conditional tense logic.

FALSE — A finished last-winter spike needs past perfect (had spiked) for a mixed link to now, or a different framing. Past simple + would … now is not the clean mixed pattern.

Tip: Past cause of a present result → if + had + V3, would + present.

TRUE — First conditional for a gated manufacturing step still ahead.

Tip: Open test gate → present + will.

FALSE — Yesterday forces a past unreal: If I had been the risk officer yesterday, I would have blocked… Was + would have mismatches the time adverb.

Tip: With yesterday/last week, prefer had been … would have, not was … would have.

TRUE — Zero conditional market rule: higher volatility, higher premiums.

Tip: Market identities → present + present.
tasks.solution_overview: Time adverbs are the tell. Last winter and yesterday demand past-perfect conditions for counterfactuals; as long as and open tests stay in first-conditional territory.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had tariffs been announced sooner, sourcing teams would already be dual-qualified now.
If the retailer offers free returns, conversion rates climb in the app.
If cash reserves are thinner, the group would cancel the dividend next week.
If the engineer had calibrated the line, scrap rates would be lower this morning.
Were investors fully informed, they would tolerate a longer payback period.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed after Had-inversion: past tariff shock → present continuous-like state (would already be dual-qualified now).

Tip: Had … been + would be … now is a valid mixed inversion.

TRUE — Zero conditional e-commerce rule linking a standing offer to conversion behaviour.

Tip: Standing commercial rules → present + present.

FALSE — Present simple are thinner with would cancel is a second-conditional mismatch; use were thinner … would cancel, or are thinner … will cancel.

Tip: Present real → will; unreal present → past/were + would — do not cross-wire them.

TRUE — Mixed: past calibration failure/success with a present scrap-rate result this morning.

Tip: Had + V3 … would be … now/this morning = mixed.

TRUE — Were-inversion second conditional on investor psychology.

Tip: Were + subject complement … would … for unreal present.
tasks.solution_overview: Real present facts take will; unreal present takes were/past + would. The false line keeps a real-present verb (are) but slips into would for next week.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the consortium bids aggressively, the city will award the concession this quarter.
If wage growth outpaced productivity last year, unit labour costs would be elevated now.
If the broker would confirm the allocation, traders will hedge by the open.
If downtime exceeds four hours, service-level credits apply automatically.
Had the insurer priced flood risk correctly, claims would not have wiped the book.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — First conditional for a live tender still in play.

Tip: Open award window → present + will.

FALSE — Last year as a factual past driver of a present state needs had outpaced, not outpaced alone, in careful mixed form: If wage growth had outpaced … would be elevated now.

Tip: For past→present mixed, upgrade the if-clause to past perfect.

FALSE — Would confirm after if plus will hedge is a first-conditional wreck; write If the broker confirms … traders will hedge…

Tip: Real pre-open plans never put would in the if-clause.

TRUE — Zero conditional SLA rule written into the contract language.

Tip: Automatic contractual consequences → present + present.

TRUE — Full third conditional on a closed underwriting mistake.

Tip: Had + V3 … would not have + V3 for finished past damage.
tasks.solution_overview: Two traps: a mixed that forgot past perfect after last year, and a first conditional polluted with would. The clean lines stay strictly first, zero, or third.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the CFO were to disclose the impairment early, analysts would reassess guidance within hours.
If negotiations break down, counsel will file for interim relief.
Had working capital been ring-fenced, the turnaround plan would succeed last month.
If order books thin further, factories will idle weekend shifts.
If I would have chaired the audit committee, related-party deals would have faced harder questions.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Were to + infinitive is an accepted formal second-conditional variant for a tentative unreal future disclosure.

Tip: If X were to + verb … would … softens an unlikely future step.

TRUE — First conditional litigation contingency still open.

Tip: Present + will for live legal forks.

FALSE — Had … been ring-fenced points to a past closed window (last month), so the result needs would have succeeded, not would succeed.

Tip: Past inversion + last month → would have + V3.

TRUE — First conditional operations response to thinning order books.

Tip: Real deterioration path → present + will.

FALSE — If I would have chaired is the textbook trap; correct: If I had chaired the audit committee…

Tip: Memorise the ban: no would have after if — ever.
tasks.solution_overview: Were to is a polished second-conditional option, not an error. Failures here under-specify a past result after Had… and recycle the if I would have chaired trap.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Even if the patent lapses, the know-how will still protect margins for a while.
If yields had climbed faster, duration risk would look worse on today's dashboard.
If the stewardess announces a delay, passengers update their onward bookings.
Supposing the lease is extended, the bakery will keep the high-street unit.
If regulators had signalled forbearance, banks would not tighten lending standards so sharply now.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Even if still follows first-conditional tenses for a real possibility that does not block the result.

Tip: Even if + present, will … keeps the same skeleton as if.

TRUE — Mixed: faster past climb in yields → present dashboard appearance (would look … today).

Tip: Had + V3 … would + present verb + today/now = mixed.

TRUE — Zero conditional passenger-behaviour rule at the gate (business-travel operations context).

Tip: Habitual responses → present + present.

TRUE — Supposing that/if-equivalent first conditional with will.

Tip: Supposing ≈ if for real future estate decisions.

TRUE — Mixed policy signal: past forbearance cue → present lending stance.

Tip: Past perfect condition + would + present verb + now.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are sound — a rare full-true card. Confirm even if / supposing keep first-conditional logic, and that both mixed lines genuinely link a past perfect cause to a present result with now/today.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the incubator mentors founders weekly, survival rates improve after year one.
If customs had cleared the consignment on Monday, shelves would not be empty this afternoon.
If I were in your position at treasury, I would ladder the maturities.
Had the pitch deck mentioned churn, the VC would ask harder questions in the room.
If spot prices rally, hedgers will roll their contracts forward.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Zero conditional describing an incubator operating model and its usual outcome.

Tip: Programme design rules → present + present.

TRUE — Mixed: Monday clearance (past perfect) versus empty shelves now (would not be … this afternoon).

Tip: Past logistics miss → present stockout: had + V3, would + be.

TRUE — Classic If I were … would … advisory second conditional in a treasury setting.

Tip: Exam gold: If I were …, I would …

FALSE — Had … mentioned sets a past counterfactual about the deck, so the room Q&A that followed needs would have asked, not would ask.

Tip: Finished past meeting → would have + V3 after Had…

TRUE — First conditional markets line for an open rally scenario.

Tip: Live price path → present + will.
tasks.solution_overview: Only the pitch-deck inversion fails by leaving the result in would ask instead of would have asked. Everything else cleanly covers zero, mixed, If I were, and first.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If carbon prices climb, cement producers pass on surcharges within the quarter.
If the syndicate had allocated more paper to retail, the aftermarket would be firmer today.
If onboarding takes longer than five days, enterprise clients will escalate to the account lead.
If the board would approve a rights issue, dilution would worry existing holders.
Were cash conversion weaker, ratings agencies would flag liquidity metrics.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Zero conditional industry pricing response.

Tip: Sector rule of thumb → present + present.

TRUE — Mixed primary-market decision (had allocated) with today's aftermarket tone (would be firmer today).

Tip: Past allocation → present trading: had + V3, would + be + today.

TRUE — First conditional SLA/escalation path still available.

Tip: Open service risk → present + will.

FALSE — Would approve after if is illegal; for unreal present write If the board approved … would worry, or for real future If the board approves … will worry.

Tip: Kill would in the if-clause, then choose second vs first consistently.

TRUE — Were-inversion second conditional on credit metrics.

Tip: Were + comparative … would … for unreal present credit stress.
tasks.solution_overview: Four lines are textbook. The false one parks would inside the if-clause before another would — double would is your red flag.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had the earn-out been structured more tightly, the acquirer would not be litigating the targets now.
If utilisation dips below seventy percent, the airline will wet-lease fewer aircraft next season.
If the controller was to restate revenue, auditors would expand sampling immediately.
If freight forwarders had digitalised documents earlier, demurrage would have been lower last peak season.
Only if collateral is topped up will the lender release the next tranche.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed Had-inversion: past earn-out design → present litigation (would not be litigating … now).

Tip: Had … been + would be + -ing + now = mixed inversion.

TRUE — First conditional fleet-planning response to utilisation.

Tip: Season-ahead ops plan → present + will.

FALSE — Formal tentative unreal prefers were to, not was to, with a singular controller in careful exam English: If the controller were to restate…

Tip: In formal papers, stick to were to (not was to) after if for this pattern.

TRUE — Pure third conditional on a finished peak-season cost outcome.

Tip: Had + V3 … would have been … for closed past peaks.

TRUE — Only if inversion in a first-conditional credit release: Only if … will + subject + verb.

Tip: Only if moves will before the subject — still a real future condition.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced packaging: mixed Had-inversion, Only if … will inversion, and the were to vs was to formality trap. Only the was to line should fall.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If goodwill had not been written down, equity ratios would look healthier on the March pack.
If the night shift finishes the batch, QC will sample before dawn.
If distributors stocked deeper inventories, stock-outs would have been rarer during last Black Friday.
If I would be less exposed to FX, I would sleep better before reporting day.
Should volumes recover, the mill will restart the idle kiln.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mixed accounting counterfactual: past write-down choice → present appearance of March ratios.

Tip: Had not + V3 … would look … on [present pack] = mixed.

TRUE — First conditional plant schedule still open tonight.

Tip: Same-night plan → present + will.

TRUE — Mixed the other way: unreal present stocking policy explaining a different past Black Friday (would have been rarer).

Tip: Present unreal → past result: if + past simple, would have + V3.

FALSE — If I would be is wrong; use If I were less exposed to FX, I would sleep better…

Tip: Replace If I would be with If I were every time.

TRUE — Should-inversion first conditional for a volume recovery path.

Tip: Should volumes … will … = If volumes … will …
tasks.solution_overview: You need both mixed directions here — past→present and present→past — plus Should-inversion. The single fail is If I would be for an unreal present state.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Were it not for the hedge, the importer would be posting large FX losses this quarter.
If the catalogue had shipped in January, spring sell-through would have peaked earlier.
If headhunters find a match, the CHRO will reopen the search committee.
Had the covenant waiver been granted, the firm will avoid a technical default last Friday.
If payment terms lengthened industry-wide, working-capital cycles would stretch for everyone.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Were it not for … is a formal second/mixed-style inversion meaning if it were not for the hedge, with would be posting now.

Tip: Were it not for X … would … = If it were not for X …

TRUE — Pure third conditional on a missed January catalogue drop.

Tip: Had + V3 … would have + V3 for closed seasonal timing.

TRUE — First conditional hiring contingency.

Tip: Open search branch → present + will.

FALSE — Had … been granted plus last Friday demands would have avoided, not will avoid.

Tip: Past waiver story → would have + V3; will cannot rewrite last Friday.

TRUE — Second conditional industry-wide counterfactual on payment terms.

Tip: Past simple + would for unreal present credit norms.
tasks.solution_overview: Were it not for is advanced but legitimate. The broken Had … will avoid line tries to put a future auxiliary on last Friday — tense suicide.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the underwriter would have priced the IPO more tightly, aftermarket volatility would have been lower.
If backlog clears by June, the yard will takes two more hulls.
If energy hedges rolled off already, spot exposure would be biting harder now.
If I would be running the category, I would delist the slowest SKUs before the reset.
Had cyber insurance been renewed on time, incident costs would have been capped.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The if-clause must not contain would have; write If the underwriter had priced the IPO more tightly…

Tip: Final reminder: if + had + V3, never if + would have.

FALSE — After will use the base verb take, not takes. Agreement -s never follows will.

Tip: will take / will ship / will hire — never will takes.

FALSE — A finished roll-off that explains present pain needs past perfect: If energy hedges had rolled off already…

Tip: Past cause of a present result → had + V3 in the if-clause.

FALSE — If I would be running is wrong; write If I were running the category, I would delist…

Tip: Replace If I would be with If I were in unreal present advice.

TRUE — Had-inversion third conditional on a missed renewal.

Tip: Had + been + V3 … would have been … seals the past counterfactual.
tasks.solution_overview: Capstone stress test: four traps (if … would have, will + -s, missing past perfect in a mixed, If I would be) and one clean Had-inversion third conditional. Hunt errors before celebrating the true line.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of overdue invoices has risen since March.
A number of suppliers was unable to meet the deadline.
Neither the buyer nor the sellers were copied on the email.
Each of the branch managers have filed a quarterly report.
There are several discrepancies in the payroll summary.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "The number of" treats the quantity as a single total, so the singular verb "has" is the right match.

Tip: Mentally replace "the number of X" with "that total" — singular almost always follows.

FALSE — "A number of" means "several," so it needs a plural verb: "were unable," not "was."

Tip: Flip the article test — "a number" ≈ many; "the number" ≈ one figure.

TRUE — With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject; "sellers" is plural, so "were" is correct.

Tip: Ignore the first noun and check only the one sitting next to the verb.

FALSE — "Each of" is always singular: "has filed," not "have filed."

Tip: "Each" picks out one member at a time, even when "of the managers" looks plural.

TRUE — "Discrepancies" is plural, so "there are" agrees correctly.

Tip: After there is/are, locate the real subject that follows the verb and match its number.
tasks.solution_overview: This set drills the core agreement traps you will see on business English exams: the number versus a number, neither…nor proximity, each, and there is/are. Read past the distracting nouns and ask what the true subject is before you choose the verb.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Every applicant for the graduate scheme receives a briefing pack.
The CFO, along with two analysts, were present at the closing.
There is a backlog of purchase orders waiting for approval.
Neither the auditors nor the treasurer has signed the letter.
A number of clients have requested an extension.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Every" forces a singular verb, so "receives" is correct even though many applicants are implied.

Tip: Treat every/each like "one person at a time."

FALSE — "Along with two analysts" is a parenthetical add-on; the subject remains singular "The CFO," so use "was present."

Tip: Cross out along with / as well as / together with and re-check the leftover subject.

TRUE — The delayed subject "a backlog" is singular, so "there is" agrees.

Tip: Do not let the plural noun inside the of-phrase ("orders") steal the agreement.

TRUE — The nearer subject after neither…nor is singular "treasurer," so "has" is right.

Tip: Proximity, not the first noun, decides the verb after neither…nor.

TRUE — "A number of clients" behaves as a plural group, so "have requested" is correct.

Tip: "A number of" ≈ several → plural verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch how add-ons like "along with" never change the head subject's number, while "every" and "a number of" pull in opposite directions. Confirm the grammatical subject first, then lock the verb.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of complaints have fallen after the recall.
Neither the warehouse nor the depots was inspected last week.
There is three outstanding claims on the policy.
Each partner in the joint venture have veto rights.
The data from the pilot survey support the forecast.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "The number of" is singular: write "has fallen," not "have fallen."

Tip: "The number" is one count; keep the verb singular.

FALSE — Nearer subject "depots" is plural, so the verb should be "were inspected."

Tip: In neither…nor chains, only the last noun controls the verb.

FALSE — "Three outstanding claims" is plural, so you need "there are," not "there is."

Tip: Count what follows the verb in there-constructions.

FALSE — "Each partner" takes singular "has veto rights."

Tip: "Each" never takes a plural verb in standard formal English.

TRUE — In formal usage "data" is plural, so "support" is the agreed verb.

Tip: On formal business exams, treat data as plural unless the prompt clearly marks informal style.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these sentences break agreement on purpose. Isolate the real subject — the number, the nearer nor-noun, the post-verbal noun after there, or each — and you will spot the mismatch quickly.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the director nor the deputies were briefed overnight.
The HR lead, together with the payroll team, has approved the bonus list.
There are no further objections from the compliance desk.
Every invoice above ten thousand pounds requires dual authorisation.
A number of interns was assigned to the summer project.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nearer subject "deputies" is plural, so "were briefed" agrees.

Tip: Cover the first noun and read from "nor" onward.

TRUE — "Together with the payroll team" does not pluralise "The HR lead"; singular "has" is correct.

Tip: Parenthetical with-phrases leave the head noun untouched.

TRUE — Plural "objections" correctly takes "there are."

Tip: "No" does not change number; match the noun that follows.

TRUE — "Every invoice" is singular, so "requires" is right.

Tip: Every/each + singular noun → singular verb.

FALSE — "A number of interns" needs plural "were assigned."

Tip: Swap in "several interns" — if that feels plural, keep the plural verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Most lines here are clean; the trap is the final "a number of" item that wrongly takes a singular verb. Use that contrast to cement the the-number / a-number distinction.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of open tickets is still above the service target.
Neither the counsel nor the witnesses was available for the hearing.
There remain several covenants that the borrower must satisfy.
The sales director, as well as the regional managers, are reviewing quotas.
Each of the subsidiaries files its own tax return.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Singular "the number" correctly pairs with "is."

Tip: Focus on "number," not "tickets."

FALSE — Nearer subject "witnesses" is plural: use "were available."

Tip: Neither…nor proximity overrides the singular feel of "counsel."

TRUE — Inverted "there remain" correctly agrees with plural "covenants."

Tip: There-constructions can use verbs other than be; still match the following subject.

FALSE — "As well as the regional managers" is parenthetical; subject "sales director" needs "is reviewing."

Tip: Strip the as-well-as phrase before you choose the verb.

TRUE — "Each of the subsidiaries" takes singular "files."

Tip: "Of the subsidiaries" is a prepositional phrase, not the subject head.
tasks.solution_overview: Difficulty rises slightly with "there remain" and "as well as." Same method: identify the grammatical subject, ignore inserts, and match number.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of bondholders have demanded an urgent call.
Neither the underwriter nor the syndicate members were ready to price the issue.
The operations head, along with her deputies, was copied on the escalation.
There is little room for further delay on this tender.
The data on churn rates indicate a seasonal pattern.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Plural sense of "a number of" → "have demanded."

Tip: "A number of" almost always takes a plural verb in exam English.

TRUE — Nearer plural "syndicate members" → "were ready."

Tip: Trust the last noun after nor.

TRUE — Head subject "operations head" stays singular despite "along with her deputies."

Tip: Commas around the insert are a clue that it is not part of a compound subject.

TRUE — Uncountable "room" is singular, so "there is" fits.

Tip: After there is/are, uncountables take singular even when the idea feels broad.

TRUE — Formal plural "data" correctly takes "indicate."

Tip: Prefer plural agreement with data in formal business writing.
tasks.solution_overview: All five sentences are grammatically sound. Use them as clean models of a number of, neither…nor, along with, there is with an uncountable, and formal plural data.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Every member of the steering committee has cast a vote.
The number of warranty claims have doubled year on year.
Neither the franchisee nor the franchisees' lenders is contesting the clause.
There are a clear timeline attached to the milestone payments.
The CEO, together with the non-executive directors, intends to resign if the bid fails.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Every member" → singular "has cast."

Tip: The of-phrase does not pluralise every/each.

FALSE — "The number of" needs singular "has doubled."

Tip: Do not agree with "claims."

FALSE — Nearer subject "lenders" is plural: "are contesting," not "is."

Tip: Possessive markers on the nearer noun do not change its plural status.

FALSE — The real subject is singular "a clear timeline," so write "there is."

Tip: Articles and adjectives after there often hide a singular head.

TRUE — Singular CEO remains the subject; "intends" is correct.

Tip: Together with never creates a plural compound subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixed correct and incorrect lines force you to slow down on proximity after neither…nor and on singular heads after there. Name the subject aloud before you judge the verb.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of retailers was late with their stocktake returns.
Neither the broker nor the clients was notified of the surcharge.
There is several annexes missing from the draft contract.
Each of the logistics hubs have its own contingency plan.
The data from last quarter's panels show a narrower spread.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use plural "were late" after "a number of retailers."

Tip: If "their" later in the sentence feels natural, the verb is almost certainly plural.

FALSE — Nearer plural "clients" needs "were notified."

Tip: Neither…nor: last noun wins.

FALSE — Plural "annexes" requires "there are."

Tip: "Several" is a strong plural cue after there.

FALSE — "Each of" → singular "has its own contingency plan."

Tip: "Its" already signals singular; keep the verb singular too.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "show."

Tip: Match data with plural verbs in exam answers unless told otherwise.
tasks.solution_overview: Four clear agreement errors surround one correct formal-data line. Scan for the usual suspects — a number, neither…nor, there is/are, each — before you mark true.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the treasurer nor the auditors have released the working papers.
The project sponsor, along with the delivery partners, has signed the charter.
There remain two conditions precedent before drawdown.
Every one of the shortlisted vendors meets the security checklist.
The number of active SKUs are being reduced this quarter.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nearer plural "auditors" → "have released."

Tip: Read only from "nor" to the verb.

TRUE — Singular sponsor + along with… → "has signed."

Tip: Parenthetical partners do not join the subject.

TRUE — Plural "conditions" correctly takes "remain."

Tip: Invert the sentence mentally: "two conditions remain."

TRUE — "Every one" is singular → "meets."

Tip: "Every one of" still points to a single unit for agreement.

FALSE — "The number of" is singular: "is being reduced."

Tip: Passive voice does not change the number of the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Mid-difficulty items combine inserts, every one of, and passive voice. Agreement still hinges on the same subject-finding habit — do not let the construction distract you.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the exporter nor the freight forwarders was listed on the bill of lading.
A number of covenants in the facility agreement has been waived.
There is too many variables still open in the pricing model.
The chair, as well as the committee secretaries, was delayed by the vote.
The data collected overnight do not yet justify a rate cut.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Nearer plural "freight forwarders" → "were listed."

Tip: Long titles after nor still keep their plural number.

FALSE — "A number of covenants" → plural "have been waived."

Tip: The of-phrase noun is plural; "a number of" takes that plurality.

FALSE — "Too many variables" is plural → "there are."

Tip: "Many" after there almost always signals a plural verb.

TRUE — Singular "chair" governs "was delayed"; secretaries are only an as-well-as insert.

Tip: Cross out the insert and re-read.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "do not yet justify."

Tip: Past participles after data ("collected") do not make the noun singular.
tasks.solution_overview: Here the distractors sit inside longer business noun phrases. Peel the sentence to its skeleton subject before you accept or reject the verb.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Each quarterly forecast submitted by the regions goes to the CFO first.
Neither the landlord nor the tenants' solicitors have consented to the break clause.
There appears to be several gaps in the supplier due-diligence file.
The marketing lead, together with two agencies, are pitching tomorrow.
The number of unsettled trades has dropped below the risk limit.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Each quarterly forecast" → singular "goes."

Tip: Long modifiers after each do not change singularity.

TRUE — Nearer plural "solicitors" → "have consented."

Tip: Possessive "tenants'" does not make the nearer noun singular.

FALSE — Although "appears" can introduce a clause, the logical subject "several gaps" is plural; prefer "there appear to be."

Tip: In there + appear/seem, still match the notional plural subject in careful exam English.

FALSE — Singular lead + together with… → "is pitching."

Tip: Agencies after together with are not co-subjects.

TRUE — "The number of" + singular "has dropped."

Tip: Keep agreeing with number, not trades.
tasks.solution_overview: "There appears to be several" is a classic soft trap: the verb looks formal but still disagrees with a plural complement. Stay strict on number even in polished phrasing.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of regional managers is attending the strategy offsite.
Neither the insurer nor the brokers was willing to extend cover.
There is only one schedule left to finalise before listing.
Every analyst on the deal team have signed the confidentiality undertaking.
The data in the appendix contradict the oral presentation.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "A number of regional managers" → "are attending."

Tip: Replace with "several managers" to hear the plural.

FALSE — Nearer plural "brokers" → "were willing."

Tip: Do not let singular "insurer" pull the verb.

TRUE — Singular "one schedule" → "there is."

Tip: "Only one" is a reliable singular signal.

FALSE — "Every analyst" → singular "has signed."

Tip: "On the deal team" is only a locator phrase.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "contradict."

Tip: Plural verbs with data are expected in formal register.
tasks.solution_overview: Contrast the clean singular "there is only one" with the false singulars after a number of and every. Pattern recognition beats word-by-word guessing.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the buyer nor the sellers' counsel has requested an adjournment.
The finance director, along with the controllers, reviews the accruals nightly.
There are still a few outstanding confirmations from counterparties.
Each of the joint venture partners retains a board seat.
The data underlying the stress test suggest limited contagion risk.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nearer singular "counsel" → "has requested."

Tip: Counsel can be singular even when plural parties are nearby.

TRUE — Singular director governs "reviews" despite along with.

Tip: Strip the insert; "the finance director reviews" must stand alone.

TRUE — Plural "confirmations" → "there are."

Tip: "A few" marks plurality after there.

TRUE — "Each of" → singular "retains."

Tip: Partners in the of-phrase do not control the verb.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "suggest."

Tip: Participial modifiers ("underlying…") never change data's formal plurality.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are correct but denser. Treat them as benchmark sentences for counsel after neither…nor, along with, there are + a few, each of, and formal data.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of unresolved exceptions are alarming the audit committee.
Neither the sponsor nor the limited partners was invited to the closed session.
There seems to be several inconsistencies between the two ledgers.
The managing partner, as well as the associates, have approved the engagement letter.
A number of warranties in the SPA survive completion.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "The number of" → singular "is alarming."

Tip: Continuous/progressive forms still follow the head subject's number.

FALSE — Nearer plural "limited partners" → "were invited."

Tip: Long second nouns after nor are still plural when marked -s.

FALSE — Prefer "there seem to be several inconsistencies" to match the plural complement.

Tip: Seem/appear after there must still track the real subject's number in careful usage.

FALSE — Singular partner + as well as… → "has approved."

Tip: Associates after as well as are not co-subjects.

TRUE — "A number of warranties" → plural "survive."

Tip: Present simple plural has no -s: survive, not survives.
tasks.solution_overview: Four failures and one clean "a number of" success. At this level, soft connectors like seems to be are designed to hide a plural complement — always check what follows.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the retailer nor its franchisees is bound by the exclusivity clause.
Every one of the contingent liabilities has been disclosed in the notes.
There remain, after the renegotiation, three material open points.
The COO, together with the divisional heads, was accountable for the overspend.
The data released this morning confirm the earlier guidance.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Nearer plural "franchisees" → "are bound."

Tip: Corporate possessives ("its") before the nearer noun do not singularise it.

TRUE — "Every one of" → singular "has been disclosed."

Tip: Passive perfect still keeps singular agreement with every one.

TRUE — Plural "three material open points" → "remain," even with a mid-sentence insert.

Tip: Ignore the comma aside and match the postponed plural subject.

TRUE — Singular COO → "was accountable."

Tip: Together with never creates a plural subject.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "confirm."

Tip: Time adjuncts ("this morning") are irrelevant to number.
tasks.solution_overview: Inserted asides and passives raise the difficulty without changing the rules. Find the subject first; the verb will usually announce itself.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of key performance indicators was revised after the board meeting.
Neither the trustee nor the beneficiaries' advisers has objected to the distribution.
