There is, contrary to the press note, several unpaid invoices still on the ledger.
Each subsidiary that operates abroad file a local compliance certificate.
The number of customer complaints has stabilised since the refunds.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "A number of … indicators" → "were revised."

Tip: Long plural noun phrases after a number of still take plural verbs.

FALSE — Nearer plural "advisers" → "have objected."

Tip: Beneficiaries' only marks possession; advisers remain plural.

FALSE — Plural "invoices" → "there are," despite the interrupting phrase.

Tip: Cross out the contrary-to aside before choosing is/are.

FALSE — "Each subsidiary" → singular "files."

Tip: Relative clauses after each do not licence a plural verb.

TRUE — "The number of" → singular "has stabilised."

Tip: Keep contrasting the number (singular) with a number (plural).
tasks.solution_overview: Interruptions and relative clauses are the main noise here. Mentally delete them, then apply the familiar agreement tests.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the parent company nor the overseas affiliates was named in the indictment.
The treasury desk, along with the front-office traders, approve large FX tickets.
There appear to be a single bottleneck in the onboarding workflow.
Every set of consolidated accounts for the group is reviewed by external counsel.
The data on which the valuation rests are drawn from audited filings.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Nearer plural "affiliates" → "were named."

Tip: International business nouns ending in -es are still plural for agreement.

FALSE — Singular "treasury desk" + along with… → "approves."

Tip: Desk is a singular institutional subject here.

FALSE — The complement "a single bottleneck" is singular → "there appears to be."

Tip: Appear/seem after there must track a singular complement too — not only plurals.

TRUE — "Every set" is singular → "is reviewed."

Tip: "Set of accounts" is one unit; every keeps it singular.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "are drawn," even inside a which-clause sandwich.

Tip: Relative clauses around data do not convert it to singular on formal papers.
highlights: There appear to be a single
tasks.solution_overview: Top band: reverse traps such as "there appear … a single" and institutional singulars like "desk." Read for the actual head noun, not the surrounding formality.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the liquidator nor the secured creditors have accepted the revised timetable.
The general counsel, together with outside counsel, has cleared the disclosure.
There remain, for the avoidance of doubt, two covenants still in force.
Each of the framework agreements provides for stepped damages.
The data furnished by the target company support a higher multiple.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nearer plural "creditors" → "have accepted."

Tip: Secured creditors is a standard plural legal subject.

TRUE — Singular general counsel governs "has cleared."

Tip: Together with outside counsel is parenthetical only.

TRUE — Plural "two covenants" → "remain" despite the formal aside.

Tip: Legal padding between there and the subject changes nothing.

TRUE — "Each of" → singular "provides."

Tip: Framework agreements in the of-phrase stay out of the verb slot.

TRUE — Formal plural data → "support."

Tip: Past participles like "furnished" do not singularise data.
tasks.solution_overview: Five correct formal-register models. Internalise how legal inserts and dual "counsel" references still leave a single grammatical subject in charge of the verb.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of material adverse change clauses was triggered overnight.
Neither the arranger nor the other lenders in the syndicate was prepared to waive the default.
There is, when one examines the schedules carefully, more than two conflicting dates.
The audit partner, as well as the engagement team, were responsible for the opinion.
The data that the model relies on have been restated twice this year.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "A number of … clauses" → "were triggered."

Tip: Dense legal noun phrases still follow the a-number-of plural rule.

FALSE — Nearer plural "lenders" → "were prepared."

Tip: Extra modifiers after the nearer noun ("in the syndicate") do not make it singular.

FALSE — "More than two conflicting dates" is plural → "there are."

Tip: Quantity phrases greater than one take plural after there.

FALSE — Singular partner + as well as… → "was responsible."

Tip: Engagement team after as well as is not a co-subject.

TRUE — Formal plural data correctly takes "have been restated."

Tip: Prefer plural agreement with data on formal business exams unless the paper allows informal singular data.
tasks.solution_overview: Four agreement failures surround one clean formal-data line. Treat plural data as the safe exam default, and strip inserts before judging neither…nor, there is/are, and as well as.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Neither the nominee director nor the shadow directors have disclosed their interests.
The number of days sales outstanding has improved after the collections drive.
There appear to be fewer exceptions in this month's reconciliation.
Every invoice that exceeds the delegated limit requires a second signature.
The CFO, along with the independent non-executives, have tabled a dissenting note.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nearer plural "shadow directors" → "have disclosed."

Tip: Legal doublets after nor still obey proximity.

TRUE — "The number of" → singular "has improved."

Tip: KPI-style of-phrases do not pluralise the number.

TRUE — Plural "fewer exceptions" → "there appear to be."

Tip: Fewer is a plural cue; match appear accordingly.

TRUE — "Every invoice" → singular "requires."

Tip: Relative clauses after every keep the verb singular.

FALSE — Singular CFO + along with… → "has tabled."

Tip: Non-executives in the insert never join the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Close on a mixed set that recycles neither…nor, the number, there appear, every, and along with. One parenthetical plural distractor remains — strip it and the error is obvious.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Applicants must submit their CV before the closing date.
The forecast might be wrong beyond any possible doubt.
You need not attend the optional compliance briefing.
The board can must approve the merger this afternoon.
We ought to revise the cash-flow projection before publication.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must" marks a hard requirement here: applicants have no choice about the CV deadline.

Tip: For company rules and absolute obligations, "must" + bare infinitive is the clean pattern.

FALSE — "Might" only signals weak possibility, so pairing it with "beyond any possible doubt" contradicts itself.

Tip: Certainty language ("beyond doubt", "without exception") never sits comfortably with "might" or "could".

TRUE — "Need not" correctly removes obligation: the briefing is optional, so attendance is not required.

Tip: "Need not" = no obligation; "must not" = prohibition — different meanings.

FALSE — Stacking "can" and "must" is ungrammatical; English allows only one modal before the main verb.

Tip: Choose one modal that fits the meaning — ability ("can") or obligation ("must"), never both.

TRUE — "Ought to" + infinitive correctly advises a prudent revision before the numbers go live.

Tip: "Ought" always needs "to" before the base verb: "ought to revise", never "ought revise".
tasks.solution_overview: This set mixes clear obligation, weak possibility, and a double-modal trap. Read each sentence for one job only: does the modal match the certainty or duty the rest of the sentence claims?

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Staff must to complete the e-learning module by Friday.
You must not to enter the server room without a pass.
The delay may stem from overlapping shipment schedules.
They must have knew about the pricing leak earlier.
The results could confirm the hypothesis in every scenario without exception.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Must" takes a bare infinitive: "must complete", not "must to complete".

Tip: Pure modals never take "to" before the main verb.

FALSE — After "must not", use the bare infinitive: "must not enter", not "must not to enter".

Tip: Modals take a bare verb; only "ought" and "need to" / "have to" patterns bring "to".

TRUE — "May" hedges carefully: overlapping schedules are a possible cause, not a proven one.

Tip: Use "may" or "might" when evidence is incomplete and you want a cautious claim.

FALSE — Modal perfect needs a past participle: "must have known", not "must have knew".

Tip: Pattern is modal + have + past participle for deductions about the past.

FALSE — "Could" expresses possibility, so it cannot guarantee an unconditional outcome "without exception".

Tip: If the claim is absolute certainty, drop the weak modal or change the wording.
tasks.solution_overview: Four traps crowd this set: illicit "to" after "must", another after "must not", a wrong past participle in modal perfect, and a weak modal that overclaims certainty. Only the cautious "may" sentence stands.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The auditor cannot have received the draft yet.
Investors might have overlooked the footnote on contingent liabilities.
We ought revise the disclosure note before filing.
Clients may request a refund within fourteen days.
The ministry will likely reject the bid for certain and without any doubt.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot have received" is a solid modal-perfect deduction about a past event that still has no confirmation.

Tip: Negative modal perfects ("cannot have", "could not have") deny a past possibility on logical grounds.

TRUE — "Might have overlooked" correctly softens a past deduction — possible, not proven.

Tip: "Might have" + past participle = tentative past speculation.

FALSE — "Ought" requires "to": "ought to revise", not "ought revise".

Tip: Treat "ought to" as a fixed pair before the base verb.

TRUE — "May" here marks permission/possibility for a refund request within the window.

Tip: In policy language, "may" often means "are allowed to".

FALSE — "Will likely" already hedges, so "for certain and without any doubt" clashes with that hedge.

Tip: Strip either the hedge or the certainty claim — they cannot both stand.
tasks.solution_overview: Modal perfects and permission "may" appear alongside one missing "to" after "ought" and one hedge-versus-certainty clash. Check structure first, then whether the strength of the modal fits the claim.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Contractors must wear safety gear on site at all times.
The report must indicate a recovery, though we have no evidence at all.
She could have sent the invoice before the cut-off.
You need not to renew the temporary access card today.
The panel should reconsider the launch window.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must" correctly imposes a non-negotiable site rule.

Tip: Health-and-safety rules almost always take "must", not "might".

FALSE — Strong deduction "must" cannot coexist with "no evidence at all".

Tip: No evidence → use "may"/"might", not "must".

TRUE — "Could have sent" correctly frames a past possibility that remains open.

Tip: "Could have" + past participle = past possibility or missed opportunity.

FALSE — Modal "need not" takes a bare infinitive: "need not renew", not "need not to renew".

Tip: Contrast with main-verb "need to": "You need to renew" vs "You need not renew".

TRUE — "Should" appropriately advises the panel to think again about timing.

Tip: "Should" is the default for measured professional advice.
tasks.solution_overview: Obligation, deduction, and advice sit side by side. Flag any sentence where a strong modal ("must") is undercut by weak evidence, or where an extra "to" sneaks in after "need not".

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The treasury should have flagged the currency exposure sooner.
Suppliers may not deliver on Sundays under the current contract.
He must sign the non-disclosure agreement before the kick-off.
The figures might suggest a seasonal spike rather than a structural shift.
We could reduce overheads if we consolidate the two warehouses.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Should have flagged" correctly criticises a past missed duty with modal perfect.

Tip: "Should have" + past participle = past advice not followed / mild reproach.

TRUE — "May not" here denies permission under the contract — a standard legal reading.

Tip: Context decides: "may not" can mean prohibition (permission) or weak negative possibility.

TRUE — "Must sign" correctly imposes a hard pre-kick-off requirement with a bare infinitive.

Tip: Pure modals (must, should, can, may, might, could) take the bare verb — no "to".

TRUE — "Might suggest" hedges an interpretation of the figures without overclaiming.

Tip: Soft epistemic modals protect you when data admit more than one reading.

TRUE — "Could" correctly marks a feasible cost-saving option, not a guaranteed outcome.

Tip: Possibility "could" is fine when the sentence does not claim certainty.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are sound: past missed duty, contractual "may not", hard obligation, hedged interpretation, and feasible optionality. Confirm that each modal’s strength matches the claim and that forms stay clean.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The regulator might withdraw the licence with absolute certainty.
Partners ought to disclose related-party transactions promptly.
They cannot have ignored the auditor’s yellow-flag notes.
You should of updated the risk register after the incident.
Trainees need not bring their own laptops to the induction.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Might" and "absolute certainty" cancel each other out.

Tip: Match modal strength to the adverbial claim — weak modal, weak claim.

TRUE — "Ought to disclose" correctly expresses moral/professional advisability.

Tip: "Ought to" ≈ "should" in formal compliance language.

TRUE — "Cannot have ignored" is a strong past deduction: the notes were too conspicuous to miss.

Tip: "Cannot have" + past participle denies a past scenario as logically untenable.

FALSE — The spoken slip "should of" is wrong in writing; you need "should have updated".

Tip: Always write "have", never "of", after modal perfects.

TRUE — "Need not bring" correctly lifts the obligation to bring a laptop.

Tip: Optional extras are a natural home for "need not".
tasks.solution_overview: Two errors mix strength mismatch ("might" + certainty) and the common "should of" spelling trap. The other three show clean advisability, strong past denial, and absence of obligation.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The CFO must have approved the write-off before the books closed.
Customers could claim a rebate if the shipment arrives damaged.
We may have to renegotiate the covenant after the downgrade.
She can must present the pitch deck to the investment committee.
Directors should not ignore material related-party loans.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must have approved" is a strong deduction that the write-off needed prior sign-off.

Tip: "Must have" = confident inference about the past, not a future obligation.

TRUE — "Could claim" correctly opens a conditional possibility under the damage clause.

Tip: "Could" often pairs with "if" for contingent options.

TRUE — "May have to" combines possibility with external necessity — a natural hedge about renegotiation.

Tip: "Have to" (not a pure modal) can follow "may"/"might" when necessity itself is uncertain.

FALSE — "Can must" stacks two modals illegally.

Tip: Pick ability or obligation — one modal, one meaning.

TRUE — "Should not ignore" correctly advises against overlooking material loans.

Tip: "Should not" = strong advice against an action, not a legal ban (that would be "must not").
tasks.solution_overview: Four sentences use modals cleanly for deduction, optionality, hedged necessity, and advice. Only the double modal is broken — spot it by asking whether two auxiliaries sit before one main verb.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The sample is tiny, so conclusions must be drawn with caution.
He might have been interviewing candidates all morning.
You mustn’t have parked in the visitor bay without a permit.
We ought to have circulated the minutes sooner.
The bid will win the tender for certain if it might undercut every rival.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must" here marks a methodological obligation: caution is required, not optional.

Tip: "Must" can express obligation or strong deduction — context tells you which.

TRUE — "Might have been interviewing" correctly hedges a continuous past speculation.

Tip: Modal + have been + -ing covers uncertain ongoing past activity.

FALSE — "Mustn’t have parked" is the wrong shape for a present prohibition; use "must not park".

Tip: Prohibition is "must not" + bare infinitive; "mustn’t have" is rare and usually a deduction, not a rule.

TRUE — "Ought to have circulated" correctly marks a past duty that was missed.

Tip: "Ought to have" + past participle ≈ "should have" for past advisability.

FALSE — Certainty ("for certain") cannot rest on a clause headed by weak "might".

Tip: If the outcome is framed as certain, the supporting clause needs a stronger modal or no modal hedge.
tasks.solution_overview: Distinguish obligation, past speculation, and past missed duty from misused prohibition and certainty built on "might". Progressive modal perfects are allowed when the time frame is continuous.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The insurer may well reject a claim lodged after the deadline.
Staff needn’t have attended the cancelled workshop.
The forecast could will improve once rates stabilise.
Managers should distinguish obligation from mere possibility in the memo.
They mustn’t disclose client data to third parties.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "May well" is an idiomatic hedge meaning "is quite likely to" — fine for a late claim.

Tip: "May well" strengthens possibility without claiming certainty.

TRUE — "Needn’t have attended" correctly says attendance turned out unnecessary (workshop cancelled).

Tip: "Needn’t have" + past participle = past action that was unnecessary in hindsight.

FALSE — "Could will" illegally stacks two modals.

Tip: Future possibility is "could improve" or "will improve", never both.

TRUE — "Should" correctly frames the advice to keep obligation and possibility distinct in wording.

Tip: Meta-advice about modal choice still uses a normal advisory "should".

TRUE — "Mustn’t disclose" is a clear prohibition on sharing client data.

Tip: Confidentiality rules usually take "must not" / "mustn’t".
tasks.solution_overview: Idiomatic "may well" and past "needn’t have" are legitimate; the broken item is the double modal "could will". Treat confidentiality language as prohibition, not soft advice.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The syndicate cannot have underpriced the issue by that margin.
You ought not to ignore the whistle-blower’s email.
She may has submitted the expense claim already.
Borrowers should repay the facility if covenants are breached.
The downturn might deepen, though nothing is certain yet.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot have underpriced" strongly rules out a past pricing error of that size.

Tip: Use "cannot have" when evidence makes the past scenario unreasonable.

TRUE — "Ought not to ignore" correctly advises against dismissing the email.

Tip: Negative "ought" keeps "to": "ought not to" + bare infinitive.

FALSE — After "may", use the bare infinitive: "may have submitted", not "may has submitted".

Tip: Modal perfect is always modal + have (not has/had) + past participle.

TRUE — "Should repay" correctly marks the expected remedial action after a breach.

Tip: Covenant language often prefers "should"/"must" over "might".

TRUE — "Might deepen" hedges a future risk while the second clause keeps certainty off the table.

Tip: Explicit uncertainty markers ("nothing is certain") pair cleanly with "might".
tasks.solution_overview: One conjugation slip ("may has") breaks an otherwise tidy set. Check that every modal perfect uses invariant "have", and that negative "ought not to" keeps its "to".

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The committee must decide today; delay is not an option.
He could of renegotiated the lease before renewal.
We may not have captured every contingent liability in the note.
Analysts should have spotted the inventory build-up earlier.
The pilot scheme might succeed beyond all doubt if funding holds.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must decide" plus "delay is not an option" consistently mark hard obligation.

Tip: When the rest of the sentence bans alternatives, "must" is the matching modal.

FALSE — Write "could have renegotiated", never "could of".

Tip: "Of" after a modal is always a spelling error for "have".

TRUE — "May not have captured" cautiously admits a possible gap in the disclosure.

Tip: Negative modal perfects hedge incomplete past work without confessing certainty of failure.

TRUE — "Should have spotted" criticises a past analytical miss.

Tip: Use this shape for retrospective professional standards that were not met.

FALSE — "Might" cannot support "beyond all doubt".

Tip: Absolute success claims need stronger wording than a weak epistemic modal.
tasks.solution_overview: Obligation and retrospective criticism are fine; the traps are "could of" and a weak modal carrying an absolute success claim. Align modal strength with any certainty phrase in the same sentence.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Vendors need not resubmit paperwork already on file.
The board shall must vote before markets open.
She might not have seen the revised term sheet.
We should to escalate any suspected fraud immediately.
The warehouse could have been sealed overnight after the audit.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Need not resubmit" correctly waives a redundant filing step.

Tip: Process guides often use "need not" for steps that are already covered.

FALSE — "Shall must" stacks two obligation markers illegally.

Tip: Formal "shall" already expresses obligation; do not add "must".

TRUE — "Might not have seen" softens a past negative deduction.

Tip: Keep "have" + past participle after "might not".

FALSE — "Should" takes a bare infinitive: "should escalate", not "should to escalate".

Tip: Extra "to" after "should"/"must"/"can" is a frequent L2 slip.

TRUE — "Could have been sealed" correctly frames a past passive possibility.

Tip: Modal + have been + past participle covers uncertain past passives.
tasks.solution_overview: Look for stacked obligation ("shall must") and an illicit "to" after "should". Absence of obligation, soft past denial, and passive modal perfects are all legitimate here.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The underwriter must have been reviewing the dossier when the call came in.
You may enter the trading floor only after clearing compliance.
They should have been told about the lock-up period in advance.
The model could predict returns with total certainty in every market.
We needn’t renew the redundant software licence this quarter.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must have been reviewing" is a confident deduction about an ongoing past activity.

Tip: Progressive modal perfect = strong inference about what was happening at a past moment.

TRUE — "May enter" grants conditional permission after compliance clearance.

Tip: Access policies often encode permission with "may".

TRUE — "Should have been told" correctly marks a past passive duty that was missed.

Tip: Modal + have been + past participle works for past passive obligations too.

FALSE — "Could" cannot deliver "total certainty in every market".

Tip: Strip the absolute phrase or upgrade the verb — weak possibility ≠ universal certainty.

TRUE — "Needn’t renew" correctly drops the obligation to keep a redundant licence.

Tip: Cost-cutting memos are a natural setting for "need not" / "needn’t".
tasks.solution_overview: Progressive and passive modal perfects appear alongside permission and waived obligation. Only the overclaiming "could … with total certainty" fails the certainty-versus-possibility test.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The subsidiary cannot have filed accounts that omit the intra-group loan.
Advisers ought to have warned the client about currency risk.
He must not have access the vault after hours without two keys.
The tender might attract more bids than last year’s round.
Employees should have completed onboarding before their first client call.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot have filed" strongly rejects the idea that such an omission slipped through.

Tip: Use this when documentation rules make the past scenario implausible.

TRUE — "Ought to have warned" marks a past professional duty that was not met.

Tip: "Ought to have" = formal past advisability parallel to "should have".

FALSE — Word order/form break: prohibition needs "must not access", not "must not have access" as a bare rule statement.

Tip: For present rules, prefer "must not" + bare infinitive; reserve "must not have" for past deductions.

TRUE — "Might attract" hedges a future turnout comparison without overpromising.

Tip: Comparative forecasts are a classic home for "might"/"may".

TRUE — "Should have completed" states a past expectation that onboarding precede client work.

Tip: Sequencing rules often surface as "should have" + past participle by the relevant deadline.
tasks.solution_overview: Past deduction and past advisability are clean. The broken sentence muddles prohibition with a modal-perfect shape — decide first whether you are stating a rule or inferring about the past.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The desk may have been mispricing the option all week.
You mustn’t to override the four-eye check on payments.
Partners should not have signed without reading the side letter.
The bond could repay early under the call schedule.
We might must revise the guidance after the profit warning.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "May have been mispricing" hedges a continuous past operational error.

Tip: Progressive modal perfect softens blame while still naming a possible ongoing fault.

FALSE — "Mustn’t to override" inserts an illegal "to" after the modal.

Tip: Prohibition is "mustn’t override" — bare infinitive only.

TRUE — "Should not have signed" criticises a past decision that breached good practice.

Tip: Negative "should not have" = past action that was inadvisable.

TRUE — "Could repay" correctly marks a contractual early-repayment option.

Tip: In finance docs, "could" often tracks optionality rather than prediction.

FALSE — "Might must" stacks conflicting modals.

Tip: Hedge necessity with "might have to revise", not "might must".
tasks.solution_overview: Two sentences fail on form: an extra "to" after "mustn’t" and the double modal "might must". The others correctly hedge past mispricing, criticise a past signature, and mark contractual optionality.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The trustee must distribute income in line with the deed.
She could not have known about the insider tip at that stage.
We ought have sought counsel before announcing the bid.
Clients may well have underestimated the onboarding lead time.
The swap should hedge interest-rate risk if structured properly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must distribute" correctly encodes a fiduciary obligation under the deed.

Tip: Trust and mandate language almost always prefers "must" for core duties.

TRUE — "Could not have known" denies past knowledge on timing grounds.

Tip: "Could not have" + past participle = past impossibility of awareness/action.

FALSE — Missing "to": "ought to have sought", not "ought have sought".

Tip: Keep the full chain: ought + to + have + past participle.

TRUE — "May well have underestimated" idiomatically strengthens a past hedge.

Tip: "May well have" ≈ "quite possibly did" without claiming proof.

TRUE — "Should hedge" states the expected function of a properly structured swap.

Tip: Here "should" is predictive/expected outcome, not moral advice.
tasks.solution_overview: Fiduciary obligation, past impossibility, and idiomatic "may well have" are sound. Only "ought have" fails — restore the mandatory "to" before "have".

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The syndicate mustn’t have priced the tranche with no book at all — that would be reckless beyond belief, yet the tape shows exactly that outcome.
You need not have paid the expedited fee; standard clearing would have sufficed.
They might have been being briefed when the leak broke.
The covenant could not of been waived without lender consent.
Directors ought not have deferred the solvency review another quarter.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The sentence tries to force "mustn’t have" as a past prohibition narrative while also asserting the reckless outcome happened; the modal logic collapses into incoherence.

Tip: Use "must not" for rules, "must have" for deductions — don’t blend prohibition and past certainty in one muddled claim.

TRUE — "Need not have paid" correctly says the expedited fee was unnecessary in hindsight.

Tip: Past unnecessary action = "need not have" / "needn’t have" + past participle.

TRUE — "Might have been being briefed" is rare but grammatical for tentative past progressive passive speculation.

Tip: Awkward stacking is allowed if each piece (might + have been + being + past participle) earns its place.

FALSE — "Could not of been" must be "could not have been".

Tip: Never write "of" for "have" in modal perfects, active or passive.

FALSE — "Ought not have" misses "to": write "ought not to have deferred".

Tip: Negative past "ought" always keeps "to" before "have".
tasks.solution_overview: Hard mode: past unnecessary action is fine, and even a heavy progressive-passive speculation can stand. Failures come from muddled prohibition-plus-deduction logic, "of" for "have", and a missing "to" after "ought not".

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The compliance officer cannot but have noticed the repeated overrides.
We should have had the valuations independently verified before closing.
She may to have understated the contingent tax exposure.
Borrowers mustn’t have drawn the facility once the default notice was live — and the ledger proves they did not.
The broker might well have front-run the client order.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot but have noticed" is a formal idiom meaning "must inevitably have noticed".

Tip: "Cannot but" + bare infinitive / perfect is literary but grammatical for inevitability.

TRUE — "Should have had … verified" correctly frames a past double-duty expectation (causative have).

Tip: Modal perfect can wrap causative "have + object + past participle".

FALSE — "May to have" inserts an illegal "to" after the modal.

Tip: Pattern is "may have understated", never "may to have".

TRUE — Here "mustn’t have drawn" works as a past prohibition reading supported by evidence that the draw did not occur.

Tip: Context and corroboration matter: past "must not have" can deny a past action that rules forbade.

TRUE — "Might well have front-run" idiomatically strengthens a serious past suspicion.

Tip: "Might well have" = "it is quite possible that … did".
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced idioms ("cannot but", "might well have") and causative modal perfects are acceptable. Reject only the stray "to" after "may". Read past "mustn’t have" carefully against the evidence clause.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rating agency must have been about to downgrade when the injection was announced.
You needn’t to have retained both counsel and a separate disclosure adviser.
They could have been going to refinance before rates jumped.
The prospectus should not of omitted the going-concern warning.
We may as well have published the unredacted annex for all the good the cuts did.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must have been about to downgrade" correctly deduces an imminent past plan interrupted by news.

Tip: "Be about to" can sit inside a modal perfect for near-future-in-the-past deductions.

FALSE — Drop the "to": "needn’t have retained", not "needn’t to have retained".

Tip: Modal "need not/needn’t" never takes "to" before the verb chain.

TRUE — "Could have been going to refinance" hedges a past intention that never completed.

Tip: "Be going to" can nest under modal perfects for aborted plans.

FALSE — "Should not of omitted" must be "should not have omitted".

Tip: Same rule every time: "have", never "of".

TRUE — "May as well have published" idiomatically means the redaction achieved nothing useful.

Tip: "May as well have" + past participle = ironic "it would have made little difference".
tasks.solution_overview: Nested near-future and "be going to" inside modal perfects are advanced but valid. Failures are form-only: an extra "to" after "needn’t" and another "of" for "have". The ironic "may as well have" idiom is fine.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The auditors cannot have been other than sceptical of the revenue recognition.
She should must escalate any sanctions hit to the committee the same day.
We ought to have been updating the sanctions list continuously, not quarterly.
He mightn’t have realised the payment routed through a blocked intermediary.
The firm need not have to maintain two parallel reporting systems after the merger.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot have been other than sceptical" is a formal double negation meaning they must have been sceptical.

Tip: "Cannot have been other than …" = strong positive deduction dressed in formal negation.

FALSE — "Should must" stacks two obligation modals.

Tip: Use "should escalate" or "must escalate" — never both.

TRUE — "Ought to have been updating" correctly criticises a past continuous practice that fell short.

Tip: Progressive past advisability: ought to + have been + -ing.

TRUE — "Mightn’t have realised" softens a past negative deduction about awareness.

Tip: Contracted "mightn’t have" is acceptable in less formal business prose.

FALSE — "Need not have to maintain" double-marks absence of obligation; write "need not maintain" or "do not have to maintain".

Tip: Pick one no-obligation marker — "need not" or "have to" (negated), not both stacked.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal double-negative deduction and progressive "ought to have been" are legitimate advanced shapes. Reject stacked obligation ("should must") and the redundant "need not have to" pairing — one marker of waived duty is enough.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The regulator fined the firm. → The firm was fined by the regulator.
The quarterly results were announced yesterday. → The CFO announced the quarterly results yesterday, and we know that for certain.
Several discrepancies were identified by the auditors.
The photograph was altered before publication. → The photograph altered itself before publication.
The board approved the restructuring plan. → The restructuring plan was approved by the board.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Object becomes subject, past simple becomes was + past participle, and the original agent stays in a by-phrase. Meaning is unchanged.

Tip: Keep the agent only when the active sentence actually names one.

FALSE — The passive names no agent, so the rewrite invents both a speaker and certainty. A fair active would not claim you know who.

Tip: Agentless passives must stay agentless unless the source names the doer.

TRUE — Clear be + past participle with an explicit agent: were identified by the auditors.

Tip: Plural subjects take were, not was, in past passive.

FALSE — Photographs do not alter themselves; the rewrite invents a reflexive agent and drops the implied human editor.

Tip: Never turn a missing agent into the patient acting on itself.

TRUE — Clean active→passive: approved → was approved, agent retained as by the board.

Tip: Match tense: past simple active → past simple passive.
tasks.solution_overview: Treat each arrow as a meaning check, not a creative rewrite. Ask whether the second sentence keeps the same tense, the same participants, and the same certainty. If the first side hides the doer, the second side must not invent one.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The contract was signed last Friday.
Mistakes were made during the compliance review. → The review made mistakes deliberately.
Legal counsel drafted the non-disclosure agreement. → The non-disclosure agreement was drafted by legal counsel.
The merger was announced yesterday. → Someone announced the merger yesterday, and we know exactly who.
The budget proposal been approved by finance last week.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correct past passive focusing on the contract; no agent is required.

Tip: Agentless passive is fine when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

FALSE — Mistakes were made does not say the review caused them on purpose. The rewrite adds agency and intent that were never stated.

Tip: Do not smuggle deliberately into a neutral passive.

TRUE — Meaning-preserving transformation with agent kept: was drafted by legal counsel.

Tip: Watch participle form: draft → drafted.

FALSE — Knowing exactly who fabricates information the passive never supplied.

Tip: Someone… and we know exactly who is almost always a fake-agent trap.

FALSE — Missing was/has: need was approved or has been approved, not bare been approved.

Tip: Passive always needs a form of be before the participle.
tasks.solution_overview: Start with form: is there a proper be + past participle? Then check meaning: any by-phrase or active rewrite must come from words already on the page, not from guesswork about who did it or why.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Engineers designed the prototype. → The prototype was designed by engineers.
The policy was introduced in 2020.
Customer complaints are handled by the support desk.
The invoice paid by accounts payable yesterday.
The committee rejected the bid. → The bid was rejected by the committee.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Active object becomes passive subject; designed → was designed; agent retained.

Tip: Keep subject–verb number: the prototype was, not were.

TRUE — Grammatical agentless past passive stating when the policy appeared.

Tip: Time phrases like in 2020 sit naturally with past passive.

TRUE — Present simple passive with a clear agent: are handled by…

Tip: Habitual processes often use present passive in business English.

FALSE — Needs was paid (or has been paid). A lone past participle is not a finite passive clause.

Tip: If you can ask Was it paid?, you still need the was in the sentence.

TRUE — Rejected → was rejected; committee stays as by-agent.

Tip: Match the original tense when you flip voice.
highlights: are handled by the support desk
tasks.solution_overview: Most items are form checks: past or present be + participle, with or without by. Spot the line that drops the auxiliary entirely — that is not a complete passive clause.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The forecast was published online. → The forecasting model published itself online.
No conclusions can be drawn from this dataset. → This dataset prevents anyone from drawing conclusions deliberately.
The press release was issued by the communications team. → We know the CEO personally issued the press release.
The warehouse was damaged during the storm. → The storm damaged the warehouse.
The applicants were notify of the delay on Monday.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Reflexive rewrite is nonsense; a model does not publish itself.

Tip: Patient ≠ agent; do not force the subject to do the action to itself.

FALSE — Modal passive can be drawn is neutral. The rewrite invents prevention and intent.

Tip: Modal passives must keep the same modality and force.

FALSE — by the communications team does not entail that the CEO did it personally.

Tip: Never upgrade a named agent into a different, more specific one.

TRUE — during the storm supplies the cause; The storm damaged the warehouse keeps that cause without inventing a human doer.

Tip: Event/cause subjects are allowed when the passive already situates the damage in that event.

FALSE — Wrong form: need were notified, not were notify.

Tip: After be, use the past participle, never the base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Four traps invent agents, intent, or wrong verb forms; only one pair keeps the same event. When you reverse passive→active, use only participants the original allows.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The shipment is being tracked by logistics.
HR has shortlisted three candidates. → Three candidates have been shortlisted by HR.
The minutes will be circulated after the meeting.
The supplier must be paid before the end of the month.
The archives were digitised by an external contractor.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present continuous passive: is being + past participle, agent retained.

Tip: Continuous passive needs being between be and the participle.

TRUE — Present perfect active → present perfect passive: have been shortlisted by HR.

Tip: Perfect passive = have/has been + past participle.

TRUE — Future passive with will be + past participle; agent optional.

Tip: will be circulated, not will circulated.

TRUE — Modal passive: must be paid. Obligation sits on the payment, not on a named payer.

Tip: Modal + be + PP is the standard obligation passive.

TRUE — Past passive with agent: were digitised by an external contractor.

Tip: British spelling digitised is fine in this bank.
highlights: were digitised by an external contractor
tasks.solution_overview: All five are well-formed passives across continuous, perfect, future, and modal patterns. Use them as clean templates: be (in the right tense) + past participle, then add by only when the agent is known.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The audit findings are still being discussed. → We know precisely which partner is discussing them.
The client sent us the revised terms. → We were sent the revised terms by the client.
The server crashed overnight. → The server was crashed overnight by itself intentionally.
New safety guidelines have been issued by the regulator.
The brochure design by marketing last quarter.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — are still being discussed hides the agent; claiming we know precisely which partner invents certainty.

Tip: Progressive agentless passives especially invite fake-agent traps.

TRUE — Double-object active allows We were sent the revised terms by the client (indirect object as subject).

Tip: With give/send/offer, either object can become the passive subject.

FALSE — Intransitive crash does not take this agentive passive, and by itself intentionally adds nonsense intent.

Tip: Many intransitive events resist a clean be + PP + by-agent rewrite.

TRUE — Present perfect passive with agent: have been issued by the regulator.

Tip: Guidelines (plural) → have been, not has been.

FALSE — Incomplete: needs was designed / were designed, not a bare design by…

Tip: by alone does not create a passive; you still need be + participle.
highlights: have been issued by the regulator
tasks.solution_overview: Watch three failure modes: inventing a discussant, forcing an intransitive into a reflexive intentional passive, and dropping be. The good lines keep agents that were already named.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board is considering the offer. → The offer is being considered by the board.
All visitors must show identification. → Identification must be shown by all visitors.
The error was occurred during overnight processing.
Management postponed the launch. → The launch was postponed by management.
The survey responses are analysed every Friday by the research team.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present continuous active → is being considered; agent retained.

Tip: Continuous passive = am/is/are being + PP.

TRUE — Modal obligation flips cleanly: must be shown by all visitors.

Tip: Keep must; do not weaken it to can or might.

FALSE — Occur is intransitive; was occurred is ungrammatical. Prefer The error occurred… or The error was detected…

Tip: Intransitives rarely form a true passive.

TRUE — Postponed → was postponed by management; meaning preserved.

Tip: Regular participle postponed matches the active verb.

TRUE — Present habitual passive with agent: are analysed by the research team.

Tip: British analysed is acceptable here.
highlights: is being considered by the board
must be shown by all visitors
tasks.solution_overview: Four transformations or stand-alone passives are sound. The odd one out forces an intransitive verb into was + past participle — a classic exam trap.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The dividend will be paid on 15 March.
IT disabled the old accounts. → The old accounts were disabled by IT.
The complaint has been escalate to senior management.
The keynote was delivered by an outside speaker.
Procurement awarded the tender to a local firm. → The tender was awarded to a local firm by procurement.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Future passive will be paid; date adverbial is fine.

Tip: will be + PP, never will + PP alone.

TRUE — Past active → past passive with agent: were disabled by IT.

Tip: Plural accounts → were, not was.

FALSE — Wrong participle form: has been escalated, not escalate.

Tip: Perfect passive = has/have been + past participle.

TRUE — Past passive with agent retained.

Tip: Delivered is the correct participle of deliver.

TRUE — Complex object pattern preserved: tender becomes subject; to a local firm stays; by procurement names the agent.

Tip: Keep prepositional complements when you flip voice.
highlights: was delivered by an outside speaker
was awarded to a local firm by procurement
tasks.solution_overview: Scan for the broken perfect passive (been + base verb). Everything else either is already a good passive or flips active→passive without changing who did what to whom.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The leak was confirmed this morning. → The communications director confirmed the leak this morning, so we know the speaker.
Staff bonuses are going to be reviewed next quarter.
The package arrived damaged. → The package was arrived damaged by the courier deliberately.
Nothing further can be done until the figures arrive. → Finance is refusing to do anything further on purpose.
The guidelines were update last night by compliance.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — was confirmed does not name the communications director; the rewrite fabricates the speaker.

Tip: so we know the speaker is a giveaway fake-agent claim.

TRUE — Going-to future passive: are going to be reviewed.

Tip: Insert be before the participle in going-to passives.

FALSE — Arrive is intransitive; was arrived is wrong, and deliberately invents intent.

Tip: Prefer The package arrived damaged or The package was damaged in transit.

FALSE — Neutral modal passive becomes an accusation of deliberate refusal — meaning not preserved.

Tip: can be done ≠ is refusing… on purpose.

FALSE — Need were updated, not were update.

Tip: Base verb after be is never enough for a passive.
tasks.solution_overview: Only one sentence is a clean future passive. The others either invent speakers and motives or break form with intransitive or base-verb passives.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The negotiators had already finalised the wording. → The wording had already been finalised by the negotiators.
Access to the portal is restricted to authorised staff.
The samples are currently test by the laboratory.
Our partners invited us to the briefing. → We were invited to the briefing by our partners.
The defective batch was withdrawn from sale immediately.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past perfect active → past perfect passive: had been finalised by the negotiators.

Tip: Perfect passive stacks been after had/has/have.

TRUE — Present passive stating a standing rule; agent optional.

Tip: is restricted to… keeps the limitation phrase.

FALSE — Need are currently being tested (or are currently tested), not are currently test.

Tip: Progressive sense wants being + PP.

TRUE — Invite allows We were invited… by our partners.

Tip: Keep the to-phrase when the original has one.

TRUE — Agentless past passive focusing on the product action.

Tip: Withdrawn is the correct irregular participle of withdraw.
tasks.solution_overview: Check the perfect and invitation passives against the originals, then catch the laboratory line that uses a base verb where a participle (and often being) belongs.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The results were announced by the process itself intentionally.
The CFO will present the outlook on Tuesday. → The outlook will be presented by the CFO on Tuesday.
Confidential files should not be left on shared drives.
The vacancy was filled last month. → We know exactly which manager filled the vacancy.
The translation is being check by a native speaker.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A process cannot intentionally announce results; agent and intent are both wrong.

Tip: by… itself intentionally is almost always false.

TRUE — Future active → will be presented by the CFO; time phrase kept.

Tip: Move the object to subject position and keep will be.

TRUE — Modal passive prohibition: should not be left…

Tip: Negation sits with the modal: should not be + PP.

FALSE — Agentless was filled does not identify the manager.

Tip: Exactly which… claims knowledge the passive never gave.

FALSE — Need is being checked, not is being check.

Tip: After being, always use a past participle.
highlights: will be presented by the CFO
tasks.solution_overview: Reject intentional process-agents and invented managers. Accept the future and modal passives that keep the original force, and fix continuous passives that use a base verb after being.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The insurance claim is being processed this week.
Security locked the building at midnight. → The building was locked at midnight by security.
Further details can be found in the appendix.
The internship offers have been accepted by both candidates.
The agenda was circulated to all attendees before noon.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present continuous passive without agent; focus on the claim.

Tip: is being processed marks an action in progress.

TRUE — Meaning-preserving past passive with agent at the end.

Tip: Time adverbial can stay before or after the by-phrase.

TRUE — Modal passive can be found; typical of formal documents.

Tip: Do not invent who finds the details.

TRUE — Present perfect passive, plural agreement: have been accepted.

Tip: Both candidates stays as by-agent.

TRUE — Past passive with recipient phrase to all attendees.

Tip: Keep to-phrases when they carry essential meaning.
highlights: was locked at midnight by security
can be found in the appendix
have been accepted by both candidates
tasks.solution_overview: A clean set of models: continuous, past with agent, modal, perfect, and recipient phrases. Use them as reference shapes when harder traps appear later.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It is said that the takeover talks collapsed overnight.
They gave the analysts revised guidance. → Revised guidance was given to the analysts.
The database crashed. → The database was crashed by the update script on purpose.
A decision has yet to be reached on the relocation.
The prototype will have been tested before the trade fair opens.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Impersonal It is said that… is a standard reporting passive; no agent needed.

Tip: It is said/believed/expected that… hedges without naming a speaker.

TRUE — Direct object as subject: Revised guidance was given to the analysts. Dropping vague they is allowed.

Tip: Omitting a vague they is fine; inventing a named VIP is not.

FALSE — Adds an agent and on purpose; the original intransitive crash states an event, not intentional causation.

Tip: Do not turn system failures into deliberate sabotage without evidence in the source.

TRUE — Perfect passive inside yet to be reached — formal and correct.

Tip: has yet to be + PP is a common business hedge.

TRUE — Future perfect passive: will have been tested before…

Tip: Future perfect passive = will have been + PP.
tasks.solution_overview: Impersonal reporting passives and future perfect passives are fair game. The crash rewrite fails because it invents both a culprit and intent the original never stated.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The figures were being finalised when the system froze. → We know the junior analyst was finalising them alone.
Nobody can be blamed for the weather delay. → The operations lead is to blame for the weather delay.
The manuscript got published without peer review. → The manuscript published without peer review by itself.
Concerns have been raised about supplier concentration.
The tokens are expired by the security protocol every night intentionally by the tokens themselves.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — were being finalised does not identify a junior analyst working alone.

Tip: Continuous passives still hide agents unless a by-phrase appears.

FALSE — Nobody can be blamed contradicts naming the operations lead as blameworthy.

Tip: Respect negation: nobody ≠ a specific person.

FALSE — Even if get-passive is colloquially fine, by itself erases any external publisher and invents self-publication.

Tip: Get-passive still implies an external process, not the patient acting alone.

TRUE — Present perfect passive Concerns have been raised… — standard and agentless.

Tip: Raising concerns often stays agentless in formal English.

FALSE — Garbled agent stack: protocol vs tokens themselves, plus intentionally — form and meaning both fail.

Tip: One clear by-agent is enough; reflexive intentional stacks are almost always wrong.
tasks.solution_overview: Four lines smuggle in named people, blame, or reflexive agents. Only the concerns sentence keeps a sober agentless perfect passive.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The embargos were lifted last week. → Last week saw the embargos lift themselves.
Stakeholders expect a decision by Friday. → A decision is expected by Friday.
The wiring diagram should have been attached to the handover pack.
Finance owns the risk register. → The risk register is owned by finance.
The samples were being store in the cold room overnight.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Reflexive lift themselves is absurd; keep were lifted or name a real authority.

Tip: Embargoes do not act on themselves.

TRUE — Expect → is expected; by Friday is a deadline, not a fake human agent.

Tip: by + time is not a by-agent; do not confuse the two.

TRUE — Modal perfect passive: should have been attached.

Tip: should have been + PP for past criticism or missed duty.

TRUE — Own passivises here in business English: is owned by finance.

Tip: Ownership passives are common in organisational descriptions.

FALSE — Need were being stored, not were being store.

Tip: being + past participle, never being + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate by-time from by-agent, accept modal perfect and ownership passives, and reject reflexive nonsense plus base verbs after being.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The shortlist will be announced tomorrow. → Tomorrow the panel chair will announce the shortlist, and that is certain.
Two seats have been reserved for the auditors.
The factory produces these components in Poland. → These components are produced in Poland.
The breach was reported anonymously. → A named executive reported the breach to take revenge.
The forms need signing before payroll runs. → The forms need to be signed before payroll runs.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — will be announced does not identify the panel chair or make that identity certain.

Tip: Certainty claims about a hidden agent fail the meaning test.

TRUE — Present perfect passive with a clear beneficiary for-phrase.

Tip: have been reserved, not has, with plural seats.

TRUE — Dropping the generic factory subject is allowed when place remains; are produced in Poland keeps the core claim without inventing a new person.

Tip: Omitting a generic producer is fine; inventing a CEO is not.

FALSE — Anonymously blocks naming an executive and inventing revenge motive.

Tip: Anonymous passives forbid named-agent actives.

TRUE — need signing and need to be signed are both acceptable obligation passives here; meaning aligns.

Tip: need signing ≈ need to be signed in formal British usage.
tasks.solution_overview: Dropping a generic producer is fine; naming a chair, executive, or revenge motive is not. Also accept the need to be signed paraphrase of need signing.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had the warning been heeded, the outage might have been avoided.
They are repairing the line now. → The line is repaired now by them as we speak.
The ambassador was shown the prototype before the press event.
It was agreed that pricing would remain unchanged for six months.
The datasets cannot be shared externally without approval.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past perfect passive in a conditional: had been heeded; might have been avoided is modal perfect passive.

Tip: Stacked passives in conditionals still need been + PP each time.

FALSE — Progressive active are repairing needs is being repaired, not is repaired, for an action in progress.

Tip: as we speak demands continuous passive, not simple passive.

TRUE — Double-object passive: The ambassador was shown the prototype…

Tip: Show/give/offer commonly allow recipient as passive subject.

TRUE — Impersonal It was agreed that… reports a decision without naming voters.

Tip: Do not invent which director agreed.

TRUE — Modal passive prohibition cannot be shared… without approval.

Tip: Keep the without-phrase; it is part of the meaning.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced shapes: conditional perfect passives, impersonal it-passives, and recipient subjects. The weak line mismatches progressive meaning with a simple passive.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The motion was passed unanimously. → Every board member who opposed it still somehow passed it deliberately.
Little progress has been made on the integration timeline. → The PMO lead personally stalled the integration timeline on purpose.
The samples were allowed to cool before testing. → The samples allowed themselves to cool before testing.
The regional HQ based in Singapore oversees APAC sales. → APAC sales are overseen by the regional HQ based in Singapore.
The password must changed every ninety days.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Unanimously already states the outcome; inventing opposing members who deliberately passed it contradicts the source.

Tip: Do not rewrite vote passives into paradoxical agent stories.

FALSE — Agentless little progress has been made does not name a PMO lead or allege purposeful stalling.

Tip: Progress passives especially attract fake-blame rewrites.

FALSE — were allowed to cool implies an external controller; allowed themselves invents reflexive agency.

Tip: Allow-passive ≠ self-action.

TRUE — Oversees → are overseen by; the same HQ remains the agent, with the Singapore detail kept.

Tip: Carry modifiers of the agent into the by-phrase when they identify which HQ.

FALSE — Missing be: must be changed, not must changed.

Tip: Modal passives always need be before the participle.
highlights: are overseen by the regional HQ
tasks.solution_overview: Only the HQ oversight pair keeps the same agent under a clean voice flip. The rest invent blame, reflexive cool-downs, or drop be after a modal.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been briefed by counsel, the directors approved the disclosure. → The directors were briefed by counsel and then approved the disclosure.
The invoices are to be settled within fourteen days.
What remains to be decided is the venue. → Someone has already decided the venue, and we know who.
The rare manuscript was being carefully restored when funding paused.
Under no circumstances should customer data be exported without encryption.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Perfect passive participle Having been briefed by counsel unpacks fairly into were briefed by counsel without inventing a new agent.

Tip: Participial passives still obey the no-fake-agent rule.

TRUE — be to + passive: are to be settled marks scheduled obligation.

Tip: are to be + PP is formal diary-style passive.

FALSE — remains to be decided means the venue is still open; claiming it is already decided by a known person reverses the meaning.

Tip: to be decided signals incompleteness, not a hidden finished decision.

TRUE — Past continuous passive was being carefully restored; agent optional.

Tip: Adverbs can sit between being and the participle.

TRUE — Modal passive after inversion still needs be: should… be exported.

Tip: Inversion does not remove the passive be.
tasks.solution_overview: Four advanced passives hold: participial, be-to, continuous, and inverted modal. The venue line fails because it turns an undecided state into a fabricated completed act.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No conclusions can be drawn from this data. → This data prevents anyone from drawing conclusions deliberately.
The interim report is expected to be published before the AGM.
They had the servers replaced overnight. → The servers were replaced overnight.
It is believed the shortfall was caused by a booking error. → We know which clerk caused the shortfall and that the clerk acted deliberately.
Were the safeguards not to be enforced, the exposure would widen. → If the safeguards were not enforced, the exposure would widen.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Neutral modal passive becomes intentional prevention; meaning and force both change.

Tip: can be drawn does not accuse the data of deliberate obstruction.

TRUE — Nested passives: is expected + to be published — both layers are well formed.

Tip: Expect + to-infinitive passive is common in formal forecasts.

TRUE — Causative had… replaced pairs with a plain passive The servers were replaced overnight without inventing who did the work.

Tip: Causative get/have + object + PP often aligns with a simple passive of the object.

FALSE — It is believed hedges; naming a clerk and alleging deliberate action fabricates agent and intent.

Tip: Belief passives especially forbid certainty-plus-motive rewrites.

TRUE — Inverted passive Were… not to be enforced paraphrases cleanly as If the safeguards were not enforced…

Tip: Formal inversion still encodes the same passive obligation/enforcement meaning.
highlights: prevents anyone from drawing conclusions deliberately
Were the safeguards not to be enforced
tasks.solution_overview: At the top band, watch nested passives and inverted conditionals that still keep meaning, and reject any rewrite that adds deliberate clerks, motives, or prevention the source never stated.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The analyst who prepared the briefing joined the call late.
The report which the committee rejected it contained outdated figures.
The bakery who opened last month already has a waiting list.
The contract that legal signed yesterday takes effect on Monday.
The stadium, that was renovated in 2019, hosted the finals.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Who" correctly refers to a person in a restrictive clause that defines which analyst you mean.

Tip: For people in defining clauses, "who" or "that" both work; pick one and stay consistent.

FALSE — Drop the extra "it": the relative already stands for the object, so write "which the committee rejected."

Tip: Never leave a leftover pronoun after a relative clause that already fills that slot.

FALSE — A bakery is a thing, so use "which" (or "that"), not "who."

Tip: Reserve "who" for people (and sometimes organisations treated as people in formal writing).

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which contract; no commas needed.

Tip: No commas = the clause is essential to identify the noun.

FALSE — After commas (non-restrictive), use "which," not "that": "The stadium, which was renovated…"

Tip: Commas signal extra information — and "that" is not welcome there.
tasks.solution_overview: Start by asking whether the clause names a person or a thing, and whether the commas mark it as essential or extra. Then check that the relative itself carries the subject or object — no leftover "it" or "them." A quick who/which/that pass catches most early mistakes.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The manager whose team hit the target received a bonus.
The auditor who's recommendations we followed has left the firm.
The proposal, which the board approved, reshapes next year's budget.
The clients that complained about delays were offered compensation.
The warehouse, who stores seasonal stock, needs new shelving.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Whose" correctly shows possession: the team belongs to the manager.

Tip: If you can rephrase as "X's Y," you almost always want "whose."

FALSE — You need possession, not "who is": write "whose recommendations."

Tip: "Who's" = who is / who has; "whose" = of whom / of which.

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" with commas correctly adds non-essential detail about the proposal.

Tip: Extra information between commas takes "which" for things, never "that."

TRUE — Restrictive "that" for people is acceptable in defining clauses.

Tip: In defining clauses about people, "who" sounds slightly more formal than "that."

FALSE — A warehouse is not a person; use "which": "The warehouse, which stores…"

Tip: Animate-looking nouns that are still things take "which," not "who."
tasks.solution_overview: Possession and person/thing choice dominate this set. Separate "who's" (contraction) from "whose" (belonging), and keep "who" for people while "which" covers places, buildings, and documents.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The merger, that investors feared, went through quietly.
The consultant whom we hired last spring redesigned the workflow.
The software which crashes during peak hours needs a patch.
The director who we briefed yesterday asked for more data.
The figures that the CFO presented them surprised the panel.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A comma-bound clause must use "which," not "that": "The merger, which investors feared…"

Tip: Spot the commas first; they ban "that" in careful British exam English.

TRUE — Formal "whom" correctly marks the object of "hired."

Tip: If the relative would be "him/her/them," "whom" is the careful choice.

TRUE — Restrictive "which" correctly defines which software; no commas required.

Tip: British formal writing often prefers "which" even in defining clauses about things.

TRUE — Informal/object "who" is widely accepted here; the sentence is grammatical as written.

Tip: Exams may still prefer "whom" after a preposition, but bare object "who" is usually fine.

FALSE — Remove the residual "them": "The figures that the CFO presented surprised…"

Tip: The relative already equals the object; a second object pronoun is always wrong.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch non-restrictive "that," object relatives (who/whom), and pronoun leftovers. If the clause already does the object’s job, nothing else should sit in that slot.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The trainee who joined in March already leads client calls.
The guidelines that HR published apply to remote staff.
The factory whose output doubled last quarter needs overtime cover.
The speaker who's opening the conference arrives at nine.
The forecast which the economists released looks optimistic.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Restrictive "who" correctly identifies the trainee.

Tip: No commas when the clause is needed to pick out which person.

TRUE — Defining "that" correctly restricts which guidelines.

Tip: "That" is a safe default in restrictive clauses about things.

TRUE — "Whose" can mark possession for things as well as people.

Tip: "The factory whose output…" = "the factory’s output."

TRUE — "Who's" correctly expands to "who is" before "opening."

Tip: Try expanding the contraction; if "who is" fits, "who's" is right.

TRUE — Restrictive "which" correctly defines the forecast.

Tip: Either "which" or "that" works in defining clauses about things.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are sound models: people with "who," things with "that/which," possession with "whose," and a genuine "who's" = who is. Use them as clean reference patterns before the traps get harder.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The partner with whom we negotiate prefers evening calls.
The dataset, that includes last year's returns, is incomplete.
Anyone who's password expires must reset it today.
The branch which we visited last week is closing for renovations.
The engineer that designed the prototype will present at noon.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Preposition + "whom" is the formal, correct pattern for a person as object.

Tip: After a preposition, prefer "whom" (people) or "which" (things), not "who" or "that."

FALSE — Non-restrictive needs "which": "The dataset, which includes…"

Tip: Commas + "that" is a classic exam fail.

FALSE — Possession requires "whose": "Anyone whose password expires…"

Tip: If "who is password" sounds nonsense, you wanted "whose."

TRUE — Defining "which" correctly identifies the branch.

Tip: Object relatives can keep "which/that" or drop the pronoun entirely in informal style.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" for a person is acceptable in defining clauses.

Tip: "Who" is often preferred for people, but "that" is not an error here.
tasks.solution_overview: Preposition + whom is the polished form; commas still forbid "that"; and "who's" vs "whose" remains a high-frequency trap. Read each clause aloud with the contraction expanded.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The supplier from which we source packaging raised its prices.
The intern whom mentors praised completed the rotation early.
The policy that HR revised last month it now covers freelancers.
Vienna, which hosts the summit, has limited hotel capacity.
The investors who capital the startup provided later withdrew.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "From which" correctly links a thing after a preposition.

Tip: Keep the preposition with "which/whom"; avoid ending with a stranded wrong relative.

TRUE — "Whom" correctly marks the intern as the object of "praised" (mentors praised the intern).

Tip: If you can replace the relative with "him/her," "whom" is justified.

FALSE — Delete residual "it": "The policy that HR revised last month now covers…"

Tip: One clause, one object slot — never both relative and "it."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Vienna.

Tip: Place names with commas almost always take "which," not "that."

FALSE — Word order collapses; write "The investors who provided the startup’s capital later withdrew."

Tip: Keep the relative clause’s internal word order like a normal statement after the relative.
tasks.solution_overview: Preposition + which, object whom, and residual pronouns dominate here. If a leftover "it" remains after the relative, cut it; if word order inside the clause collapses, rebuild the clause as a normal statement.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The lawyer to whom the letter was addressed replied within a day.
The spreadsheet who's columns are locked cannot be edited.
Staff whose badges have expired must visit reception.
The museum that we toured on Friday displays modern design.
The CEO, that announced the restructure, takes questions at four.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "To whom" is the formal object pattern after a preposition.

Tip: Preposition + whom is almost always safe for people in exam English.

FALSE — A spreadsheet’s columns need "whose," not "who's."

Tip: "Who's" never marks possession — expand it and the error is obvious.

TRUE — "Whose" correctly marks possession for people in a defining clause.

Tip: "Whose" works with plural noun heads just as with singular.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which museum.

Tip: Object "that/which" can often be omitted: "The museum we toured…"

FALSE — Non-restrictive about a person needs "who": "The CEO, who announced…"

Tip: Commas + person → "who"; commas + thing → "which"; never "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "to whom," possession with "whose," and the ban on "that" after commas are the three checks here. Expand every "who's" before you mark the sentence true.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The invoice which accounts paid yesterday still shows the old rate.
The researcher of who the paper was co-authored declined comment.
The building that overlooks the river is under offer.
Customers which request refunds must keep their receipts.
The mentor whose advice shaped the pitch will join the rehearsal.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Defining "which" correctly identifies the invoice.

Tip: Subject or object relatives both allow "which/that" for things.

FALSE — After a preposition referring to a person, use "whom": "of whom the paper was co-authored" (or better, rephrase).

Tip: "Of who" is almost never correct; "of whom" is the formal fix.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines the building.

Tip: No commas when the clause picks out which building.

FALSE — Customers are people; use "who" or "that," not "which."

Tip: "Which" for people is a strong red flag in exam marking.

TRUE — "Whose advice" correctly shows possession.

Tip: "Whose + noun" is the clean possessive relative pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: People vs things and preposition + whom are the focus. Never use "which" for customers or staff, and never leave "of who" after a preposition.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The minutes, which the secretary circulated, confirm the vote.
The candidate whom the panel shortlisted withdrew this morning.
Anyone who's still waiting should check the board outside.
The algorithm that ranks applications was updated overnight.
The office in which the interview takes place is on the third floor.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds information about known minutes.

Tip: If removing the clause still leaves a clear noun, commas + "which" are right.

TRUE — Object "whom" correctly follows the panel as subject of "shortlisted."

Tip: Swap in "him/her": if that fits, "whom" is justified.

TRUE — "Who's" = "who is" before "still waiting."

Tip: Expand the contraction; if the sentence still works, keep "who's."

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines the algorithm.

Tip: Technical nouns take the same who/which/that rules as everyday ones.

TRUE — "In which" is the formal relative after a preposition for a place.

Tip: Formal writing prefers "in which" over a stranded preposition, though both can be grammatical.
tasks.solution_overview: These are clean mid-level models: non-restrictive "which," object "whom," a genuine "who's," defining "that," and formal "in which." Compare them with nearby traps before you lock your answers.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bond, that matures next June, was issued at a discount.
The clerk to who complaints should be sent sits at desk 12.
Products whose labels lack allergen warnings must be recalled.
The witness who the prosecutor called seemed unsure.
The framework on which the appraisal rests needs revision.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "which" after commas: "The bond, which matures next June…"

Tip: Financial nouns follow the same comma rule as any other thing.

FALSE — After "to," use "whom": "to whom complaints should be sent."

Tip: Preposition + who is almost always wrong; make it "whom."

TRUE — "Whose" correctly marks possession for products/labels.
