Tip: "Whose" is fine for inanimate nouns in careful English.

TRUE — Object "who" is acceptable in modern usage for the person called.

Tip: Formal style may prefer "whom," but bare "who" as object is not marked wrong in most exams.

TRUE — "On which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Keep preposition + which together in formal answers.
tasks.solution_overview: Comma + "that," "to who," and possession for things are the main traps. Formal preposition + which/whom patterns earn easy true marks when you spot them.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The auditors with who we share draft findings signed an NDA.
London, which remains our European hub, will host the kick-off.
The dossier that compliance flagged contains personal data.
A colleague who's been seconded to Berlin still joins our stand-ups.
The prototype, which the lab tested last night, failed the stress check.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "whom" after "with": "with whom we share draft findings."

Tip: Any preposition before a person-relative wants "whom."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about London.

Tip: City names with commas take "which," not "that" or "who."

TRUE — Defining "that" correctly restricts which dossier.

Tip: Compliance and legal nouns follow ordinary relative rules.

TRUE — "Who's been" = "who has been," a correct present-perfect relative.

Tip: "Who's" covers both "who is" and "who has."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds extra detail about the prototype.

Tip: If the noun is already identified, commas + "which" are the pair.
tasks.solution_overview: One clear "with who" error sits among solid non-restrictive and defining models. Confirm each true sentence’s person/thing choice and comma pattern before moving on.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The broker through whom we placed the order confirmed the fill.
Equipment that arrives damaged must be photographed immediately.
The founder whose startup we acquired stays on as an adviser.
Anyone who's unsure about the dress code should ask HR.
The clause under which penalties apply is highlighted in bold.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Through whom" correctly marks a person after a preposition.

Tip: Formal business English loves preposition + whom for intermediaries.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which equipment.

Tip: Uncountable heads still take normal relative pronouns.

TRUE — "Whose startup" correctly shows possession.

Tip: "Whose" + noun phrase is the standard possessive relative.

TRUE — "Who's unsure" = "who is unsure."

Tip: If "who is" fits cleanly, "who's" is not a possession error.

TRUE — "Under which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Legal "under which" / "pursuant to which" patterns are exam favourites.
tasks.solution_overview: All five showcase reliable formal relatives: preposition + whom/which, defining "that," possessive "whose," and a legitimate "who's." Treat them as templates for harder items.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The committee appointed a chairperson that her experience was unmatched.
Negotiators on whom the deadline weighed most heavily requested an extension.
The portal which applicants use it times out after ten minutes.
Berlin, that we visited for the trade fair, has excellent rail links.
Shareholders whom voted against the motion still attended the lunch.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "whose": "a chairperson whose experience was unmatched," not "that her."

Tip: "That + possessive determiner" is a broken relative; switch to "whose."

TRUE — "On whom" correctly places a person after a preposition.

Tip: If stress falls on people as the object of a preposition, "whom" is the formal form.

FALSE — Remove "it": "The portal which applicants use times out…"

Tip: Residual object pronouns after relatives are always wrong.

FALSE — Non-restrictive place names need "which": "Berlin, which we visited…"

Tip: Commas + "that" fail for cities just as for documents.

FALSE — Subject relative needs "who": "Shareholders who voted…"

Tip: "Whom" is never the subject of the relative clause’s verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder traps mix broken possession ("that her"), leftover pronouns, non-restrictive "that," and subject "whom." Only the preposition + whom sentence is clean here.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The vendor with whose terms we disagreed still won the tender.
Delegates for who travel was arranged must collect vouchers by noon.
The archive in which older contracts are stored is being digitised.
A process that we streamlined last year now saves two hours a week.
The economist who's forecast we cited later revised her numbers.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "With whose terms" correctly combines preposition and possession.

Tip: "Preposition + whose + noun" is formal but fully grammatical.

FALSE — Use "whom": "Delegates for whom travel was arranged…"

Tip: After "for/to/with/from," person-relatives need "whom."

TRUE — "In which" correctly marks a place after a preposition.

Tip: Formal answers prefer "in which" over "where" in some exam styles.

TRUE — Defining "that" (object) correctly identifies the process.

Tip: Object "that/which" can be omitted: "A process we streamlined…"

FALSE — Possession needs "whose": "The economist whose forecast we cited…"

Tip: "Who's forecast" expands to nonsense; that signals "whose."
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced patterns include "with whose" and "in which," while "for who" and "who's + noun" remain frequent fails. Expand every contraction before you judge possession.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The only applicant that the firm shortlisted declined the offer.
Our Helsinki office, that opened in 2018, now employs forty people.
Investors to whom the prospectus was mailed raised further questions.
The dashboard which tracks liquidity it refreshes every minute.
Teams whose KPIs slipped this quarter must submit a recovery plan.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines the only shortlisted applicant.

Tip: "The only / the first / the last + that" is a natural defining pattern.

FALSE — Non-restrictive needs "which": "Our Helsinki office, which opened…"

Tip: Named, unique offices take commas + "which," not "that."

TRUE — "To whom" correctly marks recipients after a preposition.

Tip: Mail/send/address + to whom is a standard formal relative.

FALSE — Drop "it": "The dashboard which tracks liquidity refreshes…"

Tip: The relative clause already contains its object/subject logic; no second pronoun.

TRUE — "Whose KPIs" correctly shows possession for teams.

Tip: Collective nouns still take "whose" for belonging.
tasks.solution_overview: Defining "the only… that," formal "to whom," and "whose" for teams are solid; commas + "that" and residual "it" are the fails. Prioritise comma diagnosis first.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The regulator by whom the fine was imposed published guidance today.
Candidates which fail the compliance quiz cannot access the portal.
A policy whose wording is ambiguous invites disputes.
The seminar at which we presented drew a large audience.
Someone who's ID badge is missing should report to security.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "By whom" correctly marks the agent in a formal relative.

Tip: Passive-related "by whom" is formal but grammatical.

FALSE — People need "who/that": "Candidates who fail…"

Tip: Never use "which" for candidates, clients, or staff.

TRUE — "Whose wording" correctly marks possession for a policy.

Tip: Documents and policies commonly take "whose" in exam English.

TRUE — "At which" correctly attaches the preposition to an event.

Tip: Prefer "at which / in which" over informal "where" in formal answers when asked.

FALSE — Use "whose": "Someone whose ID badge is missing…"

Tip: "Who's ID" = "who is ID," which never works.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "by whom" / "at which" sit beside people-"which" and "who's + noun" errors. Keep person/thing and contraction checks automatic at this level.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The partner in whom's firm we invested later exited the market.
Few of the metrics on which the bonus depends are under our control.
The analyst that her model underestimated demand has revised it.
Board members whom the chair thanked stayed for photographs.
The warehouse where stock is held, that flooded last spring, is closed.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Malformed possession; write "The partner in whose firm we invested…"

Tip: Never stack "whom's"; use "whose" after the preposition.

TRUE — "On which" correctly links metrics after a preposition.

Tip: "The X on which Y depends" is a high-value formal pattern.

FALSE — Replace "that her" with "whose": "The analyst whose model underestimated…"

Tip: "That + possessive" always signals a missing "whose."

TRUE — Object "whom" correctly refers to the members thanked.

Tip: Subject of main clause + object relative "whom" is a clean formal structure.

FALSE — Mixing "where" with a second non-restrictive "that" is wrong; prefer "The warehouse where stock is held, which flooded last spring, is closed."

Tip: A second relative after commas still cannot be "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Top-band items twist possession after prepositions and stack relatives. Reject "whom's" and "that her," keep "on which," and remember a second comma-bound clause still wants "which."

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The lender to whose conditions we agreed released the funds.
Staff for whom remote work was approved must log hours weekly.
The prototype that the engineers dismantled it cannot be reassembled.
Singapore, which we use as our APAC base, hosts the regional board.
Anyone who's completed module three may sit the assessment.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "To whose conditions" correctly combines preposition and possession.

Tip: "To/with/under whose + noun" is advanced but correct.

TRUE — "For whom" correctly marks people after a preposition.

Tip: Approval/arrangement phrases often need "for whom."

FALSE — Remove "it": "The prototype that the engineers dismantled cannot be reassembled."

Tip: Even in long sentences, residual objects are still errors.

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds information about Singapore.

Tip: Country/city names with commas take "which."

TRUE — "Who's completed" = "who has completed."

Tip: Present-perfect "who's" is possession’s innocent twin — expand to check.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "to whose" / "for whom" are trustworthy when the grammar fits; the leftover "it" is the only clear fail. Expand "who's" once more to confirm "who has."

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The counsel of whom we sought advice later joined the opposing side.
A clause that its purpose is unclear should be redrafted.
Partners who the firm promoted last year now lead regional desks.
The platform via which clients upload documents went offline at noon.
The interim CFO, that arrived in May, reorganised the treasury team.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Of whom" correctly marks the person after the preposition in a formal relative.

Tip: "Of whom we sought advice" is stiff but exam-correct.

FALSE — Use "whose": "A clause whose purpose is unclear…"

Tip: "That its" is the same broken pattern as "that her."

TRUE — Object "who" for people promoted is acceptable modern usage.

Tip: Formal alternatives use "whom"; both are usually accepted without a preceding preposition.

TRUE — "Via which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Tech/process nouns take "which" after prepositions, not "who."

FALSE — Non-restrictive about a person needs "who": "The interim CFO, who arrived…"

Tip: Title + commas still bans "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "of whom" / "via which" contrast with "that its" and comma + "that" about a person. Diagnose possession failures and non-restrictive person clauses first.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The underwriters with whom we placed the issue required further disclosure.
Anyone whose laptop holds client files must enable full-disk encryption.
The jurisdiction under which the dispute will be heard is specified in clause 19.
A consultant who's already briefed the board need not attend the dry run.
The metrics against which performance is judged were agreed last autumn.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "With whom" correctly marks people after a preposition in a defining clause.

Tip: Placement/issuance language often uses "with whom we placed…"

TRUE — "Whose laptop" correctly shows possession.

Tip: Security policies love "anyone whose + noun" constructions.

TRUE — "Under which" correctly links the legal framework.

Tip: Contract English frequently uses "under which / pursuant to which."

TRUE — "Who's already briefed" = "who has already briefed."

Tip: Final check: expand "who's"; if "who has" fits, the sentence can stand.

TRUE — "Against which" correctly marks the standard of comparison.

Tip: "The X against which Y is judged" is a polished relative pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: A clean capstone of advanced but correct relatives: preposition + whom/which, possessive "whose," and "who's" = who has. Use these as your final checklist for person, thing, possession, and contraction.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The compliance team avoids discussing draft findings with suppliers before the audit closes.
Several analysts enjoy to review competitor filings after market close.
The board decided postponing the bond issue until October.
Warehouse supervisors refuse to sign off unfinished stock counts.
The agency promised delivering the campaign assets by Friday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid takes a gerund, so "avoids discussing" is the natural pattern after this verb.

Tip: Memorise avoid + -ing as a fixed pairing; an infinitive after avoid is almost always wrong.

FALSE — Enjoy needs a gerund, not an infinitive: "enjoy reviewing," not "enjoy to review."

Tip: Like, love, and enjoy all prefer -ing when the object is an activity.

FALSE — Decide takes a to-infinitive: "decided to postpone," not a gerund.

Tip: Decide / refuse / promise / plan / hope / expect all pattern with to + base verb.

TRUE — Refuse correctly takes a to-infinitive: "refuse to sign."

Tip: If the meaning is "will not do X," expect refuse + to-infinitive.

FALSE — Promise takes a to-infinitive: "promised to deliver," not a gerund.

Tip: Promise patterns like decide and refuse — to + verb, not -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: This set drills the core split: avoid and enjoy need -ing, while decide, refuse, and promise need to + verb. Check each verb's fixed pattern before you judge the sentence.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The product team is considering launching a freemium tier next quarter.
Investors enjoy reading the monthly cash-flow summary.
Legal counsel decided to challenge the indemnity clause.
The courier refused accepting parcels without a signature.
Finance promised to circulate the revised budget tonight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Consider takes a gerund: "considering launching" is correct.

Tip: Consider / avoid / enjoy / finish / suggest all take -ing when followed by a verb.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is the standard pattern: "enjoy reading."

Tip: If enjoy is followed by an activity, use -ing, not to.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to challenge."

Tip: Decision verbs (decide, agree, refuse, promise) lean toward to + base verb.

FALSE — Refuse needs a to-infinitive: "refused to accept," not a gerund.

Tip: Swap -ing for to + verb after refuse and the sentence usually repairs itself.

TRUE — Promise correctly takes a to-infinitive: "promised to circulate."

Tip: Promise + to-infinitive expresses a future commitment.
tasks.solution_overview: Four verbs here follow their textbook patterns correctly; only refuse is broken. Treat refuse like decide and promise — always to + verb.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The editor avoided to mention the leaked memo in the press release.
Trainee traders enjoy to practise scenario drills on quiet mornings.
Management is considering to outsource payroll processing.
The start-up decided expanding into two neighbouring markets.
The lender refused to extend the overdraft without fresh collateral.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Avoid takes a gerund: "avoided mentioning," not "to mention."

Tip: Avoid + -ing is non-negotiable in standard business English.

FALSE — Enjoy needs -ing: "enjoy practising," not "enjoy to practise."

Tip: British spelling "practise" (verb) is fine; the form after enjoy must still be a gerund.

FALSE — Consider takes a gerund: "considering outsourcing," not an infinitive.

Tip: Consider to + verb is a classic exam trap — rewrite with -ing.

FALSE — Decide takes a to-infinitive: "decided to expand."

Tip: After decide, reach for to + base verb every time.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to extend."

Tip: When only one sentence is right, verify the refuse / decide / promise group first.
tasks.solution_overview: Four verbs are forced into the wrong complement. Only refuse keeps the correct to-infinitive; the others need either -ing (avoid, enjoy, consider) or to + verb (decide).

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Auditors avoid relying on verbal assurances alone.
The CEO enjoys chairing the quarterly town-hall meetings.
The committee considered delaying the product launch.
Procurement decided to renegotiate the three-year contract.
The supplier promised shipping replacements by courier overnight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund works: "avoid relying."

Tip: Relying is the activity being avoided — keep it as -ing.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoys chairing."

Tip: Chairing is an activity noun-form; enjoy wants that -ing shape.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct: "considered delaying."

Tip: Consider means "think about doing," so the next verb is -ing.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to renegotiate."

Tip: A firm decision points forward with to + base verb.

FALSE — Promise needs a to-infinitive: "promised to ship," not a gerund.

Tip: Promise + -ing is a frequent slip; force to + verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Gerund verbs (avoid, enjoy, consider) and decide are clean; only promise is mistyped with -ing. Swap that for to + ship and the set is solid.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The presenter stopped speaking when the fire alarm sounded.
She stopped to check the slide deck before the client call.
The analyst stopped to smoking during working hours last year.
Operations stopped updating the legacy dashboard after the migration.
He stopped asking for overtime once headcount increased.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + gerund means the activity itself ended: he quit speaking.

Tip: Stop + -ing = cease that activity.

TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive means she paused in order to check the deck.

Tip: Stop + to + verb = interrupt one action so you can do another.

FALSE — "Stopped to smoking" mixes patterns; either "stopped smoking" (quit) or "stopped to smoke" (paused in order to).

Tip: Never put to immediately before an -ing form after stop.

TRUE — Stop + gerund correctly shows they discontinued the updates.

Tip: If the meaning is "no longer do X," use stop + -ing.

TRUE — Stop + gerund again: he quit the habit of asking.

Tip: Both stop + -ing and stop + to are grammatical — the meaning decides which you need.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on stop: -ing ends an activity; to + verb means pause in order to do something. The broken item illegally stacks to with an -ing form.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Retail partners avoid stocking slow-moving SKUs before peak season.
Junior associates enjoy shadowing senior negotiators on live deals.
The board is considering appointing an interim CFO.
HR decided to freeze hiring until revenue stabilises.
The contractor refused to work without a signed purchase order.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid stocking."

Tip: Stocking is the activity avoided — keep the -ing.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoy shadowing."

Tip: Enjoy always wants -ing for activities in this register.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct: "considering appointing."

Tip: Appointing is what they are thinking about — gerund territory.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to freeze."

Tip: Freeze here is a deliberate future action after decide.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to work."

Tip: When every line looks right, still verify each verb's complement type.
tasks.solution_overview: All five sentences use the right complement. Confirm avoid/enjoy/consider → -ing and decide/refuse → to + verb, then mark them true.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The brand promised to refund customers within five working days.
She stopped to answer a compliance question mid-presentation.
Managers avoid to schedule training during month-end close.
The committee considered rewriting the whistle-blowing policy.
He enjoys to negotiate multi-year service agreements.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive is correct: "promised to refund."

Tip: Refund is the committed future action — to + verb.

TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive correctly means she paused in order to answer.

Tip: Ask whether she quit answering forever ( -ing) or paused to answer (to).

FALSE — Avoid needs a gerund: "avoid scheduling," not "to schedule."

Tip: Avoid + to is almost never acceptable in exam English.

TRUE — Consider + gerund is correct: "considered rewriting."

Tip: Rewriting is under review — that is consider + -ing.

FALSE — Enjoy needs a gerund: "enjoys negotiating."

Tip: Enjoy + to is a high-frequency learner error.
tasks.solution_overview: Promise and stop-to are fine, and consider is fine; avoid and enjoy are wrongly given infinitives. Repair those two with -ing.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The firm decided merging with a regional competitor.
Sales leads refuse handling refunds without manager approval.
Investors promised backing the round without further diligence.
The team avoided disclosing soft pipeline numbers externally.
She stopped typing when the video call connected.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Decide takes to + verb: "decided to merge."

Tip: Merge is a chosen next step — use the infinitive after decide.

FALSE — Refuse takes to + verb: "refuse to handle."

Tip: Refuse + -ing is not standard; rewrite with to.

FALSE — Promise takes to + verb: "promised to back."

Tip: Commitment language after promise wants an infinitive.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoided disclosing."

Tip: Disclosing is the behaviour they steered clear of.

TRUE — Stop + gerund correctly means typing ceased.

Tip: Here the activity ended, so -ing is the right stop pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Decide, refuse, and promise are all forced into gerunds wrongly. Avoid and stop + -ing are the only correct lines.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The logistics manager stopped to inspect damaged packaging on the dock.
We stopped printing paper invoices after clients moved to e-billing.
Counsel is considering filing an injunction before Friday.
The partner decided to withdraw from the joint venture.
Interns enjoy to draft first versions of client emails.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: he paused in order to inspect.

Tip: Purpose after an interruption = stop + to + verb.

TRUE — Stop + gerund: printing as an activity was discontinued.

Tip: "No longer do X" → stop + -ing.

TRUE — Consider + gerund: "considering filing."

Tip: Filing is the option under review.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive: "decided to withdraw."

Tip: Withdraw is the chosen next action.

FALSE — Enjoy needs a gerund: "enjoy drafting."

Tip: Drafting is an activity — keep -ing after enjoy.
tasks.solution_overview: Both stop patterns appear correctly with different meanings. Consider and decide are fine; only enjoy is broken with an infinitive.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The agency refused releasing creative files without payment.
Founders promised to share the cap table with new angels.
Risk officers avoid escalating minor breaches to the board.
She decided cancelling the overseas roadshow.
He enjoys mentoring graduate analysts each spring.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to release."

Tip: Release is what they will not do — infinitive after refuse.

TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive: "promised to share."

Tip: Share is the future commitment.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoid escalating."

Tip: Escalating is the action they try not to take.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to cancel."

Tip: Cancel is the decision outcome — use the infinitive.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoys mentoring."

Tip: Mentoring is the liked activity.
tasks.solution_overview: Refuse and decide wrongly take gerunds; promise, avoid, and enjoy follow the correct patterns.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The workshop facilitator stopped explaining when participants looked confused.
She stopped to clarify the pricing model before continuing.
Directors are considering to spin off the logistics unit.
The bank refused to waive early-repayment fees.
Staff avoid using personal devices on the shop-floor network.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + gerund: explaining ceased.

Tip: The explaining itself stopped — that is -ing.

TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: she paused in order to clarify.

Tip: Purpose after a pause = to + verb.

FALSE — Consider takes a gerund: "considering spinning," not "to spin."

Tip: Consider + to is a trap; rewrite with -ing.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive: "refused to waive."

Tip: Waive is the rejected action.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoid using."

Tip: Using is the behaviour they steer clear of.
tasks.solution_overview: Stop appears in both correct senses. Refuse and avoid are fine; only consider is broken with an infinitive.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The CFO promised circulating the variance report after lunch.
Buyers decided to switch to a dual-sourcing strategy.
Researchers enjoy testing prototypes with focus groups.
The union refused bargaining without an independent mediator.
Planners avoid double-booking scarce laboratory time.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to circulate."

Tip: Circulate is the pledged action — infinitive required.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive: "decided to switch."

Tip: Switch is the chosen next move.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoy testing."

Tip: Testing is the liked activity.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to bargain."

Tip: Bargain is what they will not do without conditions.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoid double-booking."

Tip: Double-booking is the problem behaviour avoided.
tasks.solution_overview: Promise and refuse wrongly take gerunds. Decide, enjoy, and avoid are patterned correctly.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: After the outage, engineers stopped to reboot the primary server.
They stopped rebooting servers manually once automation went live.
The committee considered to approve a smaller capital request.
Marketing decided postponing the influencer campaign.
Partners promised to disclose related-party transactions promptly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: they paused in order to reboot.

Tip: Reboot is the purpose of the pause.

TRUE — Stop + gerund: manual rebooting as a practice ended.

Tip: Same verb reboot, different pattern — meaning flips with form.

FALSE — Consider needs a gerund: "considered approving."

Tip: Approving is under consideration — use -ing.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to postpone."

Tip: Postpone is the decision — infinitive, not gerund.

TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive: "promised to disclose."

Tip: Disclose is the pledged future action.
tasks.solution_overview: Stop shows both meanings cleanly with reboot. Consider and decide are inverted; promise is correct.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Store managers avoid discounting premium lines too early in the season.
She enjoys benchmarking margins against listed peers.
The board is considering spinning the payments unit into a subsidiary.
Creditors refused to accept a haircut below thirty percent.
He stopped to smoking in the loading bay after the policy change.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoid discounting."

Tip: Discounting is the premature behaviour they dodge.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoys benchmarking."

Tip: Benchmarking is the liked analytical activity.

TRUE — Consider + gerund: "considering spinning."

Tip: Spinning off is the option under review.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive: "refused to accept."

Tip: Accept is what they will not do on those terms.

FALSE — "Stopped to smoking" is ungrammatical; use "stopped smoking" or "stopped to smoke."

Tip: After stop, choose either -ing or to + base — never to + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Four core patterns are correct. The stop line is a hybrid error — to cannot sit before an -ing form.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The client decided to escalate the dispute to arbitration.
Vendors promised updating the API documentation weekly.
She refused signing the non-compete without legal review.
He stopped reviewing emails once the out-of-office was set.
They avoided announcing earnings before the lock-up ended.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive: "decided to escalate."

Tip: Escalate is the chosen next step.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to update."

Tip: Update is the pledged recurring action.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to sign."

Tip: Sign is what she will not do yet.

TRUE — Stop + gerund: reviewing ceased.

Tip: The reviewing activity ended — -ing is right.

TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoided announcing."

Tip: Announcing early is what they steered clear of.
tasks.solution_overview: Decide, stop + -ing, and avoid are fine. Promise and refuse wrongly take gerunds and need infinitives.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Investors enjoy questioning management on capital allocation.
The firm is considering licensing its patents to a rival.
She stopped to question a figure in the cash-flow forecast.
They decided licensing the brand to franchise partners.
He promised to question any unexplained variance above five percent.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoy questioning."

Tip: Questioning is the liked activity in the meeting.

TRUE — Consider + gerund: "considering licensing."

Tip: Licensing is the option under review.

TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: she paused in order to question a figure.

Tip: Purpose mid-task = stop + to + verb.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to license."

Tip: Same lemma license/licensing — decide still wants the infinitive.

TRUE — Promise + to-infinitive: "promised to question."

Tip: Question here is a pledged future habit.
tasks.solution_overview: Questioning and licensing recur with different governing verbs. Only decide + licensing is wrong — rewrite as decided to license.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The negotiator stopped speaking to let the interpreter catch up.
The negotiator stopped to speaking when the interpreter arrived late.
Counsel avoided to commit the firm before due diligence finished.
They refused committing capital until covenants were redrafted.
She decided to commit spare capacity to the overflow warehouse.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + gerund: speaking paused so the interpreter could catch up; the form is grammatical.

Tip: "Stopped speaking" = ceased that talk; the to-let clause is purpose for pausing the speech, not a stop + to pattern.

FALSE — "Stopped to speaking" is ungrammatical; use "stopped speaking" or "stopped to speak."

Tip: Never combine to with an -ing form after stop.

FALSE — Avoid needs a gerund: "avoided committing."

Tip: Committing early is the risk they dodge — -ing after avoid.

FALSE — Refuse needs to + verb: "refused to commit."

Tip: Commit is what they will not do yet.

TRUE — Decide + to-infinitive: "decided to commit."

Tip: Commit is the chosen allocation decision.
tasks.solution_overview: Commit and speaking create denser traps. Only stop + speaking and decide to commit are clean; the other three mix complements illegally.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Analysts enjoy modelling downside scenarios before earnings calls.
The committee considered modelling a second base case overnight.
IT promised modelling the migration in a sandboxed environment.
She stopped modelling when the live feed froze.
He stopped to model a quick sensitivity before the vote.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoy modelling."

Tip: Modelling is the liked analytical activity.

TRUE — Consider + gerund: "considered modelling."

Tip: Modelling a second case is under review.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to model."

Tip: Same surface verb modelling — promise still wants an infinitive.

TRUE — Stop + gerund: modelling ceased when the feed froze.

Tip: The modelling activity ended — -ing.

TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: he paused in order to model a sensitivity.

Tip: Purpose mid-meeting = stop + to + verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Modelling is reused under five governors. Enjoy, consider, and both stop patterns work; only promise + modelling fails.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Founders avoid pitching unfinished demos to strategic buyers.
They decided pitching the seed round only after traction metrics improved.
She refused to pitch without a signed NDA.
He promised pitching the roadmap at the next investor day.
Investors enjoy pitching follow-on ideas during office hours.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Avoid + gerund: "avoid pitching."

Tip: Pitching unfinished work is the behaviour avoided.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to pitch."

Tip: Pitch is the future decision — infinitive required.

TRUE — Refuse + to-infinitive: "refused to pitch."

Tip: Pitch is what she will not do without an NDA.

FALSE — Promise needs to + verb: "promised to pitch."

Tip: Pitch is the pledged presentation — use the infinitive.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoy pitching."

Tip: Pitching ideas is the liked activity for them.
tasks.solution_overview: Pitching is held constant while governors change. Avoid, refuse, and enjoy are right; decide and promise wrongly keep the gerund.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The chair stopped to summarise the key risks before the vote.
The chair stopped summarising once the board asked for a closed session.
Risk teams are considering summarising breaches in a weekly digest.
She enjoys summarising dense contracts into one-page briefs.
He decided summarising the findings without naming individuals.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Stop + to-infinitive: paused in order to summarise.

Tip: Purpose before the vote = to + verb.

TRUE — Stop + gerund: summarising ceased when the closed session began.

Tip: The summarising activity ended — -ing.

TRUE — Consider + gerund: "considering summarising."

Tip: Summarising in a digest is the option under review.

TRUE — Enjoy + gerund: "enjoys summarising."

Tip: Summarising is the liked drafting activity.

FALSE — Decide needs to + verb: "decided to summarise."

Tip: Summarise is the chosen reporting approach — infinitive, not gerund.
tasks.solution_overview: Summarising rides under stop (both senses), consider, and enjoy correctly. Only decide + summarising is wrong — rewrite as decided to summarise.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The audit is delayed." → "She said the audit was delayed."
Direct: "Where is the briefing room?" → "He asked where was the briefing room."
Direct: "We will submit the bid by noon." → "They said they will submit the bid by noon."
Direct: "Did you see the memo?" → "She asked if I had seen the memo."
Direct: "I resigned yesterday." → "He said he had resigned yesterday."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After a past reporting verb, present simple backshifts to past simple: "is" becomes "was."

Tip: Past said/told/asked usually pulls the reported verb one step back in time.

FALSE — Embedded wh-questions keep statement order: subject before the verb. "Where was the briefing room?" is direct-question order.

Tip: Use "where the briefing room was," not "where was…"

FALSE — "Will" normally backshifts to "would" after a past reporting verb.

Tip: "They said they would submit the bid by noon."

TRUE — Yes/no questions take if/whether plus statement order, and present perfect often becomes past perfect.

Tip: "asked if/whether + subject + had + past participle."

FALSE — Time markers shift with the tense: "yesterday" becomes "the day before" (or "the previous day").

Tip: Pair backshift with deictic shifts: yesterday → the day before; tomorrow → the next day.
tasks.solution_overview: This set drills the core trio: tense backshift after said/asked, statement word order in embedded questions, and shifting time markers like yesterday. Mark each line as a legal report of the given direct speech — or not.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I can fix the spreadsheet." → "She said she can fix the spreadsheet."
Direct: "When does the tender close?" → "He asked when the tender closed."
Direct: "We must finish the draft today." → "She said they had to finish the draft that day."
Direct: "I have checked the figures." → "He said he had checked the figures."
Direct: "Are the invoices ready?" → "She asked are the invoices ready."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Ability "can" typically backshifts to "could" after a past reporting verb.

Tip: "She said she could fix the spreadsheet."

TRUE — Wh-word stays, tense backshifts, and the clause keeps subject–verb statement order.

Tip: "asked when + subject + past verb," never "when does/did…"

TRUE — Obligation "must" often becomes "had to," and "today" shifts to "that day."

Tip: Present obligation markers (must/today) usually reshape in past reports.

TRUE — Present perfect backshifts cleanly to past perfect after said.

Tip: have/has + past participle → had + past participle.

FALSE — Reported yes/no questions need if/whether and statement order, not inverted "are the invoices…"

Tip: "She asked whether the invoices were ready."
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on modal backshift (can → could, must → had to), present perfect → past perfect, and the if/whether pattern for yes/no reports. Embedded wh-questions should already feel like statements.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The board meets here tomorrow." → "He said the board met here tomorrow."
Direct: "Why did the supplier cancel?" → "She asked why did the supplier cancel."
Direct: "I am reviewing the contract now." → "He said he was reviewing the contract then."
Direct: "Do not sign the annex." → "She told me do not sign the annex."
Direct: "We may raise prices next quarter." → "They said they may raise prices next quarter."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Place and time markers usually shift: "here" → "there," "tomorrow" → "the next day" / "the following day."

Tip: "He said the board met there the following day."

FALSE — Embedded why-questions need statement order and usually past-perfect backshift: not "why did the supplier…"

Tip: "She asked why the supplier had cancelled."

TRUE — Present continuous backshifts to past continuous, and "now" becomes "then."

Tip: am/is/are + -ing → was/were + -ing; now → then.

FALSE — Negative commands in reports use told/asked + object + not + to-infinitive.

Tip: "She told me not to sign the annex."

FALSE — "May" for possibility often becomes "might," and "next quarter" should become "the following quarter."

Tip: "They said they might raise prices the following quarter."
tasks.solution_overview: Four traps stack deictics, leftover do-support, unshifted may/next, and a bare negative command. Only the continuous now→then line is clean.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Please email the client." → "He asked me to email the client."
Direct: "Who approved the budget?" → "She asked who had approved the budget."
Direct: "I will have finished by Friday." → "He said he would have finished by Friday."
Direct: "This policy starts next week." → "She said that policy started the following week."
Direct: "Have you updated the forecast?" → "He asked had I updated the forecast."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Polite requests report as asked + object + to-infinitive.

Tip: Direct "Please…" → "asked someone to…"

TRUE — Subject questions keep who as subject; the tense still backshifts.

Tip: "asked who had approved…" is statement-like and correctly shifted.

TRUE — Future perfect "will have finished" backshifts to "would have finished."

Tip: will → would even inside perfect constructions.

TRUE — "This/next" often become "that/the following" after a past report.

Tip: Demonstratives and relative time words move with the reporting frame.

FALSE — Yes/no perfect questions need if/whether + statement order, not "had I…" inversion.

Tip: "He asked whether I had updated the forecast."
tasks.solution_overview: Four solid reports cover requests, subject questions, future perfect backshift, and this/next shifts. The trap is leftover question inversion after asked.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The margin is too thin." → "The CFO told that the margin was too thin."
Direct: "How long have you worked here?" → "She asked how long I had worked there."
Direct: "We shall revise the offer." → "He said they should revise the offer."
Direct: "I saw the auditor last night." → "She said she had seen the auditor the night before."
Direct: "Can you join the call?" → "He asked could I join the call."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Tell" needs a personal object: tell someone that…; without an object, use "said that…"

Tip: said that / told us that — never bare "told that."

TRUE — Present perfect → past perfect, "here" → "there," and statement order after how long.

Tip: Bundle tense, place, and order shifts together.

TRUE — Formal "shall" for future often reports as "should" (or "would") after past said.

Tip: Treat shall like will when backshifting future meaning.

TRUE — Past simple → past perfect and "last night" → "the night before."

Tip: Relative past time phrases shift just like yesterday/tomorrow.

FALSE — Modal yes/no reports need if/whether + subject + could, not "could I…" inversion.

Tip: "He asked if I could join the call."
tasks.solution_overview: Say versus tell joins the usual backshift package. Watch for missing objects after tell and for inverted modals after asked.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Submit the form before noon." → "She told us to submit the form before noon."
Direct: "I may be late." → "He said he might be late."
Direct: "Where have they put the samples?" → "She asked where they had put the samples."
Direct: "We were discussing the merger." → "He said they had been discussing the merger."
Direct: "I leave for Vienna tonight." → "She said she was leaving for Vienna that night."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Imperatives report as tell/ask + object + to-infinitive.

Tip: Command verb drops; to + base verb carries the instruction.

TRUE — Possibility "may" commonly becomes "might" in past reports.

Tip: may → might is the safe exam backshift.

TRUE — Wh-word + statement order + present perfect → past perfect.

Tip: "asked where they had put…" — no auxiliary before the subject.

TRUE — Past continuous often becomes past perfect continuous after a past reporting verb.

Tip: was/were + -ing → had been + -ing when sequence needs a further step back.

TRUE — Present simple for a near arrangement can report as past continuous, with "tonight" → "that night."

Tip: Timetabled or arranged futures often surface as was/were + -ing in reports.
tasks.solution_overview: All five lines are clean reports: commands with to-infinitive, modal may→might, embedded perfect questions, past continuous deepening, and arranged-future reporting.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I must have left the badge at reception." → "He said he must have left the badge at reception."
Direct: "Will the bank renew the facility?" → "She asked would the bank renew the facility."
Direct: "These costs are rising." → "He said those costs were rising."
Direct: "I used to work in compliance." → "She said she used to work in compliance."
Direct: "Don't forget the annex." → "He reminded me not to forget the annex."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Deduction "must have" often stays unchanged because it already refers to a past conclusion.

Tip: Logical deduction with must have need not backshift further.

FALSE — Yes/no with will needs if/whether + would + subject, not "would the bank…" inversion.

Tip: "She asked whether the bank would renew the facility."

TRUE — "These" → "those" and present continuous → past continuous.

Tip: Demonstratives shift with the reporting viewpoint.

TRUE — "Used to" already marks past habit and normally stays as used to after said.

Tip: No further backshift is required for used to.

TRUE — Negative reminders use not + to-infinitive after remind/tell.

Tip: "reminded me not to forget…" mirrors "told me not to…"
tasks.solution_overview: Some forms resist further shift (must have, used to); others still demand if/whether and statement order. Separate "leave alone" cases from order traps.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Why are you delaying the launch?" → "She asked why were we delaying the launch."
Direct: "I ought to call the broker." → "He said he ought to call the broker."
Direct: "We arrived two days ago." → "They said they had arrived two days ago."
Direct: "Is this the final draft?" → "He asked if that was the final draft."
Direct: "I will phone you later today." → "She said she would phone me later that day."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Keep statement order: "why we were delaying," not "why were we…"

Tip: After asked, never reinvert the auxiliary before the subject.

TRUE — "Ought to" typically remains ought to in reported speech.

Tip: Ought to is already modal-like and usually does not change form.

FALSE — "Ago" normally becomes "before" / "earlier" in past reports; keeping "ago" clashes with the shifted frame.

Tip: "They said they had arrived two days before."

TRUE — Yes/no with if, this→that, and present→past all apply together.

Tip: Bundle if + demonstrative shift + tense shift.

TRUE — will→would and today→that day after past said.

Tip: Future markers and same-day time words both move.
tasks.solution_overview: The hard spots are inverted wh-clauses and leftover "ago." Ought to and clean if/that/will shifts show the correct pattern.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "We need not renew the licence yet." → "She said they need not renew the licence yet."
Direct: "What time does the flight leave?" → "He asked what time the flight left."
Direct: "I have been waiting since Monday." → "She said she had been waiting since Monday."
Direct: "Come back the day after tomorrow." → "They told us to come back in two days' time."
Direct: "I can't approve this invoice." → "He said he couldn't approve that invoice."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Need not" for lack of obligation often stays need not (or becomes did not need to).

Tip: Either unchanged need not or did not need to is acceptable; bare "needed not" is wrong.

TRUE — Wh-clause with statement order and present→past.

Tip: "asked what time + subject + past verb."

TRUE — Present perfect continuous backshifts to past perfect continuous.

Tip: have/has been + -ing → had been + -ing.

TRUE — "The day after tomorrow" can paraphrase as "in two days' time" / "two days later."

Tip: Distant relative time phrases are often reworded, not left literal.

TRUE — can→could and this→that in one tidy report.

Tip: Modal ability and demonstratives usually shift together after past said.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are acceptable advanced reports: need not, embedded timetable questions, perfect continuous backshift, reworded far-future time, and can/this shifts.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Who did you promote?" → "She asked who did I promote."
Direct: "The shares peaked last year." → "He said the shares had peaked the year before."
Direct: "Shall I postpone the webinar?" → "She asked if she should postpone the webinar."
Direct: "We are going to expand into Poland." → "They said they were going to expand into Poland."
Direct: "I won't sign until Friday." → "He said he won't sign until Friday."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Object questions drop do-support and use statement order: "who I had promoted."

Tip: After asked, no "did" before the subject.

TRUE — Past simple → past perfect and "last year" → "the year before."

Tip: Calendar "last…" phrases become "the … before / previous …"

TRUE — Offer/suggestion shall I… reports as if/whether + should.

Tip: "asked if she should…" is the standard mapping.

TRUE — "Be going to" backshifts was/were going to after past said.

Tip: Treat going-to futures like other present forms that shift one step.

FALSE — "Won't" should become "wouldn't" after a past reporting verb.

Tip: will/won't → would/wouldn't in standard backshift.
tasks.solution_overview: Object-question do-support and unshifted won't are the failures. Going-to futures, shall→should offers, and last-year time shifts are the models.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The analyst said, "Inflation is sticky," and later reported that inflation is sticky.
Direct: "Could you circulate the minutes?" → "She asked me if I could circulate the minutes."
Direct: "I was working when the alert sounded." → "He said he had been working when the alert had sounded."
Direct: "Whose laptop is this?" → "He asked whose laptop was this."
Direct: "We needn't have hired extra staff." → "She said they needn't have hired extra staff."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — When the situation is still true, some writers keep present tense after a past report; it is acceptable for ongoing facts.

Tip: Backshift is usual but not compulsory for permanently or still-valid truths.

TRUE — Polite could you… can report as asked + if + could + statement order.

Tip: Ability/request could often stays could inside if-clauses.

FALSE — Over-shifting both verbs to past perfect can distort simultaneous past events; keep the time-clause past simple if it marks the interrupting moment.

Tip: Prefer "had been working when the alert sounded."

FALSE — Statement order needed: "whose laptop this was," not "whose laptop was this."

Tip: Possessive wh-questions still lose inversion in reports.

TRUE — "Needn't have" for unnecessary past action commonly remains needn't have.

Tip: Perfect modal forms for past comments often stay put.
tasks.solution_overview: Optional non-backshift for still-true facts sits beside over-shifted time clauses and inverted whose-questions. Perfect need not and polite could-if reports are fine.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Let's postpone the roadshow." → "She suggested postponing the roadshow."
Direct: "I wish I knew the answer." → "He said he wished he knew the answer."
Direct: "Had you finished before the outage?" → "She asked whether I had finished before the outage."
Direct: "We thrived here last spring." → "They said they had thrived there the previous spring."
Direct: "You had better renegotiate." → "He said I had better renegotiate."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Let's…" suggestions often report as suggested + gerund (or suggested that…).

Tip: Suggest takes a gerund or a that-clause, not bare to-infinitive without that.

TRUE — Wish-clauses already sit in a past-like form; reporting them usually keeps wished + past form.

Tip: Do not force a further unnatural backshift inside wish.

TRUE — Past perfect yes/no questions report with if/whether + had + past participle and statement order.

Tip: Inversion from the direct Had you… disappears after asked.

TRUE — Past simple → past perfect plus here→there and last→previous.

Tip: Stack place and calendar shifts with the tense change.

TRUE — "Had better" for advice typically remains had better after said.

Tip: Had better does not become would better.
tasks.solution_overview: Every line is a valid report: let's→suggest + -ing, wish retention, whether + past perfect, stacked deictics, and unchanged had better.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I would rather stay remote." → "She said she would rather stayed remote."
Direct: "When will you publish the results?" → "He asked when we would publish the results."
Direct: "I might have misread the clause." → "He said he might have misread the clause."
Direct: "Stay where you are." → "Security told us to stay where we were."
Direct: "Did the regulator contact you yesterday?" → "She asked if the regulator had contacted me yesterday."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — After would rather, keep the base verb: "would rather stay," not "stayed."

Tip: Would rather + bare infinitive survives reporting.

TRUE — will→would inside a wh-clause with statement order.

Tip: "asked when + subject + would + verb."

TRUE — "Might have" for past possibility usually stays might have.

Tip: Perfect modals of speculation rarely need further change.

TRUE — Imperative plus embedded where-clause: to-infinitive outside, backshift inside the where-clause.

Tip: "to stay where we were" — both layers handled.

FALSE — "Yesterday" should become "the day before" once the reporting verb is past.

Tip: "…had contacted me the day before."
tasks.solution_overview: Would rather keeps a base verb; yesterday still must shift. Wh-future reports, might have, and nested where-clauses show controlled backshift.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I insist that the clause be rewritten." → "She insisted that the clause be rewritten."
Direct: "How much did the campaign cost?" → "He asked how much the campaign had cost."
Direct: "We will be launching next Monday." → "They said they would be launching the following Monday."
Direct: "I never said that." → "She claimed she had never said that."
Direct: "Are you being serious?" → "He asked if I was being serious."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Formal mandative subjunctive after insist often stays be + past participle in the report.

Tip: Reporting insist that… can preserve the base-form subjunctive.

TRUE — Object how-much questions drop did and backshift to past perfect with statement order.

Tip: "asked how much + subject + had + past participle."

TRUE — Future continuous will be + -ing → would be + -ing, and next → the following.

Tip: Progressive futures backshift the will piece only.

TRUE — Past simple negation becomes past perfect in a past report when the earlier speech act is prior.

Tip: "had never said" places the denial further back.

TRUE — Present continuous passive-like being → past continuous being after if.

Tip: "asked if I was being…" — statement order, tense shifted.
highlights: how much the campaign had cost
tasks.solution_overview: All five succeed: preserved mandative be, cleaned object questions, future continuous backshift, prior-speech past perfect, and continuous being after if.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I would have called if I had known." → "She said she would have called if she had known."
Direct: "Which warehouse stores the spares?" → "He asked which warehouse did store the spares."
Direct: "The offer expires the day after tomorrow." → "They said the offer expired two days later."
Direct: "Must we disclose the conflict?" → "She asked if they had to disclose the conflict."
Direct: "I am to present at nine." → "He said he was to present at nine."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Conditional perfect forms already sit far back and typically stay would have / had + past participle when reported.

Tip: Do not invent an extra layer beyond would have + past perfect.

FALSE — No do-support in the embedded clause: "which warehouse stored the spares."

Tip: Wh-determiners keep statement order without did.

TRUE — "The day after tomorrow" → "two days later" / "in two days" is a natural time rewrite.

Tip: Far deixis is often paraphrased in polished reports.

TRUE — Obligation must in questions often becomes had to after asked if.

Tip: "asked if they had to…" is the usual mapping.

TRUE — Formal "be to" for scheduled duty backshifts was/were to.

Tip: am/is/are to → was/were to after past said.
tasks.solution_overview: One illegal did in a which-clause breaks the set. Elsewhere, remote conditionals, time paraphrase, must→had to, and be-to schedules report cleanly.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "You needn't worry about the audit." → "He told me I didn't need to worry about the audit."
Direct: "Whereabouts is the server rack?" → "She asked whereabouts was the server rack."
Direct: "I have got to leave now." → "He said he had got to leave then."
Direct: "We shall have completed the roll-out by June." → "They said they would have completed the roll-out by June."
Direct: "Why must the filing be public?" → "She asked why the filing had to be public."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Needn't" can report as didn't need to / needn't after a past frame.

Tip: Personal object after told plus shifted lack-of-obligation form.

FALSE — Even with whereabouts, keep statement order: "whereabouts the server rack was."

Tip: Any wh-word still bans auxiliary-before-subject after asked.

TRUE — "Have got to" obligation backshifts to had got to, and now→then.

Tip: Treat have got to like must for backshift purposes.

TRUE — shall have + past participle (future perfect) → would have + past participle.

Tip: Future perfect always yields would have in standard past reports.

TRUE — why + must → why + had to with statement order.

Tip: Obligation questions lose must inversion and often become had to.
tasks.solution_overview: Whereabouts inversion is the sole fault. Needn't→didn't need to, have got to, future perfect, and why-must→had to are sound.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Were the covenants breached last quarter?" → "Counsel asked whether the covenants had been breached the previous quarter."
Direct: "I would prefer you not to disclose this yet." → "She said she would prefer us not to disclose that yet."
Direct: "Dare I ask for a waiver?" → "He asked if he dared ask for a waiver."
Direct: "The team will have been negotiating for six hours by then." → "She said the team would have been negotiating for six hours by then."
Direct: "What if we delay the IPO?" → "He asked what if we delayed the IPO."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Passive past yes/no → whether + past perfect passive + last→previous.

Tip: Voice stays passive; only tense and time words move.

TRUE — Would prefer + object + not to stays structurally; pronouns and this→that adjust.

Tip: Preference patterns largely keep their skeleton under reporting.

TRUE — Rare dare questions can report as if + dared + bare infinitive.

Tip: Modal-like dare often becomes a past lexical dare in reports.

TRUE — Future perfect continuous will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing.

Tip: Only will becomes would; the rest of the stack stays.

TRUE — "What if…" hypotheticals often keep what if and simply backshift the following verb.

Tip: "asked what if we delayed…" is natural exam English.
highlights: had been breached the previous quarter
tasks.solution_overview: A clean advanced sweep: passive perfect reports, prefer + not to, dare, future perfect continuous, and what-if backshift — all grammatical.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Seldom have we seen such volatility." → "She said seldom had they seen such volatility."
Direct: "I was to have signed before noon." → "He said he was to have signed before noon."
Direct: "Who should we notify first?" → "She asked who should we notify first."
Direct: "The data will still be encrypted tomorrow morning." → "He said the data would still be encrypted the next morning."
Direct: "Might the bank extend the covenant holiday?" → "They asked might the bank extend the covenant holiday."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negative inversion can survive inside the reported clause after said, with pronoun and tense already matching.

Tip: Reporting rare inverted rhetoric may keep the inverted shape.

TRUE — "Was to have + past participle" (unfulfilled plan) typically remains was to have…

Tip: This past-scheduled perfect form needs no further shift.

FALSE — Embedded object questions need statement order: "who we should notify first."

Tip: Modal should still follows the subject after asked.

TRUE — Passive future will be → would be, and tomorrow morning → the next morning.

Tip: Voice stays passive while will and time words move.

FALSE — Yes/no might needs if/whether + subject + might, not "might the bank…"

Tip: "They asked whether the bank might extend…"
tasks.solution_overview: Inverted who-should and bare might-yes/no fail. Surviving rhetorical inversion, was-to-have, and passive would-be time shifts are acceptable.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I'd rather you didn't leak this." → "She said she'd rather I didn't leak that."
Direct: "How come the hedge failed?" → "He asked how come the hedge had failed."
Direct: "We used not to disclose bonuses." → "They said they used not to disclose bonuses."
Direct: "Will you have finished by the time I call?" → "She asked if I would have finished by the time she called."
Direct: "Suppose we freeze hiring." → "He suggested that we freeze hiring."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Would rather + past clause for preference about someone else keeps that past shape; this→that adjusts.

Tip: Preferential rather-clauses are not forced into past perfect.

TRUE — Informal how come reports with statement order and optional past perfect for a prior failure.

Tip: "asked how come + subject + (had) + past participle."

TRUE — "Used not to" (or didn't use to) for past habit can remain used not to.

Tip: Habitual used to patterns are already past-oriented.

TRUE — Future perfect in a yes/no question → if + would have, and the time-clause present→past.

Tip: Both the main future perfect and the by-the-time clause shift.

TRUE — Suppose-ideas often become suggested that + base or past form in formal reports.

Tip: Mandative or tentative freeze after suggested that is exam-friendly.
highlights: how come the hedge had failed
tasks.solution_overview: All five are advanced but valid: rather + past clause, how come, used not to, nested would-have with by-the-time, and suggested that.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Not only is the covenant tight, but the waiver is costly." → "She said not only was the covenant tight, but the waiver was costly."
Direct: "I needn't have flagged every footnote." → "He said he needn't have flagged every footnote."
Direct: "Where should the escrow sit?" → "Counsel asked where should the escrow sit."
Direct: "By next March we will have been leasing the site for a decade." → "They said that by the following March they would have been leasing the site for a decade."
Direct: "Was anyone monitoring the feed then?" → "She asked was anyone monitoring the feed then."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correlative not only…but also can keep inversion after said while tenses sit in the past.

Tip: Reporting flashy inversion is optional but grammatical if pronouns and tenses align.

TRUE — Needn't have for unnecessary past action stays needn't have.

Tip: Perfect absence-of-need does not become hadn't need.

FALSE — Statement order required: "where the escrow should sit."

Tip: Modal should follows the subject in embedded wh-questions.

TRUE — next→the following and will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing.

Tip: Long future-perfect-continuous stacks only change will→would.

FALSE — Yes/no past continuous needs if/whether + statement order: "whether anyone was monitoring…"

Tip: Never leave bare "was anyone…" after asked.
tasks.solution_overview: Two order failures remain: should after where, and bare was-anyone after asked. Inverted not only, needn't have, and future perfect continuous reports are fine.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She is a auditor in the compliance team.
He bought a umbrella before the client visit.
We need an new laptop for the analyst.
The board approved an proposal this morning.
Please send me an email with the revised figures.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Auditor" begins with a vowel sound, so English needs "an auditor," not "a auditor." The rest of the sentence is fine; only the choice before the job title is wrong.

Tip: Match a/an to the sound that follows, not just the first letter on the page.

FALSE — "Umbrella" starts with a vowel sound, so the form must be "an umbrella," not "a umbrella."

Tip: First mention of one countable thing usually takes a/an — but only the matching form.

FALSE — "New" begins with a consonant sound (/n/), so English needs "a new laptop," not "an new laptop."

Tip: Adjectives do not change the a/an rule — listen to the sound right after a/an.

FALSE — "Proposal" begins with a consonant sound, so use "a proposal," not "an proposal."

Tip: Specific, already-identifiable groups like "the board" can stay; the error is only the form before proposal.

TRUE — "Email" begins with a vowel sound (/iː/), so "an email" is the correct first-mention form.

Tip: Say the next word aloud; if it starts with a vowel sound, use an.
tasks.solution_overview: This set is about choosing a versus an before a singular countable noun. Listen for vowel versus consonant sounds right after the determiner, including when an adjective comes first.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The manager asked for an honest update on the delay.
They hired a European consultant for the launch.
She completed a MBA while working full time.
We reserved an hotel near the conference centre.
He is an university lecturer in economics.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Honest" starts with a silent h, so the spoken form begins with a vowel sound and takes "an."

Tip: Silent letters still decide a/an by sound, not spelling.

TRUE — "European" begins with a /j/ sound (like "you"), which counts as a consonant sound, so "a European" is correct.

Tip: Eu- and u- words often take a when they sound like they start with "y."

FALSE — "MBA" is normally read letter by letter, starting with /em/, a vowel sound, so it needs "an MBA."

Tip: With abbreviations, base a/an on how you pronounce the first letter.

FALSE — In standard modern pronunciation, "hotel" keeps the /h/, so "a hotel" is the usual form, not "an hotel."

Tip: Prefer a before clearly sounded h- words in contemporary business English.

FALSE — "University" starts with a /j/ sound, so the correct form is "a university lecturer."

Tip: If you can hear a "y" glide at the start, choose a.
tasks.solution_overview: These sentences turn on sound, not spelling. Silent h, letter names in abbreviations, and the "y" glide in words like European and university are the traps to watch.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I read a report yesterday; the report raised several concerns.
Please close a window; it is freezing in here.
She joined the firm as a junior analyst in 2022.
Could you pass me a salt from the tray?
They opened an office in Lisbon last spring.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — First mention uses "a report"; the second mention switches to "the report" because the same document is now identified.

Tip: a/an introduces; the points back to something already specified.

FALSE — In this situation the window is a specific one in the room, so English expects "the window," not "a window."

Tip: When both speakers can identify the thing, prefer the.

TRUE — Job titles after "as" commonly take a/an for one role among many: "as a junior analyst."

Tip: Roles and occupations usually need a/an in this pattern.

FALSE — At the table, "salt" is a specific shared item, so "the salt" is the natural choice.

Tip: Shared, obvious objects in the immediate setting take the.

TRUE — "An office" correctly introduces one new branch; the city name needs no determiner here.

Tip: First mention of one countable workplace unit takes a/an.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on whether the noun is newly introduced or already clear to both speakers. First mention and shared, obvious objects follow different patterns.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The sun was still low when the shift began.
Moon looks unusually bright tonight over the harbour.
She is only person who reviewed the contract.
This is same clause we flagged last week.
He is the tallest candidate in the shortlist.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Unique celestial bodies take "the": "the sun." The workplace noun "the shift" is also definite in context.

Tip: One-of-a-kind referents almost always need the.

FALSE — "Moon" in this sense needs "the moon"; leaving it bare is not standard.

Tip: Pair the with unique natural landmarks and celestial objects.

FALSE — "Only" before a singular noun requires "the only person."

Tip: Patterns with only, same, next, and last usually need the.

FALSE — The fixed pattern is "the same clause," not bare "same clause."

Tip: "Same" almost never stands without the in this use.

TRUE — Superlative forms take "the": "the tallest candidate."

Tip: If you see -est or most + adjective for a unique ranking, expect the.
tasks.solution_overview: Unique things, superlatives, and words like only and same strongly prefer the. Check whether the noun points to one identifiable item in the world or in the set.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The team received useful advice from the mentor.
She gave me an advice about the presentation slides.
We still need more informations before we decide.
The laboratory ordered new equipment last month.
They bought an furniture for the meeting room.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Advice" is uncountable, so it appears with zero article here and is modified by "useful," not by a/an.

Tip: Uncountable abstract nouns often take zero article when used in a general sense.

FALSE — "Advice" cannot take "an"; say "some advice" or "a piece of advice."

Tip: If you need a countable unit, use a piece/bit/item of + uncountable noun.

FALSE — "Information" has no plural form in standard English; use "more information," not "informations."

Tip: Watch for false plurals on uncountable nouns.

TRUE — "Equipment" is uncountable and correctly appears without a/an; "new" simply describes the mass noun.

Tip: Zero article + adjective + uncountable noun is a common correct pattern.

FALSE — "Furniture" is uncountable, so "an furniture" is impossible; use "furniture" or "a piece of furniture."

Tip: Do not place a/an directly before classic uncountables like furniture, equipment, or advice.
tasks.solution_overview: Uncountable nouns reject a/an and usually reject plural -s. Prefer zero article for general reference, or a quantifying phrase such as a piece of when you need a unit.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Progress on the merger has been slower than expected.
The news were surprising for the whole department.
Research shows that remote audits can save time.
We lack an evidence to support that claim.
Traffic was heavy on the way to the airport.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Progress" is uncountable and correctly used with zero article for a general process underway.

Tip: Zero article is normal with progress, research, and similar abstracts.

FALSE — "News" is uncountable and takes a singular verb: "The news was surprising." The determiner "the" can stay; the verb must agree.

Tip: "News" looks plural but behaves as singular.

TRUE — General research findings use zero article: "Research shows…"

Tip: When you mean research as a field or body of work in general, omit a/the.

FALSE — "Evidence" is uncountable, so "an evidence" is wrong; use "evidence" or "a piece of evidence."

Tip: Legal and audit English still treats evidence as uncountable.

TRUE — "Traffic" is uncountable and takes zero article in this general statement about conditions.

Tip: Mass nouns for weather, traffic, and similar conditions usually need no a/an.
tasks.solution_overview: Several everyday business nouns are uncountable even when they end in -s or feel countable. Keep zero article for general reference and avoid a/an before evidence, progress, and traffic.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Children need clear routines at home.
The customers expect faster replies during peak season.
Oil is still a major export for the region.
She drinks the coffee every morning before stand-up.
Managers should document key decisions carefully.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Plural nouns in a general sense take zero article: "Children need…"

Tip: General plurals usually omit the.

TRUE — Here "the customers" can refer to the company's known customer base, so the is acceptable and natural.

Tip: The + plural is fine when the group is definite in context.

TRUE — Uncountable "oil" used generically takes zero article.

Tip: Materials and commodities in general statements often need no determiner.

FALSE — Habitual general coffee-drinking uses zero article: "She drinks coffee every morning," not "the coffee," unless a specific coffee is meant.

Tip: Do not force the onto uncountables used in a general habitual sense.

TRUE — Plural "Managers" in a general professional statement correctly takes zero article.

Tip: Job-title plurals meaning "managers in general" stay bare.
tasks.solution_overview: General plurals and general uncountables prefer zero article. Use the only when the group or substance is already limited to a known set.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He goes to work by bus on most weekdays.
She travelled to Paris by a train last Friday.
They sent the samples by courier overnight.
I usually go to the home after the evening shift.
We went to school together in the same district.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Fixed patterns "go to work" and "by bus" both use zero article.

Tip: Memorise by + transport and go to work/school/bed as zero-article chunks.

FALSE — The transport pattern is "by train," not "by a train."

Tip: After by for means of transport, do not insert a/an.

TRUE — "By courier" follows the same zero-article transport/delivery pattern.

Tip: By + service/means is typically bare.

FALSE — The fixed expression is "go home," never "go to the home" in this meaning.

Tip: Home after go/arrive/get normally takes no to and no the.

TRUE — "Go to school" with zero article means attendance as a student, which fits this sentence.

Tip: Purpose-of-institution uses often drop the.
tasks.solution_overview: Several high-frequency chunks freeze the determiner choice: by bus/train, go to work/school, and go home. Treat them as fixed patterns rather than building them word by word.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Her brother is still in hospital after the operation.
We drove past the hospital on our way to the plant.
Three board members are in the prison for fraud.
The prison on the hill dates from the nineteenth century.
She stayed in bed until noon because of a migraine.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — British English uses zero article in "in hospital" when the person is there as a patient.

Tip: Purpose (patient/prisoner/student) often means zero article with the institution.
