TRUE — When the building itself is meant as a location landmark, "the hospital" is correct.

Tip: Switch to the when you mean the building, not the institutional purpose.

FALSE — As inmates, the natural British pattern is "in prison," not "in the prison."

Tip: Purpose reading → zero; building reading → the.

TRUE — Referring to a specific building as a landmark correctly takes "the prison."

Tip: Physical description and location cues usually signal the building reading.

TRUE — "In bed" for resting/sleeping takes zero article in the standard idiom.

Tip: In bed / in church / in hospital follow the same purpose logic.
tasks.solution_overview: Institution nouns flip between zero article (purpose: patient, prisoner) and the (the building as a place). Read the sentence for purpose versus physical location.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She plays the piano at company events.
He plays the football for the local amateur side.
They listen to the radio during the morning commute.
I watched a television until midnight after the audit.
She is learning the violin with a private tutor.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Musical instruments take "the" in this general ability/habit pattern: "play the piano."

Tip: play + the + instrument is the default.

FALSE — Sports use zero article: "play football," not "play the football."

Tip: Contrast instruments (the) with sports and games (zero).

TRUE — "Listen to the radio" is the standard pattern for the medium.

Tip: the radio / the news are common fixed media patterns.

FALSE — Habitual or general TV watching is "watch television," not "watch a television," unless you mean one physical set.

Tip: Medium versus device: medium often takes zero; a specific device can take a/the.

TRUE — "Learn the violin" follows the same instrument rule as play the piano.

Tip: Keep the with named instruments after play/learn.
tasks.solution_overview: Instruments prefer the; sports prefer zero. Media words like radio and television also have preferred patterns—do not invent a/an forms where the medium itself is meant.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Most employees supported the flexible-hours pilot.
The most of staff opposed the unpaid overtime plan.
Half of the budget has already been committed.
Both candidates gave a strong closing statement.
All of data must be encrypted before transfer.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Most" + plural noun takes zero article when speaking generally about the majority: "Most employees…"

Tip: most + noun (no the) for general majorities.

FALSE — Do not say "the most of staff"; use "most of the staff" or "most staff."

Tip: After most of, you normally need the + definite noun phrase.

TRUE — "Half of the budget" correctly combines the quantifier with a definite noun phrase.

Tip: half/most/some of + the + specific noun is a safe pattern.

TRUE — "Both candidates" needs no article before both; "a strong closing statement" correctly introduces one speech each.

Tip: both/all/each have their own determiner rules—do not stack the before both.

FALSE — "All of data" is incomplete; write "all of the data" or "all data."

Tip: all of must be followed by a determined noun phrase (often with the).
tasks.solution_overview: Quantifier patterns interact with determiners: most + noun, most of the + noun, half of the +, and all of the +. Avoid blending those frames.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She is studying economics at a well-known university.
He majored in the history before joining the museum.
They offer a course in business ethics this term.
The mathematics in this model is unexpectedly elegant.
She teaches the English at a private college.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Academic subjects usually take zero article: "studying economics."

Tip: Subject names in general study contexts stay bare.

FALSE — As a field of study, use "history," not "the history," unless a specific history is meant.

Tip: Zero article for subjects; the only when the noun is narrowed (the history of X).

TRUE — "Business ethics" as a course subject correctly appears without a/the before the subject name; "a course" is the countable shell.

Tip: Count the course, not the subject noun itself.

TRUE — Here "the mathematics" refers to the specific maths in this model, so the is justified.

Tip: The + subject is fine when limited by a postmodifier or clear context.

FALSE — Language subjects in general take zero article: "teaches English," not "teaches the English."

Tip: Language names as school subjects are usually bare.
tasks.solution_overview: Subject and language names are bare in general academic use, but the appears when the noun is limited to a specific body of material. Separate the countable "course" from the subject label.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The Netherlands remains a key logistics hub for the firm.
She moved to United Kingdom after the acquisition.
Their warehouse is just outside Hague, near the port.
We opened a branch in Brazil two years ago.
The Amazon is critical to several of our suppliers' routes.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Country names that are plural or include a common noun often take "the": "the Netherlands."

Tip: the with Netherlands, United Kingdom, United States, Philippines, etc.

FALSE — The standard form is "the United Kingdom," not bare "United Kingdom" after to.

Tip: Full political names with Kingdom/States/Republic usually need the.

FALSE — The city is "The Hague," so the sentence needs "outside The Hague."

Tip: A few place names include The as part of the name.

TRUE — Most single-name countries take zero article: "in Brazil."

Tip: Default for country and city names is zero unless the name belongs to a the-group.

TRUE — Famous rivers take "the": "the Amazon."

Tip: the with rivers, seas, oceans, and canal names.
tasks.solution_overview: Geography has compact rules: most countries and cities are bare, but plural/political names and many waterways take the. A handful of names include The as part of the proper noun.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Lake Victoria appears in several of our regional case studies.
They sailed across Atlantic on a freighter.
Mount Everest still attracts extreme-tourism clients.
We spent a week in Alps after the summit.
The Sahara stretches across much of North Africa.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Individual lakes usually take zero article: "Lake Victoria."

Tip: Lake + name → typically zero; the Great Lakes is an exception as a group.

FALSE — Oceans and seas need "the": "the Atlantic."

Tip: the Atlantic / the Pacific / the Mediterranean.

TRUE — Mountains named with Mount take zero article: "Mount Everest."

Tip: Mount/Mt + name = zero; mountain ranges take the.

FALSE — Mountain ranges take "the": "the Alps."

Tip: Ranges and island groups usually need the.

TRUE — Deserts take "the": "the Sahara."

Tip: the Sahara / the Gobi follow the desert pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Natural features split cleanly: lakes and Mount-names are often bare; oceans, ranges, deserts, and many seas take the. Learn the groups rather than guessing per word.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Poverty remains a structural challenge in several markets we serve.
The life is unpredictable for freelance consultants.
Society must balance growth with environmental limits.
She values the honesty above everything else in negotiations.
Innovation drives long-term competitiveness in this sector.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Abstract nouns used in a general sense take zero article: "Poverty remains…"

Tip: General abstracts (poverty, society, innovation) are usually bare.

FALSE — General "life" does not take the: "Life is unpredictable…"

Tip: Use the life only when limited (the life of a consultant, the life she wanted).

TRUE — "Society" in a broad general claim correctly appears without a/the.

Tip: Zero article signals the concept as a whole.

FALSE — As a general virtue, prefer "honesty," not "the honesty," unless a specific instance is meant.

Tip: Abstract virtues in general statements stay bare.

TRUE — "Innovation" as a general driver of competitiveness takes zero article.

Tip: If no postmodifier narrows the abstract, omit the.
tasks.solution_overview: General abstract nouns prefer zero article. Add the only when a of-phrase or clear context turns the abstract into a specific instance.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The advice she received from counsel was unusually clear.
Equipment that arrived yesterday is still in customs.
An information in the appendix contradicts the summary.
The research published last week challenges our assumptions.
We need a progress before the next steering meeting.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Uncountable "advice" can take "the" when a relative clause identifies a specific body of advice.

Tip: Uncountable + the is fine once the noun is made specific.

TRUE — "Equipment" remains uncountable; zero article works even with a defining relative clause when the noun is used as a mass.

Tip: You may also say "the equipment that arrived…" — both can be acceptable; bare is not wrong here.

FALSE — "Information" cannot take "an"; use "information" or "a piece of information."

Tip: Specificity does not magically make an uncountable noun countable with a/an.

TRUE — "The research published last week" correctly uses the because the postmodifier identifies a particular study set.

Tip: Postmodifiers often licence the with otherwise general uncountables.

FALSE — "Progress" is uncountable, so "a progress" is wrong; say "progress" or "some progress."

Tip: Never place a/an directly before progress.
tasks.solution_overview: Uncountables can take the when narrowed by context, but they still reject a/an. Specificity changes zero versus the, not countability itself.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She was appointed the CEO of a mid-sized fintech firm.
He became a head of legal after the reorganisation.
They elected her treasurer of the local trade association.
She is a only accountant who signed off on the figures.
He remains the unique bidder still active in round three.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After appoint/elect/name, English often uses "the" + unique role: "appointed the CEO."

Tip: Unique office titles after appoint/elect frequently take the.

FALSE — Prefer "the head of legal" for a unique post, or rephrase; "a head of legal" sounds like one of several equal heads.

Tip: Unique organisational roles usually take the, not a.

TRUE — Zero article is also possible after elect/appoint when the title follows directly: "elected her treasurer."

Tip: Both "elected her treasurer" and "elected her the treasurer" appear; bare title after the object is standard.

FALSE — "Only" requires "the only accountant," not "a only." Also, "only" begins with a vowel sound, so a would be wrong even without that rule.

Tip: the only is a fixed determiner pattern.

FALSE — Native wording prefers "the only bidder" (or "the sole bidder"); "the unique bidder" is awkward in this ranking sense.

Tip: For exclusivity in a set, only/sole beats unique with the.
tasks.solution_overview: Titles and unique roles have special determiner habits after appoint/elect and with only. Aim for the with unique posts, and keep the only as a locked chunk.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of clients have requested clearer invoices.
The number of open tickets fell after the release.
She has a knowledge of Portuguese that helps in negotiations.
He has knowledge of Portuguese from years in Lisbon.
We saw a rise in demand after the product redesign.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "A number of" means "several" and correctly pairs with a plural noun; the determiner pattern itself is standard.

Tip: a number of + plural is a fixed quantifying frame.

TRUE — "The number of" correctly refers to a specific total; here the noun phrase is fully determined and grammatical.

Tip: Contrast a number of (several) with the number of (the total count).

TRUE — "A knowledge of" is an accepted pattern when knowledge is limited to a field: "a knowledge of Portuguese."

Tip: Some abstracts allow a when followed by of + field.

TRUE — Zero-article "knowledge of" is equally natural for the same idea.

Tip: Both a knowledge of and knowledge of can be correct; meaning stays general-competence.

TRUE — Countable "rise" correctly takes "a" for a newly mentioned increase: "a rise in demand."

Tip: Singular countable nouns need a determiner in this slot.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch fixed frames such as a number of versus the number of, and notice when abstracts optionally take a before of-phrases. Singular countables like rise still need a determiner.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Next week we will finalise the vendor shortlist.
The next week we will finalise the vendor shortlist.
In 1990s many retailers still relied on paper ledgers.
In the 1990s many retailers still relied on paper ledgers.
On Monday morning the team ships the first batch.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Time expressions like "next week," "last year," and "this morning" take zero article in standard adverbial use.

Tip: next/last/this + time unit → usually zero.

FALSE — "The next week" is wrong in this future-plan adverbial; keep bare "next week."

Tip: Save the next for sequenced items inside a known series (the next slide), not for calendar next week.

FALSE — Decades need "the": "in the 1990s."

Tip: the + decade/century is the normal historical pattern.

TRUE — "In the 1990s" correctly includes the.

Tip: Same pattern for the 1800s, the twentieth century, etc.

TRUE — Days and parts of days used adverbially are often bare: "On Monday morning…"

Tip: on Monday / in summer / at night frequently take zero article.
tasks.solution_overview: Time phrases are highly patterned: next/last week stay bare, while decades and centuries take the. Do not import the into calendar adverbials where English expects zero.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She is in charge of marketing for the northern region.
He was hit on head during the warehouse inspection.
They shook hands after settling the dispute.
Please write the report from beginning to the end carefully.
We need to keep costs under control this quarter.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "In charge of marketing" uses zero article before the functional area in this common workplace pattern.

Tip: Many be/in + noun phrases freeze without a/the (in charge, in debt, in trouble).

FALSE — Body-contact idioms take possessive or the: "on the head" / "on his head," not bare "on head."

Tip: on the + body part is the usual set phrase after verbs like hit/pat.

TRUE — "Shake hands" is a fixed zero-article idiom.

Tip: Learn hands/arms/legs idioms as chunks; do not insert the automatically.

FALSE — The paired idiom is "from beginning to end" (both bare) or "from the beginning to the end"; mixing bare beginning with "the end" is inconsistent.

Tip: Keep both sides of a fixed pair parallel in determiner choice.

TRUE — "Under control" is a zero-article prepositional idiom.

Tip: under control / in progress / on schedule are typically bare.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced accuracy often means recognising idioms where determiner choice is frozen. Prefer the set phrase over building articles logically word by word.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Many applicants submitted their forms before the deadline.
There is much interest in the new graduate programme.
Much candidates failed the first screening round.
Few of the invoices were paid on time.
We received little feedback after the pilot launch.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Many" correctly quantifies the plural countable noun "applicants".

Tip: many + countable plural (applicants, invoices, meetings).

TRUE — "Much" correctly quantifies the uncountable noun "interest".

Tip: much + uncountable (interest, feedback, progress).

FALSE — "Candidates" is countable plural, so "much" is wrong; use "many candidates".

Tip: never pair much with a bare plural countable.

TRUE — "Few of" + plural countable is grammatical (here: few of the invoices).

Tip: few/a few work with countables; little/a little with uncountables.

TRUE — "Little" correctly quantifies uncountable "feedback".

Tip: little = not much (uncountable); few = not many (countable).
tasks.solution_overview: This opener drills the core split: many/few with countables, much/little with uncountables. Scan each noun first—if it can take -s as a plural, avoid much and little.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The amount of waste has decreased since last quarter.
The number of complaints has risen sharply.
The amount of complaints has decreased this month.
A large number of investors attended the briefing.
There was a large amount of traffic on the motorway.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Amount of" pairs correctly with uncountable "waste".

Tip: amount of + uncountable mass nouns.

TRUE — "Number of" pairs correctly with countable "complaints" and takes singular "has".

Tip: the number of + plural noun → singular verb.

FALSE — "Complaints" is countable; prefer "the number of complaints," not "amount of".

Tip: amount → uncountable; number → countable.

TRUE — "A large number of" correctly introduces plural countable "investors".

Tip: a number of + plural usually takes a plural verb.

TRUE — "Amount of" correctly quantifies uncountable "traffic".

Tip: traffic, advice, information, and news are typically uncountable.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on amount versus number. If you can count the units (complaints, investors), use number; if you measure a mass (waste, traffic), use amount.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: All of the equipment is new.
The equipments in the lab need updating.
We bought three new pieces of equipment.
There are many evidences against the claim.
The evidence supports the auditor's conclusion.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Uncountable "equipment" takes a singular verb ("is").

Tip: equipment never takes a plural -s in standard English.

FALSE — "Equipment" is uncountable; do not write "equipments".

Tip: use "pieces of equipment" when you need a count.

TRUE — "Pieces of equipment" is the correct count expression.

Tip: piece/item of + uncountable lets you count units.

FALSE — "Evidence" is uncountable; avoid "evidences" and "many evidences".

Tip: say "much evidence" or "several pieces of evidence".

TRUE — Uncountable "evidence" correctly takes a singular verb.

Tip: evidence, information, and research behave as singular masses.
tasks.solution_overview: Classic exam traps: equipment and evidence are uncountable. Count them only with piece/item of, and keep the verb singular when the noun is the subject.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Less information was available than we expected.
Fewer meetings were scheduled this week.
Less noise was reported after the renovation.
There is little doubt about the board's decision.
There is little doubt about the merger timeline.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Less" correctly pairs with uncountable "information".

Tip: less + uncountable; fewer + countable plural.

TRUE — "Fewer" correctly pairs with countable "meetings".

Tip: if the noun is plural and countable, prefer fewer.

TRUE — "Noise" is uncountable, so "less noise" is the right pair.

Tip: less + mass nouns (noise, traffic, waste).

TRUE — "Little doubt" is the correct uncountable pattern with singular "is".

Tip: there is little + uncountable.

TRUE — Same pattern again: uncountable "doubt" with singular "is" and "little".

Tip: there is/are must match whether the noun is countable plural.
tasks.solution_overview: All five sentences are correct here: less/little with uncountables (information, noise, doubt) and fewer with countable meetings. Use this set as a clean baseline before the later traps.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We still need much more data before we publish.
How many staff attended the compliance workshop?
How much staff attended the compliance workshop?
Only a few suppliers met the new quality criteria.
Only a little suppliers met the new quality criteria.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Much" correctly quantifies uncountable "data" in formal business English.

Tip: in exams, treat data as uncountable with much/little.

TRUE — "How many" correctly asks about countable people (staff as plural headcount).

Tip: how many + countable; how much + uncountable.

FALSE — "Staff" here is treated as people you can count; use "how many," not "how much".

Tip: if you could answer with a number of people, use many.

TRUE — "A few" correctly quantifies plural countable "suppliers".

Tip: a few = some (positive); few = not many (negative tone).

FALSE — "Suppliers" is countable plural; "a little" is reserved for uncountables.

Tip: a little progress / a few suppliers.
tasks.solution_overview: Questions with how much/how many and the a few/a little contrast show up constantly. Decide whether the noun is a countable set of people/items or a mass quantity.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Much of the report was incomplete.
Much of the reports was incomplete.
Many of the reports were incomplete.
Several of the proposals were rejected.
A great deal of research has been published on pricing.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Much of" + singular/uncountable-style unit ("the report") is fine with singular "was".

Tip: much of the + singular noun ≈ a large part of it.

FALSE — With plural "reports," prefer "many of the reports were," not "much of … was".

Tip: much of + singular/mass; many of + plural.

TRUE — "Many of the reports were" correctly matches plural countable + plural verb.

Tip: of-phrases still need verb agreement with the counted noun.

TRUE — "Several" quantifies plural countable "proposals" with plural "were".

Tip: several always implies more than two countables.

TRUE — "A great deal of" pairs with uncountable "research" and singular "has".

Tip: a great deal of ≈ much; use with uncountables.
tasks.solution_overview: Of-phrases (much of / many of / several of) force you to look at the noun after of. Match the quantifier and the verb to that noun's countability and number.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She gave me some useful advice on the presentation.
She gave me some useful advices on the presentation.
We need more detailed information from the supplier.
We need more detailed informations from the supplier.
The news was announced after markets closed.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Advice" is uncountable; "some useful advice" is correct.

Tip: one piece of advice / some advice—never advices.

FALSE — Do not pluralise "advice" as "advices" in standard English.

Tip: count advice with piece(s) of advice.

TRUE — "Information" is uncountable and correctly used without -s.

Tip: information never takes a plural -s in exam English.

FALSE — "Informations" is ungrammatical; keep "information" uncountable.

Tip: bits/pieces of information if you need a count.

TRUE — "News" looks plural but is uncountable and takes singular "was".

Tip: the news is … (not are).
tasks.solution_overview: Advice, information, and news are high-frequency uncountables that learners over-pluralise. Keep them singular and use piece/bit of when you must count.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There is too much paperwork in this department.
There are too many paperworks in this department.
We have made little progress on the integration plan.
We have made few progress on the integration plan.
Only a little time remains before the filing deadline.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Paperwork" is uncountable, so "too much" + singular "is" is correct.

Tip: much/little with mass nouns like paperwork and progress.

FALSE — "Paperworks" is not standard; keep "paperwork" uncountable.

Tip: if it feels like a pile of admin, treat it as a mass noun.

TRUE — "Little progress" correctly uses little with uncountable "progress".

Tip: progress is never "progresses" in this sense.

FALSE — "Progress" is uncountable, so "few" is wrong; use "little progress".

Tip: few needs a plural countable noun.

TRUE — "A little time" correctly quantifies uncountable "time".

Tip: a little = some (positive); little = not much (negative).
tasks.solution_overview: Mass nouns from office life—paperwork, progress, time—take much/little, not many/few. Watch the positive "a little" versus the negative bare "little".

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Fewer employees than expected enrolled in the scheme.
Less employees than expected enrolled in the scheme.
The firm spent less money on marketing this year.
The firm spent fewer money on marketing this year.
There were fewer errors in the revised draft.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Employees" is countable plural, so "fewer" is the precise choice.

Tip: fewer people / fewer errors / fewer days.

FALSE — Prefer "fewer employees"; "less" with plural people is a common trap.

Tip: exams still reward fewer + countable plural.

TRUE — "Money" is uncountable here, so "less money" is correct.

Tip: less + money/time/space; fewer + pounds/hours/rooms when counted.

FALSE — "Money" as a mass noun takes "less," not "fewer".

Tip: fewer only works if the noun is plural and countable.

TRUE — "Errors" is countable plural, so "fewer errors" is correct.

Tip: if you can put a number in front, use fewer.
tasks.solution_overview: Less vs fewer is a classic BBE trap. Count the noun: plural countables want fewer; mass quantities like money want less.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A large amount of evidence was presented in court.
A large number of evidence was presented in court.
Several pieces of evidence were disclosed yesterday.
The equipment have already been installed.
Most of the furniture was damaged in transit.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Amount of evidence" correctly treats evidence as uncountable with singular "was".

Tip: amount of + evidence/equipment/furniture.

FALSE — "Evidence" is not a countable plural; do not use "number of evidence".

Tip: number of + plural countables only.

TRUE — "Pieces of evidence" is the correct countable paraphrase with plural "were".

Tip: piece of unlocks counting for uncountables.

FALSE — "Equipment" is uncountable and needs singular "has," not "have".

Tip: all the equipment is … / has been …

TRUE — "Furniture" is uncountable and correctly takes singular "was".

Tip: furniture, luggage, and equipment share this pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Evidence, equipment, and furniture stay uncountable even when you mean several items. Use amount/pieces of, and keep agreement singular unless you count with piece/item.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There is not much time left to revise the budget.
There are not many times left to revise the budget.
We have plenty of opportunities to renegotiate.
We have plenty of opportunitys to renegotiate.
Hardly any of the respondents supported the change.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Uncountable "time" (duration) correctly pairs with "much" and singular "is".

Tip: not much time = little time remaining.

FALSE — "Times" changes the meaning awkwardly; for remaining duration use "much time," not "many times".

Tip: many times = frequency; much time = duration.

TRUE — "Plenty of" works with plural countable "opportunities".

Tip: plenty of works with both countables and uncountables.

FALSE — Spelling/count error: the plural is "opportunities," not "opportunitys".

Tip: watch irregular -y → -ies plurals on countables.

TRUE — "Hardly any of" + plural countable is a natural negative quantifier pattern.

Tip: hardly any ≈ almost no/none.
tasks.solution_overview: Time as duration is uncountable (much time), while opportunities are countable. Negative quantifiers like hardly any still require the right noun type underneath.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A few of the analysts raised valuation concerns.
Few of the analysts raised valuation concerns, which surprised the board.
Little of the budget remains for contingency spending.
A little of the budget remains for contingency spending.
Few of the budget remains for contingency spending.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "A few of" + plural countable correctly signals a small but real number.

Tip: a few = some (neutral/positive).

TRUE — Bare "few of" is grammatical and stresses scarcity (negative tone).

Tip: few vs a few is tone, not grammar—both need countables.

TRUE — "Little of" + uncountable "budget" correctly stresses almost none remains.

Tip: little of the + uncountable.

TRUE — "A little of" + uncountable is also grammatical and more positive (some remains).

Tip: a little = some; little = not much.

FALSE — "Budget" is uncountable here; "few of the budget" mixes few (countable) with a mass noun.

Tip: few of the funds/items; little of the budget/money.
tasks.solution_overview: A few/few and a little/little are all grammatical in the right environments—the trap is swapping them across the countable/uncountable line, especially with budget/money.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of remote workers is increasing every year.
The number of remote workers are increasing every year.
A number of remote workers are requesting flexible hours.
A number of remote workers is requesting flexible hours.
The amount of remote workers is increasing every year.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "The number of" is a singular subject, so "is" is correct.

Tip: the number of + plural noun → singular verb.

FALSE — Do not use plural "are" after "the number of".

Tip: lock the verb to number (singular), not to workers.

TRUE — "A number of" means several and normally takes a plural verb.

Tip: a number of ≈ some/several → plural verb.

FALSE — With "a number of workers," prefer plural "are," not singular "is".

Tip: contrast the number (singular) vs a number (plural).

FALSE — "Workers" are countable people; use "number of," not "amount of".

Tip: amount of work; number of workers.
highlights: A number of remote workers are
A number of remote workers is
tasks.solution_overview: This task stacks two traps: the number vs a number (verb agreement) and amount vs number (countability). Read the determiner before "number," then check whether people should be counted with number at all.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Much of what the consultant recommended has already been implemented.
Many of what the consultant recommended has already been implemented.
None of the evidence points to intentional fraud.
None of the evidences point to intentional fraud.
Both of the equipment need replacing before the audit.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Much of what…" treats the content as an uncountable mass and takes singular "has".

Tip: much of what / much of the advice → singular.

FALSE — "What the consultant recommended" is not a plural countable set; "many of what" is unnatural.

Tip: many of those points / many of the recommendations.

TRUE — "None of the evidence" with uncountable evidence commonly takes singular "points".

Tip: none of + uncountable → singular verb in careful formal English.

FALSE — "Evidences" is wrong; keep evidence uncountable.

Tip: none of the evidence / none of the pieces of evidence.

FALSE — "Equipment" is uncountable, so "both of the equipment" fails; say "both pieces of equipment".

Tip: both needs two countable units.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced of-phrases: much of what…, none of the evidence, and both… only work when the noun after of can be counted the way the quantifier requires.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We have received a great deal of positive feedback.
We have received a great number of positive feedback.
There was a large quantity of liquid waste in the tank.
There were a large quantity of liquid waste in the tank.
Only a small proportion of respondents chose option C.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "A great deal of" correctly quantifies uncountable "feedback".

Tip: a great deal of ≈ much.

FALSE — "Feedback" is uncountable; "a great number of feedback" is wrong.

Tip: a great number of comments/responses; a great deal of feedback.

TRUE — "Quantity of" with a mass noun and singular "was" is correct.

Tip: quantity/amount often take singular agreement with mass nouns.

FALSE — Singular "quantity" as subject takes "was," not "were".

Tip: there was a large quantity of …

TRUE — "Proportion of" + plural countable "respondents" is a standard research quantifier.

Tip: proportion/percentage of + plural noun is common in reports.
tasks.solution_overview: Deal/number/quantity/proportion look similar but select different noun types and verb forms. Match the head noun's countability, then agree the verb with the quantifier phrase.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Research shows that hybrid work can raise productivity.
Researches show that hybrid work can raise productivity.
Several researches have confirmed the same pattern.
Several studies have confirmed the same pattern.
A piece of research published last year challenged the consensus.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Uncountable "research" correctly takes singular "shows".

Tip: research is / research shows …

FALSE — Do not pluralise academic "research" as "researches" in this sense.

Tip: use studies/projects when you need a plural countable.

FALSE — "Several researches" is unidiomatic; prefer "several studies" or "several research projects".

Tip: several needs a countable plural.

TRUE — "Studies" is the countable counterpart you need after "several".

Tip: research (mass) vs studies (count).

TRUE — "A piece of research" is an acceptable count expression for one study.

Tip: piece of research / item of research in formal prose.
tasks.solution_overview: Research behaves like evidence: keep it uncountable, switch to studies when you need several, or use a piece of research for a single unit.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Far fewer applicants than last year met the language requirement.
Far less applicants than last year met the language requirement.
Considerably less paperwork is required under the new rules.
Considerably fewer paperwork is required under the new rules.
There has been far too much speculation and far too few facts.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Far fewer" intensifies fewer with countable "applicants".

Tip: far/much/considerably can modify fewer/less.

FALSE — Plural countable "applicants" needs "fewer," not "less".

Tip: far fewer people; far less interest.

TRUE — "Considerably less paperwork" correctly uses less with uncountable paperwork.

Tip: intensifiers do not change the countable rule.

FALSE — "Paperwork" is uncountable, so "fewer paperwork" is wrong.

Tip: fewer forms; less paperwork.

TRUE — Parallel contrast: much + uncountable speculation; few + countable facts.

Tip: mixed quantifiers in one sentence still obey each noun's type.
tasks.solution_overview: Intensifiers (far, considerably, too) dress up the same less/fewer and much/few choices. Strip the adverb and decide from the noun alone.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Each item of equipment must be labelled before shipment.
Each equipment must be labelled before shipment.
No further evidence is required at this stage.
No further evidences are required at this stage.
A substantial amount of capital has already been committed.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Item of equipment" correctly creates a countable unit after "each".

Tip: each needs a singular countable noun.

FALSE — "Each equipment" fails because equipment is uncountable.

Tip: each piece/item of equipment.

TRUE — "Evidence" stays uncountable with singular "is".

Tip: no further evidence is …

FALSE — Avoid plural "evidences" and the plural verb that follows it.

Tip: further pieces of evidence if you insist on counting.

TRUE — "Amount of capital" treats capital as an uncountable mass with singular "has".

Tip: capital, funding, and liquidity often behave as uncountables.
tasks.solution_overview: Determiners like each and no further expose uncountable nouns quickly. If the determiner demands a countable unit, insert piece/item of before equipment or evidence.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Scarcely any of the luggage was recovered after the delay.
Scarcely any of the luggages were recovered after the delay.
A surprising number of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.
A surprising amount of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.
Too little attention has been paid to operational risk.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Luggage" is uncountable; "scarcely any of the luggage was" is correct.

Tip: luggage/baggage like furniture: no plural -s.

FALSE — "Luggages" is non-standard; keep luggage uncountable with singular agreement.

Tip: pieces of luggage if you need a count.

TRUE — "Criteria" is plural; "a surprising number of the criteria were" matches countability and plural verb.

Tip: criterion (singular) / criteria (plural).

FALSE — Prefer "number of the criteria"; amount is for mass nouns, not plural criteria.

Tip: amount of inconsistency; number of criteria.

TRUE — "Too little attention" correctly uses little with uncountable attention.

Tip: little attention / much attention; few comments.
tasks.solution_overview: Mixes luggage (uncountable) with criteria (plural countable) and attention (uncountable). Identify each head noun's class before choosing any/number/amount/little.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board found insufficient evidence to proceed with sanctions.
The board found insufficient evidences to proceed with sanctions.
There remains a large number of unresolved issues in the contract.
There remains a large amount of unresolved issues in the contract.
Fewer than ten percent of the equipment have been calibrated.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Insufficient evidence" correctly keeps evidence uncountable.

Tip: sufficient/insufficient + uncountable evidence/information.

FALSE — "Evidences" is wrong in this legal/business sense.

Tip: insufficient pieces of evidence if counting is required.

FALSE — "A large number of unresolved issues" is plural in sense, so prefer "there remain," not singular "remains".

Tip: there remain + plural; there remains + singular/mass.

FALSE — "Issues" are countable, so "amount of unresolved issues" is off, and singular "remains" still clashes.

Tip: number of issues remain; amount of uncertainty remains.

FALSE — Double error: equipment is uncountable (not "fewer than ten percent of the equipment have"); prefer "less than ten percent of the equipment has been calibrated" or "fewer than ten pieces of equipment have…".

Tip: percent of + uncountable → singular; fewer needs countable units.
tasks.solution_overview: The hardest set combines evidence, number vs amount, there remain(s), and percent-of agreement with equipment. Resolve countability first, then force verb agreement to follow.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The revised bid is more cheaper than the competitor's offer.
This warehouse is larger than the one we leased last year.
Of the twelve suppliers, Apex delivered the worse service.
The new courier route is less congested than the old one.
She performed more better in the Q3 review than in Q2.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Cheaper" already carries the comparative; "more cheaper" is a double comparative. Use "cheaper" alone.

Tip: Drop "more" when the adjective already takes -er.

TRUE — One-syllable "large" correctly forms the comparative with -er: "larger."

Tip: Short adjectives usually take -er, not "more."

FALSE — With a group larger than two, you need the superlative "worst," not the comparative "worse."

Tip: Of three or more → worst / best / least; of two → worse / better / less.

TRUE — "Less" + adjective correctly forms a comparative of inferiority for a two-item comparison.

Tip: "Less … than" compares two; "least" ranks among many.

FALSE — "Better" is already comparative; "more better" doubles the marking. Use "better" alone.

Tip: Never stack "more" with an irregular comparative.
tasks.solution_overview: Read each sentence for how comparison is marked. Watch for double marking (more + -er), and check whether the form is comparative (two items) or superlative (a group). Irregulars like better/worse have their own shapes — do not add "more."

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Among the five regional offices, Singapore posts the highest utilisation rate.
The renovated lobby looks gooder than it did before the fit-out.
Payroll costs were lower this month than in February.
The board found the revised forecast less optimistic than the first draft.
This is the most fastest checkout process the retailer has trialled.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Highest" is the correct superlative for ranking one office among five.

Tip: Use -est / most when ranking within a group of three or more.

FALSE — The irregular comparative of "good" is "better," not "gooder."

Tip: Memorise good → better → best; never invent -er on irregulars.

TRUE — One-syllable "low" correctly takes -er: "lower."

Tip: One-syllable adjectives almost always use -er / -est.

TRUE — "Less optimistic than" correctly compares two forecasts on a multi-syllable adjective.

Tip: Multi-syllable adjectives take more/less, not -er.

FALSE — "Fastest" is already a superlative; "most fastest" doubles it. Use "the fastest."

Tip: Never pair "most" with an -est form.
tasks.solution_overview: Check whether the adjective needs -er/-est or more/most, and whether any irregular (good/better/best) is mangled. Double superlatives like "most fastest" are always wrong.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is more smarter than the other analysts on the desk.
Of all the tenders, this one is the less expensive.
The updated brochure is more informative than the previous edition.
Customer complaints rose more worser after the outage.
This prototype runs gooder under peak load than the pilot build.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Smarter" already marks the comparative; drop "more."

Tip: If you see "more" + -er together, mark FALSE.

FALSE — Among many tenders you need "the least expensive," not "the less expensive."

Tip: less = two; least = three or more.

TRUE — Multi-syllable "informative" correctly takes "more … than."

Tip: Three-or-more-syllable adjectives: more/most + base form.

FALSE — "Worse" is the comparative of "bad"; "more worser" is a double error. Use "worse."

Tip: bad → worse → worst — no "more," no "worser."

FALSE — Use "better," the irregular comparative of "good."

Tip: "Gooder" is never acceptable in formal English.
tasks.solution_overview: This set leans on common traps: double comparatives, less/least with group size, and irregular good/bad. Only one sentence is clean — find the correctly formed "more … than."

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Fuel efficiency is higher in the hybrid fleet than in the diesel fleet.
It is the most affordable packaging option among the three quotes.
The new tower is more taller than the adjacent block.
Of the three neighbourhoods, this one has the least traffic noise.
The newer design is significantly lighter than its predecessor.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correct comparative "higher … than" for a one-syllable adjective.

Tip: higher/lower are safe one-syllable comparatives.

TRUE — Correct superlative with "most" for multi-syllable "affordable."

Tip: most + long adjective is the standard superlative pattern.

FALSE — Double comparative: use "taller," not "more taller."

Tip: Delete "more" before any -er form.

TRUE — Correct superlative of inferiority with "least" among three.

Tip: least + noun/adjective ranks the lowest in a group.

TRUE — Correct comparative "lighter" for one-syllable "light."

Tip: -er on short adjectives is the default.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of five are well-formed. Isolate the one double comparative ("more taller") and confirm the rest use -er, most, or least correctly.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Unit labour costs fell further than management had projected.
The audit trail is clearer than the one in last year's system.
This hedge fund is more volatile than the balanced portfolio.
Among all listed brands, ours remains the best known in the region.
Margins were thinner than in the previous quarter.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Further" is a correct irregular comparative for degree or extent.

Tip: further/farther both work for figurative extent in business English; further is common.

TRUE — Adjective "clear" correctly takes -er: "clearer."

Tip: Adjectives ending in -r still take -er (clearer, nearer).

TRUE — Multi-syllable "volatile" correctly takes "more … than."

Tip: more + adjective + than for longer adjectives.

TRUE — Irregular superlative "best" is correct for ranking fame among many.

Tip: good → better → best; best known is a common compound.

TRUE — Comparative "thinner" (double n + -er) is correctly formed.

Tip: Short adjectives with a short vowel often double the final consonant: thin → thinner.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are correct this time. Use it as a checklist of clean patterns: further, -er, more + long adjective, irregular best, and consonant doubling.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Sales were more higher in June than in May.
The compliance pack is the least complex of the four templates.
Their offer is the most unique proposal we have ever received.
Cash reserves are stronger now than they were at year-start.
This KPI is more worse than last month's reading.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Higher" already marks comparison; "more higher" is wrong. Use "higher."

Tip: more + -er is always a red flag.

TRUE — "Least complex" correctly ranks inferiority among four.

Tip: least + adjective for the lowest degree in a set.

FALSE — In careful exam English, "unique" is not normally graded; avoid "most unique." Prefer "unique" alone or "most distinctive."

Tip: Absolutes like unique/perfect rarely take more/most in formal marking.

TRUE — Correct comparative "stronger … than."

Tip: strong → stronger is a regular one-syllable pattern.

FALSE — Use "worse," not "more worse."

Tip: Irregulars do not take "more."
tasks.solution_overview: Look for stacked markers (more higher, more worse) and absolute adjectives that should not be graded. Two sentences are sound.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Delivery times are shorter with the overnight service than with standard shipping.
Of the two candidates, Maya is the most experienced.
The revised fee schedule is less punitive than the original.
That was the worst quarterly result the division has posted.
Inventories are more larger than the safety-stock target.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correct comparative "shorter … than."

Tip: short → shorter is regular.

FALSE — For exactly two people, prefer the comparative: "the more experienced."

Tip: Two items → comparative; three or more → superlative.

TRUE — Correct "less … than" comparative of inferiority.

Tip: less + adjective + than for two-way comparison.

TRUE — Irregular superlative "worst" is correct.

Tip: bad → worse → worst.

FALSE — Double comparative: use "larger."

Tip: Strip "more" before -er.
tasks.solution_overview: Group size matters: two candidates take "the more …," while a full history of quarters can take "the worst." Spot the double comparative as well.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The eastern plant is farther from the port than the western plant.
Customer churn is the lowest it has been in five years.
The software is more easier to deploy than the legacy suite.
This bond is less risky than the emerging-market alternative.
Among all departments, Finance submitted the most detailed budget narrative.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Farther" correctly compares physical distance between two sites.

Tip: farther often = physical distance; further often = figurative — both accepted.

TRUE — Correct superlative "lowest" for a multi-year ranking.

Tip: low → lower → lowest.

FALSE — "Easier" already comparative; drop "more."

Tip: Double comparative trap.

TRUE — Correct "less risky than" for a two-way comparison.

Tip: less + adjective + than.

TRUE — Correct "most detailed" superlative among many departments.

Tip: most + multi-syllable adjective.
tasks.solution_overview: Confirm distance (farther), rankings (lowest/most), and inferiority (less). Only the "more easier" line fails.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The sooner we close the books, the more better the audit will go.
She is elder than her co-manager by two years.
The denser the traffic near the depot, the slower the turnaround time becomes.
This solution is more preferable to the in-house alternative.
Of every branch in the network, Leeds performed more poorly.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The idiom is "the sooner … the better"; "more better" is wrong.

Tip: In the … the … patterns, use bare comparatives: the sooner, the better.

FALSE — For age comparison use "older than," not "elder than." "Elder" is mainly attributive (elder sister).

Tip: older than (predicative); elder mainly before a noun.

TRUE — Correct double-comparative pattern: the + comparative, the + comparative.

Tip: the X-er …, the Y-er … is a standard correlative comparative.

FALSE — "Preferable" already implies comparison; avoid "more preferable." Say "preferable to" or "more desirable than."

Tip: Do not grade adjectives that already encode preference.

FALSE — Ranking among all branches needs a superlative such as "the most poorly" / "the worst," not a bare comparative without a than-clause.

Tip: Among all → superlative form.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder traps: the … the … correlatives, elder vs older, and adjectives that already contain comparison (preferable). Only one line is fully correct.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Lead times grew longer after the supplier consolidation.
The least attractive clause in the contract is the early-termination fee.
Output per shift is better than the industry median.
Spot prices became increasingly sensitive to fuel costs as demand rose.
This tranche carries a higher coupon than the previous issue.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correct comparative "longer" when the baseline is clear from context.

Tip: Comparatives can stand without an explicit than-phrase if the contrast is obvious.

TRUE — Correct "least attractive" for ranking among contract clauses.

Tip: least + adjective for lowest appeal.

TRUE — Irregular comparative "better" is correctly used.

Tip: good → better.

TRUE — "Increasingly sensitive" correctly intensifies the adjective without a faulty double comparative.

Tip: increasingly + adjective is cleaner than "increasingly more" in exam prose.

TRUE — Correct "higher … than."

Tip: high → higher.
tasks.solution_overview: A clean set emphasising least, better, higher, and progressive intensification. Treat each as a model form when you revise.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The revised SLA is as strict as the previous agreement.
This server rack is more compacter than the old chassis.
Fewer customer tickets were opened this week than last week.
The meeting ran more longer than scheduled.
Of the six bids, ours was the least aggressive on price.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Equality comparative "as … as" is correctly formed.

Tip: as + adjective + as compares equal degree — no -er here.

FALSE — Do not combine "more" with -er: use "more compact" or, if accepted, "compacter" — not both.

Tip: Pick one marking system, never both.

TRUE — "Fewer" correctly compares countable tickets.

Tip: fewer + countable plural; less + uncountable (usually).

FALSE — Double comparative: use "longer."

Tip: more + -er → FALSE.

TRUE — Correct "least aggressive" among six.

Tip: least + adjective for the lowest degree in a set.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on as … as equality, few/less with countable nuance in comparative frames, and whether -er is wrongly replaced by more. Three items are correct.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Between the two warehouses, Dock B has the largest capacity.
There is less downtime on the night shift than on the day shift.
This is the most cheapest freight forwarder on the shortlist.
Staff retention is better here than at the previous employer.
We need a more better buffer against currency swings.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — For exactly two, prefer "the larger capacity," not the superlative "largest."

Tip: Between two → comparative; among many → superlative.

TRUE — "Less" correctly compares uncountable downtime between two shifts.

Tip: less + uncountable; fewer + countable.

FALSE — Double superlative: use "the cheapest."

Tip: most + -est is always wrong.

TRUE — Irregular "better" is correct.

Tip: good → better → best.

FALSE — Use "better," not "more better."

Tip: Irregular comparative already includes the degree marker.
tasks.solution_overview: Check two-item vs many-item forms, irregular little/less/least, and whether "most" is wrongly attached to an -est word. Two are correct.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The least expensive option still meets the safety specification.
The revised deck is more clear than the first draft.
Among the pilot sites, Manchester showed the most consistent uptime.
Demand proved weaker than the seasonal model predicted.
The CFO argued that a smaller inventory float would free working capital.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correct "least expensive" for ranking cost among options.

Tip: least + long adjective is standard.

FALSE — Prefer "clearer than" for one-syllable "clear"; "more clear" is awkward in careful marking.

Tip: One-syllable adjectives normally take -er, not more.

TRUE — Correct "most consistent" superlative among several sites.

Tip: most + multi-syllable adjective.

TRUE — Correct comparative "weaker."

Tip: weak → weaker.

TRUE — Correct comparative "smaller."

Tip: small → smaller.
tasks.solution_overview: Subtler business traps: absolute adjectives, wrong syllable strategy (more + short adj), and clean least/most. Four sentences pass.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The more transparent the disclosure, the greater the investor confidence.
We received less invoices this quarter than in Q1.
Fraud losses were worse than anything recorded in the prior decade.
This covenant is the most strictest in the entire facility agreement.
Shipping via rail is more economical than air freight for bulk loads.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correct correlative comparative: the more …, the greater ….

Tip: Keep parallel comparative forms on both sides of the correlative.

FALSE — "Invoices" is countable; use "fewer invoices," not "less invoices."

Tip: less → uncountable; fewer → countable plurals.

TRUE — Irregular comparative "worse" is correct.

Tip: bad → worse → worst.

FALSE — Double superlative: use "the strictest."

Tip: most + -est → FALSE.

TRUE — Correct "more economical than" for a longer adjective.

Tip: more + adjective + than.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch correlative the … the …, double marking on irregulars, and whether "less" is used where "fewer" is required with count nouns. Three are correct.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Of the two frameworks, GDPR is the most restrictive for our data flows.
Turnover became more bad after the product recall.
The least disruptive migration path is a weekend cutover.
Their elder warehouse sits nearer the motorway than the new hub.
This algorithm is more simpler than the neural-net alternative.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — With exactly two frameworks, prefer "the more restrictive."

Tip: Two → comparative; many → superlative.

FALSE — Use "worse," not "more bad."

Tip: Irregular: bad → worse.

TRUE — Correct "least disruptive" ranking among migration options.

Tip: least + adjective for minimal impact.

FALSE — "Elder" is wrong for buildings/age of sites; use "older warehouse."

Tip: elder is mainly for people in fixed phrases; older is the general comparative.

FALSE — Double comparative: use "simpler."

Tip: more + -er → FALSE.
tasks.solution_overview: Difficulty climbs: mixed syllable rules, false friends like "elder," and ranking with least/most. One sentence only is fully correct.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Among all SKUs, the seasonal gift set generates the best margin.
The team responded more quicker than the vendor's support desk.
Idle cash balances were the lowest across the group's ten entities.
A less aggressive hedge ratio left more upside on the table.
This was the worse breach in the company's history.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Irregular superlative "best" correctly ranks among many SKUs.

Tip: good → better → best.

FALSE — "Quicker" already comparative; use "more quickly" (adverb) or "quicker" — not "more quicker."

Tip: Do not stack more with -er on adverbs either.

TRUE — Correct superlative "lowest" among ten entities.

Tip: low → lower → lowest.

TRUE — Correct "less aggressive" comparative of inferiority.

Tip: less + adjective for reduced degree.

FALSE — History implies many incidents: use "the worst breach," not "the worse."

Tip: worse = of two; worst = of many / of all time.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced ranking and irregulars. Confirm best/worst/least and whether "more" wrongly modifies an already comparative adverb.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The redesign is not as costly as the full platform rebuild.
Please escalate this ticket furtherest up the chain.
Our stance is more perfect now that legal has signed off.
Credit spreads widened further after the downgrade.
Of the many scenarios, base case is the less probable.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correct negated equality: "not as … as."

Tip: not as + adjective + as is the standard equality negation.

FALSE — The superlative of "far" is "furthest" / "farthest," not "furtherest."

Tip: far → further/farther → furthest/farthest.

FALSE — "Perfect" is an absolute; avoid "more perfect." Prefer "closer to perfect" or "improved."

Tip: Absolutes (perfect, unique, complete) resist more/most in careful English.

TRUE — Correct irregular comparative "further."

Tip: further for figurative distance/degree is standard in finance copy.

FALSE — Among many scenarios use "the least probable," not "the less probable."

Tip: less (two) vs least (many).
tasks.solution_overview: Exam-level nuance: as … as negation, far/further, and absolute grading. Two statements survive.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The broader the distribution network, the harder it is to keep service levels uniform.
Warranty claims proved fewer than the actuarial model assumed.
The board preferred a more safer capital structure.
This covenant package is the most onerous the bank has tabled this year.
Latency is lower on the fibre link than on the microwave backup.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correct the … the … correlative with two -er forms.

Tip: Match comparative morphology on both halves.

TRUE — "Fewer" correctly compares countable claims.

Tip: fewer + countable plural.

FALSE — Double comparative: use "safer."

Tip: more + -er → FALSE.

TRUE — Correct "most onerous" among this year's packages.

Tip: most + multi-syllable adjective.

TRUE — Correct comparative "lower … than."

Tip: low → lower.
tasks.solution_overview: Near-exam intensity: correlatives, syllable choice, and double marking on irregulars. Four are correct — find the single fault.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The more diversified the client base, the less exposed the firm is to a single sector shock.
Among rival platforms, ours remains the least intrusive for end users.
Settlement risk looks worse under T+0 than under T+2.
Peak load is heavier on Fridays than on midweek trading days.
This is the most pragmatic workaround until the core system is replaced.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correct correlative with more … and less ….

Tip: the more …, the less … is a valid correlative pattern.

TRUE — Correct "least intrusive" ranking among rivals.

Tip: least + adjective for minimal intrusion.

TRUE — Irregular comparative "worse … than" is correct for a two-way contrast.

Tip: worse for two; worst for many.

TRUE — Correct comparative "heavier … than" (y → i + -er).

Tip: heavy → heavier is the standard spelling change.

TRUE — Correct "most pragmatic" superlative among workarounds.

Tip: most + long adjective.
tasks.solution_overview: Highest band: mixed traps including wrong superlative for two items, invented irregulars, and clean least/most. Five true answers — treat as a gold-standard set.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Between Paris and Lyon, Paris is the busiest logistics node for us.
Returns were more worse in apparel than in electronics.
Of all the pilots, the Dublin trial produced the best conversion rate.
The dashboard is more user-friendlier after the redesign.
That clause is the most complete indemnity we can offer.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Exactly two cities → prefer "the busier logistics node," not "the busiest."

Tip: Between A and B → comparative.

FALSE — Use "worse," not "more worse."

Tip: No more before irregular comparatives.

TRUE — Irregular superlative "best" correctly ranks among all pilots.

Tip: good → better → best.

FALSE — Do not combine "more" with -er on a compound: use "more user-friendly" or "user-friendlier," not both.

Tip: One comparative marker only.

FALSE — "Complete" is treated as absolute in careful exam English; avoid "most complete." Prefer " fullest" only when grading extent, or rephrase as "the most comprehensive."

Tip: Watch absolute adjectives under most/more.
tasks.solution_overview: Final stretch: absolute grading, double marking, two-vs-many, and one clean irregular superlative. Only one statement is correct.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Despite the rising costs, the company expanded into two new markets.
Despite of the rising costs, the company expanded into two new markets.
Although the rising costs, the company expanded into two new markets.
Because the delay, the product launch slipped by three weeks.
The plan failed owing insufficient demand in the pilot region.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Despite" takes a noun phrase directly, so "Despite the rising costs" is well formed before the main clause.

Tip: If you can replace the linker with "in spite of," you almost always want a noun, not a full clause.

FALSE — Never write "despite of." Use "despite the rising costs" or "in spite of the rising costs."

Tip: "Despite of" is one of the most common exam traps — delete "of" on sight.

FALSE — "Although" needs a clause with a verb: "Although costs rose," not a bare noun phrase.

Tip: Ask "is there a finite verb after although?" If not, switch to despite / in spite of.

FALSE — "Because" introduces a clause; for a noun use "because of the delay" (or "Because there was a delay").

Tip: "Because" + noun is almost always wrong — insert "of" or rebuild as a full clause.

FALSE — The fixed pattern is "owing to" + noun: "owing to insufficient demand."

Tip: Treat "owing to" as one unit; if "to" is missing, the sentence fails.
tasks.solution_overview: This set checks whether you pick the right linker shape: noun after despite / because of / owing to, and a full clause after although / because. Read each connector and ask what kind of material follows it before you mark true or false.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of the budget freeze, the research team finished the prototype.
Although the mid-year funding cut, the research team finished the prototype.
Costs rose; however, the firm still hired two analysts.
Costs rose, however the firm still hired two analysts without any stronger punctuation.
The merger stalled owing regulatory objections from two agencies.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "In spite of" + noun phrase is the correct concessive pattern here.

Tip: "In spite of" and "despite" are interchangeable before a noun; neither takes a bare clause.

FALSE — "Although" needs a clause with a verb: "Although funding was cut mid-year…"

Tip: A noun after although is almost always a despite transplant — rewrite or switch linker.

TRUE — As a conjunctive adverb, "however" sits well after a semicolon (or full stop) between two independent clauses.

Tip: Semicolon / period + however + comma is the clean formal pattern.

FALSE — A bare comma before conjunctive "however" is weak or wrong in formal writing; prefer a semicolon or a new sentence.

Tip: If however could start a new sentence, do not glue it with only a comma.

FALSE — Restore the full linker: "owing to regulatory objections."

Tip: "Owing" without "to" is never complete in this pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Contrast linkers come in two families: despite / in spite of (noun) versus although (clause), plus however between full sentences. Check punctuation around however and whether owing to is complete.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Because of the customs backlog, shipments arrived five days late.
Because shipments were delayed at customs, the warehouse ran short of stock.
Even though risks remained, the board approved the acquisition.
Even though the remaining risks, the board approved the acquisition.
Whereas revenue climbed, operating margins narrowed.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Because of" + noun phrase correctly gives the reason.

Tip: Use because of before nouns; reserve bare because for clauses.

TRUE — "Because" + full clause is the other correct reason pattern.

Tip: If you already have subject + verb after because, do not add "of."

TRUE — "Even though" takes a clause, and "risks remained" supplies one.

Tip: Even though ≈ although: both want finite clauses.

FALSE — "Even though" cannot take a noun phrase alone; write "even though risks remained."

Tip: Swap even though → despite when only a noun follows.

TRUE — "Whereas" contrasts two full clauses cleanly.

Tip: Whereas needs clause + clause; "whereas rising revenue" without a verb is wrong.
tasks.solution_overview: Cause and concession each have a clause form and a noun form. Match because / even though / whereas to clauses, and because of to nouns — that single check resolves most of these items.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Despite of repeated warnings, the supplier missed every milestone.
In spite the repeated warnings, the supplier missed every milestone.
Although the supplier missed every milestone, the contract was renewed.
The audit was postponed because of staff shortages in the regional office.
Demand collapsed; however, inventory levels stayed high through May.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Drop "of": "Despite repeated warnings…"

Tip: Despite never partners with of; in spite always needs of.

FALSE — The full phrase is "in spite of," not "in spite" alone.

Tip: Remember the trio: despite / in spite of / although — learn the prepositions as fixed spelling.

TRUE — Although + clause correctly sets up the contrast with the main clause.

Tip: When the concessive idea has its own verb, although is usually safer than despite.

TRUE — Because of + noun phrase is the right causal linker here.

Tip: Staff shortages is a noun phrase, so because of (not bare because) is required.

TRUE — Semicolon + however correctly joins two contrasting independent clauses.

Tip: Read however as a sentence adverb: it likes strong punctuation before it.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch the spelling pairs: despite (no of) versus in spite of (of required). Then confirm although and however are doing clause-level work with proper punctuation.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Owing to weak consumer confidence, retailers cut promotional budgets.
Because of weak consumer confidence, retailers cut promotional budgets.
Despite consumer confidence remaining weak, retailers still cut budgets.
Although consumer confidence remained weak, retailers still cut budgets.
However, the board delayed the dividend announcement until June.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Owing to" + noun phrase correctly states the cause.

Tip: Formal reports love owing to / because of before abstract nouns like confidence.

TRUE — "Because of" + noun phrase is an equally correct causal pattern here.

Tip: Because of and owing to are near-interchangeable before nouns.

TRUE — Despite can take a gerund noun phrase ("consumer confidence remaining weak").

Tip: Despite + -ing phrase is fine; despite + finite clause usually is not.

TRUE — Although + finite clause ("remained weak") is the clean concessive form.

Tip: If you can hear a tensed verb after although, the clause test usually passes.

TRUE — Sentence-initial "However," with a following comma correctly opens a contrast.

Tip: Starting with However is fine; just do not leave it mid-sentence with only a weak comma before it.
tasks.solution_overview: Here the traps sit in small words: the missing to after owing, and the wrong follow-on after although versus despite. Read the material after each linker as carefully as the linker itself.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bid failed because of the incomplete disclosure package.
The bid failed because the disclosure package was incomplete.
The bid failed because of the disclosure package was incomplete.
In spite of incomplete disclosure, the committee advanced the bid to diligence.
Whereas the disclosure package was incomplete, the financial model looked solid.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Because of + noun phrase correctly explains the failure.

Tip: Incomplete disclosure package is a noun — because of fits.

TRUE — Because + clause is equally correct when you spell out subject + verb.

Tip: Both because and because of can be right; the grammar after them decides.

FALSE — Do not stack "because of" onto a full clause; drop "of" or rewrite the clause as a noun.

Tip: "Because of + subject + verb" is almost always a false hybrid.

TRUE — In spite of + noun phrase is the right concessive frame.

Tip: Incomplete disclosure is a noun idea — in spite of / despite both work.

TRUE — Whereas contrasts two complete clauses about disclosure versus the model.

Tip: Use whereas for side-by-side contrasts, not for simple cause.
highlights: because of the disclosure package was
tasks.solution_overview: Cause linkers are easy until someone glues because of onto a whole clause. Check that after because of you only have a noun idea, and after because / whereas you have a real clause.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Despite the fact that cash flow was tight, payroll was met on time.
Despite that cash flow was tight, payroll was met on time.
Although cash flow was tight, payroll was met on time.
Cash flow was tight. However, payroll was met on time.
Cash flow was tight however payroll was met on time.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Despite the fact that" + clause is an accepted formal workaround when you need a clause after despite.

Tip: Prefer plain although when you can; despite the fact that is wordy but grammatical.

FALSE — "Despite that" + clause is non-standard in careful exam English; use although or despite the fact that.

Tip: If you want a clause, switch to although rather than forcing despite.

TRUE — Although + clause is the cleanest concessive choice here.

Tip: When both options work, although is usually shorter and safer than despite the fact that.

TRUE — A full stop before However correctly separates the contrasting sentences.

Tip: Period + However + comma is as strong as semicolon + however.

FALSE — Running however between clauses with no strong punctuation is incorrect in formal writing.

Tip: Never leave however floating between clauses with zero commas or stops.
tasks.solution_overview: Despite wants nouns; although wants clauses; however wants sentence-level punctuation. These five lines test those three habits in a cash-flow story.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Owing to the currency swing, imported components became markedly dearer.
Because of the currency swing, imported components became markedly dearer.
Although the currency swing, imported components became markedly dearer.
In spite of the currency swing, the pricing team held list prices steady.
Whereas the currency swing, the pricing team held list prices steady.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Owing to + noun correctly marks the cause of the cost rise.

Tip: Owing to and because of are near twins before nouns.

TRUE — Because of + noun is equally correct in the same slot.

Tip: Either linker works; do not mix them with although’s clause rule.

FALSE — Although needs "Although the currency swung" or similar, not a bare noun.

Tip: Currency swing is a noun — feed it to despite / because of / owing to instead.

TRUE — In spite of + noun correctly frames the concession.

Tip: Holding prices steady despite a swing is a classic despite / in spite of pattern.

FALSE — Whereas requires a full clause, not a noun phrase.

Tip: Rewrite as "Whereas the currency swung…" or switch to despite.
tasks.solution_overview: Same noun idea — the currency swing — can follow owing to, because of, or in spite of, but not although or whereas. Let the linker dictate the grammar of what follows.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The pilot succeeded despite early scepticism from the regional managers.
The pilot succeeded in spite of early scepticism from the regional managers.
The pilot succeeded although early scepticism from the regional managers.
Early scepticism was widespread; however, the pilot still met its adoption target.
Early scepticism was widespread, the pilot however still met its adoption target with no change in word order.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Despite + noun phrase correctly expresses concession after the main clause.

Tip: Mid- or end-sentence despite is fine when a noun follows.

TRUE — In spite of mirrors despite before the same noun phrase.

Tip: Prefer one style consistently in a report; both are grammatical.

FALSE — Although cannot take "early scepticism…" without a verb.

Tip: "Although managers were sceptical" would repair it.

TRUE — Semicolon + however correctly contrasts scepticism with the success metric.

Tip: Keep a comma after however in this pattern.

FALSE — Dropping however into the middle without proper clause punctuation / inversion patterns makes the sentence clumsy and formally wrong here.

Tip: Put however at the clause edge with a semicolon or period, not as a loose insert.
tasks.solution_overview: Concession after a success statement usually wants despite / in spite of + noun. Although needs a clause, and however needs clear sentence boundaries — do not bury it mid-clause.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Because of rising energy tariffs, the plant shifted production overnight.
Because rising energy tariffs, the plant shifted production overnight.
Owing to rising energy tariffs, the plant shifted production overnight.
Despite rising energy tariffs, overnight shifts were not authorised.
Although rising energy tariffs forced a review, overnight shifts were not authorised.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Because of + noun phrase correctly states the cause.

Tip: Rising energy tariffs is a noun phrase headed by tariffs.

FALSE — Bare because needs a clause: "Because energy tariffs rose…"

Tip: Missing of after because before a noun is an automatic false.

TRUE — Owing to + noun phrase is a formal alternative to because of.
