Tip: In board minutes, owing to often sounds slightly more formal than because of.

TRUE — Despite + noun phrase correctly marks concession.

Tip: Same noun can follow despite or because of depending on whether you mean contrast or cause.

TRUE — Although + full clause ("rising energy tariffs forced a review") is grammatical.

Tip: Once a verb appears after although, the clause test is passed.
tasks.solution_overview: One topic — energy tariffs — appears after cause, concession, and clause linkers. Decide first whether the sentence argues cause or contrast, then whether what follows is a noun or a clause.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The forecast was revised downward owing to softer order books in Q3.
The forecast was revised downward owing softer order books in Q3.
Softer order books reduced visibility; however, hiring plans stayed unchanged.
Softer order books reduced visibility, however hiring plans stayed unchanged.
In spite of softer order books, the firm kept its graduate intake.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Owing to + noun phrase correctly explains the revision.

Tip: Soft order books = noun idea → owing to / because of.

FALSE — Restore "to": "owing to softer order books."

Tip: Scan every owing for its partner to.

TRUE — Semicolon + however correctly contrasts visibility with hiring.

Tip: Two independent clauses around however need strong punctuation.

FALSE — A lone comma before however is not enough in formal exam style.

Tip: Upgrade the comma to a semicolon or start a new sentence.

TRUE — In spite of + noun phrase correctly frames the concession.

Tip: Keeping intake despite soft books is a textbook in spite of use.
tasks.solution_overview: Forecast language often pairs owing to with commercial nouns and however with policy contrasts. Check the little words — to after owing, and the stop before however.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Although the syndicate disagreed on valuation, talks continued into Friday night.
Despite the syndicate disagreed on valuation, talks continued into Friday night.
Despite the syndicate's disagreement on valuation, talks continued into Friday night.
Because of the syndicate's disagreement on valuation, talks nearly collapsed.
Whereas the syndicate disagreed on valuation, the strategic fit was never in doubt.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Although + clause correctly introduces the concession.

Tip: Disagreed is a finite verb — although is happy.

FALSE — Despite cannot take a finite clause directly; use although or turn the idea into a noun.

Tip: "Despite + subject + verb" is a high-frequency false pattern.

TRUE — Despite + noun phrase ("the syndicate's disagreement") is correct.

Tip: Nominalise the clause (disagreed → disagreement) when you insist on despite.

TRUE — Because of + noun phrase correctly states the near-collapse cause.

Tip: Same noun phrase can follow despite (contrast) or because of (cause).

TRUE — Whereas contrasts two full clauses about valuation versus strategic fit.

Tip: Whereas is for contrast, not cause — meaning must also fit.
tasks.solution_overview: The key subtlety is despite versus although: a finite clause after despite fails until you nominalise it. Because of and whereas then reuse the same content with different meanings.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Even though the underwriters demanded extra warranties, the issuer refused to reopen the prospectus.
Even though the underwriters' demand for extra warranties, the issuer refused to reopen the prospectus.
In spite of the underwriters demanding extra warranties, the issuer kept the prospectus closed.
The issuer refused; however, the underwriters still allocated a full book.
The issuer refused however the underwriters still allocated a full book without stops or commas.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Even though + clause correctly marks strong concession.

Tip: Even though is a more emphatic cousin of although — same clause rule.

FALSE — Even though needs a verb-bearing clause, not a noun phrase.

Tip: Switch to despite / in spite of before "the underwriters' demand."

TRUE — In spite of + gerund noun phrase is grammatical.

Tip: "X demanding Y" after in spite of / despite is a useful compact pattern.

TRUE — Semicolon + however correctly contrasts refusal with allocation.

Tip: Keep both sides of however able to stand alone as sentences.

FALSE — However needs stronger punctuation than a bare run-on join.

Tip: Insert a semicolon/period and a comma after however.
highlights: In spite of the underwriters demanding
tasks.solution_overview: Capital-markets wording hides the same linker rules: even though wants clauses, in spite of can take -ing phrases, and however still needs sentence punctuation.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Because the compliance filter flagged three counterparties, onboarding paused for a week.
Because of the compliance filter flagged three counterparties, onboarding paused for a week.
Owing to the compliance filter flagging three counterparties, onboarding paused for a week.
Despite the compliance filter flagging three counterparties, senior managers pressed ahead.
Although the compliance filter flagging three counterparties, senior managers pressed ahead.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Because + finite clause correctly gives the reason.

Tip: Flagged is past simple — perfect after because.

FALSE — Because of cannot introduce a finite clause; remove of or nominalise.

Tip: Spot the illegal "because of + subject + verb" stack.

TRUE — Owing to + -ing noun phrase is acceptable formal cause marking.

Tip: Gerund phrases after owing to / because of / despite are common in reports.

TRUE — Despite + -ing phrase correctly marks concession.

Tip: Same -ing phrase can mean cause (owing to) or contrast (despite) depending on the linker.

FALSE — Although needs a finite verb: "Although the compliance filter flagged…"

Tip: -ing after although is usually a despite transplant — reject it.
highlights: Because of the compliance filter flagged
Owing to the compliance filter flagging
tasks.solution_overview: Compliance scenarios often use long noun phrases. Keep because for finite clauses, and reserve because of / owing to / despite for noun or -ing phrases — not the other way round.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Whereas domestic bookings surged, outbound leisure travel remained subdued.
Whereas domestic bookings, outbound leisure travel remained subdued.
Domestic bookings surged. However, outbound leisure travel remained subdued.
Despite domestic bookings surging, marketing spend on outbound routes rose.
Although domestic bookings surging, marketing spend on outbound routes rose.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whereas contrasts two finite clauses about travel segments.

Tip: Both halves need a verb when whereas opens the sentence.

FALSE — Whereas cannot take a bare noun; add a verb ("surged").

Tip: Incomplete whereas clauses are easy to miss if you only read the second half.

TRUE — Separate sentences with However correctly mark the contrast.

Tip: Short sentences around however are often clearer than a long semicolon join.

TRUE — Despite + -ing noun phrase is grammatical concession.

Tip: "Despite X -ing" compresses "although X -ed."

FALSE — Although needs "Although domestic bookings surged…"

Tip: Do not copy despite’s -ing pattern onto although.
tasks.solution_overview: Travel-data contrasts use whereas and however for clause-level opposition, while despite can take an -ing phrase. Although still refuses that -ing shortcut.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of having little collateral, the start-up secured a bridging facility.
Despite of having little collateral, the start-up secured a bridging facility.
Although having little collateral, the start-up secured a bridging facility.
Although it had little collateral, the start-up secured a bridging facility.
The start-up had little collateral; however, lenders still offered a bridging facility.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — In spite of + gerund phrase ("having little collateral") is correct.

Tip: Perfect for concise concession before a surprising result.

FALSE — Remove of: "Despite having little collateral…"

Tip: Despite + -ing is fine; despite of + -ing is not.

FALSE — Although does not take a bare -ing phrase in careful formal English; add a subject + finite verb.

Tip: "Although having…" is a common L2 transfer error from despite.

TRUE — Although + full clause repairs the previous pattern.

Tip: Insert a clear subject (it / the firm) after although when in doubt.

TRUE — Semicolon + however correctly contrasts weak collateral with lender appetite.

Tip: Keep however’s comma after the linker.
tasks.solution_overview: Gerund concessions after in spite of / despite are elegant, but although still wants a full clause. Watch the fake "despite of" and the fake "although -ing" twins.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bond issue cleared, owing to last-minute support from two anchor investors.
The bond issue cleared owing last-minute support from two anchor investors.
Last-minute support arrived; the pricing, however, stayed inside the marketed range.
Last-minute support arrived, however the pricing stayed inside the marketed range with only a comma before however.
Despite last-minute support arriving, several smaller accounts still cancelled orders.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Mid-sentence "owing to" + noun phrase correctly states the cause.

Tip: A comma before owing to is common when the cause follows the result.

FALSE — Missing to: write "owing to last-minute support."

Tip: End-of-sentence owing still needs its to.

TRUE — Parenthetical however between commas correctly contrasts support with pricing.

Tip: Mid-clause however with commas is allowed when it does not join two bare clauses with a weak comma alone.

FALSE — Using however as a coordinator with only a preceding comma remains poor formal style.

Tip: Distinguish parenthetical however (commas both sides) from clause-joining however (semicolon/period).

TRUE — Despite + -ing phrase correctly marks concession.

Tip: "Despite X arriving" ≈ "although X arrived."
tasks.solution_overview: Harder however items distinguish parenthetical mid-clause use from illegal comma splices. Pair that with a clean owing to check and a despite -ing concession.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Because of how abruptly the corridor closed, logistics costs jumped overnight.
Because how abruptly the corridor closed, logistics costs jumped overnight.
Although how abruptly the corridor closed surprised planners, contingency stock covered the gap.
In spite of how abruptly the corridor closed, contingency stock covered the gap.
The corridor closed abruptly. Owing to that disruption, contingency stock was released.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Because of + free relative noun clause ("how abruptly…") is grammatical.

Tip: Wh-clauses can act as nouns after because of / despite / in spite of.

FALSE — Bare because needs a normal clause, not "because how…" without of.

Tip: If a how/what clause follows, you usually need because of, not bare because.

TRUE — Although + clause including "how abruptly…surprised" is fine.

Tip: Here how-clause is inside a larger finite clause — although is satisfied.

TRUE — In spite of + how-clause (noun-like) correctly marks concession.

Tip: In spite of how / despite what are polished formal patterns.

TRUE — Sentence-initial Owing to + noun correctly links to the prior disruption.

Tip: Pointing back with "that disruption" keeps owing to attached to a noun.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced items use how-clauses as noun objects of because of / in spite of. Bare because still wants an ordinary subject–verb clause — do not drop of before how.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Notwithstanding the delayed filings, the exchange allowed trading to resume — and despite the same delay, analysts kept their overweight ratings.
Despite delayed filings, analysts kept overweight ratings; however, several funds reduced exposure overnight.
Although delayed filings, analysts kept overweight ratings, however several funds reduced exposure overnight.
Owing to the delayed filings, the exchange postponed the opening auction.
Because of delayed filings were incomplete, the exchange postponed the opening auction.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Despite + noun works in the second half; the sentence remains grammatical (notwithstanding is outside our trap set but does not break the despite use).

Tip: Focus on the despite + noun chunk — it is correctly formed.

TRUE — Despite + noun and semicolon + however are both well formed.

Tip: Stacking two contrast tools is fine if each obeys its own rule.

FALSE — Although lacks a clause, and however is joined with only a weak comma.

Tip: Two linker errors can hide in one sentence — check each separately.

TRUE — Owing to + noun correctly states the auction delay cause.

Tip: Exchange notices often prefer owing to for formal tone.

FALSE — Because of + finite clause is illegal; write "Because filings were delayed" or "Because of incomplete delayed filings."

Tip: If a verb like were sits after because of, rewrite immediately.
tasks.solution_overview: Dense market sentences may contain two linkers. Score each linker on its own rule — noun versus clause, and however’s punctuation — rather than judging the sentence by overall "feel."

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Whereas headcount rose in shared services, front-line capacity fell — a split that, however, the CEO refused to call a contradiction.
Despite headcount rose in shared services, front-line capacity fell.
In spite of headcount rising in shared services, front-line capacity fell.
Because of headcount rising in shared services, training budgets were ring-fenced.
Although headcount rising in shared services, training budgets were ring-fenced.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whereas opens a proper clause contrast, and parenthetical however is correctly set off with commas.

Tip: Parenthetical however does not replace a missing verb after whereas.

FALSE — Despite cannot take the finite clause "headcount rose…"

Tip: Change to although, or to "despite the rise in headcount."

TRUE — In spite of + -ing phrase correctly compresses the contrast.

Tip: Rising turns the clause idea into a noun-like phrase for in spite of.

TRUE — Because of + -ing phrase correctly marks cause.

Tip: Same -ing phrase can follow because of (cause) or in spite of (contrast).

FALSE — Although still needs "Although headcount rose…" with a finite verb.

Tip: Final check on every although: find the tensed verb or mark false.
tasks.solution_overview: The last set mixes whereas, despite, in spite of, because of, and although around one workforce story. Name the linker, name what follows it, and the true/false call becomes mechanical even at exam speed.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The quarterly report was clear, concise, and persuasive.
The proposal was both innovative and it reduced overhead.
Staff must clock in on time, finish assigned tasks, and following safety rules.
She enjoys analysing spreadsheets, drafting briefs, and to present findings.
The manager not only approved the budget but also extended the deadline.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three adjectives sit in matching form, so the list is parallel.

Tip: When listing qualities, keep each item the same part of speech.

FALSE — "Both…and" joins an adjective to a full clause ("it reduced overhead").

Tip: Match structures after both…and: both innovative and cost-saving.

FALSE — The list shifts from bare infinitives (clock in, finish) to a participle (following).

Tip: After a shared modal, keep every verb in the same bare form: follow, not following.

FALSE — Two gerunds are paired with an infinitive ("to present").

Tip: Keep enjoy + -ing throughout: analysing, drafting, and presenting.

TRUE — "Not only…but also" links two matching past-tense verb phrases.

Tip: Place the same kind of phrase after each half of the correlative.
tasks.solution_overview: Read each sentence as a list or a paired construction. Ask whether every item shares the same grammatical shape. Correlatives such as both…and and not only…but also are correct only when the two sides match.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Investors valued its stability, its growth potential, and its transparency.
The goal was to cut costs, improving morale, and increase output.
He is skilled at negotiating contracts but weak in managing teams.
The policy aims to protect consumers, encourage competition, and boosting innovation.
She likes reading market reports and writing executive summaries.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three noun phrases share the same pattern with repeated "its."

Tip: Repeating a determiner can help keep noun lists visibly parallel.

FALSE — An infinitive series is broken by the gerund "improving."

Tip: After "to," keep bare infinitives: cut, improve, and increase.

TRUE — Adjective + preposition + gerund appears on both sides.

Tip: Parallel comparisons often reuse the same preposition pattern (at… / in…).

FALSE — The final item shifts from infinitives to a gerund ("boosting").

Tip: Finish the series with boost, not boosting.

TRUE — Two gerund phrases sit after "likes" in matching form.

Tip: Prefer reading… and writing… rather than mixing -ing with to-infinitives.
highlights: stability, its growth potential, and its transparency
tasks.solution_overview: Check lists of nouns, infinitives, and gerunds one item at a time. A single mismatched form is enough to mark the sentence false, even if the meaning is clear.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The training covers how to operate the machine, how to log incidents, and how to report faults.
Candidates should be reliable, motivated, and have experience.
The firm both restructured its debt and renegotiated supplier terms.
Our priorities are recruiting talent, retaining clients, and to expand overseas.
The auditor asked whether the figures were complete, accurate, and timely.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Three "how to" infinitive clauses form a clean parallel series.

Tip: Repeating "how to" before each verb keeps the list balanced.

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a verb phrase ("have experience").

Tip: Use three adjectives (reliable, motivated, and experienced) or three verb phrases.

TRUE — "Both…and" joins two matching past-tense verb phrases.

Tip: Place the shared subject once, then keep both verbs in the same tense and form.

FALSE — Two gerunds collide with an infinitive ("to expand").

Tip: Keep gerunds throughout: recruiting, retaining, and expanding.

TRUE — Three adjectives modify the figures in matching form.

Tip: Short adjective lists are easiest when every item is a single adjective.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch for mixed categories: adjectives slipping into verb phrases, or gerunds mixed with infinitives. Correct parallelism keeps one pattern from the first item to the last.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The launch was delayed by weak demand, rising costs, and because suppliers missed deadlines.
Either accept the revised offer or continue negotiating in good faith.
The brief must be short, focused, and without unnecessary jargon.
Neither the forecast nor the cash-flow model supports the expansion.
We need a plan that is realistic, affordable, and can be implemented quickly.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a because-clause.

Tip: Keep causes as nouns: weak demand, rising costs, and missed supplier deadlines.

TRUE — "Either…or" links two bare imperatives.

Tip: After either…or, use the same verb form on both sides.

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a prepositional phrase.

Tip: Prefer three adjectives: short, focused, and jargon-free.

TRUE — "Neither…nor" joins two noun subjects; the nearer singular noun takes a singular verb.

Tip: Parallel correlatives still need subject–verb agreement with the nearer noun.

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a modal clause ("can be implemented").

Tip: Stay with adjectives: realistic, affordable, and quick to implement.
tasks.solution_overview: Clauses and prepositional phrases often sneak into adjective or noun lists. If the first two items are adjectives or nouns, the third must be too.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The committee decided to postpone the vote, to request further evidence, and that members should abstain.
Success depends on careful planning, disciplined execution, and continuous review.
The app is designed for browsing catalogues, placing orders, and to track deliveries.
She is responsible for preparing the slides and for presenting them to the board.
The memo was both poorly timed and written in an aggressive tone.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two infinitives are followed by a that-clause.

Tip: Keep infinitives: postpone, request, and ask members to abstain — or rewrite as three that-clauses.

TRUE — Three noun phrases follow "depends on" in matching form.

Tip: After a preposition, noun or gerund lists usually work best when every item matches.

FALSE — Two gerunds are paired with an infinitive ("to track").

Tip: Use tracking deliveries to keep the -ing series intact.

TRUE — "For" + gerund appears twice in matching form.

Tip: Repeating the preposition before each gerund makes the parallelism explicit.

FALSE — "Both…and" joins an adverb–adjective pair to a past-participial clause of different shape.

Tip: Prefer both poorly timed and aggressively written.
highlights: careful planning, disciplined execution, and continuous review
for preparing the slides and for presenting
tasks.solution_overview: Infinitive series and gerund series are easy to break with a stray that-clause or to-infinitive. Name the pattern of the first item, then force every later item to match it.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The director wants employees who are punctual, who communicate clearly, and dedicated.
Not only did the firm cut headcount, but it also renegotiated leases.
Please submit the form online, attach supporting documents, and a covering letter.
The package includes flights, accommodation, and airport transfers.
He prefers to negotiate directly rather than relying on intermediaries.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two relative clauses are followed by a bare adjective.

Tip: Keep relative clauses throughout: who are punctual, who communicate clearly, and who are dedicated.

TRUE — Fronted "not only" uses inversion, and "but also" continues with a matching verb phrase.

Tip: After inverted not only…, keep but also + parallel predicate.

FALSE — Two imperatives are followed by a noun phrase.

Tip: Use three verbs: submit, attach, and include a covering letter.

TRUE — Three noun objects form a simple parallel list.

Tip: Ordinary product lists are correct when every item is a noun phrase.

FALSE — An infinitive ("to negotiate") is contrasted with a gerund ("relying").

Tip: Match forms: to negotiate… rather than to rely…, or negotiating… rather than relying…
tasks.solution_overview: Comparisons with rather than and lists that mix clauses with adjectives are frequent traps. Keep the grammatical category constant across the join.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The role involves reviewing contracts, advising clients, and attendance at hearings.
We are looking for someone who can think strategically, act decisively, and communicate persuasively.
The surplus will be used both to rebuild reserves and financing new projects.
Her strengths are attention to detail, calm under pressure, and solving problems creatively.
The board voted to approve the merger, to appoint an interim CEO, and to defer the dividend.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two gerunds are followed by a noun phrase ("attendance").

Tip: Use attending hearings to keep the gerund pattern.

TRUE — Three bare infinitives after "can" form a matching series.

Tip: Shared modals (can/must/should) demand the same bare verb form each time.

FALSE — "Both…and" joins an infinitive to a gerund.

Tip: Both to rebuild… and to finance…, or both rebuilding… and financing…

FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a gerund phrase.

Tip: Use creative problem-solving so all three items are nouns.

TRUE — Three infinitives after "voted to" stay in parallel.

Tip: Repeating "to" before each verb is optional but often clearer.
highlights: think strategically, act decisively, and communicate
both to rebuild reserves and financing
to approve the merger, to appoint
tasks.solution_overview: Job descriptions and board resolutions often hide mixed lists. Convert every item into the same type—gerund, infinitive, or noun—before you judge the sentence true.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The campaign was effective in raising awareness, in generating leads, and sales increased.
Applicants must either enclose a portfolio or they submit a link to an online gallery.
The analyst is known for rigorous methods, clear writing, and ethical judgement.
We aim not only to grow revenue but also market share.
The workshop taught participants to define objectives, to map stakeholders, and to draft a pilot plan.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two "in + gerund" phrases are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Keep the preposition pattern: in raising…, in generating…, and in increasing sales.

FALSE — "Either…or" joins a bare infinitive to a full clause with a new subject.

Tip: Either enclose a portfolio or submit a link — same subject, same verb form.

TRUE — Three noun phrases follow "known for" in parallel.

Tip: After "for," noun lists are usually the safest parallel choice.

FALSE — "Not only…but also" joins an infinitive to a bare noun.

Tip: Not only to grow revenue but also to grow market share — or not only revenue but also market share.

TRUE — Three infinitives after "taught…to" match cleanly.

Tip: Repeat "to" when it keeps each learning outcome equally weighted.
highlights: rigorous methods, clear writing, and ethical judgement
to define objectives, to map stakeholders, and to draft
tasks.solution_overview: Correlatives fail when one side is a phrase and the other is a clause, or when one side has "to" and the other does not. Balance the two halves before you look at meaning.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The tender requires bidders to demonstrate capacity, to provide references, and financial statements for three years.
Whether by email, by phone, or in person, clients must receive a reply within one working day.
The restructuring plan is ambitious, controversial, and it may fail.
She speaks fluently in English, in German, and Mandarin.
The software can schedule meetings, share files, and integrate with payroll systems.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two infinitives are followed by a noun phrase without "to provide."

Tip: Add to provide financial statements, or turn all three into nouns after "demonstrate."

TRUE — Three prepositional routes stay parallel after "whether."

Tip: Keep the same preposition pattern (by… / by… / in…) when listing channels.

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a clause.

Tip: Use three adjectives: ambitious, controversial, and risky.

FALSE — "In" appears before the first two languages but not the third.

Tip: Repeat in before Mandarin, or drop in before all three.

TRUE — Three bare infinitives after "can" form a matching list.

Tip: Shared auxiliaries make parallel verb lists especially clear.
highlights: by email, by phone, or in person
schedule meetings, share files, and integrate
tasks.solution_overview: Missing repeated prepositions and trailing clauses after adjective pairs are subtler errors. Read the list aloud; an abrupt change of rhythm usually signals a break in form.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The CFO argued that costs were rising, that margins were shrinking, and cash was scarce.
He is not only a capable negotiator but also leads the compliance team.
The checklist covers opening the till, reconciling receipts, and locking the safe.
Our partners expect transparency, responsiveness, and that we escalate issues promptly.
To succeed in this market, firms must innovate constantly and listen carefully to customers.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two that-clauses are followed by a bare clause without "that."

Tip: Repeat that before cash was scarce, or drop that before all three.

FALSE — "Not only…but also" joins a noun phrase to a verb phrase.

Tip: Not only a capable negotiator but also the compliance lead — or not only negotiates… but also leads…

TRUE — Three gerund phrases describe procedures in matching form.

Tip: Process lists after "covers" work well as -ing forms.

FALSE — Two nouns are followed by a that-clause.

Tip: Use three nouns: transparency, responsiveness, and prompt escalation.

TRUE — Two bare infinitives after "must" stay parallel.

Tip: Two-item lists still need matching forms after a shared modal.
highlights: not only a capable negotiator but also leads
opening the till, reconciling receipts, and locking
tasks.solution_overview: That-clause series and not only…but also mismatches are classic exam items. Decide whether you are linking nouns or verbs, then refuse any hybrid.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The consultant recommended streamlining processes, automating reports, and that the firm outsource payroll.
As much by design as by accident, the platform became the industry standard.
The keynote was informative, entertaining, and left the audience motivated.
Managers should praise good work publicly and criticise mistakes privately.
The contract prohibits disclosing trade secrets, soliciting clients, and to hire rival staff.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two gerunds are followed by a that-clause.

Tip: Prefer outsourcing payroll so all three recommendations are gerunds.

TRUE — "As much…as" joins two matching "by + noun" phrases.

Tip: Correlative comparisons need identical structures after each as.

FALSE — Two adjectives are followed by a verb phrase.

Tip: Use three adjectives: informative, entertaining, and motivating.

TRUE — Two parallel verb phrases contrast public praise with private criticism.

Tip: Matching adverbs (publicly / privately) reinforce the parallel design.

FALSE — Two gerunds after "prohibits" are followed by an infinitive.

Tip: Use hiring rival staff to keep the gerund series.
highlights: As much by design as by accident
praise good work publicly and criticise
tasks.solution_overview: Legal and advisory prose often piles gerunds after verbs like recommend or prohibit. One infinitive or that-clause at the end will break an otherwise solid series.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The pilot succeeded because of careful scoping, because of clear ownership, and dedicated testers.
She neither confirmed the rumour nor denied it outright.
What the board wants is faster decisions, clearer metrics, and that risks are flagged early.
The new policy applies to permanent staff, to contractors, and interns.
Rather than delaying the launch, the team shipped a limited release and gathered feedback.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two "because of + noun" phrases are followed by a bare noun without "because of."

Tip: Repeat because of before dedicated testers, or drop because of before the first two and use a noun list.

TRUE — "Neither…nor" joins two matching past-tense verbs.

Tip: Keep the same tense and complement pattern after each half.

FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a that-clause after "what…is."

Tip: Use three nouns: faster decisions, clearer metrics, and earlier risk flags.

FALSE — "To" appears before the first two groups but not the third.

Tip: Repeat to before interns, or omit to before all three.

TRUE — "Rather than + gerund" is followed by two matching past-tense actions.

Tip: The contrast is with delaying; the main clause then keeps shipped and gathered parallel.
highlights: neither confirmed the rumour nor denied
tasks.solution_overview: Repeated prepositions and correlatives like neither…nor reward careful scanning. If a marker appears twice, check whether the third item still carries it.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The memorandum asks readers to note the assumptions, question the projections, and whether the model is stress-tested.
Both the marketing plan and the sales forecast were updated overnight.
The internship offers mentoring, networking opportunities, and you will receive a stipend.
Investors want founders who can raise capital, who can scale operations, and who can retain talent.
The revision was neither complete nor it was internally consistent.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two infinitives after "asks…to" are followed by a whether-clause.

Tip: Use to check whether the model is stress-tested so the third item stays an infinitive.

TRUE — "Both…and" joins two matching noun subjects with a plural verb.

Tip: Both X and Y take a plural verb when the subjects are plural in sense.

FALSE — Two noun objects are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Use three nouns: mentoring, networking opportunities, and a stipend.

TRUE — Three matching relative clauses begin with "who can."

Tip: Repeating who can keeps a long relative series clearly parallel.

FALSE — "Neither…nor" joins an adjective to a full clause.

Tip: Neither complete nor internally consistent — two adjectives.
highlights: Both the marketing plan and the sales forecast
who can raise capital, who can scale
tasks.solution_overview: At this level, errors often hide inside long relative or infinitive chains. Isolate the shared frame (asks to… / who can…) and test whether every continuation fits that frame.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The audit found discrepancies in inventory counts, in accounts receivable, and payroll records were incomplete.
Not only the CFO but also the controllers were briefed before the announcement.
We measure success by how quickly we resolve tickets, how rarely issues recur, and customer satisfaction scores.
The brief should explain what changed, why it changed, and how teams should respond.
She is admired for working efficiently, for communicating clearly, and her integrity.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two "in + noun" phrases are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Keep in payroll records, or rewrite as three noun objects of "in."

TRUE — "Not only…but also" joins two noun subjects; the nearer plural subject takes were.

Tip: Agreement follows the nearer noun after not only…but also.

FALSE — Two "how" clauses are followed by a noun phrase.

Tip: Add how high customer satisfaction scores remain, or turn all three into nouns.

TRUE — Three matching wh-clauses answer what, why, and how.

Tip: Parallel wh-clauses are a strong pattern for instructional briefs.

FALSE — Two "for + gerund" phrases are followed by a bare noun.

Tip: Use for her integrity so every item follows for.
highlights: Not only the CFO but also the controllers
what changed, why it changed, and how
tasks.solution_overview: Wh-clause lists and not only…but also with compound subjects reward precise reading. Do not let a correct agreement pattern distract you from a broken list elsewhere in the set.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The firm’s culture rewards people who take initiative, who share credit, and deliver results without drama.
Either the warranty covers accidental damage or it does not; the brochure cannot claim both.
Objectives for the quarter are reducing churn, increasing average order value, and to reopen two stores.
The mediator asked each side to listen carefully, to summarise the other’s position, and then propose a compromise.
His presentation was organised around three questions: where demand is shifting, which segments are growing, and what pricing can sustain.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two "who" clauses are followed by a bare verb phrase missing "who."

Tip: Write who deliver results without drama to keep the relative pattern.

TRUE — "Either…or" contrasts two matching clauses about coverage.

Tip: Full clauses can be parallel when both sides share the same clause shape.

FALSE — Two gerunds are followed by an infinitive.

Tip: Use reopening two stores to finish the gerund list.

FALSE — Two "to" infinitives are followed by a bare infinitive after "then."

Tip: Write to propose a compromise, or drop to before all three verbs after asked…to.

TRUE — Three matching wh-clauses form a parallel agenda.

Tip: Parallel questions make a presentation structure easy to follow and grammatically clean.
highlights: where demand is shifting, which segments
tasks.solution_overview: Omitted relative pronouns and dropped infinitive markers are easy to miss in long sentences. Mentally restore the shared word before the last item; if it no longer fits, the sentence is false.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The partnership agreement obliges each party to share data promptly, to notify material breaches, and confidentiality must be maintained.
She proved herself both in crisis management and when markets were calm.
The dashboard tracks conversion rates, bounce rates, and how long users stay on the site.
To attract talent, to retain clients, and to protect the brand remain the stated priorities.
The lawyer advised against signing the clause, against waiving notice, and against accepting unlimited liability.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two infinitives are followed by an independent clause with a new modal.

Tip: Use to maintain confidentiality so the obligation stays an infinitive series.

FALSE — "Both…and" joins a prepositional phrase to a when-clause.

Tip: Both in crisis management and in calm markets — two prepositional phrases.

FALSE — Two noun objects are followed by a how-clause.

Tip: Use session duration so all three metrics are noun phrases.

TRUE — Three infinitive phrases function as a parallel compound subject.

Tip: Infinitive subjects can be parallel when every infinitive carries the same role.

TRUE — Three matching "against + gerund" phrases follow "advised."

Tip: Repeating against before each gerund locks the parallel pattern.
highlights: both in crisis management and when
To attract talent, to retain clients, and to protect
against signing the clause, against waiving
tasks.solution_overview: Legal and analytics English mixes nouns, infinitives, and clauses freely in drafts. Your job is to refuse that mixing: pick one frame and hold it through every item.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The turnaround hinged not so much on cutting costs as restoring customer trust through service.
Executives debated whether to refinance the debt, whether to seek an equity partner, or liquidating non-core assets.
The new code of conduct forbids accepting gifts, soliciting favours, and using insider information for personal gain.
Her mandate is as much about rebuilding culture as it is about hitting quarterly targets.
The motion was neither seconded promptly nor was it discussed on the merits.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Not so much…as" joins "on cutting" to a bare gerund without "on."

Tip: Not so much on cutting costs as on restoring trust — repeat on.

FALSE — Two "whether to" infinitives are followed by a gerund.

Tip: Or whether to liquidate non-core assets keeps the pattern.

TRUE — Three gerund phrases after "forbids" stay parallel.

Tip: Long gerund objects remain correct when every item is -ing + complement.

TRUE — "As much…as" balances two "about + gerund/noun" ideas with matching "it is."

Tip: Correlative as much…as often needs mirrored about-phrases.

FALSE — "Neither…nor" joins a past participle phrase to an inverted clause.

Tip: Neither seconded promptly nor discussed on the merits — two past participles.
highlights: accepting gifts, soliciting favours, and using
as much about rebuilding culture as it is about
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced correlatives (not so much…as, as much…as, whether to…) fail when the second half drops a preposition or switches to a different verb form. Match the scaffolding, not just the topic.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The prospectus promises investors clearer disclosures, tighter governance, and that dividends will resume within two years.
By training supervisors early, by publishing escalation paths, and by auditing outcomes quarterly, the firm reduced complaints.
The candidate was praised for how she handled objections, how she framed trade-offs, and her closing summary.
We will either migrate the legacy system this year or postpone the project until budgets allow.
The clause requires that vendors deliver on time, that they maintain insurance, and invoices be submitted monthly.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two noun phrases are followed by a that-clause.

Tip: Use resumption of dividends within two years as a third noun phrase.

TRUE — Three matching "by + gerund" phrases form a parallel means list.

Tip: Repeating by before each gerund keeps the causal list balanced.

FALSE — Two "how" clauses are followed by a noun phrase.

Tip: Add how she delivered her closing summary to keep the how-pattern.

TRUE — "Either…or" joins two matching bare infinitives after "will."

Tip: Shared will + either…or needs the same bare verb form on both sides.

FALSE — Two "that" clauses are followed by a bare subjunctive clause missing "that."

Tip: Repeat that before invoices be submitted monthly.
highlights: By training supervisors early, by publishing
either migrate the legacy system this year or postpone
tasks.solution_overview: Prospectus and contract language often stacks that-clauses. If that appears twice, the third clause almost always needs it too—or all three should be rewritten as nouns.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The strategy rests less on aggressive pricing than expanding the service network.
Not only did revenue recover in the second half, but operating margins also widened.
Stakeholders asked for a timeline that is realistic, that is funded, and achievable without overtime.
The committee prefers meeting in person on Mondays and to convene online on Thursdays.
A credible plan must specify who owns each workstream, what resources are required, and when progress will be reviewed.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Less…than" joins "on + gerund/noun" to a bare gerund without "on."

Tip: Less on aggressive pricing than on expanding the service network.

TRUE — Inverted "not only" is balanced by "but…also" with a parallel past-tense verb phrase.

Tip: Keep both predicates finite and matching after not only…but also.

FALSE — Two "that is" relatives are followed by an adjective missing "that is."

Tip: Write that is achievable without overtime.

FALSE — A gerund ("meeting") is paired with an infinitive ("to convene").

Tip: Prefer meeting… and convening…, or to meet… and to convene…

TRUE — Three matching wh-clauses specify ownership, resources, and timing.

Tip: Parallel wh-clauses are ideal for plans that must answer who, what, and when.
highlights: who owns each workstream, what resources
tasks.solution_overview: Comparative frames (less…than) and relative-clause chains demand the same marker on every branch. When in doubt, rewrite the last item so it could replace the first without changing structure.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board authorised management to pursue a sale, to explore a joint venture, and filing for a dual listing if talks stalled.
Just as the firm invests in product research, so too does it invest in after-sales support.
Performance will be judged on whether targets are met, whether risks are logged, and staff development plans exist.
The brief is neither to defend the status quo nor to dismiss every criticism wholesale.
She left the firm because of limited promotion prospects, because of a toxic team culture, and her commute had become unmanageable.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Two infinitives after "authorised…to" are followed by a gerund.

Tip: Use to file for a dual listing to keep the infinitive series.

TRUE — "Just as…so too" balances two matching invest + in + noun patterns with inversion on the second clause.

Tip: Correlative just as…so too needs mirrored clause structure.

FALSE — Two "whether" clauses are followed by a bare clause missing "whether."

Tip: Repeat whether before staff development plans exist.

TRUE — "Neither…nor" joins two matching infinitives after "is."

Tip: Keep to + bare verb on both sides of neither…nor.

FALSE — Two "because of + noun" phrases are followed by an independent clause.

Tip: Use because of an unmanageable commute so every reason stays a noun phrase.
highlights: and filing for a dual listing
neither to defend the status quo nor to dismiss
tasks.solution_overview: Final-band items combine correlatives, repeated subordinators, and long infinitive chains. Name the opening structure of each sentence, then reject any ending that cannot wear the same grammatical clothes.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board recommended that the proposal be reviewed before the vote.
It is essential that every applicant submits the form by Monday.
The committee insisted that the report is finalised within a week.
The manager demanded that the supplier pays the outstanding invoice immediately.
It is crucial that the sample remains uncontaminated during transit.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After "recommended that," the formal subjunctive takes the base form "be reviewed," not a present indicative.

Tip: Mandative triggers (recommend, insist, demand…) want the bare verb, even after a third-person singular subject.

FALSE — "It is essential that" requires the base form: "every applicant submit," not "submits."

Tip: Impersonal adjectives (essential, crucial, imperative) still trigger the same base-form pattern.

FALSE — After "insisted that," use "be finalised," not indicative "is finalised."

Tip: Passive subjunctive needs "be" + past participle, never "is/are" + past participle.

FALSE — After "demanded that," use "pay," not the indicative "pays."

Tip: Drop the third-person -s after any mandative that-clause.

FALSE — Use base form "remain," not "remains," after "it is crucial that."

Tip: Stative verbs (remain, stay, keep) still lose -s in the formal subjunctive.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan each sentence for a mandative trigger—recommend, insist, demand, or "it is essential/crucial that." After that that-clause, the verb should be a bare base form (or "be" + participle), not a normal present indicative. Mark TRUE only when the base form is already in place.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The regulator required that the bank disclose the contingency figures.
The panel proposed that the hearing is postponed until Friday.
It is imperative that the results be verified independently.
The council requested that the contractor submits revised drawings.
She suggested that he reconsiders the timeline before signing.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Required that" correctly takes the base form "disclose."

Tip: Require, request, and demand behave like recommend: that + base form.

FALSE — After "proposed that," write "be postponed," not "is postponed."

Tip: "Is/are + past participle" is indicative passive; the subjunctive passive needs "be."

TRUE — "It is imperative that… be verified" uses the correct subjunctive passive.

Tip: Impersonal "it is + adjective + that" is a classic mandative frame.

FALSE — After "requested that," use "submit," not "submits."

Tip: Do not add -s even when the subject of the that-clause is singular.

FALSE — After "suggested that," use "reconsider," not "reconsiders."

Tip: Suggest and propose are softer verbs but still trigger the formal subjunctive in exam English.
tasks.solution_overview: These items mix require, propose, request, suggest, and "it is imperative that." Treat them all the same way: look past the subject of the that-clause and check that the verb is base form. Indicative -s and "is postponed" are the FALSE marks.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It was recommended that the policy remain unchanged until the audit ended.
The ministry insisted that the tender documents are published online.
The ethics board demanded that the researcher withdraw the contested claim.
It is vital that every participant arrives fifteen minutes early.
The partners asked that the clause be redrafted in clearer language.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past-tense "was recommended that" still takes present base form "remain," not "remained."

Tip: The mandative subjunctive does not backshift with the main verb's tense.

FALSE — Use "be published," not "are published," after "insisted that."

Tip: Agreement with a plural subject does not licence indicative "are" in this pattern.

TRUE — "Demanded that… withdraw" is correct base-form usage.

Tip: Active subjunctive often looks identical to the infinitive without "to."

FALSE — After "it is vital that," write "arrive," not "arrives."

Tip: Vital, essential, and necessary all suppress the third-person -s.

TRUE — "Asked that… be redrafted" correctly uses the subjunctive passive.

Tip: Ask that + clause (formal) follows the same rule as request that.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch for past-tense reporting verbs and impersonal "it is vital that." Neither changes the rule: the that-clause verb stays in the base form. Flag any -s or "are/is" as incorrect.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The auditor recommended that management strengthen internal controls.
It is necessary that the warranty covers accidental damage as well.
The chair insisted that the minutes be circulated the same day.
Stakeholders demanded that the firm issues a public apology.
The guidance states that it is important that staff report conflicts of interest promptly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Recommended that… strengthen" is the expected base form.

Tip: Abstract subjects like "management" still take bare verbs after recommend.

FALSE — Use "cover," not "covers," after "it is necessary that."

Tip: Necessary and essential never keep indicative agreement in careful exam usage.

TRUE — "Insisted that… be circulated" is correct subjunctive passive.

Tip: Time adverbials ("the same day") do not change the verb form.

FALSE — After "demanded that," write "issue," not "issues."

Tip: A plural organisation noun ("firm") still takes a bare verb in the that-clause.

TRUE — Nested "it is important that staff report" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: The trigger can sit inside a larger sentence; find the that-clause first.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of five sentences already use the mandative base form. The false ones keep ordinary present agreement ("covers," "issues") after necessary/demand—those are the traps to strike.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The tribunal ordered that the defendant disclose the email archive in full.
Counsel advised that the witness remains available for cross-examination.
It is desirable that the questionnaire be anonymous.
The lender stipulated that the borrower repay the facility within ninety days.
The memo urges that each division updates its contingency plan quarterly.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Ordered that… disclose" follows the mandative pattern.

Tip: Legal and formal verbs (order, stipulate, decree) are reliable subjunctive triggers.

FALSE — After "advised that" in this mandative sense, use "remain," not "remains."

Tip: Advise that + base form is the formal pattern tested here; do not keep -s.

TRUE — "It is desirable that… be anonymous" correctly uses "be."

Tip: Desirable, advisable, and preferable work like essential.

TRUE — "Stipulated that… repay" is the correct bare form.

Tip: Contract language often hides subjunctives—check the that-clause carefully.

FALSE — After "urges that," write "update," not "updates."

Tip: Urge, recommend, and insist share the same base-form rule.
tasks.solution_overview: Legal and advisory wording (order, advise, stipulate, urge) still triggers the formal subjunctive. Read past the institutional subject and verify the that-clause verb is bare.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board moved that the dividend be suspended for one quarter.
Investors requested that the CEO explains the sudden revision.
It is critical that access logs be retained for seven years.
The supervisor insisted that nobody leave the site until clearance was given.
The circular recommends that departments consolidates overlapping budgets.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Moved that… be suspended" is correct parliamentary/board subjunctive.

Tip: "Move that" in meeting minutes almost always takes the base form.

FALSE — Use "explain," not "explains," after "requested that."

Tip: A singular title ("the CEO") is a frequent bait for -s.

TRUE — "It is critical that… be retained" uses the right passive subjunctive.

Tip: Critical and crucial are interchangeable triggers for this pattern.

TRUE — "Insisted that nobody leave" correctly uses the bare verb after a negative indefinite.

Tip: Nobody/everybody still take base form, not "leaves."

FALSE — After "recommends that," write "consolidate," not "consolidates."

Tip: Plural subjects do not need -s—and the subjunctive forbids it anyway.
tasks.solution_overview: Meeting language ("moved that") and negative subjects ("nobody") still demand the base form. The errors here are ordinary present endings after request/recommend.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The protocol requires that each sample be labelled before freezing.
It is essential that the chairperson opens the session punctually.
Shareholders proposed that the buy-back programme commence next month.
The inspector demanded that unsafe scaffolding were dismantled at once.
We recommended that the candidate not be shortlisted without references.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Requires that… be labelled" is correct.

Tip: Require that + passive subjunctive is standard in procedures and SOPs.

FALSE — Use "open," not "opens," after "it is essential that."

Tip: Job titles after essential/imperative still take the bare verb.

TRUE — "Proposed that… commence" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: Formal verbs like commence are fine; keep them bare after propose.

FALSE — After "demanded that," use "be dismantled," not "were dismantled."

Tip: Do not confuse mandative "be" with the unreal "were" subjunctive.

TRUE — Negation sits before the base form: "not be shortlisted."

Tip: Write "that X not + base," never "that X does not" in the formal pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: This set adds negation and a "were" trap. Mandative English wants "be," not past "were," and negatives use "not" + base form rather than "does not."

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The ombudsman recommended that the agency apologise to the complainant.
It is advisable that travellers avoids unmarked border crossings.
The contract provides that either party give thirty days' written notice.
The faculty insisted that the thesis is submitted in electronic form only.
Her counsel urged that the injunction be lifted pending appeal.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Recommended that… apologise" uses British base-form spelling correctly.

Tip: Spelling (apologise/apologize) is separate from the subjunctive test—focus on the ending.

FALSE — After "it is advisable that," write "avoid," not "avoids."

Tip: Advisable and preferable suppress -s exactly like essential.

TRUE — "Provides that… give" is a legal mandative with a bare verb.

Tip: "Either party" is singular in meaning but still takes base form here, not "gives."

FALSE — Use "be submitted," not "is submitted," after "insisted that."

Tip: Academic instructions often hide indicative passives—swap "is" for "be."

TRUE — "Urged that… be lifted" is correct.

Tip: Court and counsel English is rich in formal subjunctives.
tasks.solution_overview: Legal "provides that" and counsel "urged that" sit beside the usual recommend/insist frames. Correct items keep the bare verb; incorrect ones keep -s or indicative "is."

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The compliance officer insisted that every gift above €50 is logged.
It is important that the appendix include the raw survey responses.
The syndicate demanded that interest payments resumes immediately.
Directors resolved that the subsidiary be wound up voluntarily.
The brief suggested that counsel prepares a chronology overnight.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — After "insisted that," use "be logged," not "is logged."

Tip: Threshold phrases (€50, 10%, etc.) distract—still check the verb form.

TRUE — "It is important that… include" correctly drops -s.

Tip: Important is among the highest-frequency impersonal triggers in exams.

FALSE — Use "resume," not "resumes," after "demanded that."

Tip: Plural "payments" can tempt "resume" vs "resumes"—subjunctive wants bare "resume" either way.

TRUE — "Resolved that… be wound up" is correct board-resolution English.

Tip: Resolve/move/order that + be + participle is a fixed formal pattern.

FALSE — After "suggested that," write "prepare," not "prepares."

Tip: Soft verbs (suggest, recommend) still forbid indicative -s in the that-clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Only two sentences already use the base form. Hunt for indicative "is" and third-person -s after insist, demand, and suggest—those are your FALSE marks.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The watchdog recommended that lobbying contacts be disclosed quarterly.
It is mandatory that visitors wear protective footwear in the plant.
The arbitrator directed that both parties exchange witness lists by noon.
Management asked that overtime claims is filed before payroll closes.
The statute requires that the minister lay the report before Parliament.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Recommended that… be disclosed" is correct.

Tip: Frequency adverbs (quarterly) do not affect the subjunctive form.

TRUE — "It is mandatory that visitors wear" uses the bare plural verb correctly.

Tip: With plural subjects the base form looks like a normal present—confirm the trigger first.

TRUE — "Directed that… exchange" is the right base form.

Tip: Direct, order, and instruct that all behave mandatively.

FALSE — Use "be filed," not "is filed," after "asked that."

Tip: Singular collective objects ("overtime claims" as a batch) still take "be," not "is," in the passive subjunctive.

TRUE — "Requires that the minister lay" correctly uses bare "lay."

Tip: Parliamentary English ("lay a report") is a classic formal-subjunctive habitat.
tasks.solution_overview: Four items are already correct; the single error is an indicative passive ("is filed") after "asked that." When the that-clause looks almost normal, still verify "be" versus "is."

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The lender insisted that the covenant remains in force after refinancing.
Researchers proposed that the pilot study be extended by six weeks.
It is preferable that feedback is collected anonymously.
The union demanded that shift differentials be restored retrospectively.
The editor requested that the author cite the primary dataset explicitly.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — After "insisted that," use "remain," not "remains."

Tip: "Remain in force" is a set phrase—still strip the -s in mandative clauses.

TRUE — "Proposed that… be extended" is correct.

Tip: Research English frequently uses propose that + be + participle.

FALSE — Use "be collected," not "is collected," after "it is preferable that."

Tip: Preferable/advisable + that still demand the subjunctive passive with "be."

TRUE — "Demanded that… be restored" is correct.

Tip: Labour-relations wording often packs adjectives around a clean "be" + participle core.

TRUE — "Requested that… cite" correctly uses the bare verb.

Tip: Academic request that + base form is standard formal style.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on "remain(s)" and passive "is/be collected." Indicative endings after insist and preferable are the FALSE answers; the rest already show proper base forms.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The court decreed that the assets be frozen pending further order.
It is essential that confidentiality is maintained throughout the tender.
Partners agreed that the valuation methodology be revisited annually.
The coach insisted that every player arrives forty minutes before kick-off.
Guidance notes recommend that applicants enclose certified translations.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Decreed that… be frozen" is correct formal subjunctive.

Tip: Decree, ordain, and enjoin are strong legal triggers.

FALSE — Use "be maintained," not "is maintained," after "it is essential that."

Tip: Abstract nouns (confidentiality) still take "be," not "is," in the that-clause.

TRUE — "Agreed that… be revisited" correctly uses "be."

Tip: Agree that can be factual or mandative; here the annual revision is a prescribed action.

FALSE — After "insisted that," write "arrive," not "arrives."

Tip: Sports or workplace deadlines do not change the grammar rule.

TRUE — "Recommend that applicants enclose" uses the bare plural verb correctly.

Tip: When the subject is plural, correct and incorrect forms differ only after singular subjects—still confirm the trigger.
tasks.solution_overview: Legal "decreed that" and softer "agreed/recommend that" share one test: base form after that. The two FALSE items keep indicative "is" and "arrives."

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The trustee recommended that the beneficiary not receive further advances.
It was vital that the vaccine were stored below eight degrees.
The panel insisted that discrepancies be reconciled before sign-off.
Auditors required that inventory counts takes place under dual control.
She asked that the embargo remain in place until the filing date.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negated subjunctive "not receive" is correctly formed.

Tip: Place "not" immediately before the base verb; do not insert "do/does."

FALSE — After "it was vital that," use "be stored," not "were stored."

Tip: Past-tense "was vital" does not licence past "were"; mandative still wants "be."

TRUE — "Insisted that… be reconciled" is correct.

Tip: Plural abstract subjects (discrepancies) still take "be," not "are."

FALSE — Use "take," not "takes," after "required that."

Tip: Subject–verb lookalikes ("counts takes") are noise—strip to "counts take."

TRUE — "Asked that… remain" correctly keeps the base form.

Tip: "Remain in place" after ask/insist is a frequent correct pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder traps appear: negation without "do," and past "were" after "it was vital that." Remember the mandative form is tenseless "be" / bare verb, not a past indicative or unreal "were."

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The statute provides that the authority publish the tariff annually.
It is crucial that no one tamper with the sealed evidence bags.
The board directed that bonuses be withheld pending the investigation.
Counsel recommended that the client waive privilege only in writing.
The notice requires that complaints be lodged within fourteen days.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Provides that… publish" is bare-form statutory English.

Tip: Singular institutional subjects ("the authority") still take no -s here.

TRUE — After "it is crucial that," "no one tamper" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: Indefinites (no one, everyone, anybody) still suppress -s in mandative clauses.

TRUE — "Directed that… be withheld" correctly uses the subjunctive passive.

Tip: Plural objects ("bonuses") still take "be," not "are," after direct that.

TRUE — "Recommended that… waive" is correct.

Tip: Legal "waive" after recommend is a high-frequency exam item.

TRUE — "Requires that… be lodged" correctly uses "be" + participle.

Tip: Plural "complaints" still take "be" in the passive subjunctive.
tasks.solution_overview: Every sentence here already uses the mandative base form or "be" + participle. Confirm the trigger, confirm the bare verb, and mark all five TRUE—do not invent errors that are not on the page.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The committee moved that standing orders be suspended for the vote.
It is imperative that the nominee declares all related-party interests.
Underwriters required that the prospectus be amended before circulation.
The mediator suggested that each side makes one further concession.
Clinicians insisted that the dosage remain constant during the trial.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Moved that… be suspended" is correct.

Tip: Procedural motions almost always use the formal subjunctive.

FALSE — After "it is imperative that," use "declare," not "declares."

Tip: Nominee/applicant/candidate after imperative are classic -s traps.

TRUE — "Required that… be amended" is correct.

Tip: Capital-markets English loves require that + be + participle.

FALSE — Use "make," not "makes," after "suggested that."

Tip: "Each side" is singular in form—exam writers plant -s here deliberately.

TRUE — "Insisted that… remain" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: Clinical protocols often keep "remain" after insist/require.
tasks.solution_overview: Three correct mandatives and two indicative -s errors after imperative and suggest. "Each" and job-title subjects are the usual bait for an unwanted ending.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The regulator stipulated that intermediaries not solicit retail clients cold.
It is necessary that the escrow account be opened in both names.
Shareholders demanded that the chairperson steps down forthwith.
The brief urged that exhibits be paginated consecutively.
Policy guidance recommends that remote staff uses only approved VPN links.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negated mandative "not solicit" is correctly formed.

Tip: After stipulate/require, "that X not + verb" is the formal negative.

TRUE — "It is necessary that… be opened" is correct.

Tip: Banking/escrow contexts recycle the same "be" + participle frame.

FALSE — After "demanded that," write "step," not "steps."

Tip: Dramatic verbs (step down, resign) still lose -s in the that-clause.

TRUE — "Urged that… be paginated" is correct.

Tip: Litigation documents favour urge/direct that + be + participle.

FALSE — Use "use," not "uses," after "recommends that."

Tip: Collective "staff" often takes singular agreement in BrE—but the subjunctive still wants bare "use."
tasks.solution_overview: Negation without do-support and collective nouns (staff) raise the difficulty. Correct sentences already use "not" + base or "be" + participle; FALSE ones keep ordinary -s.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The injunction provides that the defendant not contact the claimant directly.
It is desirable that the questionnaire were bilingual from the outset.
Partners insisted that profit shares be recalculated after the write-down.
The assessor recommended that the candidate retakes the oral component.
Treasury directed that contingency reserves remain untouched this year.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Court English "provides that… not contact" is a correct negated subjunctive.

Tip: Injunctions and orders are prime territory for "that X not + base."

FALSE — After "it is desirable that," use "be bilingual," not "were bilingual."

Tip: Do not import the unreal "were" into mandative clauses.

TRUE — "Insisted that… be recalculated" is correct.

Tip: Finance write-downs often appear beside clean "be" + participle forms.

FALSE — Use "retake," not "retakes," after "recommended that."

Tip: Exam/assessment vocabulary is a favourite place to hide -s.

TRUE — "Directed that… remain" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: "Remain untouched/unchanged" after direct/insist is a high-yield pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: At this level, watch unreal "were" bleeding into mandative frames and -s after recommend. Negated legal "not + base" is grammatical; "were" after desirable is not.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The charter requires that the secretary keep minutes of every plenary.
It was insisted that the renegotiation starts before the bond matures.
External counsel advised that settlement talks be reopened quietly.
The syndicate proposed that voting thresholds is raised to seventy-five percent.
The protocol states that it is vital that specimens reach the lab within four hours.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Requires that… keep" is correct bare-form usage.

Tip: Officer titles (secretary, treasurer) after require are classic test items.

FALSE — After "it was insisted that," use "start," not "starts."

Tip: Passive reporting ("it was insisted") does not change the that-clause rule.

TRUE — "Advised that… be reopened" is correct.

Tip: Advise that + be + participle is formal counsel English.

FALSE — Use "be raised," not "is raised," after "proposed that."

Tip: Plural "thresholds" still take "be" in the passive subjunctive.

TRUE — "It is vital that specimens reach" correctly uses the bare plural verb.

Tip: Nested "states that it is vital that…" still ends in a mandative clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Reporting shells ("it was insisted," "the protocol states that it is vital") bury the real trigger. Unwrap to the innermost that-clause and test for base form versus indicative.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board resolved that interim dividends not be declared this half.
It is essential that whoever chairs the panel has no prior conflict.
Lenders demanded that financial covenants be tightened after the breach.
The examiner insisted that each script is double-marked independently.
Guidance recommends that the risk register be reviewed after every incident.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negated passive "not be declared" is correctly formed.

Tip: Board resolutions often negate with "not be" + participle.

FALSE — After "it is essential that," use "have," not "has," even after "whoever."

Tip: Free relatives (whoever) still sit under the mandative rule—no -s.

TRUE — "Demanded that… be tightened" is correct.

Tip: Covenant language after demand/require is almost always subjunctive.

FALSE — Use "be double-marked," not "is double-marked," after "insisted that."

Tip: Exam-administration passives are a favourite "is" trap.

TRUE — "Recommends that… be reviewed" is correct.

Tip: Risk and compliance manuals recycle this frame constantly.
tasks.solution_overview: The sharpest trap is "whoever… has": the free relative does not cancel the mandative. Strip -s / swap "is" for "be" wherever essential, insist, or recommend governs the clause.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The articles provide that directors declare interests at the first opportunity.
It is critical that the spill kit remains sealed until an incident occurs.
The tribunal ordered that costs be reserved pending written submissions.
Her supervisor suggested that the abstract emphasises policy implications only.
Investors requested that management provide a bridge to the revised forecast.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Provide that directors declare" correctly uses the bare plural verb.

Tip: Articles of association are full of silent mandatives—spot the that-clause.

FALSE — After "it is critical that," use "remain," not "remains."

Tip: Safety and ops manuals often leave an indicative -s by mistake.

TRUE — "Ordered that costs be reserved" is correct.

Tip: Costs/orders/injunctions after order that almost always take "be."

FALSE — Use "emphasise," not "emphasises," after "suggested that."

Tip: Academic suggest that + -s is one of the most common exam errors.

TRUE — "Requested that management provide" correctly uses the base form.

Tip: Collective "management" still takes a bare verb in mandative English.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with statutory "provide that," tribunal "ordered that," and academic "suggested that." Only the critical/suggest items keep unwanted -s; the rest already show proper base forms.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not only she arrived late, but she also forgot the briefing pack.
Seldom the board approves a bid without a second valuation.
Never the firm had faced such regulatory scrutiny.
No sooner had the auction opened than bids flooded in.
Under no circumstances the clerk will release the client files.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Fronted "not only" needs inversion: "Not only did she arrive late…".

Tip: If "not only" sits at the start, treat it like a question for the auxiliary: did/does/had + subject.

FALSE — Needs "Seldom does the board approve…".

Tip: Negative frequency words (seldom, rarely, never) at the start almost always trigger inversion.

FALSE — Fronted "never" needs "Never had the firm faced…", not subject–verb order.

Tip: With past perfect after "never", move "had" before the subject.

TRUE — "No sooner…than" with past perfect inversion is the classic pattern here.

Tip: Pair "no sooner" with "than" (not "when") and invert: "had + subject".

FALSE — Needs "Under no circumstances will the clerk release…".

Tip: Modal + subject swaps after a negative prepositional phrase at the front.
tasks.solution_overview: These openers look formal, but the test is mechanical: a negative or restrictive phrase at the front usually forces auxiliary–subject order. Scan each line for that swap first, then check the correlative word (than/when) if "no sooner" or "hardly" appears.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hardly had the announcement been made when questions began.
Rarely we see such a sharp move in the overnight rate.
Little did the committee realise how contested the vote would be.
Not only did the report flag the risks, but it also proposed fixes.
Seldom the audit committee meets without a full pack.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Hardly had…when…" is the standard inverted past-perfect pattern.

Tip: After hardly/scarcely/barely, prefer "when" (or "before"), not "than".

FALSE — Needs "Rarely do we see…".

Tip: No auxiliary visible? Add do/does/did and place it before the subject.

TRUE — "Little did…" correctly inverts after a restrictive opener.

Tip: "Little" meaning "not at all" behaves like a negative fronting word.

TRUE — Fronted "not only" takes inversion, and "but also" keeps the second clause parallel.

Tip: Check both halves: inversion after "not only", then a matching "but also" clause.

FALSE — Requires "Seldom does the audit committee meet…".

Tip: "Seldom" + present simple → does/do before the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Task 2 drills the core set: hardly, rarely, little, not only, seldom. Correct lines already invert; wrong ones leave ordinary subject–verb order after a fronted negative. Fix those by inserting or moving the auxiliary.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Under no circumstances should this forecast be leaked before the call.
No sooner the CFO sat down than the analysts started questioning.
Never has the bank issued a profit warning mid-quarter like this.
Scarcely the project had begun before funding was frozen.
At no time the directors authorised an off-book transfer.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negative adverbial + modal inversion is clean: "should this forecast be leaked".

Tip: After "under no circumstances", expect will/should/can before the subject.

FALSE — Needs "No sooner had the CFO sat down than…".

Tip: "No sooner" almost always pairs with past perfect and inversion of "had".

TRUE — "Never has the bank issued…" correctly inverts present perfect.

Tip: Keep the participle after the subject: Never + has/have + subject + past participle.

FALSE — Needs "Scarcely had the project begun…".

Tip: Scarcely/hardly/barely fronting → had + subject + past participle.

FALSE — Needs "At no time did the directors authorise…".

Tip: "At no time" is a full negative fronting phrase; invert like a question.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on stock fronting phrases: under no circumstances, no sooner, never, scarcely, at no time. If the phrase is negative and sits first, the next word should be an auxiliary, not the subject.
