tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only after the audit closed did the errors become obvious.
Not until the contract was signed did negotiations end.
Hardly the traders had logged on when the system crashed.
On no account may staff discuss the merger outside the room.
Nowhere in the prospectus does it mention contingent liabilities.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Only after…" inverts the main clause: "did the errors become".

Tip: With only + time clause, leave the time clause alone and invert the main clause.

TRUE — "Not until…" likewise inverts only the main clause.

Tip: Do not invert inside the "not until" clause itself.

FALSE — Needs "Hardly had the traders logged on when…".

Tip: Hardly + past perfect: had before the subject.

TRUE — "On no account may staff…" is a correct formal prohibition with inversion.

Tip: "On no account" and "under no circumstances" behave the same way.

TRUE — "Nowhere…does it mention…" correctly inverts after a negative place adverbial.

Tip: Nowhere/no place at the front → does/do/did + subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these already invert correctly after only after, not until, on no account, and nowhere. The odd one out is "hardly" without "had" before the subject—fix that pattern and the rest fall into place.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No longer does the supplier dominate the regional market.
Barely had the webcast started when the feed cut out.
In no way can the warranty cover wilful misuse of the kit.
Not only was the tender late, but it also lacked the bond.
Seldom have we seen spreads tighten this fast after a hike.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "No longer" at the front takes "does the supplier dominate".

Tip: No longer + present simple → do/does before the subject.

TRUE — "Barely had…when…" mirrors the hardly pattern.

Tip: Barely/hardly/scarcely share the same inversion + "when" template.

TRUE — "In no way can the warranty…" correctly inverts the modal.

Tip: In no way / under no circumstances / on no account all pull the modal forward.

TRUE — Fronted "not only" with "was" before the subject is right, and "but also" completes it.

Tip: With be-verbs, invert be itself: Not only was the tender…

TRUE — "Seldom have we seen…" is clean present-perfect inversion.

Tip: Frequency negative + have/has + subject + past participle.
tasks.solution_overview: Every sentence here is already inverted. Use them as models: spot the fronted negative, confirm the auxiliary sits next, then note the correlative (when/but also) where relevant.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No sooner had liquidity dried up than spreads blew out.
Rarely does a mid-cap issue price without a roadshow.
Not only the CFO objected, but the counsel also raised red flags.
Under no circumstances will payroll data leave the secure vault.
Never the syndicate had allocated such a large greenshoe.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past-perfect inversion after "no sooner" plus "than" is exact.

Tip: Memorise the trio: no sooner + had + subject + than.

TRUE — "Rarely does…" correctly adds do-support for present simple.

Tip: If there is no auxiliary, invent do/does/did for the inversion.

FALSE — Needs "Not only did the CFO object, but…".

Tip: Fronted not only without an auxiliary still needs did/does/do.

TRUE — Modal inversion after "under no circumstances" is correct.

Tip: will/must/should jumps before the subject after this phrase.

FALSE — Needs "Never had the syndicate allocated…".

Tip: Never + past perfect → Never had + subject + past participle.
tasks.solution_overview: Three lines already invert; two leave the subject right after not only / never. Mentally flip those into question order and you will see the repair immediately.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hardly had the embargo lifted when rival bids appeared.
Little the investors understood about the clawback clause.
Only when the covenant was breached did lenders intervene.
Scarcely had the ink dried on the term sheet when terms shifted.
Seldom the risk desk updates its stress scenarios mid-week.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Hardly + had + subject + when is textbook.

Tip: Keep "when" (not "than") after hardly/scarcely/barely.

FALSE — Needs "Little did the investors understand…".

Tip: Little as a fronting restrictor needs did/does/do + subject.

TRUE — Only when + clause, then invert the main clause.

Tip: Invert after the time clause ends, not inside it.

TRUE — Scarcely had…when… matches the hard/barely family.

Tip: Same skeleton for scarcely, hardly, and barely.

FALSE — Needs "Seldom does the risk desk update…".

Tip: Present-simple after seldom → does/do before the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Hardly, scarcely, and only when are shown correctly; little and seldom are missing their auxiliaries. Add did/does and the pattern locks in.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not until the regulator cleared the filing the bank announced the deal.
Under no circumstances are visitors allowed in the dealing room.
No sooner had the bond priced than secondary trading surged.
At no point did management concede that guidance was wrong.
Rarely a distressed name recovers without a full restructuring.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Needs "…did the bank announce the deal" after the not-until clause.

Tip: Not until + time clause → invert the main clause with did/does/do or an auxiliary.

TRUE — Be-verb inversion after "under no circumstances" is fine: "are visitors allowed".

Tip: With be, invert be itself; no extra do-support.

TRUE — No sooner + had + than is correct again.

Tip: Watch the correlative: than after no sooner.

TRUE — "At no point did management concede…" is solid inversion.

Tip: At no point / at no time are interchangeable triggers.

FALSE — Needs "Rarely does a distressed name recover…".

Tip: Rarely + present simple → does/do + subject + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Most lines invert cleanly. The traps are "not until" without main-clause inversion and "rarely" without do-support—both classic exam misses.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only by cutting costs can the division stay solvent this year.
No sooner had the rates decision landed when futures reversed.
Not only did volumes spike, but spreads also compressed.
Under no circumstances should client passwords be reused.
Never before has the exchange halted trading for so long.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Only by…" inverts the main clause: "can the division stay".

Tip: Only + prepositional phrase at the front still forces inversion.

FALSE — "No sooner" takes "than", not "when": "…landed than futures reversed".

Tip: Correlative pairs: no sooner→than; hardly/scarcely→when.

TRUE — Not only + did + but also is correctly inverted and balanced.

Tip: Keep both verbs parallel after not only / but also.

TRUE — Modal inversion after under no circumstances is right.

Tip: should/must/will before the subject after this opener.

TRUE — "Never before has…" correctly inverts present perfect.

Tip: Never before / never again behave like never for inversion.
tasks.solution_overview: Inversion is mostly done right; the subtle miss is the correlative after "no sooner". Word order can look perfect and still fail if than/when is swapped.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hardly had the CFO finished speaking than the share price jumped.
Not until funding was secured did construction resume.
Seldom do private placements clear without intensive marketing.
On no account the intern may access production systems alone.
Little did the buy-side know a rival bid was already circulating.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Hardly pairs with "when", not "than": "…speaking when the share price jumped".

Tip: Swap than→when after hardly/scarcely/barely even if inversion looks fine.

TRUE — Not until + clause, then "did construction resume".

Tip: Main-clause inversion only; leave the time clause in normal order.

TRUE — Seldom + do-support is correct.

Tip: Frequency negatives need do/does/did when no other auxiliary exists.

FALSE — Needs "On no account may the intern access…".

Tip: Move the modal before the subject after on no account.

TRUE — Little did… is a stock restrictive inversion.

Tip: Little + did + subject + base verb is the usual template.
tasks.solution_overview: Two errors here mix correlative choice (hardly…than) with missing modal inversion (on no account). Check both word order and the linking word after the fronted phrase.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only after collateral was posted the loan facility became available.
Nowhere else will you find comparable covenants in this sector.
Scarcely had settlement completed when a dispute was filed.
Not only did the bank raise capital, it also cut its dividend.
Under no circumstances the auditors will sign without testing.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Needs "…did the loan facility become available".

Tip: Only after + time clause → invert the main clause with did + subject.

TRUE — Nowhere else + will + subject is correct.

Tip: Nowhere / nowhere else at the front always invert.

TRUE — Scarcely had…when… is the right pair.

Tip: Keep when after scarcely; keep had before the subject.

TRUE — Not only…but also (here "it also") with inversion is acceptable formal style.

Tip: "But also" can appear as "it also" if the second clause still matches.

FALSE — Needs "Under no circumstances will the auditors sign…".

Tip: will must precede the subject after this fronting phrase.
tasks.solution_overview: Only after and under no circumstances still trap people who invert late or not at all. The other three already show the target shapes—use them as anchors.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No sooner had the embargo expired than rival filings landed.
Rarely have margins recovered so quickly after a write-down.
Not only was pricing aggressive, but documentation was incomplete.
At no time were minority shareholders consulted on the spin-off.
Barely had the market opened when the halt was triggered.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — No sooner + had + than is perfect.

Tip: Drill the correlative than until it is automatic.

TRUE — Rarely + present perfect inversion is correct.

Tip: Rarely have/has + subject + past participle.

TRUE — Not only was…but… keeps be inverted and the contrast clear.

Tip: With was/were, invert be; no do-support needed.

TRUE — At no time + were + subject is correct be-inversion.

Tip: Passive or be-main verbs invert be itself.

TRUE — Barely had…when… matches the hard/scarcely family.

Tip: Barely = hardly for inversion purposes.
tasks.solution_overview: A clean model set: no sooner, rarely, not only, at no time, barely. If your own answers miss any of these shapes, rewrite the wrong ones to match these templates.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only if the guarantor signs will the facility become effective.
The report not only highlights risks but also proposes remedies.
No sooner had trading resumed than another circuit breaker hit.
Hardly the ink had dried on the SPA when a walk-away notice arrived.
Under no circumstances are personal devices permitted on the floor.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Only if + clause, then invert the main clause: "will the facility become".

Tip: Conditional "only if" at the front still triggers main-clause inversion.

TRUE — Mid-sentence "not only…but also" needs no inversion.

Tip: Invert only when "not only" is fronted; otherwise keep normal order.

TRUE — No sooner…than with past perfect inversion is correct.

Tip: Confirm than after no sooner every time.

FALSE — Needs "Hardly had the ink dried…when…".

Tip: had must sit before the subject after hardly.

TRUE — Under no circumstances + are + subject is correct.

Tip: Be-inversion after this phrase is standard in policies.
tasks.solution_overview: The key sophistication here is knowing when not to invert: mid-clause "not only…but also" is fine. The only hard fail is hardly without had-before-subject.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not until did the board approve the write-off the accounts were final.
In no circumstances should draft minutes circulate outside the committee.
Seldom has a listing attracted so many cornerstone investors.
No longer the franchise depends on a single regional distributor.
Only after did the due diligence close were funds released.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Do not invert inside the not-until clause; say "Not until the board approved the write-off were the accounts final" (or "…did the accounts become final").

Tip: Invert the main clause only—never invert the not-until/time clause itself.

TRUE — "In no circumstances should…" is the same family as under no circumstances.

Tip: In/under no circumstances both pull the modal forward.

TRUE — Seldom + present perfect inversion is correct.

Tip: Seldom has/have + subject + past participle.

FALSE — Needs "No longer does the franchise depend…".

Tip: No longer + present simple → does/do before the subject.

FALSE — Wrong placement of did; use "Only after the due diligence closed were funds released".

Tip: Keep the only-after clause normal; invert the main clause alone.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced traps put the auxiliary in the wrong clause (not until / only after). Remember: time/condition clause stays normal; the following main clause inverts.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not only did costs overrun, but timelines slipped as well.
Scarcely had the roadshow ended than subscriptions were scaled back.
Never again will the firm underwrite without independent counsel.
Little does the market appreciate how thin the order book is.
Under no circumstances the escrow agent may release funds early.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Fronted not only + did, completed by but…as well, is acceptable.

Tip: "But also / but…as well" both work if the first half inverts.

FALSE — Scarcely takes "when", not "than".

Tip: Correlative check: scarcely/hardly/barely → when; no sooner → than.

TRUE — Never again + will + subject is correct.

Tip: Never again / never before behave like never.

TRUE — Little does… correctly inverts present simple with do-support.

Tip: Little + does/do + subject + base verb.

FALSE — Needs "Under no circumstances may the escrow agent release…".

Tip: Modal before subject after under no circumstances.
tasks.solution_overview: Inversion looks right on the scarcely line, but the correlative is wrong. Pair that check with the modal-order miss on under no circumstances.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only when the ratings agencies upgraded did spreads normalise.
No sooner the prospectus was filed than the roadshow began.
At no stage were investors told about the contingent earn-out.
Rarely do we publish earnings without a simultaneous webcast.
Not only the pricing disappointed; the allocation disappointed too.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Only when + clause, then "did spreads normalise".

Tip: Invert after the when-clause finishes.

FALSE — Needs "No sooner was the prospectus filed than…" or "No sooner had the prospectus been filed than…".

Tip: No sooner requires inversion of be/had immediately after it.

TRUE — At no stage + were + subject is correct be-inversion.

Tip: At no stage / at no point / at no time are equivalent triggers.

TRUE — Rarely + do-support is correct.

Tip: Rarely do/does + subject + base verb.

FALSE — Fronted not only needs inversion: "Not only did the pricing disappoint…".

Tip: If not only leads the sentence, insert did/does/do before the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Two failures omit inversion after no sooner and not only. The survivors show only when, at no stage, and rarely done properly—mirror those.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not until the swap was unwound the hedge accounting treatment changed.
Under no circumstances may margin calls be ignored overnight.
Seldom has a distressed exchange offer cleared on the first attempt.
Only by restructuring the notes can default be avoided this quarter.
Hardly had liquidity returned than another redemption wave began.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Needs "…did the hedge accounting treatment change" (or "…was the treatment changed").

Tip: Not until → invert the main clause; do not leave subject–verb order there.

TRUE — Under no circumstances + may + subject is correct modal inversion.

Tip: After this phrase, expect may/will/should before the subject.

TRUE — Seldom + present perfect inversion is correct.

Tip: Seldom has/have + subject + past participle.

TRUE — Only by + -ing, then modal inversion in the main clause.

Tip: Only by / only with / only through all invert the following clause.

FALSE — Hardly takes "when", not "than".

Tip: Even with perfect inversion, wrong correlative still fails the item.
tasks.solution_overview: Top-band items stay inside negative/restrictive inversion: not until, under no circumstances, seldom, only by, hardly. Judge each line by whether the auxiliary moved—and whether than/when is the right partner.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Under no circumstances is front-running of client orders tolerated.
No sooner had the block crossed than the tape lit up.
Not only were fees waived, but research access was expanded.
Seldom does a secondary offering clear without price tension.
Little did counterparties expect the variation margin call overnight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Under no circumstances + is + subject is correct.

Tip: Be-main verbs invert be after this phrase.

TRUE — No sooner…than with past perfect is exact.

Tip: had + subject + than remains the gold standard.

TRUE — Not only were…but… correctly inverts were.

Tip: Plural subject → were before it after not only.

TRUE — Seldom does… is clean do-support inversion.

Tip: Frequency negative + does/do + subject + base verb.

TRUE — Little did… is the classic restrictive inversion.

Tip: Little + did + subject + base verb.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are model answers across the core triggers. Treat this task as a checklist of shapes you should be able to produce under exam pressure.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only after the lock-up expired investors were free to sell.
Not until management restated earnings did the sell-side upgrade.
Barely had the facility been drawn when utilisation hit the cap.
On no account should draft valuations leave the data room.
Never the compliance team had cleared a structure this aggressive.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Needs "…were investors free to sell" or "…did investors become free to sell".

Tip: Only after + clause → invert the main clause.

TRUE — Not until…did… is correctly inverted in the main clause.

Tip: Keep the not-until clause in normal order.

TRUE — Barely had…when… is right.

Tip: Passive past perfect still inverts had: Barely had the facility been drawn…

TRUE — On no account should… is correct modal inversion.

Tip: should/must/may before the subject after on no account.

FALSE — Needs "Never had the compliance team cleared…".

Tip: Never + past perfect → Never had + subject + past participle.
tasks.solution_overview: Two lines forget to invert after only after and never. The others show not until, barely, and on no account in full working order—match those repairs to the same templates.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Nowhere in the offering circular does it disclose related-party debt.
Not only did the issuer refinance, but it also extended the tenor.
Hardly had the blackout ended when marketing calls resumed.
Under no circumstances the trustee will waive a payment default.
No sooner had allocations been finalised than complaints arrived.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Nowhere…does it disclose… correctly inverts after a negative place adverbial.

Tip: Nowhere / no place at the front → does/do/did + subject.

TRUE — Not only did…but also… is fully inverted and parallel.

Tip: Match verb forms across both halves after not only / but also.

TRUE — Hardly had…when… is the standard pattern.

Tip: when after hardly; had before the subject.

FALSE — Needs "Under no circumstances will the trustee waive…".

Tip: Final check on every under-no-circumstances item: modal before subject.

TRUE — No sooner had…than… closes the set correctly.

Tip: than after no sooner; had before the subject.
highlights: Nowhere in the offering circular does
tasks.solution_overview: Four model inversions and one classic miss: under no circumstances without modal–subject swap. If you catch that last pattern every time, this topic is exam-ready.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having reviewed the quarterly figures, the analyst revised the forecast.
Walking into the boardroom, the presentation slides were already on screen.
Concerned about liquidity, the bond issue was delayed until spring.
Having been delayed by customs, several complaints were logged online.
Frustrated by the slow response, several emails were sent overnight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The analyst is the logical subject of Having reviewed, so the opening participle attaches cleanly.

Tip: Ask who did the -ing / having action — that person must be the grammatical subject.

FALSE — The slides were not walking; rewrite as Walking into the boardroom, the directors found the slides already on screen.

Tip: If the subject cannot perform the participle, it is dangling.

FALSE — A bond issue cannot feel concerned; Concerned about liquidity, the treasurer delayed the bond issue until spring.

Tip: Past participles (Concerned, Exhausted) still need a human or animate logical subject.

FALSE — Complaints were not delayed by customs; Having been delayed by customs, the shipment prompted several online complaints.

Tip: Passive participles need the thing that underwent the delay as subject.

FALSE — Emails cannot feel frustrated; say Frustrated by the slow response, the manager sent several emails overnight.

Tip: Emotions + inanimate subject = classic dangling trap.
tasks.solution_overview: For each opener, name the implied doer of the participle, then check whether that doer is the grammatical subject. Only the first sentence matches; the rest dangle.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Delayed by fog, the flight departed three hours late.
Having analysed the survey data, several inconsistencies were noted.
Exhausted after the night shift, the nurse went straight home.
Reading the contract carefully, a hidden penalty clause became obvious.
Surprised by the sudden downturn, capital was withdrawn overnight.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The flight is a logical patient of Delayed; the participle attaches correctly.

Tip: Passive -ed openers are fine when the subject was delayed, damaged, approved, etc.

FALSE — Inconsistencies did not analyse the data; use Having analysed the survey data, the team noted several inconsistencies.

Tip: Having + PP needs the analyser as subject, not the findings.

TRUE — The nurse is exhausted; subject and participle align.

Tip: Tired / Exhausted / Relieved almost always need a person as subject.

FALSE — A clause cannot read; rewrite Reading the contract carefully, the lawyer spotted a hidden penalty clause.

Tip: Present participles imply an agent who can act.

FALSE — Capital cannot be surprised; Surprised by the sudden downturn, investors withdrew capital overnight.

Tip: Keep the experiencer as subject across the comma.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan for Having + past participle and bare -ing openers. Only two sentences keep a matching subject; the others put findings, clauses, or capital in the doer slot.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having crossed the border, the travellers presented their passports.
Startled by the alarm, the meeting was adjourned at once.
Reviewing the bids, three suppliers were shortlisted immediately.
Published last spring, several updates remain outstanding.
Hoping to cut costs, overtime was banned across the division.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Travellers both crossed and presented; perfect participle is anchored.

Tip: Having + PP marks an earlier completed action by the same subject.

FALSE — A meeting cannot be startled; Startled by the alarm, the chair adjourned the meeting at once.

Tip: Emotion participles need people, not events or institutions as experiencers.

FALSE — Suppliers were not reviewing; Reviewing the bids, the procurement lead shortlisted three suppliers immediately.

Tip: Keep the reviewer as subject when the opener is Reviewing…

FALSE — Updates were not published last spring in this wording; Published last spring, the guidelines still leave several updates outstanding.

Tip: Past-participle openers need the thing that was published as subject.

FALSE — Overtime cannot hope; Hoping to cut costs, management banned overtime across the division.

Tip: Intent verbs (hoping, intending, aiming) need a human subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Only the travellers sentence attaches. Emotion, reviewing, published, and hoping openers all fail when the wrong noun follows the comma.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Entering the warehouse, the temperature dropped sharply.
Having missed the filing deadline, the applicant was disqualified.
Written in plain English, the privacy notice is easier to follow.
Driving to the site, a tyre burst on the motorway.
Based on last year's audit, the risk rating was lowered.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Temperature did not enter; Entering the warehouse, the inspectors noticed the temperature drop.

Tip: Motion -ing + weather/measurement subject is a textbook dangler.

TRUE — The applicant missed the deadline and was disqualified.

Tip: Perfect participle + same person as subject is usually safe.

TRUE — The notice is what was written; reduced relative works.

Tip: Written / Drafted / Signed + document subject is typically grammatical.

FALSE — A tyre cannot drive; Driving to the site, she had a tyre burst on the motorway.

Tip: Vehicles and parts are not drivers.

TRUE — The rating is based on the audit; Based on… correctly modifies the subject.

Tip: Based on / According to openers are fine when the subject is the conclusion or rating.
tasks.solution_overview: Three sentences hang on a person or document that matches the participle; two put the wrong noun after the comma. Fix danglers by renaming the subject to the real actor.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having negotiated all night, the delegates signed the protocol at dawn.
Seated near the exit, the observers left as soon as the vote was called.
Funded by the ministry, the pilot scheme ran for eighteen months.
Looking at the chart, the analysts called the downward trend unmistakable.
Realising the error too late, the clerk circulated a corrective memo.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Delegates negotiated and signed; sequence is clear.

Tip: Having + PP then main verb shows earlier → later for one subject.

TRUE — Observers were seated and then left; logical match.

Tip: Past participles of position (seated, located) often describe the subject’s state.

TRUE — The scheme was funded; patient subject fits.

Tip: Funded / Sponsored / Led by… + project subject is standard.

TRUE — Analysts can look at the chart; perception participle matches the subject.

Tip: Perception -ing (looking, listening) needs a perceiver as subject.

TRUE — The clerk realises and circulates; mental-state participle is anchored.

Tip: Mental-state participles need minds, not documents.
tasks.solution_overview: All five attach cleanly: perfect participle, position participle, patientive Funded…, perception Looking…, and mental Realising… each keep a matching subject.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been briefed by counsel, the directors approved the settlement.
Turning the corner, the head office came into view.
Charged with fraud, the former CFO denied every allegation.
Comparing the two drafts, several typos stood out immediately.
Prepared under time pressure, the slides still covered the key risks.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Directors were briefed (passive perfect) and then approved.

Tip: Having been + PP = earlier passive experience of the subject.

FALSE — The head office did not turn; Turning the corner, we saw the head office come into view.

Tip: Motion openers need a mover as subject.

TRUE — The former CFO is the one charged; attachment is sound.

Tip: Legal past participles (charged, accused, convicted) take the person as subject.

FALSE — Typos do not compare drafts; Comparing the two drafts, the editor spotted several typos immediately.

Tip: Comparing / Examining + findings-as-subject is a frequent dangler.

TRUE — The slides were prepared; patient subject works.

Tip: Prepared / Written / Compiled under… + document subject is fine.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch motion and comparison openers especially — they almost never attach to buildings or typos. Passive perfect and patientive past participles are usually safe.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Working from home, productivity rose by twelve percent.
Having submitted the tender, the consortium waited for clarification questions.
Alarmed by the breach, the IT team isolated the affected servers.
Stored in a cool warehouse, the samples remained stable.
Opening the spreadsheet, an unexpected formula error appeared.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Productivity does not work from home; Working from home, staff raised productivity by twelve percent.

Tip: Abstract nouns (productivity, morale, demand) rarely do -ing actions.

TRUE — The consortium submitted and waited.

Tip: Institutional subjects can take Having + PP when the organisation is the actor.

TRUE — The IT team can be alarmed and isolate servers.

Tip: Emotion + team/person subject is grammatical.

TRUE — Samples were stored; state participle matches.

Tip: Stored / Kept / Held + physical object is a clean reduced relative.

FALSE — An error cannot open a spreadsheet; Opening the spreadsheet, the analyst found an unexpected formula error.

Tip: Instrumental -ing needs the user, not the discovery.
tasks.solution_overview: Reject any sentence where an abstract result or error is doing the opening action. Keep sentences where the organisation, team, or physical object is a plausible subject of the participle.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having checked the inventory twice, the warehouse supervisor closed the system.
Standing on the balcony, the harbour lights looked magnificent.
Issued in March, the interim report already needs an update.
Determined to meet the target, overtime was authorised until Friday.
Speaking off the record, the minister confirmed the draft timetable.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Supervisor checked then closed; perfect participle is anchored.

Tip: Same actor before and after the comma.

FALSE — Harbour lights were not standing; Standing on the balcony, we thought the harbour lights looked magnificent.

Tip: Location -ing needs the person located there.

TRUE — The report was issued; reduced relative is correct.

Tip: Issued / Released / Circulated + document subject = OK.

FALSE — Overtime cannot be determined; Determined to meet the target, management authorised overtime until Friday.

Tip: Determined / Eager / Keen require a willful subject.

TRUE — The minister is speaking; attachment is clear.

Tip: Speaking / Writing as openers need the speaker/writer as subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Attitude participles (Determined…) and posture participles (Standing…) are dangler magnets. Document participles (Issued…) and speech participles with a named speaker are usually fine.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been warned about volatility, the traders reduced their exposure.
While reviewing the ledger, several duplicate invoices surfaced.
Built in 2012, the data centre still meets current standards.
Convinced by the evidence, the panel upheld the sanction.
Arriving late to the briefing, the key slides had already been discussed.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Traders were warned and then reduced exposure.

Tip: Having been + PP correctly marks earlier passive experience.

FALSE — Invoices do not review; While reviewing the ledger, the auditor found several duplicate invoices.

Tip: While + -ing still needs the reviewer as subject.

TRUE — The centre was built; patient subject fits.

Tip: Built / Constructed / Renovated + place/building is standard.

TRUE — The panel can be convinced and uphold a sanction.

Tip: Convinced / Persuaded take the decision-maker as subject.

FALSE — Slides did not arrive late; Arriving late to the briefing, she found the key slides had already been discussed.

Tip: Time-of-arrival openers need the latecomer.
tasks.solution_overview: While + participle does not excuse a dangling structure — the logical subject rule still applies. Buildings and people attach cleanly; discoveries and slides usually do not.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having finalised the disclosure letter, counsel filed it before noon.
Running the stress test overnight, several capital shortfalls emerged.
Buried in the appendix, the critical assumption went unnoticed.
Pleased with the pilot results, the board extended funding.
Climbing the stairs to the lab, the samples began to thaw.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Counsel finalised and filed; same actor.

Tip: Perfect participle + professional subject is usually solid.

FALSE — Shortfalls do not run tests; Running the stress test overnight, the risk team found several capital shortfalls.

Tip: Process -ing + result-as-subject = dangler.

TRUE — The assumption was buried; reduced relative works.

Tip: Buried / Hidden / Nested in… + detail/subject is fine.

TRUE — The board can be pleased and extend funding.

Tip: Emotion adjective-participles still need a capable subject.

FALSE — Samples do not climb stairs; Climbing the stairs to the lab, the researchers noticed the samples beginning to thaw.

Tip: Never let cargo or samples perform locomotion openers.
tasks.solution_overview: Two danglers put results or samples in the doer slot. The other three keep counsel, an assumption, and the board as coherent subjects of their participles.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been rejected twice, the proposal was withdrawn without debate.
Using the new template, formatting errors fell by half.
Signed by both parties, the amendment took effect immediately.
Worried about reputational risk, a press embargo was imposed.
Following the guidelines strictly, the assessors scored each criterion.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The proposal was rejected and then withdrawn; patient subject is consistent.

Tip: Having been + PP can take a document as subject when that document underwent the action.

FALSE — Errors do not use templates; Using the new template, editors cut formatting errors by half.

Tip: Using / Applying tools needs a user subject.

TRUE — The amendment was signed; reduced relative is correct.

Tip: Signed / Ratified / Endorsed + agreement subject is clean.

FALSE — An embargo cannot worry; Worried about reputational risk, communications imposed a press embargo.

Tip: Emotional openers + policy-as-subject fail.

TRUE — Assessors follow and score; attachment holds.

Tip: Following… as a manner opener needs the follower as subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Instrumental Using… and emotional Worried… are the usual fail points here. Document subjects work for passive perfect and signed-amendment patterns.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having consulted the stakeholders, the project lead revised the scope.
Seen from the river, the campus looks surprisingly compact.
Expecting a soft landing, asset prices were left unchanged.
Drawn from internal surveys, the chart understates regional gaps.
Leaving the building, the fire doors locked automatically behind them.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Project lead consulted and revised.

Tip: Having + PP of a deliberate action needs that actor as subject.

TRUE — Campus is what is seen; passive participle of perception is fine.

Tip: Seen from / Viewed from + place/building subject is idiomatic and grammatical.

FALSE — Prices do not expect; Expecting a soft landing, the committee left asset prices unchanged.

Tip: Expecting / Anticipating require a planner, not a price.

TRUE — The chart’s data were drawn from surveys; reduced relative sense holds.

Tip: Drawn from / Taken from + figure/chart subject is acceptable.

FALSE — Fire doors do not leave; Leaving the building, they heard the fire doors lock automatically.

Tip: Leaving / Entering need the people moving.
tasks.solution_overview: Seen from… and Drawn from… are legitimate patientive openers. Expecting… and Leaving… are not — restore a human subject for those.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been promoted mid-year, she inherited a strained budget.
Judging by the margins, the product line is barely viable.
Covered by insurance, the damaged consignment was written off.
Intending to reassure investors, calm wording was chosen for the release.
Once approved by compliance, the campaign can go live.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — She was promoted and inherited the budget.

Tip: Having been + PP + same person is a safe pattern.

TRUE — Judging by… is a fixed, impersonal evaluative opener; no dangling actor is required.

Tip: Judging by / Considering / Given are often absolute-style and exam-accepted.

TRUE — Consignment was covered; patient subject matches.

Tip: Covered / Protected / Guaranteed by… + asset subject works.

FALSE — Wording cannot intend; Intending to reassure investors, the team chose calm wording for the release.

Tip: Intending / Meaning to… always need a willful subject.

TRUE — Once approved… is a reduced passive clause with the campaign as patient.

Tip: Once / When + PP often equals once it has been + PP.
tasks.solution_overview: At this level, distinguish true danglers from conventional absolute openers like Judging by…. Only Intending… fails the logical-subject test here.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having restructured the debt, interest costs fell sharply in Q3.
Granted under the emergency scheme, the waiver expires in June.
All things considered, the merger still looks premature.
Assuming constant demand, unit costs decline with scale.
Walking through the plant, safety violations were everywhere.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Interest costs did not restructure the debt; Having restructured the debt, the firm saw interest costs fall sharply in Q3.

Tip: Perfect participles of corporate actions need the firm/board as subject, not the metric.

TRUE — The waiver was granted; patient subject is correct.

Tip: Granted / Awarded / Issued under… + licence/waiver subject is fine.

TRUE — All things considered is a set absolute construction, not a dangling modifier of a missing person.

Tip: Memorise a few absolutes: all things considered, weather permitting, that said.

TRUE — Assuming… here sets a modelling condition; the main clause states the model’s implication with unit costs as subject in a scientific register.

Tip: Assuming / Holding constant… can introduce hypothetical premises in analysis writing.

FALSE — Violations do not walk; Walking through the plant, inspectors found safety violations everywhere.

Tip: Still apply the walking-subject rule even in denser prose.
tasks.solution_overview: Absolutes and modelling openers (All things considered, Assuming…) are grammatical conventions. Having restructured… still needs the restructurer, and Walking… still needs the walker.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been delayed by industrial action, passengers were offered vouchers.
Taken at face value, the forecast looks overly optimistic.
Tired of endless revisions, the draft was abandoned overnight.
Weather permitting, the site visit will go ahead on Tuesday.
Having identified the bottleneck, throughput improved within a week.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Passengers were delayed (passive perfect) and then offered vouchers.

Tip: Having been delayed can take people as patients.

TRUE — The forecast is what is taken at face value; reduced relative sense.

Tip: Taken / Read / Interpreted as… + claim/forecast subject is OK.

FALSE — A draft cannot feel tired; Tired of endless revisions, the author abandoned the draft overnight.

Tip: Tired of / Fed up with need experiencers.

TRUE — Weather permitting is a classic absolute; no dangling actor.

Tip: Absolute noun + participle stands free of the main subject.

FALSE — Throughput did not identify anything; Having identified the bottleneck, operations improved throughput within a week.

Tip: Perfect participle of problem-finding needs the finder.
tasks.solution_overview: Mix patientive perfects, evaluative Taken…, and an absolute (Weather permitting). Reject Tired… and Having identified… when the subject is the draft or the KPI.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Properly trained, junior analysts can handle the first-line review.
Having lost the original invoices, a reconstruction was attempted from bank statements.
Other things being equal, higher tariffs reduce import volumes.
Relieved at the outcome, celebrations continued late into the night.
Designed for remote audits, the checklist omits on-site sampling steps.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Junior analysts are the ones trained; conditional past-participle opener attaches correctly.

Tip: Properly trained / If trained… often reduces If they are trained…

FALSE — A reconstruction cannot lose invoices; Having lost the original invoices, the accounts team attempted a reconstruction from bank statements.

Tip: Having lost / mislaid needs the loser as subject.

TRUE — Other things being equal is an absolute used in economics writing.

Tip: Absolutes have their own subject (other things) inside the phrase.

FALSE — Celebrations cannot feel relieved; Relieved at the outcome, the staff continued celebrating late into the night.

Tip: Emotion + event-as-subject remains dangling.

TRUE — The checklist was designed for that purpose; patient subject fits.

Tip: Designed for / Intended for + tool/document subject is standard.
tasks.solution_overview: Absolutes carry an internal subject; reduced conditionals like Properly trained… still share the main subject. Emotion and loss participles must not attach to celebrations or reconstructions.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having been briefed only that morning, several directors still asked basic questions.
The committee, having adjourned for lunch, resumed at two o'clock.
Considering the tight deadline, an extension seems justified.
Struck by the inconsistency, further sampling was ordered at once.
There being no quorum, the vote was postponed until Thursday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Directors were briefed; even if they still asked questions, they remain the logical patients of Having been briefed.

Tip: A surprising outcome does not make a matching subject into a dangler.

TRUE — Mid-clause Having adjourned clearly modifies the committee.

Tip: Participles after the subject (…, having…,) are often clearer than sentence-initial ones.

TRUE — Considering… functions like Given… / In view of… as an evaluative absolute-style opener.

Tip: Considering / Given / Regarding often need no separate human subject.

FALSE — Sampling cannot be struck by inconsistency; Struck by the inconsistency, the lead auditor ordered further sampling at once.

Tip: Struck by / Surprised by need experiencers.

TRUE — There being no quorum is an absolute with its own existential subject.

Tip: There being / It being constructions stand apart from the main subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced items mix mid-clause participles, Considering…, and There being… absolutes. Only Struck by… fails because further sampling is not an experiencer.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The report having been leaked, the ministry brought the announcement forward.
Although exhausted, the final chapter was finished before midnight.
Not knowing the password, access to the shared drive was impossible.
Broadly speaking, the reform has improved filing discipline.
Having once worked in compliance, she spotted the gap immediately.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Absolute: the report having been leaked has its own subject (the report).

Tip: Noun + having been + PP before the comma is a full absolute, not a dangler.

FALSE — A chapter cannot be exhausted; Although exhausted, she finished the final chapter before midnight.

Tip: Although / While + adjective still needs the experiencer as main subject.

FALSE — Access cannot know a password; Not knowing the password, they could not access the shared drive.

Tip: Negated participles (Not knowing / Never having…) still need the knower.

TRUE — Broadly speaking is a fixed discourse absolute.

Tip: Broadly / Generally / Frankly speaking are conventional and accepted.

TRUE — She worked in compliance and spotted the gap; perfect participle matches.

Tip: Having once / previously + PP marks prior experience of the subject.
tasks.solution_overview: Absolutes with their own noun subject (The report having been…) and discourse markers (Broadly speaking) are grammatical. Although exhausted… and Not knowing… still dangle when the subject is a chapter or access.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The data having been cleaned, the model was re-estimated overnight.
Without realising the conflict, the consultancy accepted both mandates.
Seated behind the glass, proceedings were hard to hear.
That said, the pilot should still proceed on a smaller scale.
Having never audited a bank before, the assignment felt daunting.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Absolute with the data as its own subject; main clause subject is the model.

Tip: Absolute subject ≠ main-clause subject by design.

TRUE — The consultancy is the one not realising and accepting.

Tip: Without + -ing still needs the non-realiser as subject.

FALSE — Proceedings were not seated; Seated behind the glass, observers found proceedings hard to hear.

Tip: Seated / Standing location participles need people.

TRUE — That said is a discourse absolute meaning nevertheless.

Tip: That said / That being so link ideas without dangling.

FALSE — An assignment cannot have audited; Having never audited a bank before, she found the assignment daunting.

Tip: Experience participles need the person with the experience.
tasks.solution_overview: Absolutes and That said are free-standing. Without realising… is fine with a firm as subject; Seated… and Having never audited… are not fine with proceedings or the assignment as subjects.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The figures having been reconciled, payroll was released the same afternoon.
Not having received a reply, a second reminder was issued on Friday.
Strictly speaking, the clause does not cover consequential loss.
Being the largest bidder, the consortium's offer set the reserve price.
Once the minutes had been approved, having no further business, the chair closed the meeting.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Absolute (figures having been reconciled) plus a separate main subject (payroll).

Tip: If the participle phrase has its own noun subject, it is an absolute, not a dangler.

FALSE — A reminder cannot fail to receive a reply; Not having received a reply, the clerk issued a second reminder on Friday.

Tip: Not having + PP needs the non-recipient as subject.

TRUE — Strictly speaking is a fixed evaluative absolute.

Tip: Strictly / Technically / Legally speaking pattern like Broadly speaking.

FALSE — The offer was not the bidder; Being the largest bidder, the consortium set the reserve price with its offer. As written, Being… wrongly modifies offer.

Tip: Being + role must modify the person/organisation, not their bid or document.

TRUE — Having no further business mid-clause clearly modifies the chair after the minutes clause.

Tip: Placement after the subject (the chair) removes dangling ambiguity.
tasks.solution_overview: Finish by separating absolutes and discourse markers from true danglers. Not having received… and Being the largest bidder… fail when they attach to a reminder or an offer instead of the clerk or the consortium.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The sample is small enough to raise concerns.
The sample is enough small to support firm conclusions.
It was such a clear result that no further test was needed.
It was so a clear result that no further test was needed.
The briefing was too technical for the audience.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Adjective + enough is the standard order before a to-infinitive. Small enough to raise concerns is grammatical and natural.

Tip: Remember enough after adjectives: adj + enough (+ to…).

FALSE — Enough cannot sit before the adjective here. Swap to small enough (or too small if you mean excess).

Tip: Never write enough + adjective; flip it.

TRUE — Such a + adjective + singular countable noun + that-clause is the classic pattern.

Tip: Such takes the noun phrase; so takes the adjective alone.

FALSE — So does not combine with a before a noun. You need such a clear result, or so clear that… without the noun.

Tip: So a / so an is almost always wrong — use such a/an.

TRUE — Too + adjective (+ for…) correctly marks excess relative to a purpose or audience.

Tip: Too = excess; enough = sufficiency.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan for the intensifier first: so, such, too, or enough. Then check what follows — adjective alone, noun phrase, or word-order with enough. Most easy traps are so a… and enough + adjective.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The results were so clear that no further test was needed.
There was such demand that the venue expanded capacity.
There was so demand that the venue expanded capacity.
He is not experienced enough for this role.
He is not enough experienced for this role.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So + adjective + that-clause correctly intensifies and links a result.

Tip: So + adj/adv (+ that…); keep the noun out of that slot.

TRUE — Such + uncountable noun (demand) + that is standard without an article.

Tip: Such + noun; no a/an with uncountables.

FALSE — So cannot modify a bare noun. Use such demand or so much demand.

Tip: So + noun needs much/many (or a determiner phrase).

TRUE — Experienced enough places enough after the adjective before for.

Tip: Adj + enough + for / to…

FALSE — Enough experienced reverses the required order.

Tip: If you hear enough first, check whether a noun follows (enough time) — not an adjective.
tasks.solution_overview: Pair each intensifier with its partner: so with adjectives, such with nouns, enough after adjectives. When so sits before a noun with no much/many, mark it false.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It was such an important meeting that everyone attended.
It was so an important meeting that everyone attended.
The sample is too small to support firm conclusions.
The briefing was too much technical for the audience.
She spoke so quickly that few colleagues could follow.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Such an before a vowel-sound adjective + noun is correct (important → an).

Tip: Such a/an agrees with the following sound, not with so.

FALSE — So an is ungrammatical; replace with such an important meeting or so important that…

Tip: Article + noun belongs with such, not so.

TRUE — Too + adjective + to-infinitive expresses excess preventing a result.

Tip: Too…to often means "so…that not".

FALSE — Do not insert much between too and a single adjective. Too technical is enough; too much modifies nouns (too much noise).

Tip: Too much + noun; too + adjective.

TRUE — So + adverb + that-clause is parallel to so + adjective.

Tip: Quickly is an adverb, so so quickly that… is fine.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on article choice with such and the too much trap. If the word after too is an adjective, much should not be there unless you are quantifying a noun.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We had enough time to finish the audit.
The margin was so thin that finance delayed the launch.
She spoke so quickly speech that few followed.
The pitch was such convincing that investors signed immediately.
The warehouse is large enough for the extra inventory.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Enough + noun is the correct order when enough quantifies a noun (enough time).

Tip: Enough + noun vs adjective + enough — two different slots.

TRUE — So + adjective + that correctly builds cause and result.

Tip: Thin is adjectival; so thin that… fits.

FALSE — So quickly speech mixes adverb pattern with a noun. Use so quickly that… or such quick speech that…

Tip: Do not park a noun right after so + adverb.

FALSE — Such needs a noun phrase: such a convincing pitch, not such convincing alone before that.

Tip: Such + (a/an) + (adj) + noun.

TRUE — Adjective + enough + for + noun phrase is grammatical.

Tip: Enough for X / enough to V — both common after adjectives.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate noun-quantifying enough from adjective-modifying enough. Then catch hybrid errors like so + adverb + noun and such + bare adjective without a noun.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There was so much interest that registration closed early.
There were so many applicants that HR extended the deadline.
The clause is too vaguely to enforce in court.
The offer was not attractive enough to retain the candidate.
It was such bad weather that the site visit was cancelled.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So much + uncountable noun (+ that) is the correct so + noun pattern.

Tip: Uncountable → so much; plural countable → so many.

TRUE — So many + plural countable noun is parallel to so much.

Tip: Count the noun before choosing much/many.

FALSE — Too must modify an adjective or adverb in base form usable as a complement: too vague to enforce, not too vaguely when you mean the clause itself.

Tip: After linking be, use too + adjective, not too + -ly adverb.

TRUE — Attractive enough to… places enough correctly after the adjective.

Tip: Not + adj + enough to… is a common exam pattern.

TRUE — Such + adjective + uncountable noun (weather) needs no article.

Tip: Such bad weather / such good news — no a/an.
tasks.solution_overview: When so modifies quantity, check much vs many. When too follows be, prefer an adjective. Such before uncountable noun phrases usually drops the article.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The dashboard loads too slowly to be useful in live meetings.
The data were such unreliable that the model was shelved.
We do not have enough evidence to overturn the ruling.
The fee is so high a barrier that startups leave the market.
The room was enough quiet for confidential negotiations.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Too + adverb + to-infinitive correctly marks excess manner blocking a purpose.

Tip: Too slowly to… parallels too small to…

FALSE — Such unreliable lacks a noun head. Use such unreliable data or so unreliable that…

Tip: Such wants a noun; so wants an adjective.

TRUE — Enough + uncountable noun (evidence) is correct before to.

Tip: Enough evidence / enough capital — noun after enough.

TRUE — So + adjective + a + noun (+ that) is a formal but grammatical pattern (so high a barrier).

Tip: So adj a noun ≈ such a adj noun; both appear in careful English.

FALSE — Quiet is an adjective, so use quiet enough, not enough quiet.

Tip: Enough before adjectives is a word-order error.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch for such + bare adjective and enough + adjective. The formal so + adj + a + noun pattern is acceptable — do not mark it false just because such a… is more common.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The timeline is tight enough that any slip will delay launch.
It was so efficient process that costs fell within a month.
The vendor responded too late for us to revise the tender.
Such were the risks that the committee demanded a second opinion.
The brief is too much short for a full board pack.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Adj + enough + that-clause is acceptable in modern usage alongside enough to…

Tip: Enough that… and enough to… both appear; meaning stays "sufficient".

FALSE — So efficient process misses the article/noun patterning. Use such an efficient process or so efficient that…

Tip: So + adj + noun without a is a classic miss.

TRUE — Too + adverb/adjective + for + object + to-infinitive is a solid excess pattern.

Tip: Too late for X to V = X cannot V in time.

TRUE — Inversion such were the risks that… is formal but grammatical.

Tip: Such + be + noun phrase + that is literary/formal, not an error.

FALSE — Too much short wrongly inserts much before an adjective. Use too short.

Tip: Too much ≠ intensifier before adjectives.
tasks.solution_overview: Most items still hinge on word order and partners of so/such/too. One formal inversion with such is correct — do not reject unusual word order if the grammar holds.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The memo was not clear enough for junior staff to act on.
They made so rapid progress that the pilot finished early.
They made such rapid progress that the pilot finished early.
The server is too heavily to handle peak traffic without scaling.
We retained enough experienced analysts to cover both regions.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Not + adj + enough + for + noun + to-infinitive is fully grammatical.

Tip: Enough often licenses a for…to… complement.

TRUE — So + adjective + uncountable/mass-like noun phrase (rapid progress) without a is acceptable in many styles; progress is uncountable.

Tip: So + adj + uncountable noun can work; contrast so efficient process (countable need).

TRUE — Such + adjective + uncountable noun is the safer textbook twin of the previous pattern.

Tip: Such rapid progress is the exam-safe default.

FALSE — Too heavily is an adverb where an adjective is needed after be: too heavy / too heavily loaded…

Tip: Linking verb → too + adjective.

TRUE — Enough + adjective + plural noun quantifies how many qualified people you have.

Tip: Enough experienced analysts = sufficient number of that type.
tasks.solution_overview: Distinguish countable vs uncountable after so/such, and adjective vs adverb after be. Enough before a noun phrase (enough experienced analysts) is fine — that is not the enough + adjective error.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The discount was so generous as to surprise the procurement team.
The discount was such generous as to surprise the procurement team.
The factory is not automated enough to cut night-shift costs.
It was too a complex model for a one-page summary.
There has been such an uptick in churn that marketing paused spend.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So + adjective + as to + infinitive is a formal result pattern parallel to so…that.

Tip: So…as to… ≈ so…that someone does…

FALSE — Such does not take as to after a bare adjective. Use so generous as to… or such a generous discount that…

Tip: Such pairs with nouns; so…as to pairs with adjectives.

TRUE — Not + past participle used adjectivally + enough + to… is correct.

Tip: Participial adjectives still take enough after them.

FALSE — Too a complex is wrong; use too complex a model or such a complex model.

Tip: Too + adj + a + noun is possible (too complex a model), but too a… never is.

TRUE — Such an + noun (+ that) correctly intensifies a countable singular.

Tip: Uptick is countable → such an uptick.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal so…as to… is fair game. Check that such is not forced into that frame, and that too never precedes the article directly (too a…).

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The proposal is too complex a document for a five-minute slot.
Clients left because the wait was such long.
We arrived early enough to secure seats near the interpreters.
The board found the forecast so optimistic that it ordered a stress test.
She is enough senior to chair the steering committee.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is a formal pattern matching so adj a noun.

Tip: Too complex a document = such a complex document in meaning of excess.

FALSE — Such long needs a noun: such a long wait, or so long that…

Tip: Bare such + adjective without noun is incomplete.

TRUE — Adverb early + enough + to-infinitive is correct (enough after the adverb).

Tip: Adv + enough mirrors adj + enough.

TRUE — So + adjective + that after a reporting verb is clean.

Tip: Found X so adj that… keeps so on the adjective.

FALSE — Senior is an adjective → senior enough, not enough senior.

Tip: Same flip rule as enough small.
tasks.solution_overview: Accept the formal too/so + adj + a + noun shapes when articles land after the adjective. Reject such + bare adjective and enough + adjective.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The outage was so serious as that regional clients filed complaints.
The outage was so serious that regional clients filed complaints.
We lacked enough liquidity to meet the margin call.
It was such a poorly designed interface that users abandoned checkout.
The targets are too ambitious for the team complete this quarter.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — So…as that mixes two patterns. Choose so…that or so…as to, not both markers.

Tip: Never stack as and that after so.

TRUE — Clean so + adjective + that result clause.

Tip: One linker only: that or as to.

TRUE — Enough + noun (liquidity) before to-infinitive is correct.

Tip: Financial uncountables still take enough + noun.

TRUE — Such a + adverb + adjective + noun is fine when the adverb modifies the adjective inside the noun phrase.

Tip: Such a poorly designed X = noun phrase after such.

FALSE — Missing to before the infinitive: too ambitious for the team to complete…

Tip: For + object needs to before the verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Hunt blended patterns (as that) and missing to after for + object. Such a + heavily modified noun phrase can still be correct.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hiring froze because attrition became so high.
Hiring froze because attrition became such high.
The clause is worded carefully enough to limit liability.
There were too few inspectors to cover every site weekly.
The deck contained so few charts that the story felt thin.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So + adjective can stand without a that-clause when the result is implied by context.

Tip: That-clause is common but not obligatory after so/such/too/enough.

FALSE — Such high needs a noun (such high attrition) or switch to so high.

Tip: After become, prefer so + adjective.

TRUE — Carefully enough places enough after the adverb modifying the participle/adjective phrase.

Tip: Adv + enough + to… works like adj + enough.

TRUE — Too few + plural noun expresses insufficiency (excess of scarcity).

Tip: Too few ≈ not enough; grammar differs from too much + adj.

TRUE — So few + plural noun + that is grammatical and parallel to so many.

Tip: Few/little pair with so the same way many/much do.
tasks.solution_overview: Result clauses are optional. Focus on whether such has a noun and whether few/little sit correctly after so/too.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The warranty is such that replacements ship within forty-eight hours.
The warranty is so that replacements ship within forty-eight hours.
Investors pulled out, the valuation having become too uncertain to defend.
She left enough of a buffer to absorb currency swings.
The API is not enough documented for external partners.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Such that meaning "of a kind that" is a fixed formal pattern without an adjective.

Tip: Noun + is such that… = the nature of X means…

FALSE — So that expresses purpose ("in order that"), not the "of a kind that" reading. Here such that is required.

Tip: So that ≠ such that; different jobs.

TRUE — Too + adjective + to-infinitive inside a participial absolute is still grammatical.

Tip: Too…to… keeps its shape in reduced clauses.

TRUE — Enough of a + singular countable noun is idiomatic.

Tip: Enough of a buffer / enough of an issue — of a(n) before singular count nouns.

FALSE — Documented is adjectival here → not documented enough, not not enough documented.

Tip: Flip enough after adjectives even with not.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder items distinguish such that (nature/result) from so that (purpose), and test enough of a… plus adjective–enough order under negation.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Morale fell so low as staff began refusing overtime.
Morale fell so low that staff began refusing overtime.
The export licence proved too costly a requirement for the pilot.
We cannot move forward without such information as the auditor requests.
The rebuild was enough extensive that downtime doubled.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — So…as without to needs a comparative/manner reading or as to; here a result clause should use that (or so low as to cause…).

Tip: So adj as + finite clause is not standard for result.

TRUE — So + adjective + that correctly states the result.

Tip: Default result linker after so/such is that.

TRUE — Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is grammatical formal English.

Tip: Too costly a requirement ≈ an excessively costly requirement.

TRUE — Such…as meaning "the kind that" with a relative-like clause is correct.

Tip: Such information as X requests = the information that X requests.

FALSE — Enough extensive reverses order; need extensive enough that…

Tip: Enough never precedes the adjective in this frame.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate result that from faulty so…as + clause, and recognise formal such…as and too adj a noun. Keep policing enough + adjective.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The settlement was so structured as to minimise tax exposure.
Cash on hand is barely enough for payroll, let alone expansion.
It was too little time remaining to renegotiate the covenants.
There was too little time remaining to renegotiate the covenants.
The brand became such synonym with reliability that rivals copied the slogan.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So + past participle/adjective + as to + infinitive expresses designed result.

Tip: So structured as to… = structured in such a way that…

TRUE — Enough for + noun works; barely intensifies sufficiency without breaking grammar.

Tip: Modifiers like barely/almost can precede enough.

FALSE — It was too little time is awkward/wrong; time needs there was / we had too little time, or too little time remained.

Tip: Watch dummy it with quantity noun phrases.

TRUE — There was too little + uncountable noun (+ to…) is the natural existential pattern.

Tip: Prefer there-insertion with too little/much + noun.

FALSE — Needs an article: such a synonym with… (or so synonymous with…).

Tip: Countable singular after such almost always needs a/an.
tasks.solution_overview: Judge existential framing with too little + noun, article requirements after such, and formal so…as to…. Surface similarity can hide a missing there or a/an.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The KPI is defined such that regional managers cannot game the metric.
The KPI is defined so that regional managers cannot game the metric.
Demand proved elastic enough that a small cut lifted volume sharply.
He spoke with so a confident tone that objections faded.
We kept the briefing short enough not to overrun the slot.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Defined such that… means "in such a way that" and is standard in technical/policy English.

Tip: Verb + such that ≈ configured so that.

TRUE — Defined so that… expressing purpose/result is also grammatical.

Tip: Here so that and such that can both work with slightly different nuance.

TRUE — Adj + enough + that-clause is acceptable.

Tip: Elastic enough that… = sufficiently elastic that…

FALSE — So a confident tone is wrong; use such a confident tone or so confidently that…

Tip: So a… returns as a trap even in longer NPs.

TRUE — Adj + enough + not to-infinitive correctly encodes avoidance.

Tip: Enough not to… = sufficiently… to avoid…
tasks.solution_overview: Both so that and such that can be right after verbs of defining/designing. Still fail so a…, and accept enough not to… as a valid negative infinitive pattern.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Seldom is a market so fragmented that no price signal emerges.
The escrow proved insufficiently funded enough to reassure sellers.
Her objection was not so much legal as procedural.
The delay was such that, had we waited, the option would have expired.
They priced the add-on too expensively for mid-market buyers to justify.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Inversion with seldom does not break the inner so…that pattern.

Tip: Judge the so/such/too/enough core even inside inversion shells.

FALSE — Insufficiently funded enough doubles the sufficiency marker. Use insufficiently funded or not funded enough — not both.

Tip: One sufficiency tool per adjective phrase.

TRUE — Not so much X as Y is an established correlative; so is required in this idiom.

Tip: Not so much…as… ≠ ordinary so + adjective, but it is grammatical.

TRUE — Such that introducing a counterfactual continuation is formal and correct.

Tip: Such that can host complex follow-ons, including inverted conditionals.

TRUE — Too + adverb + for + noun + to-infinitive marks excess manner/cost.

Tip: Too expensively for X to V parallels too expensive for X to V (adj vs adv choice depends on what is modified).
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced packaging: inversion, correlative not so much…as…, and stacked markers. Reject double intensifiers like insufficiently…enough while keeping legitimate idioms with so.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No other bidder moved so swiftly as to lock exclusivity overnight.
No other bidder moved such swiftly as to lock exclusivity overnight.
The covenant is drawn tightly enough that refinancing needs consent.
We had rather too little runway for a full product redesign.
The interface was so intuitive a design as users needed no training.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — So + adverb + as to + infinitive correctly states result after a comparative frame.

Tip: So…as to… works with adverbs as well as adjectives.

FALSE — Such does not modify adverbs; such swiftly is impossible.

Tip: Such → noun phrases only (or such that).

TRUE — Adv/adj + enough + that remains grammatical in legal/business register.

Tip: Tightly enough that… = sufficiently tightly that…

TRUE — Rather too + adjective/determiner phrase is idiomatic mild criticism.

Tip: Rather/a bit/far can modify too.

FALSE — So intuitive a design as + finite clause mismatches; use so intuitive a design that… or so intuitive that…, or so intuitive as to need…

Tip: So adj a noun pairs with that or as to, not bare as + clause.
highlights: so intuitive a design as users
tasks.solution_overview: Stress-test so…as to… with adverbs, block such + adverb, and require the right linker after so adj a noun. Degree modifiers before too are allowed.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only then did costs become high enough for restructuring to look rational.
The algorithm was trained on so biased a sample that fairness checks failed.
The algorithm was trained on such biased a sample that fairness checks failed.
Cash reserves look healthy enough; still, they may prove too thin under stress.
He is too much of a perfectionist to ship an imperfect MVP.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Inversion only then did… leaves high enough for… intact and grammatical.

Tip: Embedded enough patterns survive fronting and inversion.

TRUE — So + adjective + a + noun + that is the formal pattern inside a prepositional phrase.

Tip: So biased a sample = such a biased sample.

FALSE — Such biased a sample mis-orders the article; need such a biased sample (article before the adjective).

Tip: Such a + adj + noun, never such adj a noun.

TRUE — Two coordinated judgments: adj + enough, and too + adj, both well formed.

Tip: Enough and too can contrast in one sentence without clashing.

TRUE — Too much of a + noun + to-infinitive is a fixed evaluative idiom.

Tip: Too much of a X to V = excessively X-like to V.
tasks.solution_overview: Article placement separates so adj a noun (correct) from such adj a noun (incorrect). Also recognise the idiom too much of a… to…

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had the collateral been liquid enough, the bank would have waived the fee.
The revision cycle grew so protracted as nobody could finalise wording.
Whatever the brand promises, delivery is seldom swift enough to match it.
It remains too early a stage for full automation of claims.
Their reply was so that we escalated the dispute at once.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Adj + enough inside an inverted third conditional is grammatical.

Tip: Enough keeps adjective-final order even in had-conditionals.

FALSE — So…as + finite clause is wrong for result; use so protracted that… or so protracted as to prevent…

Tip: As to + infinitive, or that + clause — not as + clause after so + adj.

TRUE — Seldom… enough to… correctly denies sufficiency.

Tip: Frequency adverb + enough pattern is fine.

TRUE — Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is formal but correct.

Tip: Too early a stage = an excessively early stage.

FALSE — So that marks purpose ("in order that"), not the nature/result reading needed here. Use such that we escalated… or Their reply was so blunt that we escalated…

Tip: Reply/situation + such that = character/result; so that = purpose.
tasks.solution_overview: Final set mixes conditionals, formal too adj a noun, and result-linker discipline after so. Prefer that or as to for results, and keep such that vs so that distinct.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Success depends of careful planning before the launch.
She is responsible of the quarterly budget review.
They are interested on the revised merger proposal.
Despite of the delay, the audit was completed on time.
The firm was accused of misleading retail investors.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "depends on," not "depends of," for this fixed dependency pattern.

Tip: After "depend," lock in "on" — "of" is a common L1 transfer trap.

FALSE — Use "responsible for," not "responsible of."

Tip: Pair "responsible" with "for" + noun/gerund; "of" is wrong here.

FALSE — The fixed pattern is "interested in," not "interested on."

Tip: Interest takes "in"; "on" belongs with focus/concentrate.

FALSE — "Despite" never takes "of"; write "Despite the delay" or "In spite of the delay."

Tip: "Despite of" is always wrong — drop "of" or switch to "in spite of."

TRUE — "Accused of" + gerund/noun is the standard legal collocation.

Tip: Accuse/charge of wrongdoing; do not swap in "for" after "accused."
tasks.solution_overview: Scan each sentence for a fixed verb/adjective + preposition lock. Ask whether the preposition matches the standard pattern, and watch for the classic "despite of" false friend. Correct any mismatch before you mark TRUE.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He insisted on seeing the raw sales data.
The outcome differs of last year's forecast.
We apologised about the shipping delay to the client.
The report focuses to cost control measures.
She participated in the compliance workshop.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Insist on" + gerund is the fixed pattern here.

Tip: After "insist," use "on" + -ing, not a bare infinitive.

FALSE — Use "differs from," not "differs of."

Tip: Differ/different → from; do not write "differ of."

FALSE — Prefer "apologised for the shipping delay" in careful exam English.
