Tip: Apologise for a fault or inconvenience; "about" is weaker and often marked wrong.

FALSE — Use "focuses on," not "focuses to."

Tip: Focus/concentrate take "on," never "to."

TRUE — "Participated in" correctly names involvement in an event.

Tip: Participate/join/engage → in an event or activity.
tasks.solution_overview: These items test high-frequency business collocations. Match each verb to its locked preposition, and rewrite any false friend before deciding TRUE or FALSE.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They objected against the indemnity clause.
The consultant is capable of handling the negotiation.
Managers must be aware of the new disclosure rules.
She is good in presenting quarterly results.
We look forward to receiving your comments.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "objected to the clause," not "against."

Tip: Object to X; "against" belongs with protest/argue in other patterns.

TRUE — "Capable of" + gerund is correct.

Tip: Capable/incapable take "of," not "to."

TRUE — "Aware of" correctly introduces the known fact or risk.

Tip: Aware/conscious → of; "about" is looser and often weaker in exams.

FALSE — Say "good at presenting," not "good in."

Tip: Good/bad/skilled → at + -ing for ability.

TRUE — "Look forward to" + gerund is fixed; "to" is a preposition here.

Tip: After "look forward to," keep -ing, never a bare infinitive.
tasks.solution_overview: Adjective and verb patterns lock specific prepositions. Check whether "of," "to," "at," or "in" is the required partner, especially after capable, aware, good, and look forward.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The project succeeded in cutting overhead by eight percent.
The package consists of three separate modules.
The forecast is based on conservative assumptions.
These findings are related to last quarter's results.
According with the auditor, the controls are adequate.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Succeed in" + gerund names the achievement.

Tip: Succeed in doing X; do not write "succeed to do."

TRUE — "Consists of" correctly lists the parts.

Tip: Consist of / be composed of — never "from" after consist.

TRUE — "Based on" correctly introduces the foundation of the claim.

Tip: Base/based → on evidence or assumptions.

TRUE — "Related to" is the fixed comparison/link pattern.

Tip: Related/similar → to; "with" is a common trap after related.

FALSE — Use "According to the auditor," not "according with."

Tip: According to + person/document; never "according with" for this meaning.
tasks.solution_overview: Report-writing English leans on a small set of locked phrases. Verify each preposition against the standard business pattern before you accept the sentence.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The deputy is in charge of the regional rollout.
Investors rely on timely disclosures from management.
The team must deal with customer complaints promptly.
Nothing will prevent us from meeting the deadline.
Higher rates resulted in weaker loan demand.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "In charge of" correctly marks responsibility for a domain.

Tip: In charge of X ≈ responsible for X.

TRUE — "Rely on" is the fixed dependency pattern.

Tip: Rely/depend → on; both reject "of" in exam English.

TRUE — "Deal with" correctly introduces the problem handled.

Tip: Deal with a problem or person; "about" does not replace "with" here.

TRUE — "Prevent … from" + gerund is correct.

Tip: Prevent/stop/discourage someone from doing X.

TRUE — Outcomes "result in" an effect; that direction is right here.

Tip: Result in = cause → effect; result from = effect ← cause.
tasks.solution_overview: These workplace phrases are almost mechanical once you know the lock. Confirm each verb/adjective still carries its standard preposition before marking TRUE.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Our approach is similar to the peer group's model.
This year's margin is different than last year's by a wide gap.
The campaign aims for increasing brand recognition only.
She is dedicated for improving internal controls.
New hires quickly became accustomed to remote tools.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Similar to" is the standard comparison pattern.

Tip: Similar to X; "with" is wrong after similar.

FALSE — Careful exam English prefers "different from" (or "different to" in some BrE), not "different than" in this frame.

Tip: On WU-style papers, choose "different from" and avoid "than" after different.

FALSE — Prefer "aims at increasing" or "aims to increase," not "aims for increasing."

Tip: Aim at / aim to are the safe exam pairs; "aim for" usually takes a noun goal.

FALSE — Use "dedicated to improving," not "for."

Tip: Dedicated/committed/devoted → to + -ing.

TRUE — "Accustomed to" correctly marks the habit pattern.

Tip: Accustomed/used → to; "with" is a frequent trap.
tasks.solution_overview: Comparison and attitude adjectives often lock "to" or "from." Read past the content words and test only the preposition that follows the key adjective.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board congratulated her for completing the turnaround.
Staff complained about the abrupt schedule change.
Please apply to the vacancy before Friday.
They applied for the graduate scheme in June.
The memo refers on last week's minutes.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Congratulate someone for/on" an achievement both occur; "for completing" is acceptable here.

Tip: Congratulate + person + for/on + achievement.

TRUE — "Complain about" correctly names the grievance.

Tip: Complain about X; complain to a person.

FALSE — Jobs and schemes take "apply for"; "apply to" targets an organisation or address.

Tip: Apply for a post; apply to a company/university.

TRUE — "Applied for the graduate scheme" is the correct job-application pattern.

Tip: For + what you want; to + who receives the application.

FALSE — Use "refers to last week's minutes," not "refers on."

Tip: Refer to a document or point; "on" belongs with focus/comment in other patterns.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply/refer/complain change meaning with the preposition. Decide what the object is — a job, a person, or a document — then pick the locked partner.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The policy benefits from clearer wording.
Clients benefit from lower transaction fees.
We agreed on a revised delivery window.
They agreed with the supplier's new terms.
She insisted to reopen the closed account.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Benefit from" correctly marks the source of advantage.

Tip: Benefit from X; never "benefit of" as the verb pattern.

TRUE — Verb "benefit" takes "from" for the source of the gain.

Tip: "Be of benefit to" is a different structure — do not mix it with the verb.

TRUE — "Agree on" a plan, date, or figure is standard.

Tip: Agree on a thing; agree with a person/opinion.

TRUE — "Agree with" the supplier's terms correctly accepts another's position.

Tip: With + person/opinion; on + joint decision.

FALSE — Use "insisted on reopening," not "insisted to reopen."

Tip: Insist on + -ing; the infinitive after insist is a classic trap.
tasks.solution_overview: Small preposition swaps change meaning or break the pattern entirely. Separate "agree on" from "agree with," and keep gerunds after "insist on."

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite the headwinds, revenue still grew.
Despite of rising costs, margins held steady.
She disapproves against remote-only onboarding.
The committee approved against the contingency plan.
Despite the headwinds, revenue still grew.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "In spite" must be followed by "of"; write "In spite of the headwinds."

Tip: In spite of = despite; never drop of from the three-word phrase.

FALSE — "Despite of" is ungrammatical; drop "of" or use "in spite of."

Tip: If you hear "of," the safe rewrite is "in spite of."

FALSE — Use "disapproves of," not "against."

Tip: Approve/disapprove of X; "against" belongs with be/argue.

FALSE — Use "approved of the plan" (attitude) or "approved the plan" (formal decision) — not "against."

Tip: Approve of an idea; do not invent "approve against."

TRUE — "Despite" + noun phrase is correct and needs no "of."

Tip: Despite ≠ despite of — never add "of" after despite.
tasks.solution_overview: Concession phrases and approval verbs are frequent exam traps. Confirm that "despite" stands alone, that "in spite of" keeps its of, and that approve/disapprove take "of" when an attitude is meant.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The delay was due to a supplier outage.
Owing to the outage, shipments slipped by two days.
Because of the outage last Tuesday, filings slipped.
He was blamed for the reporting error.
In spite of the outage, the team filed on time.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Due to" + noun correctly states the cause after a linking verb.

Tip: Due to / owing to + noun; not + bare clause.

TRUE — "Owing to" + noun is a formal cause marker.

Tip: Owing to ≈ because of; both need a noun phrase.

TRUE — "Because of" + noun correctly marks the cause.

Tip: Because + clause; because of + noun.

TRUE — "Blamed for" an error is the fixed responsibility pattern.

Tip: Blame someone for X; be blamed for X — not "of."

TRUE — "In spite of" + noun is the complete three-word concession phrase.

Tip: Mirror check: if despite works, in spite of should too — with of included.
tasks.solution_overview: Cause and concession patterns look similar but lock different partners. Check that due to/owing to/because of take nouns, and keep blamed for distinct from accused of.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The analyst is familiar with the IFRS disclosure notes.
Few staff are familiar to the new CRM workflow.
He specialised in cross-border tax structuring.
The firm specialises on logistics software.
We must comply to the updated privacy regulation.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Familiar with" correctly marks knowledge of a topic.

Tip: Familiar with X; "to" belongs with "familiar to someone" in a different frame.

FALSE — People are "familiar with" a system; a system can be "familiar to" people — here you need "with."

Tip: Subject = person → familiar with; subject = thing → familiar to + person.

TRUE — "Specialise in" a field is the fixed pattern.

Tip: Specialise/major → in a subject area.

FALSE — Use "specialises in," not "on."

Tip: On appears with focus/concentrate; specialise stays with in.

FALSE — Use "comply with" a regulation, not "comply to."

Tip: Comply with rules; never "comply to" on careful papers.
tasks.solution_overview: Expertise and compliance language uses a narrow set of prepositions. Watch the familiar with/to swap and keep specialise/comply on their locked partners.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The warranty covers damage resulting from misuse.
Better training resulted in fewer service tickets.
The shortage resulted of a warehouse fire.
They congratulated the team on winning the tender.
Please comment the draft before noon.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Resulting from" correctly marks the cause of the damage.

Tip: Result from = come from a cause.

TRUE — "Resulted in" correctly marks the effect produced.

Tip: Result in = lead to an outcome.

FALSE — Causes take "resulted from," not "of."

Tip: Never write "result of" as a verb pattern; "be the result of" is a noun pattern.

TRUE — "Congratulate … on" an achievement is fully standard.

Tip: On/for both appear after congratulate; on + -ing is very common.

FALSE — You "comment on the draft," not "comment the draft" in this exam register.

Tip: Comment on / make comments on a document.
tasks.solution_overview: Result in vs result from is a direction test: effect versus cause. Finish by checking whether transitive-looking verbs still need a preposition, as with comment on.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The CFO is committed to reducing leverage this year.
They are opposed to selling the subsidiary now.
She is keen on expanding into adjacent markets.
He is keen in expanding into adjacent markets.
We are accustomed to filing reports every Friday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Committed to" + gerund shows firm intention.

Tip: To after committed/dedicated is a preposition, so -ing follows.

TRUE — "Opposed to" + gerund correctly states resistance.

Tip: Opposed to X / to doing X — keep the gerund.

TRUE — "Keen on" + gerund is the usual BrE ability/interest pattern.

Tip: Keen on -ing; keen to + infinitive is a different but also valid frame.

FALSE — Not "keen in"; use "keen on" or "keen to."

Tip: In does not partner with keen for this meaning.

TRUE — "Accustomed to" + gerund matches the fixed habit pattern.

Tip: Accustomed/used to + -ing (prepositional to).
tasks.solution_overview: Attitude adjectives followed by "to" or "on" still take gerunds because that "to" is a preposition. Reject any swap that inserts "in" where "on" or "to" is locked.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Nothing will stop the bank from raising its forecast.
The clause prohibits staff from sharing client files externally.
Higher volumes translated into stronger fee income.
The discussion centred on pricing strategy.
Investors look forward to hearing the revised guidance.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Stop … from" + gerund is correct.

Tip: Stop/prevent/keep someone from doing X.

TRUE — "Prohibits … from sharing" is the fixed pattern.

Tip: Prohibit/ban/discourage from -ing — not to + infinitive.

TRUE — "Translate into" an outcome is a standard figurative collocation.

Tip: Translate into = result in; "to" is weaker here.

TRUE — "Centred on" correctly names the topic focus.

Tip: Centre/focus/concentrate → on a topic.

TRUE — "Look forward to" + gerund remains fixed in formal updates.

Tip: After look forward to, keep -ing because to is a preposition.
tasks.solution_overview: Restriction verbs almost always take "from" + gerund. Pair that with topic verbs that lock "on," and you can clear most of this set quickly.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Whether we expand depends of next quarter's cash flow.
He takes pride of mentoring junior analysts.
The review will take account to seasonal effects.
She was blamed of the reporting error.
The bonus depends on whether targets are met.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Still "depends on," even before a clause — never "of."

Tip: The clause after depend does not change the locked preposition.

FALSE — Not "pride of"; that mixes "proud of" with "take pride in."

Tip: Keep the pairs intact: pride in ≠ proud of.

FALSE — Use "take account of," not "to."

Tip: Take account of X; take into account is the sibling pattern.

FALSE — Not "blamed of"; that pattern belongs with accused/suspected.

Tip: Blamed for ≠ accused of — keep the pairs separate.

TRUE — "Depend on whether…" correctly introduces a condition.

Tip: Depend on + noun/whether-clause; the preposition stays "on."
tasks.solution_overview: Fixed phrases stay fixed even when a clause follows. Watch for crossed pairs such as pride in vs proud of, and keep "depend on" through every continuation.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The recommendation rests on three independent studies.
Their case rests in three independent studies.
We cannot dispense with the interim audit this year.
The plan provides for a mid-year stress test.
The plan provides of a mid-year stress test.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Rest on" evidence or assumptions is correct.

Tip: Rest on / be based on — both take "on."

FALSE — Use "rests on," not "in," for this meaning.

Tip: In would suggest location; the argumentative sense needs on.

TRUE — "Dispense with" (= do without) is a fixed formal pattern.

Tip: Dispense with X; do not invent "dispense of."

TRUE — "Provide for" a contingency means make arrangements for it.

Tip: Provide for = make provision; provide someone with = supply.

FALSE — Not "provides of"; use "provides for" or "provides … with."

Tip: Of after provide is almost always wrong in exam English.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal report verbs hide fixed prepositions. Rest on, dispense with, and provide for each lock one partner — treat any other preposition as a trap.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board will not enter into a binding commitment yet.
They entered in negotiations without legal counsel.
Investors put pressure on management to clarify guidance.
The delay put pressure to the operations team.
She was charged for insider trading last month.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Enter into" an agreement or commitment is the formal pattern.

Tip: Enter into a contract/talks; enter a room needs no into.

FALSE — Negotiations take "entered into," not "entered in."

Tip: For abstract agreements and talks, keep into.

TRUE — "Put pressure on" someone is fixed.

Tip: Pressure on a person/organisation; not "to" the person.

FALSE — Use "put pressure on the operations team," not "to."

Tip: On marks the target of pressure; to marks direction elsewhere.

FALSE — Use "charged with" an offence, not "for."

Tip: Charged with ≈ accused of; keep each pair as learned.
tasks.solution_overview: Legal and negotiation English mixes "enter into," "charged with," and "pressure on." These are memorised locks — if the preposition feels improvised, it is probably wrong.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The division accounts for nearly forty percent of revenue.
Poor controls accounted to several reporting breaches.
We must allow for currency swings in the model.
The schedule does not allow of further slippage.
Despite the fact that costs rose, cash flow improved.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Account for" a share or proportion is correct.

Tip: Account for = constitute / explain.

FALSE — Explanations also "account for" events — not "account to."

Tip: Account to someone = report to them; account for something = explain it.

TRUE — "Allow for" a risk means include it in planning.

Tip: Allow for = make provision for.

TRUE — Formal "allow of" (= permit) is rare but grammatical in this sense.

Tip: Allow of = admit the possibility of; different from allow for.

TRUE — "Despite the fact that" correctly introduces a full clause after despite.

Tip: Despite + noun, or despite the fact that + clause — still no "despite of."
tasks.solution_overview: Account for vs account to, and allow for vs allow of, are advanced pairs with different meanings. Read for sense, then confirm the preposition matches that sense — including the legal "despite the fact that" workaround.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The committee insisted that the clause be revised, and the lawyer insisted on seeing the redraft.
She was suspected of leaking the memo to the press.
The flotation went ahead in spite of the delays.
She takes pride in mentoring junior analysts.
Notwithstanding the objections, the board adopted the policy.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Two different "insist" patterns can coexist: subjunctive that-clause, and "insist on" + gerund.

Tip: Insist that + base form ≠ insist on + -ing — both are fixed, but they are not interchangeable.

TRUE — "Suspected of" + gerund is the legal collocation.

Tip: Suspected/accused/convicted of wrongdoing.

TRUE — "In spite of the delays" is fully correct.

Tip: Mirror check: if despite works, in spite of should too — with of included.

TRUE — "Take pride in" + gerund is fixed.

Tip: Pride in / proud of — different heads, different prepositions.

TRUE — "Notwithstanding" works like despite and takes a noun phrase with no extra of.

Tip: Notwithstanding X ≈ despite X; do not write "notwithstanding of."
tasks.solution_overview: High-band items mix near-identical frames correctly. Separate insist that from insist on, keep suspected of and pride in, and leave notwithstanding without a trailing of.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Please refrain to call the client until legal has cleared the script.
The bonus pool is contingent of meeting group targets.
She was suspected for leaking the memo to the press.
In spite the delays, the flotation went ahead.
The lenders will refrain from calling the loan if covenants hold.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Not "refrain to call"; use "refrain from calling."

Tip: From + -ing after refrain/abstain.

FALSE — Use "contingent on," not "of."

Tip: Of after contingent is a depend-of style transfer error.

FALSE — Use "suspected of," not "for."

Tip: Suspected/accused of wrongdoing — keep for for blame.

FALSE — "In spite" must be followed by "of"; "in spite the delays" is incomplete.

Tip: In spite of = despite; never drop of from the three-word phrase.

TRUE — "Refrain from" + gerund is the fixed restraint pattern.

Tip: Refrain from doing X; never a bare infinitive after refrain.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with formal restraint and condition traps. Refrain from and contingent on behave like depend on; strip away every false of/for/to before accepting a sentence.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wonder where he is.
I wonder where is he.
Could you tell me what time the meeting starts?
Could you tell me what time does the meeting start?
She asked whether the figures were final.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After wonder, the clause keeps statement order: where + subject + verb (where he is), not question inversion.

Tip: Embedded wh-clauses look like statements, not questions.

FALSE — where is he inverts auxiliary and subject, which belongs in a direct question, not after I wonder.

Tip: Drop the inversion: where he is.

TRUE — Polite frame Could you tell me… embeds what time the meeting starts with subject before the verb.

Tip: No does inside the embedded clause.

FALSE — does the meeting start is direct-question word order jammed into an indirect question.

Tip: Use what time the meeting starts.

TRUE — whether correctly introduces a yes/no embedded clause with statement order (the figures were).

Tip: whether/if + subject + verb — never invert.
tasks.solution_overview: Indirect questions keep statement word order after the question word or whether/if. Scan for stray do/does/did or swapped auxiliary–subject pairs — those belong only in direct questions.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Do you know if the report has been filed?
Do you know if has the report been filed?
Please explain why costs rose.
Please explain why did costs rise.
They could not decide which option was safer.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — if embeds a yes/no clause with normal order: the report has been filed.

Tip: After if/whether, never move has/is/will before the subject.

FALSE — if has the report… wrongly inverts the auxiliary into the embedded clause.

Tip: Keep if the report has…

TRUE — why costs rose is statement order after explain; no auxiliary is needed.

Tip: Embedded why-clauses do not take did unless the original had do-support for another reason.

FALSE — why did costs rise mirrors a direct question; the embedding verb already carries the interrogative force.

Tip: why + subject + past: why costs rose.

TRUE — which option was safer keeps subject–verb order inside the embedded choice question.

Tip: which + noun + verb — no extra it.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on if/whether and wh-clauses after know, explain, and decide. Correct items keep subject before the finite verb; wrong ones smuggle direct-question inversion (has…?, did…?) into the subordinate clause.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The question is how the firm will respond.
The question is how will the firm respond?
I am not sure what caused the outage.
I am not sure what did cause the outage.
She asked whether were the figures final.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After The question is, how the firm will respond uses statement order (subject firm before will).

Tip: Noun-phrase frames still take embedded statement order.

FALSE — how will the firm respond? is a direct question glued onto The question is.

Tip: how + subject + modal: how the firm will respond.

TRUE — what is the subject of caused, so no do-support is required or allowed.

Tip: Subject wh-clauses never need did.

FALSE — what did cause forces unnecessary do-support into an embedded subject question.

Tip: what caused, not what did cause.

FALSE — whether were the figures… inverts were and the subject after whether.

Tip: whether the figures were…
tasks.solution_overview: Watch two classic traps: modal inversion after how (will the firm…) and fake did in subject questions (what did cause…). Correct embedded clauses read like calm statements inside a larger sentence.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They could not decide which option was it safer.
I'd like to know when the auditors arrive.
I'd like to know when do the auditors arrive.
Can you remind me where the spare keys are kept?
Can you remind me where are the spare keys kept?
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Extra pronoun it after was breaks the clause; which option was safer is already complete.

Tip: Never add a dummy it after the verb in an embedded which-clause.

TRUE — when the auditors arrive keeps subject–verb order after I'd like to know.

Tip: Softeners like I'd like to know still take statement order.

FALSE — when do the auditors arrive inserts do-support as if the clause were a direct question.

Tip: Delete do: when the auditors arrive.

TRUE — where the spare keys are kept is passive statement order inside a polite question.

Tip: are stays after the subject keys.

FALSE — where are the spare keys… flips are before the subject inside the embedded clause.

Tip: where + subject + are/is…
highlights: where the spare keys are kept
tasks.solution_overview: Polite frames (I'd like to know, Can you remind me) do not license inversion inside the embedded clause. Also reject dummy it after which… was — the option is already the subject.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Nobody could say who had authorised the transfer.
Nobody could say who had the transfer been authorised by.
We need to establish whether the supplier can meet the deadline.
We need to establish whether can the supplier meet the deadline.
Tell me how much the upgrade will cost.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — who is subject of had authorised; statement order is natural and correct.

Tip: Subject who/what never invert with the verb.

FALSE — who had the transfer been… forces awkward inversion and a stranded by that belongs in a rewritten object question.

Tip: Prefer who had authorised… or by whom the transfer had been authorised.

TRUE — whether the supplier can meet… keeps modal can after the subject.

Tip: whether + subject + modal + verb.

FALSE — whether can the supplier… is direct yes/no inversion after whether.

Tip: Never put the modal before the subject in an embedded clause.

TRUE — how much the upgrade will cost is statement order after Tell me.

Tip: how much/how many + noun phrase + verb — no will-fronting.
highlights: how much the upgrade will cost
tasks.solution_overview: Subject wh-words (who authorised…) stay simple; modal yes/no embeds keep can/will after the subject. Reject any whether can… or how much will… fronting inside the subordinate clause.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tell me how much will the upgrade cost.
The memo does not say how long the outage lasted.
The memo does not say how long did the outage last.
Investors asked what the board intended to do next.
Investors asked what did the board intend to do next.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — how much will the upgrade cost inverts will and the subject after Tell me.

Tip: how much the upgrade will cost.

TRUE — how long the outage lasted is a clean embedded duration clause.

Tip: how long + subject + past verb.

FALSE — how long did the outage last imports direct-question did.

Tip: Drop did and keep past simple: lasted.

TRUE — what the board intended… places the subject board before the verb.

Tip: Object what still uses statement order: what + subject + verb.

FALSE — what did the board intend… is a direct object question pattern inside reported asking.

Tip: what the board intended / what the board intends.
tasks.solution_overview: how much, how long, and object what all take statement order once embedded. Any will/did sitting before the subject is a leftover from a direct question — delete the fronted auxiliary.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Have you checked whether the invoices match the purchase orders?
Have you checked whether do the invoices match the purchase orders?
I'm curious who she nominated for the panel.
I'm curious who did she nominate for the panel.
The brief should clarify which metrics matter most.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — whether the invoices match… is statement order under a yes/no main question.

Tip: The outer Have you…? does not license inversion inside whether…

FALSE — whether do the invoices… adds illegal do-support after whether.

Tip: whether + subject + verb.

TRUE — who is the object of nominated; she stays before the verb in embedded order.

Tip: Object who: who + subject + verb.

FALSE — who did she nominate is direct-question order after I'm curious.

Tip: who she nominated.

TRUE — which metrics matter most needs no auxiliary; metrics is the subject.

Tip: Subject which-phrases never take do.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate subject who/which (no do) from object who (who + subject + verb). Outer question marks on Have you…? never justify do or inversion after whether or who inside the embed.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The brief should clarify which metrics do matter most.
Staff were unsure where to send the revised draft.
Staff were unsure where should they send the revised draft.
Could you confirm if payroll has processed the bonus?
Could you confirm if has payroll processed the bonus?
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — which metrics do matter adds emphatic do that is unnecessary and exam-wrong in a neutral embed.

Tip: which metrics matter — no do.

TRUE — where to send… is a correct infinitive indirect question (no subject inversion possible).

Tip: wh- + to-infinitive is a standard compact embed.

FALSE — where should they send… inverts modal and subject as in a direct question.

Tip: where they should send… or where to send…

TRUE — if payroll has processed… keeps perfect have after the subject.

Tip: if/whether + subject + has/have…

FALSE — if has payroll… front-loads has before the subject.

Tip: Move has after payroll.
tasks.solution_overview: Infinitive embeds (where to send) are a safe alternative to full clauses. When you use a full clause, keep modals and have/has after the subject — never before.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We still do not know whose proposal the committee selected.
We still do not know whose proposal did the committee select.
It remains unclear how the breach was discovered.
It remains unclear how was the breach discovered.
Ask her whether she can join the noon call.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — whose proposal the committee selected keeps the subject committee before selected.

Tip: whose + noun + subject + verb.

FALSE — whose proposal did the committee select is direct-question do-support.

Tip: Drop did: whose proposal the committee selected.

TRUE — how the breach was discovered is passive statement order under It remains unclear.

Tip: Passive embeds still put was after the subject.

FALSE — how was the breach discovered inverts was into question position.

Tip: how the breach was discovered.

TRUE — whether she can join… is a clean yes/no embed after Ask.

Tip: Ask + whether/if + statement order.
tasks.solution_overview: whose and passive how-clauses follow the same rule as simpler embeds: subject before the finite verb. Frames like It remains unclear or Ask her do not change that order.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Ask her whether can she join the noon call.
The clients want to know what we are offering this quarter.
The clients want to know what are we offering this quarter.
No one has confirmed who will chair the session.
No one has confirmed who will the session be chaired by.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — whether can she… inverts can and she after whether.

Tip: whether she can…

TRUE — what we are offering keeps progressive are after the subject we.

Tip: Continuous embeds: what + subject + are/is + -ing.

FALSE — what are we offering is direct continuous-question order.

Tip: what we are offering.

TRUE — who will chair… treats who as subject; will stays after who.

Tip: Subject who + modal + verb is already statement-shaped.

FALSE — who will the session be chaired by awkwardly inverts and strands by; prefer who will chair… or by whom the session will be chaired.

Tip: Avoid forcing object-passive word order when a subject who is available.
tasks.solution_overview: Progressive and modal embeds fail the same way: are/will jumps before the subject. Prefer a subject who-clause (who will chair…) over a clunky inverted passive with stranded by.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Please let us know if you require further documentation.
Please let us know if do you require further documentation.
I cannot recall why the previous vendor was dropped.
I cannot recall why was the previous vendor dropped.
They debated whether to accept the counter-offer.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — if you require… is standard polite statement order after let us know.

Tip: Business closers still embed, not invert.

FALSE — if do you require… mixes a direct question into the embed.

Tip: Delete do you → if you require.

TRUE — why the previous vendor was dropped keeps passive was after the subject.

Tip: why + subject + was/were + PP.

FALSE — why was the previous vendor dropped is direct-question inversion.

Tip: why the previous vendor was dropped.

TRUE — whether to accept… is a correct infinitive yes/no embed (no subject to invert).

Tip: whether to + verb is standard for undecided choices.
highlights: why the previous vendor was dropped
tasks.solution_overview: Email-style if-clauses and why-passives must stay uninverted. whether to + infinitive is a third lawful shape — compact and free of subject–auxiliary swapping.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They debated whether should they accept the counter-offer.
She wondered how many seats were still available.
She wondered how many seats were there still available.
Do you remember what the password hint was?
Do you remember what was the password hint?
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — whether should they… inverts the modal; use whether they should… or whether to accept…

Tip: Full clause: whether + subject + modal.

TRUE — how many seats were still available places were after seats.

Tip: how many + noun + verb.

FALSE — were there is an existential inversion pattern that does not belong after wondered how many seats…

Tip: Avoid there-inversion inside how many embeds.

TRUE — what the password hint was puts was at the end in statement order (subject hint before was).

Tip: Embedded what… was keeps be last.

FALSE — what was the password hint? is direct-question be-fronting after remember.

Tip: what the password hint was.
tasks.solution_overview: Be-fronting (what was…?) and there-inversion (were there…?) are direct-question habits. Inside embeds, leave was/were after the real subject, and keep whether + subject + modal.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The analyst could not determine from which sources the rumour originated.
The analyst could not determine from which sources did the rumour originate.
We are assessing what impact the delay may have on delivery.
We are assessing what impact may the delay have on delivery.
Kindly advise when the signed copies will be returned.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Formal pied-piping from which sources the rumour originated keeps statement order after the prepositional wh-phrase.

Tip: Preposition + which + subject + verb is fine in formal embeds.

FALSE — …sources did the rumour originate adds do-support as in a direct question.

Tip: originated without did.

TRUE — what impact the delay may have keeps may after the subject delay.

Tip: what + noun + subject + modal + verb.

FALSE — what impact may the delay have front-loads may before the subject.

Tip: the delay may have, not may the delay have.

TRUE — when the signed copies will be returned is passive statement order after Kindly advise.

Tip: will stays after the subject copies.
highlights: from which sources the rumour originated
what impact the delay may have
when the signed copies will be returned
tasks.solution_overview: Formal prepositional wh-phrases and what + noun objects still forbid do-support and modal fronting. Read the embedded string aloud: if it sounds like a stand-alone question, the word order is probably wrong.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Kindly advise when will the signed copies be returned.
It is unclear to whom the confidential annex was circulated.
It is unclear to whom was the confidential annex circulated.
Management queried how often the backups are tested.
Management queried how often are the backups tested.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — when will the signed copies… inverts will after Kindly advise.

Tip: when the signed copies will…

TRUE — Formal to whom the confidential annex was circulated keeps was after the subject.

Tip: to whom + subject + verb (formal object question).

FALSE — to whom was the confidential annex… inverts was into question position.

Tip: Keep was after annex.

TRUE — how often the backups are tested is statement order for frequency embeds.

Tip: how often + subject + verb.

FALSE — how often are the backups tested is direct-question inversion.

Tip: how often the backups are tested.
highlights: to whom the confidential annex was
how often the backups are tested
tasks.solution_overview: Formal whom-phrases and how often-clauses still use statement order. Inversion after to whom or how often is a direct-question reflex — wrong once the clause is embedded.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The auditor asked under what conditions the discount would apply.
The auditor asked under what conditions would the discount apply.
Nobody knows which of the two bids the panel prefers.
Nobody knows which of the two bids does the panel prefer.
Please specify where the temporary files should be stored.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — under what conditions the discount would apply keeps would after the subject.

Tip: Long wh-phrases still take subject + modal order.

FALSE — under what conditions would the discount apply is direct modal inversion.

Tip: …conditions the discount would apply.

TRUE — which of the two bids the panel prefers places prefers after panel.

Tip: which of… + subject + verb.

FALSE — which… does the panel prefer inserts do-support.

Tip: Drop does: the panel prefers.

TRUE — where the temporary files should be stored keeps should after the subject.

Tip: where + subject + modal + be + PP.
highlights: under what conditions the discount would
which of the two bids the panel prefers
where the temporary files should be stored
tasks.solution_overview: Longer wh-openers (under what conditions, which of the two bids) tempt writers to invert as if starting a new question mid-sentence. Resist: finish with subject + verb, not would/does + subject.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Please specify where should the temporary files be stored.
Researchers examined whether or not the sample was representative.
Researchers examined whether or not was the sample representative.
I need to find out who the message was intended for.
I need to find out who was the message intended for.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — where should the temporary files… inverts should after specify.

Tip: where the temporary files should…

TRUE — whether or not the sample was representative is a standard yes/no embed with or not.

Tip: whether or not + subject + verb.

FALSE — whether or not was the sample… wrongly inverts was.

Tip: Keep was after sample.

TRUE — Informal stranded for is acceptable: who the message was intended for with statement order.

Tip: who + subject + was + PP + preposition.

FALSE — who was the message intended for? is direct-question be-fronting.

Tip: who the message was intended for.
highlights: whether or not the sample was
whether or not was the sample
who the message was intended for
who was the message intended for
tasks.solution_overview: whether or not does not unlock inversion. Stranded-preposition object questions (who… for) still keep was after the subject — only the outer sentence may look interrogative.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board inquired how soon a revised forecast could be produced.
The board inquired how soon could a revised forecast be produced.
It is debatable whether such a clause should even be included.
It is debatable whether should such a clause even be included.
Few partners recalled what assumptions underpinned the valuation model.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — how soon a revised forecast could be produced keeps could after the subject.

Tip: how soon/how quickly + subject + modal…

FALSE — how soon could a revised forecast… is direct modal inversion.

Tip: …forecast could be produced.

TRUE — whether such a clause should even be included is statement order with focusing even.

Tip: Adverbs like even stay inside; they do not trigger inversion.

FALSE — whether should such a clause… front-loads should before the subject.

Tip: whether such a clause should…

TRUE — what assumptions underpinned… treats what assumptions as subject — no do needed.

Tip: Subject what + noun takes the verb directly.
highlights: how soon a revised forecast could
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced how soon and whether… should embeds fail only when the modal jumps left of the subject. Subject what-noun phrases (what assumptions underpinned…) remain do-free.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Few partners recalled what assumptions did underpin the valuation model.
Counsel sought clarification as to why the indemnity had been narrowed.
Counsel sought clarification as to why had the indemnity been narrowed.
The survey asked respondents how satisfied they were with remote support.
The survey asked respondents how satisfied were they with remote support.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — what assumptions did underpin… inserts unnecessary did into a subject clause.

Tip: what assumptions underpinned…

TRUE — as to why the indemnity had been narrowed is a formal embed with past perfect passive statement order.

Tip: as to why + subject + had been + PP.

FALSE — as to why had the indemnity… inverts had before the subject.

Tip: why the indemnity had been…

TRUE — how satisfied they were… is the standard adjectival how-clause order.

Tip: how + adjective + subject + be.

FALSE — how satisfied were they… is direct-question be-inversion.

Tip: how satisfied they were…
highlights: why the indemnity had been narrowed
tasks.solution_overview: Formal as to why and survey how + adjective patterns still ban auxiliary fronting. Fake did in subject what-clauses is another advanced trap — delete it.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Regulators questioned on what basis the exemption had been granted.
Regulators questioned on what basis had the exemption been granted.
We must decide which vendor we should engage first.
We must decide which vendor should we engage first.
The minutes do not record who seconded the motion.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — on what basis the exemption had been granted keeps had after the subject.

Tip: on what basis/grounds + subject + verb.

FALSE — on what basis had the exemption… is direct perfect inversion.

Tip: …basis the exemption had been granted.

TRUE — which vendor we should engage first keeps should after we.

Tip: which + noun + subject + modal + verb.

FALSE — which vendor should we engage is direct-question order after decide.

Tip: which vendor we should engage.

TRUE — who seconded the motion is a subject clause with no inversion and no do.

Tip: Subject who + past verb.
highlights: on what basis the exemption had
on what basis had the exemption
tasks.solution_overview: Prepositional wh-openers (on what basis) and object which-clauses (which vendor we should…) both fail when the auxiliary precedes the subject. Subject who remains the simplest correct pattern.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The minutes do not record who did second the motion.
Partners remain divided over whether the spin-off itself makes strategic sense.
Partners remain divided over whether does the spin-off itself make strategic sense.
I wonder where the CFO is during the blackout window.
I wonder where is the CFO during the blackout window.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — who did second… adds emphatic/wrong do to a subject question.

Tip: who seconded — never who did second in this embed.

TRUE — whether the spin-off itself makes… keeps makes after the subject; itself is just a focusing pronoun.

Tip: Extra focus words do not change embedded order.

FALSE — whether does the spin-off… invents do-support after whether.

Tip: whether the spin-off makes…

TRUE — where the CFO is… is the classic wonder pattern with statement order.

Tip: I wonder where + subject + is.

FALSE — where is the CFO… reverts to direct-question inversion after wonder.

Tip: where the CFO is — the core contrast of this topic.
tasks.solution_overview: Close on the signature contrast: wonder where the CFO is (statement order) versus where is the CFO (direct inversion). Along the way, reject fake do after who or whether — embeds do not need it.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Give the briefing pack to whoever requests it first.
The analyst, who's spreadsheet we checked, spotted the error.
Rising rates affect borrowing costs across the sector.
Between you and I, the forecast looks optimistic.
Fewer complaints were logged after the redesign.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is the subject of requests, so the nominative form is required even after to.

Tip: Ignore the preposition; judge case inside the clause.

FALSE — Use possessive whose, not who's (= who is/has): whose spreadsheet.

Tip: If you cannot expand to who is, write whose.

TRUE — Affect as a verb correctly means influence.

Tip: Most exam sentences want the verb affect, not the noun effect.

FALSE — After the preposition between, use object case: Between you and me.

Tip: Strip you and — you would never say between I.

TRUE — Fewer correctly modifies the countable plural complaints.

Tip: Countable plural → fewer; mass noun → less.
tasks.solution_overview: Work through each sentence as a quick case check: which form fits the grammar slot? Look for subject vs object, possession vs contraction, influence vs result, object pronouns after prepositions, and countable vs mass nouns.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Award the contract to whomever submits the lowest compliant bid.
The director, whose memo clarified the timeline, left early.
The reform will effect consumer confidence overnight.
Between you and me, the merger talks stalled.
The selection criteria is listed on page two.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The relative is the subject of submits, so use whoever, not whomever.

Tip: Find the verb in the clause; if the wh-word does the action, choose whoever.

TRUE — Whose correctly marks possession before memo.

Tip: Whose works for people and organisations in formal English.

FALSE — For influence, use the verb affect: will affect consumer confidence.

Tip: Reserve verb effect for bring about / cause to happen.

TRUE — Object pronouns after between are correct: you and me.

Tip: Formal speech still uses me here — I is the hypercorrection.

FALSE — Criteria is plural; use are: The selection criteria are listed.

Tip: Singular form is criterion.
tasks.solution_overview: These five hinge on classic swap traps. Ask: is the wh-word a subject? Is the 's a contraction or a possessive? Does the sentence mean influence or bring about? Is the pronoun after a preposition? Is criteria treated as plural?

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Whoever finishes the audit should file the summary today.
Who's responsible for signing the disclosure?
The board hopes the new policy will effect a change in reporting.
Less invoices were rejected this month.
The hiring criteria are transparent and published online.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever correctly acts as the subject of finishes.

Tip: Start-of-sentence subject slots almost always need whoever.

TRUE — Who's expands cleanly to who is before responsible.

Tip: Test expansion before you accept who's.

TRUE — Verb effect meaning bring about is correct with a change.

Tip: Effect a change/reform/improvement is the rare but valid pattern.

FALSE — Invoices are countable; use Fewer invoices.

Tip: If you can count the noun, prefer fewer.

TRUE — Plural criteria correctly takes are.

Tip: Formal WU-style English keeps criteria plural.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these are standard correct forms; one countable/mass slip remains. Confirm each pair quickly: whoever subject, who's = who is, effect = bring about, fewer with countables, criteria + plural verb.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Invite whomever the panel nominates as keynote speaker.
Please identify the stakeholder who's concerns were ignored.
Currency swings affect export margins immediately.
Keep this confidential between you and me.
We need less paperwork before the audit begins.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whomever is the object of nominates, so the object form is traditionally correct.

Tip: If another subject does the verb, the wh-word is often the object.

FALSE — Need possessive whose concerns, not who's (= who is).

Tip: Who's concerns never expands sensibly.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence.

Tip: Ask whether something influences something else.

TRUE — Object pronouns after between are required.

Tip: Business English still marks between you and I wrong.

TRUE — Paperwork is uncountable, so less is appropriate.

Tip: Mass nouns (time, money, paperwork) take less.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch the one genuine object-case whomever and the mass-noun less. The rest are possession, influence, and prepositional object pronouns — mark false only where the wrong member of a pair appears.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Forward the files to whomever is on duty tonight.
The firm whose shares surged published a cautious outlook.
Higher tariffs will effect domestic demand for imports.
This matter stays between the counsel and I.
One key criterion is still missing from the checklist.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Is needs a subject: use whoever is on duty.

Tip: To + whomever + is is almost always wrong.

TRUE — Possessive whose correctly links the firm to shares.

Tip: Whose is fine with inanimate subjects in formal prose.

FALSE — Meaning is influence → will affect domestic demand.

Tip: No a change/result noun after the verb? Prefer affect.

FALSE — Object of between must be me: between the counsel and me.

Tip: Same rule as between you and me.

TRUE — Singular criterion correctly pairs with is.

Tip: One item → criterion; several → criteria.
tasks.solution_overview: Difficulty steps up slightly: check clause subjects after to, possessive whose with companies, affect vs effect, object pronouns after between, and criterion vs criteria.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We will hire whoever the committee recommends.
Who's been updating the risk register this week?
The announcement had little effect on trading volumes.
Fewer than twelve suppliers met the new standard.
These criteria was drafted after the consultation.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is widely accepted as the object of recommends and is the safer exam default when case is contested.

Tip: Markers rarely accept whomever as a subject; they often accept whoever as an object.

TRUE — Who's = who has before the past participle been.

Tip: Who's been is a standard contraction.

TRUE — Noun effect meaning result/impact is correct after little.

Tip: Article/quantifier + effect usually signals the noun.

TRUE — Countable suppliers take fewer than.

Tip: Fewer than + number + plural noun is the careful form.

FALSE — Plural criteria needs were, not was.

Tip: Never pair criteria with a singular verb in formal answers.
tasks.solution_overview: Four statements are solid; one plural agreement error with criteria. Confirm contractions, the noun effect, fewer with numbers of countable items, and plural verb agreement.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Assign the ticket to whoever the system flags as owner.
The auditor who's laptop crashed lost an hour of work.
Interest-rate cuts affect mortgage applications with a lag.
Less staff were retained after the restructuring.
The evaluation criteria remain unchanged this year.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever functions acceptably as the object of flags in modern exam English.

Tip: Prefer whoever unless the object case is unmistakable and required.

FALSE — Possessive needed: whose laptop, not who's (= who is).

Tip: Expand every who's before you accept it.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence.

Tip: Subject influences object → affect.

FALSE — Headcount treated as plural people needs Fewer staff were retained.

Tip: Headcount plurals → fewer.

TRUE — Plural criteria correctly takes plural remain.

Tip: Watch subject–verb number with Latin plurals.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan for the possessive/contraction slip and the fewer/less headcount error. The affect and criteria lines should read clean if you keep influence and plural agreement in mind.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Congratulate whomever you select for the award.
A regulator whose remit includes banks issued the notice.
Management intends to effect several procedural reforms.
Please discuss the offer only between you and me.
We observed less delays on the delivery route.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whomever is the object of select, so the object form is traditionally correct.

Tip: Subject you + verb select → object whomever.

TRUE — Whose remit correctly shows possession for an institution.

Tip: Whose + noun is the safe possessive pattern.

TRUE — Verb effect meaning bring about fits reforms.

Tip: Effect + concrete result noun is the cue.

TRUE — Between you and me uses correct object pronouns.

Tip: Hypercorrect I fails after prepositions.

FALSE — Delays are countable: fewer delays.

Tip: Plural -s nouns almost always take fewer.
tasks.solution_overview: Most lines are carefully correct, including a legitimate object-case whomever and verb effect. The single miss is less with a countable plural — swap it mentally to fewer.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hand the microphone to whomever finishes speaking next.
Tell me who's attending the closing session.
The scandal did not affect the share price for long.
The dispute should stay between the CFO and I.
Each criterion carries equal weight in the scorecard.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Subject of finishes must be whoever.

Tip: Verb immediately after the wh-word usually signals subject case.

TRUE — Who's = who is before attending.

Tip: Progressive after who's → contraction is fine.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence the share price.

Tip: Markets, prices, and demand are typically affected.

FALSE — Use me: between the CFO and me.

Tip: Coordinated pronouns keep the same case.

TRUE — Singular criterion correctly takes singular carries.

Tip: Each + singular noun reinforces criterion.
tasks.solution_overview: Two traps are classic: whomever used as a subject, and I after between. The remaining three are clean contractions, affect-as-influence, and singular criterion agreement.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Support will go to whoever presents the strongest case.
Name the partner who's proposal we rejected.
The new levy may effect small retailers disproportionately.
Fewer working days remain before the filing deadline.
The admission criteria have been tightened again.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is the subject of presents.

Tip: Subject + verb right after whoever is the clean pattern.

FALSE — Possessive required: whose proposal.

Tip: Who's proposal cannot mean who is proposal.

FALSE — Influence meaning needs may affect small retailers.

Tip: Adverb of manner after the verb often follows affect, not effect.

TRUE — Countable working days take fewer.

Tip: Calendar units in the plural prefer fewer.

TRUE — Plural criteria correctly takes have.

Tip: Have/are/were are the safe plural partners.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on the two false lines: a who's/whose possession error and affect miswritten as effect. The whoever-subject, fewer-days, and criteria-have lines should all read true.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We contacted whomever the client had authorised to negotiate.
The committee, whose chair resigned yesterday, postponed the vote.
Severe weather can affect logistics across the region.
Between you and me and the rest of the team, morale is fragile.
There is less evidence than we expected in the file.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whomever is the object of had authorised, so object case is traditionally right.

Tip: Past perfect clauses often bury the object — find who receives the action.

TRUE — Non-defining whose chair correctly marks possession.

Tip: Commas do not change the whose/who's rule.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence logistics.

Tip: Weather/events affect systems and people.

TRUE — All coordinated pronouns after between stay in object case; me is correct.

Tip: Adding more nouns does not license I.

TRUE — Uncountable evidence takes less.

Tip: Evidence, information, and research are mass nouns.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are carefully correct. Use this set to lock in the right members of each pair: object whomever, possessive whose, verb affect, object me, and less with a mass noun.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Credit the bonus to whomever meets the quarterly target.
Who's signature appears on the final page?
The mediation failed to effect an early settlement.
Less than forty applications arrived before noon.
Several criteria needs revision before publication.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Subject of meets requires whoever.

Tip: Target-meeting clauses are subject cases.

FALSE — Ask whose signature, not who's (= who is).

Tip: Noun after the wh-word → almost always whose.

TRUE — Verb effect meaning bring about fits a settlement.

Tip: Effect + indefinite article + result noun is classic.

FALSE — Countable applications prefer Fewer than forty applications.

Tip: Exam English still prefers fewer with countable plurals after numbers.

FALSE — Plural subject needs need: Several criteria need revision.

Tip: Several + plural noun → plural verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Only one sentence is true — the effect a settlement pattern. The other four mix subject/object, possession/contraction, fewer/less with numbers, and criteria agreement.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Delegate authority to whoever you believe can close the deal.
An investor who's portfolio includes bonds asked for details.
Oil prices affect airline operating costs within days.
The settlement must remain between the claimant and me.
We have fewer inventory than last quarter.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is the subject of can close inside the nested clause.

Tip: Case is decided in the innermost clause, not by to.

FALSE — Possessive needed: whose portfolio.

Tip: Portfolio/assets after the wh-word → whose.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence costs.

Tip: Prices affect costs is a stock exam pattern.

TRUE — Object pronoun me after between is correct.

Tip: Legal/business between X and me is standard.

FALSE — Inventory is typically uncountable here → less inventory (or fewer inventory items).

Tip: Do not use fewer with a mass noun.
tasks.solution_overview: Nested clauses and mass/count swaps raise the difficulty. Decide case inside you believe can…, fix the who's/whose slip, keep affect and between…me, and reverse the fewer/inventory mismatch.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Offer the internship to whomever the mentors shortlist.
The NGO whose funding was cut suspended two programmes.
The announcement will effect investor sentiment tomorrow.
Keep the draft between you and I until Friday.
The scoring criteria are applied uniformly to all bids.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whomever is the object of shortlist.

Tip: Mentors shortlist someone → object case.

TRUE — Whose funding correctly shows possession.

Tip: Organisation + whose + noun is fine.

FALSE — Sentiment is influenced → will affect investor sentiment.

Tip: Abstract reactions (sentiment, confidence) take affect.

FALSE — Object case required: between you and me.

Tip: Until Friday does not change pronoun case.

TRUE — Plural criteria correctly takes are applied.

Tip: Passive voice still needs plural agreement.
tasks.solution_overview: Two false lines misuse effect for influence and I after between. Confirm the object-case whomever, the possessive whose, and plural criteria in the passive.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Promote whoever has delivered consistent results this year.
Who's been responsible for the overdue reconciliations?
Sanctions are beginning to effect trade with the region.
There were fewer discrepancies in the second sample.
This single criteria determines eligibility on its own.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is the subject of has delivered.

Tip: Perfect aspect does not change the case rule.

TRUE — Who's been = who has been.

Tip: Been after who's almost always means who has.

FALSE — Influence meaning → beginning to affect trade.

Tip: Progressive frames usually host affect.

TRUE — Countable discrepancies take fewer.

Tip: Audit/sample count nouns prefer fewer.

FALSE — Singular is criterion: This single criterion determines…

Tip: Single/one/each before the noun forces criterion.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch the subtler affect/effect slip inside a progressive construction and the false plural criteria after single. The whoever, who's been, and fewer lines are sound.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We will brief whomever is appointed as interim chair.
A supplier whose invoices arrived late was fined.
The task force hopes to effect lasting improvements in compliance.
Please keep the valuation between the advisers and me.
Managers reported less absences after flexible hours began.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Subject of is appointed must be whoever.

Tip: Passive is appointed still needs a subject form.

TRUE — Whose invoices correctly marks possession.

Tip: Supplier/company + whose is standard.

TRUE — Verb effect meaning bring about fits improvements.

Tip: Lasting/major + noun after effect is a good cue.

TRUE — Object pronoun me after between is correct.

Tip: Parallel advisers and me, never I.

FALSE — Countable absences need fewer absences.

Tip: Attendance counts are countable.
tasks.solution_overview: Passive clauses hide subject-case whoever traps, and countable absences tempt less. Hold onto whose, effect-as-bring-about, and between…me as the true anchors.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Allocate overtime to whoever the roster shows as available.
Identify the officer who's remit covers cross-border payments.
Liquidity shocks quickly affect short-term funding markets.
The negotiation is strictly between you and me at this stage.
Fewer capital was available after the rating downgrade.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whoever is acceptable as the object of shows; when object case is unclear, whoever remains the safer exam form.

Tip: When object case is unclear, whoever rarely costs marks.

FALSE — Possessive whose remit is required.

Tip: Remit/mandate/portfolio after the wh-word → whose.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence markets.

Tip: Shocks/events affect markets is a frequent stem.

TRUE — Between you and me is the correct object-case pair.

Tip: At this stage is irrelevant to case.

FALSE — Uncountable capital takes Less capital.

Tip: Capital, liquidity, and funding are mass nouns.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder items flip the usual fewer/less intuition: capital is mass, so fewer is wrong. Also catch the remit possession error while confirming whoever, affect, and between you and me.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Send the draft to whomever you think should review it first.
The bank whose bonds were downgraded issued a statement.
Further delays will effect the project timeline severely.
Confidential pricing stays between procurement and me.
The shortlisting criteria leave little room for discretion.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Innermost clause: who should review — subject case → whoever you think should review it.

Tip: Ignore you think; case belongs to the embedded verb.

TRUE — Whose bonds correctly expresses possession.

Tip: Financial nouns after whose are routine.

FALSE — Influence on the timeline → will affect the project timeline.

Tip: Severely/significantly after the verb often follows affect.

TRUE — Object pronoun me after between is correct.

Tip: Department names do not change pronoun case.

TRUE — Plural criteria correctly takes plural leave.

Tip: Criteria + plural verb is the default formal choice.
tasks.solution_overview: The nested you think should… clause is the main trap — the wh-word is a subject, so whoever is required. Pair that with an affect/effect influence error; the remaining three are solid.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We interviewed whomever the headhunter had shortlisted for CFO.
Who's attending on behalf of the supervisory board?
The restructuring may effect a reduction in overlapping roles.
Between you and I, the valuation model is flawed.
One of the criteria are inconsistent with the statute.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Whomever is the object of had shortlisted.

Tip: Headhunter shortlisted someone → object case.

TRUE — Who's attending = who is attending.

Tip: Expansion test passes cleanly.

TRUE — Verb effect meaning bring about fits a reduction.

Tip: Effect + a + noun of result is intentional formal diction.

FALSE — Object case: Between you and me.

Tip: Informal tone does not excuse I.

FALSE — One of the criteria takes a singular verb: is inconsistent.

Tip: One of + plural noun → singular verb for one.
tasks.solution_overview: Two advanced traps: hypercorrect between you and I, and singular agreement after one of the criteria. The object-case whomever, who's contraction, and effect-a-reduction lines are correctly written.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Appoint whoever the board considers capable of leading the turnaround.
A client who's invoices remain unpaid will lose credit terms.
Currency volatility continues to affect hedging strategies.
All discussions must stay between the counsel and me.
We now require less formal approvals than before the overhaul.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — With consider X capable, prefer whoever in careful exam answers.

Tip: Nested complements after consider usually favour whoever.

FALSE — Possessive whose invoices is required.

Tip: Invoices/accounts after the wh-word → whose.

TRUE — Verb affect correctly means influence strategies.

Tip: Continues to + affect is a common formal stem.

TRUE — Object pronoun me after between is correct.

Tip: Counsel and me is a frequent legal stem.

FALSE — Approvals are countable → fewer formal approvals.

Tip: If the noun is plural and countable, choose fewer even with adjectives in between.
tasks.solution_overview: Finish with a dense mix: a board-considers clause, a who's/whose slip, solid affect and between…me, and a sneaky less before a countable plural. Only mark true when each confusable pair is already the right member.
